# Sūrah al-Aʿrāf (Chapter 7) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sūrah of the Heights**

Al-Aʿrāf, "the Heights," is the seventh chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 206 verses, and it stands as one of the great mid-length Makkan sūrahs whose structure resembles a vast architectural plan: a broad statement of the Law, then a series of rooms — narrative suites in which the sacred history of the prophets is told again and again, each time widening the circle of warning. The name comes from the word *al-aʿrāf* in verses 46 and 48, the "heights" from which certain men will look across a partition between the Garden and the Fire, identifying the people of both sides "by their marks." Classical commentators differ on what these heights are: some say a ridge or terrace between Paradise and Hell, others say a level of Paradise from which its inhabitants survey all that is below. Whatever the precise identification, the image gives the sūrah its name and one of its deepest psychological tones: the standing, unresolved middle — the place of those whose outcome is not yet the reward they hoped for, who can see the blessed and the damned, and who must watch. It is a name that keeps the sūrah, and everyone who reads it, out of comfort.

**A Late Makkan Composition with a Subtler Edge**

In the order of revelation al-Aʿrāf is counted among the later Makkan sūrahs, and many scholars place it just before al-Anʿām, with some authorities reporting that verses 163–167 were revealed in Madinah. Its immediate audience is the same as al-Anʿām's: the idolatrous Quraysh who refused to accept Muḥammad ﷺ as a prophet. But where al-Anʿām argues directly with the arguments of its opponents, al-Aʿrāf takes a subtler, less polemical course. It does not meet the Makkans point for point; instead it turns them toward the past and says, in effect: look at what your story has always looked like, from the first of the prophets to the last of the cities. The sūrah's central thesis, stated and restated in many forms, is that the consequences of rejecting the signs of God are not hypothetical; they are historical, and they are repeatable. The chapters of sacred history — Adam, Noah, Hūd, Ṣāli, Lūt, Shuʿayb, Mūsā and Pharaoh — are arranged not as antiquarian material but as a courtroom record, each case closed the same way.

**The Shape of the Sūrah**

The opening verses (1–10) state the case of the Book: it is sent down for the Prophet's breast, for warning, and for the remembrance of the believers; it is followed by the fate of destroyed towns, by the questioning of messengers and their peoples, and by the weighing of deeds. Then the first great narrative begins (11–28): the creation of Adam, the refusal of Iblīs, the temptation in the Garden, the descent, and the clothing that follows. From the clothing the sūrah moves to adornment and temperance (31–33), to the appointed term of every nation (34–39), and then to the famous passage of the Hereafter in which the people of the Garden call out to the people of the Fire, and the men on the Heights call to those they know by their marks (44–50). A brief discourse on the signs of God in creation (52–58) introduces the long procession of the destroyed peoples (59–93): Noah, the people of the well and the palm-grove (Hūd), the she-camel of Ṣāli, the transgression of the people of Lūt, and the commerce and religion of Shuʿayb. The Mūsā narrative (103–156) is the sūrah's longest and most detailed suite: the staff and the white hand, the confrontation with Pharaoh, the magicians, the plagues, the parting of the sea, the drowning, the mountain, the golden calf, and the covenant of the elders. A verse identifies the Prophet as the "unlettered" Muḥammad ﷺ written in the Torah and the Gospel (157). The sūrah then returns to Israel's later history — the breach of the covenant, the punishment of the Sabbath-breakers, the city in the land (161–67) — and closes, after a passage on the character of the Prophet and his mission (158–188), with the great verses of the Covenant of the Looms (172), the story of the two brothers and the field (176–77), the parable of the dog in the Cave (178–81), and the final, serene vision of the angels in the Presence of God, who are not too proud to worship Him, glorifying Him and prostrating to Him (206). The arc of the sūrah — from the letters that open the Book to the angels that close it — is deliberate: it begins with the mystery of Divine speech and ends with the order of Divine worship, and between the two, every human story that could carry the warning is told at length.

**The Method of Its Warning**

What distinguishes al-Aʿrāf from its neighbors is the patience of its method. It does not once say "you Makkans will be destroyed" in so many words in the narrative sections; it simply tells the case files and lets the listener recognize himself. This is a warning designed to bypass the defender's defenses: when a man is told directly that he is wrong, he prepares his answer; when he is told a story of a people he knows, he watches it, and in the watching, he confesses. The sūrah trusts its evidence and its order. It also pairs the narratives with the present address constantly — "O Children of Adam" — so that every story is also a mirror. The result is a sūrah that reads less like a sermon than like a history written by God for the use of His creatures, in which the past is not the past but a live demonstration, and in which the last page, the page of the angels and of the final reckoning, is the only page that is already finished.

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:1

> **Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Four Letters, and Only These, Before This Book**

The seventh sūrah of the Qur'an does not begin with a word, a name, a blessing, or a story. It begins with four letters of the Arabic alphabet, recited by their own names in that order: *Alif, Lām, Mīm, Ṣād* — a combination that belongs to this sūrah alone. Of the twenty-nine sūrahs that open with the so-called "separated letters" (*al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt*), no other carries precisely this quartet. Alif, Lām, Mīm together open the second, third, and twenty-ninth chapters; Mīm alone opens others; and ṣād opens chapter thirty-eight. But the four-letter sequence *ʾalif lām mīm ṣād* stands in the muṣḥaf exactly once, and that once is here, at the gate of al-Aʿrāf. The repetition of the formula across the Book establishes that the letters are not a scribal accident but a standing feature of Divine speech in the Qur'an; the singularity of this particular combination then marks this sūrah with its own signature, as though the Book announced, before a single sentence was spoken, that what follows is a specific and unrepeatable message.

**A Signature of Mystery**

The commentators' first instinct was the same as it was for every set of the separated letters: to acknowledge that the letters are true, real, and weighty, and to acknowledge that their precise meaning is one of the points in which God has concealed knowledge from us. It is transmitted among the early authorities that the meaning of the letters is a *munkarat* — a mystery that the Prophet ﷺ did not explain and that therefore was not to be forced. Some of the later reporters, as the sources gather them, held that the opening letters are a name of God, and that this particular sequence may stand for the "Greatest Name" (*al-Ism al-Aʿẓam*), the name by which God is known to Himself before He is known to creation. Others held that the letters are a name for the Qur'an itself, the Book signing its own opening with the raw material of its own language. Neither opinion is demonstrable; both are preserved in the tradition as reverent conjecture. The soundest course, and the one the older commentators consistently favored, is to hold what is certain: that God opened His Book with these letters, that no meaning has been authentically fixed to them, and that their silence at the threshold is itself a teaching.

**The Challenge Under the Surface**

What can be said with confidence is the function the letters serve in the pattern of the Book. In most of the sūrahs that open with the separated letters, the very next verse mentions the Book or the revelation: *Alif Lām Mīm, this is the Book of which there is no doubt*; *Alif Lām Mīm, a Book We have sent down unto you*; and here, *Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād — [this is] a Book sent down unto thee*. The letters, in other words, are the herald of the Book, the sound the Book makes before it speaks. And there is a second, deeper function that the later commentators drew out at length. The letters are the very letters of the Arab's own tongue. The Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic of the Quraysh, and the Quraysh were the masters of Arabic, the people whose poetry was the measure of eloquence. By opening sūrah after sūrah with the alphabet itself, the revelation performs a quiet demonstration: here are your own letters, your own sounds, your own material, in the hand of your own tongue's Speaker — and from this material, a Book of this order. The explicit challenge, *bring a sūrah like it*, comes elsewhere; here the challenge is implied by the opening itself, the way a master archer lays a bow at the feet of his rivals without saying a word.

**A Pause Before the Storm**

There is also a spiritual function, one the practical commentators of the devotional strain emphasized. A sūrah that opens with isolated letters forces the reciter into a moment of pure voice before meaning: the lips form sounds that do not yet signify, and in that gap the heart is suspended between the letter and the word, between the sound and the sense. For the worshipper this is a small discipline with a large effect. The sūrah that follows these four letters is among the sternest in the Qur'an — it will recount destroyed cities, a fallen devil, a drowned pharaoh, a people cursed in their fields and their sabbaths. To approach it, God has placed a pause: four letters, no meaning, only Presence. The listener is given, in the first second of the sūrah, the posture the entire sūrah demands — the posture of a witness who has not yet heard the verdict. That is the office of these letters at the gate of al-Aʿrāf: to make the reader still, to mark the Book as a Book from above, and to open the page.

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:2

> **˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺— do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it—so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺, and as a reminder to the believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Book Named at Its Own Gate**

The four letters of the opening are not left hanging in the air. The very next word names what they herald: *This is a Book* (*hādhā kitābun*). Grammarians note the figure in the phrase: the noun *kitāb* is in the state of explanation (*ṣila al-bayān*) to the demonstrative *hādhā*, as though the Book is so near that it is pointed at, so present that it is shown rather than described. And it is immediately qualified with the passive participle *anẓala* — "sent down" — which does two things at once: it declares the Book's origin (it is not produced, compiled, or composed by any hand in this world) and its direction (it descends, it comes from above, it is addressed downward to the human level). The combination — "˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺" — is the Qur'an's own self-introduction in miniature, and it is the first complete sentence of the sūrah. Everything that follows in al-Aʿrāf — the destroyed towns, the prophets, the Hereafter — is the unfolding of a single claim that is made in this verse: that a Book has come from God, and that it has come to one man first, and through him to the rest of the world.

**The Constriction in the Breast**

The address now turns to the Prophet ﷺ, and it turns to the most sensitive place in him: *do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it*. The word is *ḥaraj* — hence the translation's "anxiety into your heart" — or, in the common reading, the sense of *ḍayq*: a narrowing, a tightening, a closing-in, as when a chest constricts under fear or grief so that the breath grows short. The Qur'an elsewhere places the *ṣadr*, the breast or chest, precisely as the organ of this kind of distress: it is where the word that is too heavy to bear "weighs down" (2:255, where the recitation of the signs is a *ṣadr ḍīq* — "a narrow breast"), and it is where the heart sits. The Qur'an's psychology is bodily before it is abstract: the distress of the messenger is not a thought but a physical tightening, the kind of compression a person feels in the pit of the chest when he sees his own people turn away from the very thing that could save them.

This is not a hypothetical. The history of the first years of the mission is a history of constriction. The Prophet ﷺ had come down from the cave of Ḥirā with a breast that, by his own account to Khadija, was afraid for itself; he had stood before the Quraysh and seen the faces of men he loved harden against him; he had been stoned, insulted, and blocked in the streets of Makkah. The constriction this verse speaks of is not doubt about the Book — that question never troubled him — it is the sorrow and fear of the messenger who carries a warning his people will refuse. And the command *“do not let anxiety into your heart”* (7:2) is not a command to stop feeling; it is a command to locate the feeling correctly. The Qur'an elsewhere treats exactly this kind of messenger's distress with the same medicine: *do not grieve over them* (16:127), *do not be in distress* (28:21, 56), and the famous prayer taught for the very condition — when a believer's heart tightens, he is taught to say, "O God, Lord of the Throne, Lord of the Might, Lord of the Greatness" — a dhikr whose name in the sources is the *dhikr al-ḍiqq*, the remembrance for constriction. The cure for a constricted breast is not less feeling but the transfer of the feeling to its proper object: the One who owns the constriction and can open it.

**Warning as Purpose, Remembrance as Result**

The verse then states the Book's double office in one sentence. First: *so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺*. The root is *n-z-r*, and the word *nadhīr* carries the sense of one who gives notice of a coming harm, the one who stands at the gate and says, a caravan of trouble is coming, and the door is this. Warning is forward-looking: it addresses a future that can still be avoided. The Book was sent down, on this account, so that the Prophet would perform the function of the warners — *nadhīr* is one of his standing titles in the Qur'an, as it is of Noah, Hud, and all the prophets told the same story in this sūrah. Second: *and as a reminder to the believers*. The word is *dhikrā*, from the root *d-h-r*, remembrance. If warning looks forward to the punishment that is avoided, remembrance looks present and inward: it is the keeping of God in the heart, the repeated turning back to the source. The same Book therefore performs two different functions on two different hearers. For the one who has not entered the path, it is a warning: it shows the fate of the destroyed towns and the weighing of deeds. For the one who has entered, it is a remembrance: it keeps the heart warm, the direction steady, and the gratitude fresh. The sentence is a complete map of the Qur'an's relationship to its two audiences, and it is a map that the sūrah will then spend 205 verses walking.

**The Logic of the Command**

There is a logic here worth stating plainly, for it is the logic that holds the whole prophetic enterprise together. The Book was sent down "to you ˹O Prophet˺" — to one man — and the reason given for not letting his breast constrict is the task itself: *so with it you may warn*. The messenger must be free of the constriction of fear of his people's answer, because a messenger whose chest is closed by the fear of rejection will deliver a diminished warning, or delay it, or soften it into something his people can swallow. God's command is thus a command about the conditions of effective communication: the message must be carried whole. And the same law, by the pattern of the verse, extends beyond the Prophet to every person who has received the message and carries it. The believer who speaks the truth he has been given and feels his breast constrict at the cost he will pay — the cost of the family's disapproval, the office's disfavor, the crowd's laughter — is addressed by the same verse in the same way: the constriction is real, the feeling is not a sin, and the cure is to place the feeling before the One who sees the breast and opens it. The verse, in other words, is not only a Makkan command to one man; it is a standing statute for every messenger of the Book in every age, including the private age in which the message is carried by an individual rather than a state.


A Book Named at Its Own Gate: The Same Opening in al-Baqarah

7:2 opens the sūrah by naming the thing the reader holds, and al-Baqarah opens in the same way: *“This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺”* (2:2). The two openings agree on three points

The task is stated in two verbs, warning and reminding, and the verse attaches a command to the one who performs them: let there be no constriction in the breast on account of it. The prohibition concerns the weight of the task, and it is addressed before any difficulty has been reported

The audience named in 2:2 is the mindful, and the audience named in 7:2 is the believers, with the warning directed elsewhere. The sūrah's long account of the towns supplies the third party: those to whom the warning was given and who refused it


Reminders Benefit the Believers

The second function named at 7:2 has a rule stated elsewhere: *“But ˹continue to˺ remind. For certainly reminders benefit the believers.”* (51:55). The verse of adh-Dhāriyāt gives the reminder a beneficiary, as 7:2 does by attaching it to the believers

What this adds to the sūrah's opening is an account of its own method. Al-Aʿrāf reminds by narrating, and the narration is long because the reminder is addressed to a people who will recognise themselves in it

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:3

> **Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him. How seldom are you mindful!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Address Widens**

The previous verse spoke to the Prophet in the singular. This verse speaks in the plural, and the shift is deliberate: the command now reaches the community, and beyond the community, all people. *Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord* — the "you" is the collective "you" of every person who has received the Book and stood in the light of it. The object of the command is the revealed Book, the very Book named in the preceding verse, and the verb is *ittabiʿū*, "follow," from the root *ṭ-w-y*, which pictures walking behind someone on a path: to follow is to place oneself on the same track as the one you follow, to let his footfall set your pace. To "follow" a revealed Book is therefore not an abstract approval of its truth but a practical alignment: one makes the Book the route of one's life, the direction of one's choices, the standard by which one measures what to take and what to leave. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the following of the prophets and the following of the law, and the pattern is constant: faith in the Book without following it is like knowing the map and walking a different road.

**Protectors Besides God**

The negative half of the verse is the one that carries the weight: *and do not take others as guardians besides Him*. The word is *awliyāʾ*, the plural of *walī*, from the root *w-l-y*, which means closeness — a wali is literally a close one, and the word has grown in Arabic to cover the whole family of relations: the guardian, the patron, the ally, the protector, the friend who has authority over a person or a cause. To *take* (*ittakhadhū*) protectors other than Allah is to place oneself in a relation of closeness, dependence, and loyalty toward something or someone other than God, such that one's security, direction, and love are attached to that other thing. The Qur'an returns to this phrase again and again, and each use clarifies the range of what the *protectors* can be. For the disbelievers, *“their guardians are false gods”* (2:257); whoever *“turns a blind eye to the Reminder of the Most Compassionate”* is given *“a devilish one as their close associate”* (43:36); and Iblīs and his descendants are taken *“as patrons instead of Me”* (18:50); and in this very sūrah, a few verses later, the same sentence is repeated with the subject made explicit: *“They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah— thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided”* (7:30). But the classical commentators broadened the phrase further than the literal, and rightly so. In the early Muslim community the *protectors* other than Allah were often not idols at all but human beings — the associates, friends, and kindred who incited the Companions to their old religion, whose approval was the real currency of safety, and whose disapproval was the real punishment. The *walī* in this verse is whatever stands between a person and God in the distribution of his loyalty, whether it is a carved stone, a demon of the unseen, or a living human being whose pleasure is sought as a god is sought.

The Qur'an gives the logic of the error in one of its sharpest parables, in Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt:

> *"The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is that of a spider spinning a shelter. And the flimsiest of all shelters is certainly that of a spider, if only they knew."* (29:41)

The image is precise. The spider believes in the strength of its web; the web is the strongest thing in the world to the spider, and the frailest in the world to everything else. The "protectors" apart from God are exactly this: they feel like the whole of security to the person attached to them, and they are the weakest possible thing at the moment of need. When the hour comes in which a protector is tested — the illness, the loss, the death, the hour in which the money cannot be commanded and the status cannot be summoned — the web is cut, and the one who took the spider for a house has no house. The verse's command is therefore not a matter of doctrine but of engineering: attach your security to that which is actually strong.

**The Rebuke of the Unreflecting**

The verse closes with a rebuke that is short and very old in the Qur'an: *How seldom are you mindful!* The word is *taʿqilūn*, from the root *ʿ-q-l*, the same root as *ʿaql*, the intellect, and the word *taʿqīl* — to reason, to judge, to grasp, to hold a thing in the mind and weigh it. The rebuke is not against the existence of the intellect but against its non-use. The logic of the whole verse is a piece of reasoning: if the Book is from God, and if God is the only protector that is real, then to follow the Book and to take no other protector is the only rationally consistent position; to follow the Book in words while attaching one's life to other protectors is to hold two incompatible directions at once. And the person who does this is not ignorant; he is one who has chosen not to reflect. The Qur'an repeats this rebuke in the same short form in several places — "Yet you are hardly mindful!" (27:62, 40:58; 69:42, and dozens of close variants) — and the repetition is itself a teaching: the central failure of the human heart is not a lack of intelligence but a refusal to apply it to the things that matter.

**The Two Loyalties in Modern Form**

The verse's structure — one positive command and one negative prohibition, joined by the logic of exclusive loyalty — is the structure of every real allegiance in human life. A citizen who follows the constitution and also follows a criminal gang is not a citizen in any sense, even if the gang is beloved and the constitution is distant. A person who says he serves God and serves money in the same hour is in the same position, and the Qur'an's phrase for it is the one in this verse: he has taken *awliyāʾ* apart from God. The modern form of the disease is not less real than the Makkah form; it is only better dressed. The "protectors" of a modern life — the career that must not be risked, the reputation that must not be damaged, the crowd that must not be opposed, the money that must not be questioned — are taken in exactly the way the Quraysh took their idols: not as objects of worship in a temple, but as objects of dependence in the heart, the things one actually turns to when the crisis comes. And the cure is the one the verse names: *taʿqīl*, reflection, the simple and brutal test that every real protector fails — *what will this thing do for me in the hour in which I am alone?* The idol, the status, the money, the friend all fail that test; only the One the verse names passes it. To reflect, in the sense this verse requires, is to run that test honestly, and to let the result arrange one's loyalties.


Follow What Is Revealed: The Command to the Messenger

7:3 issues two commands in one sentence, the first directed at following: follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord. The Book puts the same command to the Prophet: *“Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you ˹all˺ do.”* (33:2)

The command's object is a thing sent down, which fixes the relation between follower and followed. A person who follows what has been revealed is not following an opinion or a custom but a text with a stated source

The sūrah's towns failed at both commands in the reverse order: they took guardians before they refused to follow


Guardians Instead of Believers: The Prohibition Stated

The second command forbids taking others as guardians beside Him, and the Book states the same prohibition in a social form: *“Believers should not take disbelievers as guardians instead of the believers—and whoever does so will have nothing to hope for from Allah”* (3:28)

The two verses establish that guardianship is not a neutral arrangement. The sūrah's towns took their customs, chiefs, and gods as guardians, and each taking is reported as a failure of following rather than an addition to it

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:4

> **˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed! Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rhetoric of the Many**

The verse opens with a rhetorical plural in the form of a question: *˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed!* The Arabic word is *kaẓīr*, and the figure is the one the grammarians call the *mabnāʾ li-ḍamīr al-kathīrah* — a form that does not expect an answer, because the answer is not a number but a volume: many, so many that counting has stopped being possible. The construction is deliberate. The Qur'an does not say "I destroyed your town" or "I destroyed one town"; it says *how many*, and the listener's mind is immediately placed in front of a procession of cities, a city after a city, each one with its own name and its own end. This is the sūrah announcing its own method. The long narrative suite that follows — the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Lot, the people of Shuayb, and then the people of Pharaoh — is the gallery that this single verse opens. The verse is the door of the exhibit: step in, and the walls are lined with the cases of the destroyed towns.

The "town" (*qaryah*) is the unit of the Qur'an's moral history. In the Qur'an, sin is not primarily an individual act in the modern sense; it is a communal condition. A town is destroyed, not a man; a city is struck, not a household. The reason is logical: the corruption that merits destruction is never the corruption of one man but the corruption of a whole order of life — the judges who have sold judgment, the markets that have cheated by measure, the pulpit that has mocked the messenger, the whole civic fabric that has made the false into the normal and the true into the offense. When the Qur'an says *how many societies*, it is naming the scale at which its history is written: the scale of the community, where the moral health of a place is a fact that can be seen from a distance, and where the punishment, when it comes, is the settlement of a communal account.

**The Hour of the Strike**

The verse then names the hour of the destruction, and the naming is one of the most pointed things in the Qur'an: *Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday*. The word for "torment" here is *ʿaẓāb* — punishment, and more than punishment, the punishment that displays a power: it is the word used for the divine strikes that the Qur'an recounts in its narrative suites, the wind that took a whole people in their beds, the flood that rose over the high places, the earthquake that overthrew a city with its dwellings. And the verb rendered "took them by surprise" (*jāʾahum*, literally "it came upon them") is the word of the unexpected: it came *upon* them, not toward them, not as a thing they had arranged for — it fell on them.

The two hours named are the two hours in which a people is furthest from readiness. By night: the hour of rest, the hour when the senses are closed, the hour when no one is watching and no one is on guard. At midday, *˹while sleeping˺* — the Arabic is *qāʾilūn*, from the midday rest (*qaylūlah*) — the hour of ease, of a people that has settled into the rhythm of its own comfort and is attending to its own pleasures. The logic of the two hours is the same: it is in the hour of maximum relaxation that the heart is farthest from the awareness of God, and it is in that hour that the account is closed. The Qur'an's teaching is not that God strikes the sleeping or the playing man as a cruelty; it is that the man who has rejected the warning has already chosen the hour of his own account. He has spent his days in the ease that the verse names, and the ease is the opposite of the readiness for which the warning was sent. When the warning is rejected, the man has, in effect, said: I will not be ready. And the destruction, when it comes, comes at the hour that is the true shape of his choice: the hour in which he is not ready.

The Qur'an's own narratives keep the two hours in view. Lot's people are told to *“travel with your family in the dark of night”* (15:65) and *“the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise”* (15:73), and Sūrat al-Qamar states the same dawn from the side of the punished — *“by the early morning they were overwhelmed by an unrelenting torment”* (54:38); the flood of Noah rose in the hour of their deepest security. The pattern is constant and it is the pattern of this verse: the destruction does not come with a second notice, and it does not come at a convenient hour. It comes when the people is at rest, because the people that has rejected the messenger has already made the rest its religion.

**The Warning of the Hour**

There is a law here that extends beyond the literal destruction of the towns, and the classical commentators drew it out. The law is this: once God has sent the warning and the people has refused it, the man is under no obligation to the man's comfort any longer. The comfort is the man's own, and the man has chosen to spend it in the rejection. The "ease at midday" is therefore not a description of God's method but a description of the man's state. The town that is destroyed at midday is the town that had been at ease at midday for years, and the midday of the destruction is only the last midday of a long noon of ease. The verse, applied to the individual life, is a warning about the hour in which a person feels most at ease with himself — the hour in which the career is secure, the health is good, the friends are pleased, and the question of the account has been pushed to the far side of the calendar. That hour is the hour the verse names, and the verse says the account can close in it, without notice, in the middle of the ease, in the very moment the man is furthest from the preparation. The practical consequence is not fear but readiness: the man who keeps the awareness of the account open does not sleep without the awareness, and he does not play without the awareness, and the destruction that "comes upon" the unready does not come upon him, because he is, in the Qur'an's word, the one who has been *prepared* — and the prepared man is not caught by the hour, in either world.


Night and Midday: The Two Hours of the Sūrah's Destructions

7:4 states the number of destroyed societies and then the hour of their destruction: at night or while they rested at midday

The choice of hours is what gives the verse its force. Night and midday rest are the two periods in which a town is least organised, and in both the population is dispersed and asleep. A punishment arriving at either hour arrives without an assembly, without a defence, and without warning

What the verse adds to the accounts is the number. How many a society We have destroyed: the plurality is stated before the individual cases, and the sūrah then supplies the cases one by one. The reader is thus given a quantity and then a series of examples, which is the structure of an argument rather than of a narrative


With or Without Warning: The Question in al-Anʿām

The suddenness of 7:4 is put as a question elsewhere: *“who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers?”* (6:47), asked of a punishment that would overwhelm a people with or without warning. The verse of al-Anʿām isolates the variable the sūrah's verse treats as settled, namely the warning

This is the answer to the question 7:4 leaves standing. A town destroyed at night is not destroyed because it was asleep; it is destroyed because it was destroyed-worthy, and the night is the hour at which the fact becomes visible

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:5

> **Their only cry—when overwhelmed by Our torment—was, “We have indeed been wrongdoers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence That Arrives Too Late**

The fourth verse of the sūrah left the destroyed towns asleep in their beds or resting at midday; this fifth verse reports what they said when the Might of God arrived. The Arabic is *fa-mā kāna daʿwāhum idh jāʾahum baʾsunā illā an qālū innā kunnā ẓālimīn*. The translation "plea" renders *daʿwā*, a noun from the root *d-ʿ-w*, to call out. Its lexical range is instructive: in the market and the courtroom of the Arabs the same word meant a *claim* — the assertion a man entered on his own behalf. What the verse records, then, is not a prayer. It is the last claim the townspeople filed before a court whose session had already ended.

The grammar carries the weight. *Mā kāna … illā* is a restrictive construction: the whole of their speech was *nothing but* that one clause. Not a defence, not a bargain, not an appeal to ancestry or custom — the entire content of their final hour collapsed into four words: *we were wrongdoers*.

**Why the Confession Cannot Help Them**

The word rendered "wrongdoers" is *ẓālimūn*, from *ẓ-l-m*. Its primary sense is not cruelty but displacement: to put a thing where it does not belong. A man is a *ẓālim* in this Qur'anic sense when he installs himself in a station that is not his — when he sits in judgment over what belongs to God, treats his own desire as the standard, and answers for an account that was never his to settle. The confession in the verse is therefore exact. The townspeople do not confess a list of crimes; they confess a mislocation, a life spent in a place that was not theirs.

The tragedy is that the words are true and the time is gone. The Qur'an draws the line between two confessions with unmistakable clarity. Repentance belongs to the living hour: *“repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, ‘Now I repent!’”* (4:18). Pharaoh made this confession with the water at his throat — *“I believe!”* — and the answer still echoes: *“Now you believe? But you always disobeyed and were one of the corruptors”* (10:90–91). The dead cry out for a second term: *“My Lord! Let me go back, so I may do good in what I left behind”* — and the door answers: *“Never!”* (23:99–100).

Across those scenes the pattern is one anatomy in three parts: the recognition is genuine, the repair is impossible, and the verdict is unchanged. The verse therefore does not describe penitence; it describes penitence's counterfeit — the moment when agreement with God's judgment costs nothing, because nothing can any longer be rescued by it.

**The Clock Inside the Verse**

Read this way, 7:5 stops being a report about vanished nations and becomes a measurement of the reader's own position. The sentence *we were wrongdoers* has two lives. Spoken inside the season of the open door, it is the beginning of the turning; spoken after the closing, it is the final entry in a ledger already sealed. The same words, one hour apart, are two different acts — and the two verses before this one established that no one controls the hour, since the torment came at night or at midday, unannounced.

The Qur'an places the cure beside the diagnosis. *“Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”* (4:110) is what the townspeople could have said and did not, in the years when saying it would have worked. The Prophet ﷺ described God's reception of such a turning in terms that make this verse's warning land: *“God is more joyful at the repentance of His servant than one of you who finds his camel that he had lost in the desert.”* (Muslim 2747, from Anas ibn Mālik).

The destroyed town and the returning servant say the same sentence and end in opposite places. What separates them is not the sincerity of the tone but their position on the clock of mercy — and the reader of this verse stands, by definition, in the part of the hour where the sentence still works.

**The Ruins the Sūrah Tells Its Readers to Read**

The sūrah does not leave the destroyed towns in the past tense of a report. It tells its audience that the evidence is still lying around them. *“Say: Travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers”* (6:11; see also 16:36; 27:69; 29:20; 30:42), and Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ makes the same point with the remains in view: *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly.”* (28:58).

The traders of Makkah rode north and south every season, and the caravan routes of the peninsula ran through the territories of peoples the Qur'an names as examples: ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the people of the ditch. The sūrah's argument in these first verses is not that God is capable of punishing nations; it is that He already has, in the neighbourhood, and that the ruins are readable to anyone who stops. Verse 96 will state the law that explains the ruins: *“Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful of Allah, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth”* (7:96). The verse of the cry, then, is not a piece of ancient history. It is an interpretation of the landscape the sūrah's first listeners crossed on their way to market.


**The Same Cry in al-Anbiyāʾ**

The confession is not unique to this sūrah, and the other account shows how short the interval between it and the end is. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ reports the cry and then the mowing: *“Woe to us! We have surely been wrongdoers.”* (21:14), *“They kept repeating their cry until We mowed them down, ˹leaving them˺ lifeless.”* (21:15).

The two verses answer a question this verse leaves open. A confession repeated until the mowing arrives is not a repentance that failed; it is a recognition that arrived after the term. The commentators draw the distinction from the Book’s rule that a return is accepted only while the term is still running, and the sequence in al-Anbiyāʾ supplies the picture: the words are true, they are spoken, and they change nothing, because the moment in which they could have changed anything has closed. This verse states the same fact in one clause, calling the confession the towns’ only cry, which is what remains of a speech that once had a use.


**The Word for a Cry**

The word the verse uses for what the towns said is *daʿwā*, from the root for calling or claiming, and it denotes both an invocation and an assertion. The Book uses the same word of the last speech of the people of Paradise, where it denotes a praise rather than a confession: *“All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds!”* (10:10).

The pairing is worth holding because it fixes what a *daʿwā* is: the sentence a person arrives at when nothing else remains to be said. In the Garden it is praise, and the verse in Yūnus describes it as the closing of a prayer; in the destroyed towns it is an admission of wrongdoing, and this verse describes it as the only thing their cry amounted to. The same word carries both because both are last words. The sūrah’s readers are being shown the two endings of the same act of speech, and the difference between them is not the vocabulary but the time at which the sentence was reached.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:6

> **We will surely question those who received messengers and We will question the messengers ˹themselves˺.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Interrogations, One Order**

The previous verse left the nations with a confession; this one opens the court in which the confession is taken. The emphatic form is deliberate: *la-nasʾalanna* is an oath-future reinforced by *nūn al-tawkīd*, the strongest way Arabic has of saying *this will certainly happen*. The parties are named in a fixed order — first *those unto whom the message was sent*, then *the messengers* themselves.

The order is the argument. The community stands first because the question at issue is what it did with what reached it; the messengers stand second because their testimony closes the door on every plea of ignorance. No one will be able to say that the warning never came, because the same court will call the carrier who brought it.

**What the Messengers Are Asked**

The Qur'an describes the messengers' interrogation, and it is narrow: *“the Day Allah will gather the messengers and say, ‘What response did you receive?’”* (5:109). The question is not whether they were eloquent or successful — success was never theirs to engineer — but whether the message was delivered. The Book states their commission in the same short form again and again: *“your duty is only to deliver the message”* (13:40); *“then your duty ˹O Prophet˺ is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly.”* (16:82). A messenger's account is settled by the delivery, and the delivery is what leaves the community without an excuse.

**Why the People Are Questioned at All**

The classical commentators took seriously a difficulty that other verses create: some passages seem to say the guilty will not be questioned. *“On that Day there will be no need for any human or jinn to be asked about their sins”* (55:39). A witness will be brought from every faith-community (4:41; 16:84), the record will be laid open (39:69). How can there be interrogation if there is nothing to ask?

The answer the exegetes gave is the key to this verse: the questioning is not an investigation. God does not ask in order to learn; the account is already complete, and the very next verse says so — *“Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge—for We were never absent.”* (7:7) The questioning of 7:6 is the arraignment: the moment the evidence is put to the person and the person is made to stand inside it. That is why 16:84 ends with the disbelievers allowed neither to plead nor to appeal — the interrogation exposes the excuse; it does not discover the fact.

**The Interrogation That Has No Interpreter**

The Prophet ﷺ described the setting of that encounter with the precision of an eyewitness: *“There is none among you except that Allah will speak to him, with no interpreter between Him and him. He will look to his right and see nothing except what he has sent forth, and to his left nothing except what he has sent forth, and ahead of him nothing but the Fire — so protect yourselves from the Fire even with half a date.”* (al-Bukhārī 7443; the command to ward off the Fire with half a date is at al-Bukhārī 1413 and Muslim 1016 — all three from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim).

The detail that carries this verse's weight is the absence of intermediaries. Human power is screened: secretaries, advocates, patrons, spokesmen stand between the ruler and the ruled. The court of 7:6 has none. The question is put by the Lord directly to the servant, with the witnesses and the messengers present — and every layered defence a person spent a lifetime building (*my father did so*, *my people did so*, *no one told me*) has already been answered by the earlier session of the same court, in which the carriers were asked and the delivery was confirmed.

In two clauses, then, the verse gives the whole architecture of accountability: a message that arrived, carriers who delivered it, and a meeting in which both sides answer — the carriers for the delivery, the receivers for the response, and no one else to blame.

**The Question That Will Be Put to the Messengers**

The interrogation of verse 6 runs in two directions at once, and the Qur'an returns to it at several points in the Book. *“Consider the Day Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What response did you receive?'”* (5:109). *“And watch for the Day He will call to them, asking, 'What response did you give to the messengers?'”* (28:65). Sūrat al-Naḥl adds that a witness will be produced from every faith-community (16:84), and the Prophet himself is told that he is one of them: *“So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours?”* (4:41).

The doctrinal consequence is not a technicality about procedure. A message delivered by a messenger creates a record on both sides of the transmission: what the messenger actually said, and what the recipients actually did with it. The second half of the questioning — the messengers themselves — protects the integrity of the whole system, because it establishes that the account being examined is what was in fact delivered, not what the recipients later claimed to have heard.

Any reader who has ever complained that a preacher failed to explain something will find the verse uncomfortable in a useful way. The Book constructs a courtroom in which the accused cannot plead that the message never arrived, and in which the one sent can be asked what he passed on. Both halves of the evidence are on the record, and the record is held by a clerk who was never out of the room.


**The Witness Brought From Every Community**

The verse announces two interrogations; the Book elsewhere describes the setting in which they occur. An-Nisāʾ: *“So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours?”* (4:41). The questioning of 7:6 takes place with witnesses present, and the witnesses include the messengers themselves.

That answers the exegetes’ question about what the messengers are asked. They are not asked to explain themselves; they are asked to testify. Their interrogation is the discharge of an office — the office of the one who was sent, who saw what his people did, and who will be asked what he delivered and what they answered. 4:41 supplies the term the sūrah leaves implicit: *shahīd*, witness, from the root *sh-h-d*, the one who was present and who speaks from presence.


**Voices Hushed Before the Questioning**

The sūrah describes an interrogation; the Book describes the sound of the Day. Ṭāhā: *“On that Day all will follow the caller for assembly, and none will dare to deviate. All voices will be hushed before the Most Compassionate. Only whispers will be heard.”* (20:108). An-Nabaʾ: *“on the Day the holy spirit and the angels will stand in ranks. None will talk, except those granted permission by the Most Compassionate and whose words are true.”* (78:38).

The two verses supply what 7:6 leaves unstated: the questioning occurs in a silence, and speech on that Day is licensed. 20:108 describes voices hushed and whispers only; 78:38 adds the condition — permission, and truth in what is said. Read together with 7:6 they explain why the verse says nothing about answers. The interrogation is not a debate; it is a proceeding in which the right to speak is granted and the content is fixed.

This is also why the sūrah’s phrase at 7:7 — the recounting with knowledge, from a Witness who was never absent — matters to the scene. In a proceeding where speech is licensed and the record is complete, no party can improve its position by what it says. The commentators’ observation that the interrogation admits no interpreter (7:6) is the same fact stated from the other side: there is no gap in the record for an advocate to work in.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:7

> **Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge—for We were never absent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Recounting That Matches the Fact**

From the question the verse moves to the narration: *fa-la-naquṣṣanna ʿalayhim bi-ʿilm*. The verb is *qaṣṣa*, to follow a thing step by step — the root that also gives *qiṣṣah*, a story, because a story is a tracing of events in their order. To recount in the Arabic of the Qur'an is not to summarize; it is to reproduce the sequence so faithfully that the hearer recognizes his own life inside it. The instrument is named: *with knowledge* — not evidence reconstructed after the fact, not inference from testimony, but the knowledge that was present when the act itself occurred.

The final clause states the ground of that completeness: *wa-mā kunnā ghāʾibīn* — We were never absent. *Ghāʾib* is the one who is elsewhere; the negation removes not merely a lapse but the whole category of distance. The Qur'an expresses the same fact elsewhere in images the imagination can hold: *“We are closer to them than their jugular vein”* (50:16); *“Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth or anything—green or dry—but is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record.”* (6:59). The Book does not say that God was informed afterwards. It says that the record was never left unwritten.

**The Reading of the Record**

The sequence of this sūrah — question, recounting, weighing — matches the courtroom imagery the Qur'an uses for the final accounting. The record is brought out and opened: *“And the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, and you will see the wicked in fear of what is ˹written˺ in it”* (18:49). Each person is handed his own book: *“We have bound every human's destiny to their neck, and on the Day of Judgment We will bring forth to each person a record which they will find laid open”* (17:13) — and is told: *“Read your record. You alone are sufficient this Day to take account of yourself”* (17:14). Before the prophets and witnesses are brought forward, the earth shines with the light of its Lord and judgment is passed (39:69).

The purpose of that architecture is that a person is not merely judged; he is made to read. The recounting of 7:7 is that reading, and *with knowledge* is why it cannot be contested. No one can plead that the file was mistaken or that a context was missing or that the intention was better than the deed — because the One who recounts was present at the intention as well.

**The Hours No One Saw**

The Prophet ﷺ gave this certainty a name and a set of questions. The feet of the servant will not move on the Day of Judgment, he said, until he is asked about his life and how he spent it, his body and how he wore it out, his wealth and how he earned it and where he spent it, and his knowledge and what he did with it (al-Tirmidhī 2417, from Abū Barzah al-Aslamī; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by al-Tirmidhī and daʿīf by Dār al-Salām. The fourfold version reported from Muʿādh ibn Jabal in al-Dārimī is judged weak by the critics, and al-Dāraquṭnī preferred to read it as the companion’s own words). Not one of those four can be answered by reputation. All of them belong to the interior — to hours that no one but God observed.

That is the practical force of *We were never absent*. Human accountability is limited to what can be seen; the divine recounting is not — and this is a mercy before it is a dread. A person who did good that nobody ever learned of has lost nothing at all, and a person who kept an evil behind a locked door has hidden it from everyone except the One who is now doing the recounting. The verse makes secret-keeping as impossible as it already was, and makes integrity a matter of fact rather than of performance: the only kind that survives the reading of the record.

**The Account Written by Observers Who Never Left**

The clause *with sure knowledge* — *ʿalā ʿilm* — rests on a doctrine the sūrah assumes but states elsewhere: the deed was never unobserved. *“He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you”* (6:61). *“Not a word does a person utter without having a vigilant observer ready to write it down”* (50:18). *“While you are certainly observed by vigilant, honourable angels, recording ˹everything˺. They know whatever you do.”* (82:10–12). Sūrat al-Zukhruf adds that not even an unspoken thought escapes the record: *“Or do they think that We do not hear their ˹evil˺ thoughts and secret talks? Yes ˹We do˺! And Our messenger-angels are in their presence, recording ˹it all˺.”* (43:80).

The Book's picture of the accounting on the Day incorporates the book itself: the record is laid open before its owner, who reads it without disputing a line — *“And the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, and you will see the wicked in fear of what is ˹written˺ in it. They will cry, ‘Woe to us! What kind of record is this that does not leave any sin, small or large, unlisted?” They will find whatever …’* (18:49). The sūrah's *full account* of verse 7 is therefore not a reconstruction made after the fact from fragmentary evidence. It is the presentation of a document.

There is a practical corollary the early Muslims drew from this and repeated in their instruction of children: a person's private life is the part of the record he does not control. Public reputation, in a Book that keeps scribes on both shoulders, is not the file that will be read out.


**Simultaneous Rather Than Retrospective**

The verse grounds the recounting in God’s presence: *“for We were never absent.”* (7:7). The Book states the same presence at length in Yūnus: *“There is no activity you may be engaged in ˹O Prophet˺ or portion of the Quran you may be reciting, nor any deed you ˹all˺ may be doing except that We are a Witness over you while doing it.”* (10:61). The verse enumerates three cases — an affair, a recitation, a deed — and puts the witnessing inside each of them, with the participle *īdh tafīḍūna fīh*: while you are engaged in it.

Al-Mujādilah states it in the form the exegetes quote most often: *“If three converse privately, He is their fourth. If five, He is their sixth. Whether fewer or more, He is with them wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Judgment, He will inform them of what they have done.”* (58:7). The verse runs from the smallest private gathering to the Day on which it is reported, and its final clause is 7:7’s clause: the informing is the consequence of the presence.


**The Sūrah’s Own Method Stated**

7:6 and 7:7 together give the procedure of the Day: questioning, then recounting with knowledge by a Witness who was never absent. The same two verbs govern the sūrah’s own procedure. It questions its readers through its histories — every town’s exchange is a question put to the one reading — and it narrates with knowledge, in the first person plural, of events none of its audience saw.

The parallel is not a coincidence of vocabulary but a claim. A book that says *“We will surely question those who received messengers”* (7:6) and then narrates the towns in detail is performing, in its own register, the procedure it announces. The histories are the questioning; the narration is the recounting with knowledge; and the sūrah’s repeated appeal to its readers — *laʿallakum tattaqūn*, *laʿallakum tashkurūn*, *fa-kayfa kāna ʿāqibat al-mukadhdhibīn* — is the form the question takes in a text.

This is why 7:7’s final clause matters for the reading of the whole sūrah. *Wa-mā kunnā ghāʾibīn* (we were never absent) is spoken by the narrator of the histories. The one who tells the story of Midian and Thamūd and the towns whose names are not preserved was present at all of them, and the sūrah is His report. The reader is not being given a chronicle to assess but a testimony to answer.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:8

> **The weighing on that Day will be just. As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺, ˹only˺ they will be successful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day That Weighs**

This verse sets the third action of the sūrah's courtroom: after the question (v. 6) and the recounting (v. 7), the weighing. The syntax puts the verdict first: *wa-l-waznu yawmaʾidhin al-ḥaqq* — the weighing on that Day will be just. *Ḥaqq* does double duty here. It means the scales are real, not a metaphor that dissolves on inspection; and it means they are true — exact, uncorrupted, incapable of registering a false weight.

The choice of the scale as the instrument of judgment answers the audience of this Makkan sūrah. Al-Aʿrāf speaks to a mercantile city whose life ran on balances: measured grain, weighed silver, a handshake over a pan. The Qur'an takes the instrument of the market and moves it to the last Day, where it is operated by the One who cannot be bribed. The point is sharpened in another sūrah, where woe is pronounced on traders who demand full measure when they buy and short it when they sell (83:1–3). The market's scale is precisely where men learn to weigh for advantage — which is why it is a scale that is set up on the Day of Judgment, and why the verse insists that the measuring there is *ḥaqq*.

**The Scale That Weighs What Scales Cannot**

The Qur'an describes the operation of this balance with mechanical precision: *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And even if a deed is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth”* (21:47). It will register an atom's weight (4:40; 99:7–8), and its verdicts are given in the very phrasing used here: *“As for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺, it is they who will be successful. But those whose scale is light, they will have doomed themselves, staying in Hell forever”* (23:102–103); and in Sūrat al-Qāriʿah, *“So as for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺, they will be in a life of bliss”* (101:6–7).

What, then, is weighed? The Prophet ﷺ answered with an image no arithmetic can hold. A man is brought before God with ninety-nine scrolls of sins, each stretching as far as the eye can see, and a single card bearing the witness *there is no god but God*. The scrolls are placed on one pan and the card on the other: the scrolls rise, the card descends — *“nothing is heavier than the Name of God”* (al-Tirmidhī 2639, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr; graded ḥasan gharīb by al-Tirmidhī and ṣaḥīḥ by Dār al-Salām; Ibn Mājah 4300 records it as well).

That image is this verse's commentary. The scales of the hereafter do not weigh quantity, so that whoever piles up the most acts wins; they weigh reality — the actual worth of what a life was aimed at. A mountain of activity performed for display can rise like chaff, while one sincere confession of the One God can descend with the weight of a lifetime. This is why the Day can be called *the truth*: it is the moment when things are measured as they are, and not as they were advertised.

**The Prosperity of the Heavy**

The verse closes with the outcome for those whose pan descends: *fa-ulāʾika humu al-mufliḥūn*. *Mufliḥūn* comes from *f-l-ḥ*, the root of the farmer — *fallāḥ* — who splits the earth, plants, and waits. *Filāḥ*, prosperity, is the same word as cultivation, because in the Qur'an's vocabulary success is not what a man extracts from the world but what grows out of what he has planted in it. The Arabic quietly answers the mercantile image: the real trade is not the one that closes when the caravan departs, but the one whose harvest is delivered on the Day the scales are set.

Heaviness, in that grammar, is not a burden. It is the weight of the things that survive — a confession guarded in secret, a charity no one recorded, an injustice refused at the moment when it would have paid. All of it descends in the pan, in the sight of no one except the One who was never absent.

**What Is Placed on the Scale**

The scale of verse 8 is the Book's standard instrument for the reckoning and it appears in three other sūrahs with the same terminology: *“As for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺, it is they who will be successful. But those whose scale is light, they will have doomed themselves, staying in Hell forever”* (23:102–103); *“So as for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺, they will be in a life of bliss. And as for those whose scale is light, their home will be the abyss”* (101:6–9).

The Book states elsewhere the arithmetic that gives the weighing its relief: *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold, but whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one”* (6:160), and the atom of good and evil each appears on the record of the one who did it (99:7–8). But the sūrah's wording is not that deeds are counted; it is that they are *weighed*. A thing weighed has a quality as well as a quantity — sincerity, intention, the occasion, the cost — and the tradition drew precisely that conclusion. The Prophet ﷺ said of two short phrases that *they are light on the tongue, heavy in the balance, and dear to the Most Merciful: Subḥān Allāh wa biḥamdih, Subḥān Allāh al-ʿAẓīm* (al-Bukhārī 6406, from Abū Hurayrah).

For the reader of the sūrah, the scale's existence changes the size of small things. The history of the sūrah's audience is full of gestures that looked trivial at the time — a cup of water given, a harsh word withheld, a rumour passed on — and the verse tells him that each of them has been placed on an instrument that will be read out with exactness, on a Day whose justice the sūrah has already called *ḥaqq*.


**The Balance Set in the Sky**

The verse states the weighing and its justice: *“The weighing on that Day will be just.”* (7:8). Ar-Raḥmān describes the balance as something set in place before any weighing occurs: *“As for the sky, He raised it ˹high˺, and set the balance ˹of justice˺ so that you do not defraud the scales. Weigh with justice, and do not give short measure.”* (55:7–9).

The two verses connect a cosmic arrangement to a market practice. The sky is raised and the balance is set, and the purpose given is that people should not defraud the scales — the same offence the sūrah condemns in Midian (7:85). The balance of the Day is therefore not an image borrowed from trade; the trade practice is derived from the balance.

The exegetes read 55:7–9 as the ground of every statement about weighing in the Book. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse commands justice in measure because measure is itself a gift, and that the Day described at 7:8 is the occasion on which the gift is accounted for. A just weighing is thus the completion of a just market, not its replacement.


**Successful Indeed Are the Believers**

The verse’s second clause names the outcome of heaviness: *“As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺, ˹only˺ they will be successful.”* (7:8). Al-Muʾminūn opens with the same word: *“Successful indeed are the believers: those who humble themselves in prayer.”* (23:1–2).

The restriction in both verses is the same — *ʾulāʾika hum al-mufliḥūn*, those, they are the successful — and the list that follows in al-Muʾminūn gives the conduct the word is attached to. The heaviness of 7:8 is not a quantity deposited but a life described, and 23:1–9 is the Book’s own description of it.

This is why the verse is placed at the head of the sūrah’s account of the Day. 7:8–9 states the weighing and its two outcomes before any narrative begins, and the histories that follow show the two classes in the towns. The word for success is the sūrah’s positive term throughout, and its definition is given in the verses that describe what the successful do.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:9

> **But those whose scale is light, they have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lightness as a Verdict**

The verse completes the pair begun in 7:8 with an exact mirror: the heavy scale and the light. What makes a scale light is not always the absence of deeds — the scrolls and the card have already shown that volume counts for nothing — but the absence of weight. The measure of the hereafter is not the number of acts but their worth, and the worth of an act is set by the aim to which it was offered.

The fate is then stated in commercial Arabic: *alladhīna khasirū anfusahum* — those who have lost themselves. *Khusrān* is the merchant's word for a loss, and the Qur'anic usage is exact: this is not the loss of profit but the loss of capital. The person in the verse leaves the market of his life having traded away the very self he was trading with. The same ledger appears in another sūrah: those who reject the meeting with their Lord have *“their deeds void, so We will not give their deeds any weight on Judgment Day.”* (18:105). A deed with no weight to give is a loss no accounting can repair.

**The Cause: Wronging the Signs**

The verse then names the cause, and it is not the one a reader might expect. Lightness is not diagnosed here as weakness or as ignorance. It is *an ẓalamū bi-āyātinā ẓulm* — that they wronged Our signs. The noun is the same one the townspeople used of themselves in 7:5, and the echo ties the sūrah's opening to its weighing: the destruction of the first verses and the light scale here are one offense at two moments of the story. Wronging a sign (*ẓulm*) is, in the Qur'an's usage, putting it out of its place — denying it outright, or acknowledging the words while treating them as though they carried no claim, or bending their meaning toward a preferred outcome. The imperfect *yaẓlimūn* adds what "having treated wrongfully" can only hint at: this was not a single lapse but a practice.

The seriousness follows from what a sign is. The signs — the revelation, the messengers, the world itself with its dawns and its marks of design — do not merely inform; they oblige. To meet one and shrug is not neutrality; it is a decision about the One who sent it. That is why the wronging of signs is counted among the gravest acts, and why the lightness of the scale is its natural consequence: a person who spends a lifetime refusing weight arrives at the judgment with none.

**The Exactness That Spares No One**

The verses around this one guard the verdict from despair. *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least”* (21:47). *“Indeed, Allah never wrongs anyone — even by an atom's weight”* (4:40). *“So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it”* (99:7–8). The lightness of this verse is therefore no accident of arithmetic, and no one will be condemned for a gram that was never his to supply: the same Book that weighs a mustard seed also declares that God does not require of any soul more than it can bear (2:286).

What follows in the sūrah — the settlement of humanity on the earth, its brief tenure, and the return (7:10 onward) — reads as the practical conclusion of this weighing. If the scale is real, then the days in which a pan may still be loaded with something of weight are exactly the days being lived now. Verse 9 closes the ledger with a warning whose force lies in its tense: those who *were* wronging Our signs made their own lightness, one deliberate and unremarkable moment at a time.

**"They Have Doomed Themselves"**

*Khasirū anfusahum* — they have lost themselves. The phrase is one of the Qur'an's most concentrated statements of what sin does, and the Book repeats it with a variety of emphasis. *“And by the soul and ˹the One˺ Who fashioned it, then with ˹the knowledge of˺ right and wrong inspired it! Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul, and doomed is the one who corrupts it!”* (91:7–10). *“The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day. That is indeed the clearest loss.”* (39:15), a sentence Sūrat al-Shūrā echoes for the wrongdoers exposed to the Fire (42:45). Sūrat al-Baqarah uses the same vocabulary for the small-scale version of the crime in this world: the hypocrites think they are deceiving God and the believers, *“yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it”* (2:9).

The word *khasira* is drawn from trade: it is what happens to a merchant's capital. The sūrah's audience knew the sensation exactly — loss of a caravan, of a year's profit, of a stake in a market — and the Book uses their own vocabulary of catastrophe for something they did not price at all. The warning implicit in the choice is that the life of a human being is a capital sum placed in his hands at birth, and that what is done with it has the shape of an investment: it either returns or it does not.

The sūrah itself returns to this ending later, in the mouths of the condemned: *“They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”* (7:53). The two verses frame the sūrah's whole account of the last things with the same verdict, and the verb is the same in both. The difference is that the men of verse 9 could still read the sentence while it was in manuscript.


**The Scales of Justice: The Word for Weighing**

The verse’s subject is the scale — *mīzān*, from the root *w-z-n*, which gives *wazn* (weight), *wazana* (to weigh) and *mīzān* (the instrument by which weight is known). The plural in this verse and in 21:47 is *mawāzīn*. The root is the Book’s ordinary vocabulary for commercial weighing, which is why its use for deeds is so deliberate: the sūrah that condemns short measure in Midian (7:85) describes the Day in the language of the market the Midianites corrupted.

Al-Anbiyāʾ states the procedure: *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And ˹even˺ if a deed is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth.”* (21:47). The verse supplies the two features 7:9 assumes — the scales are set up by God, and their justice excludes any shortfall, down to the weight of a mustard seed. 7:9 speaks only of the outcome: heaviness and lightness.

The exegetes ask what is weighed, since deeds are not bodies. Their answers divide between the weighing of the record, the weighing of the deeds made substantial, and the weighing as a figure for exact requital


**Wronging the Self: The Reflexive in the Sūrah**

The verse’s second clause is *kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn* — *“they have doomed themselves”* (7:9), literally they were wronging their own selves. The reflexive pronoun is emphatic: *anfusahum*, their very selves. Yūnus states the rule in general terms: *“Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves.”* (10:44). The two verses make the same claim from opposite ends — one describing a class of the damned, the other stating the principle that governs every class.

The sūrah has already used this formula at its opening, in the first confession it records: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”* (7:23). Between 7:23 and 7:9 the same words describe two outcomes, and the difference is the request that follows the admission. Ādam said it and asked; the people of the light scales said it in effect and did not ask. 10:44 explains why the second case is final: the wrong was never inflicted from outside, so there is no injustice to appeal against.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:10

> **We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood. ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Courtroom Back to the Earth**

The three verses before this one stood inside the final court: the question, the recounting, the weighing. Verse 10 returns the reader to the ground he is standing on. The transition is deliberate. Before the sūrah names the first refusal in the universe (vv. 11–18), it reminds the human being of the position he occupies: he has been *settled*, and he has been *provided for*. The two facts together form the premise of every command that follows, and the pivot of the verse is the last clause, which turns provision into a question about the recipient: *˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks!*

**makkannākum: The Verb of Being Settled**

The verb is *makkanā*, from *m-k-n*, the root of place and of power. *Tamkīn* is not merely to drop someone somewhere; it is to give him a firm place, the ability to act from it, and the security to remain. The Qur'an uses the same root for the establishment of the believers in the land (22:41; 24:55) and for the power given to Joseph in Egypt (12:56). Here it is granted to humanity as such, without distinction of nation or creed.

The Qur'an describes the earth with the vocabulary of a house prepared for a guest: *“Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy”* (2:22); *“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you”* (40:64); *“He is the One Who smoothed out the earth for you, so move about in its regions and eat from His provisions”* (67:15). The last of these is the closest twin to this verse: the earth is *smooth*, *tamed*, *made traversable* — a planet whose gravity holds instead of crushing, whose atmosphere filters instead of burning, whose soil yields food when a seed is placed in it. None of that was arranged by the person who benefits from it.

**maʿāyish: Livelihood in the Plural**

Provision is named with a plural that is significant: *maʿāyish*, from *ʿ-y-sh*, to live. Not one livelihood but many, distributed across soils and climates and temperaments. The commentators drew the practical consequences. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the plural shows the variety of ways God has opened for the creature to eat — agriculture, trade, craft, pasture — so that no one is forced into a single channel and no one may claim that the earth offered him nothing. Al-Qurṭubī adds the juridical consequence: since the livelihoods are *placed* by God, they are not owed to any person by right of cleverness; they are received, and receiving creates the duty of thanks.

The verse also quietly settles a question that occupies the sūrah elsewhere. If provision is placed by God, then striving is a means, not a guarantee; effort is required, but the outcome is not owned by the effort. That single adjustment disarms both envy and arrogance at once: envy, because another's plenty is not a theft from my share; arrogance, because my plenty is not a proof of my superiority.

**The Ingratitude Clause**

The verse closes with *qalīlan mā tashkurūn* — “little is it that you give thanks.” The construction (*qalīlan mā* + imperfect) is one of the Arabic forms of emphatic rebuke, and the translation’s rendering of this verse, “˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks” (7:10), carries it. The wording is careful: the verse does not say that human beings are never grateful. It says that gratitude is *little* — occasional, partial, easily displaced by complaint. The Qur'an returns to this diagnosis repeatedly: *“If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you would never be able to number them”* (14:34; 16:18), with 14:34 ending in the same verdict — *“Indeed humankind is truly unfair, ˹totally˺ ungrateful.”*

The Qur'an also states the law that governs the relationship: *“If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe”* (14:7). The logic deserves to be stated plainly, because it is not a bargain in the manner of a merchant. Gratitude is not a payment that purchases increase; it is a *seeing* that makes increase bearable and fruitful. The person who acknowledges the Giver receives the same gift and is enlarged by it; the person who credits himself receives it and is narrowed by it, because everything he has becomes a monument to himself — and monuments have to be defended forever.

**Gratitude as a Discipline of the Eye**

Islam treats *shukr* as a practice, not a mood. The Prophet ﷺ trained his companions to compare downward rather than upward in the things of this world: *“Look at those below you and not those above you, for that is more likely to keep you from belittling the favour of God upon you.”* (Muslim 2963, from Abū Hurayrah). It is a remedy against precisely the disease this verse names. Ingratitude rarely announces itself as denial of God; it appears as a habitual focus on the one thing missing, in a life that has received a thousand things.

The circle of gratitude is also horizontal before it is vertical. *“Whoever is not grateful to the people, he is not grateful to Allah.”* (al-Tirmidhī 1954, from Abū Hurayrah). A person who cannot bring himself to thank a teacher, a parent, a driver, a colleague has already lost the reflex by which the Creator is thanked, because both are acts of the same faculty: the willingness to admit that what I have came through someone other than me.

Read in the sūrah's sequence, then, verse 10 is not a pleasant interlude before the story of Iblīs. It is the foundation of that story. The earth is prepared, the livelihoods are placed, the human being is settled in dignity — and the next thing the sūrah shows is a creature who had been given a station and lost it by believing the station was his own achievement.


**A Place of Settlement: The Same Gift Described in Ghāfir**

The verse names two gifts in two verbs: establishment on the earth and provision of livelihoods. Ghāfir describes the same pair in the same order: *“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form. And He has provided you with what is good and lawful.”* (40:64).

The verse of Ghāfir adds the sky and the shaping of the body, so that the settlement and the provision are set between two other acts — a place made and a form perfected. The two gifts of 7:10 are therefore not isolated favours but parts of an arrangement that includes the person who receives them.

40:64 ends where 7:10 begins its complaint: the arrangement is described, and then the blessing is named. The sūrah’s own summary of it is shorter — *“˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks.”* (7:10) — and the word for seldom, *qalīlan*, quantifies the response rather than denying it. The gift is plural in both verses; the thanks are few in both.


**Blessings That Cannot Be Numbered**
