The provision named in this verse is *maʿāyish*, the plural of *maʿīshah* — a means of living, what a life is lived on. An-Naḥl states the scale of what the plural contains: *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them.”* (16:18).

The verse answers an objection to 7:10 before it can be raised. A charge of ingratitude assumes that the favour is identifiable and finite; 16:18 removes the assumption, and with it the possibility of an accounting that would settle the matter. The sūrah’s own formulation is consistent with this: the establishment is stated once, the livelihoods in the plural, and the ingratitude as a habit rather than as a single refusal.

The exegetes connect the two verses by the discipline of gratitude. What cannot be counted can still be acknowledged, and acknowledgement is what *shukr* means in the Book’s usage — the favour named, and then used as it was given. Al-Qurṭubī notes that 7:10 is placed at the head of the sūrah’s histories precisely because it states the condition under which all of them are narrated.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:11

> **Surely We created you, then shaped you, then said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Why the Story of Adam Comes Here**

This verse begins the sūrah's longest narrative, the account of Adam, Iblīs, and the first disobedience — a story that will run to verse 25 and will be told again, from different angles, in al-Baqarah, al-Ḥijr, al-Isrāʾ, Ṣād, and Ṭā-Hā. Its placement here answers the verse before it. Verse 10 described a creature settled on a prepared earth and provided for; verse 11 shows what that creature *is* — the being for whom the angels were commanded to bow. The dignity is stated before the failure, so that the failure may be read correctly: not as evidence that humanity is contemptible, but as the collapse of something noble.

**Two Verbs: Created, Then Formed**

*Khalaqnākum thumma ṣawwarnākum* — We created you, then shaped you. The two verbs are not synonyms. *Khalaqa* names the bringing into being of what was not; *ṣawwara* names the giving of shape — proportion, features, the arrangement that makes a thing recognizable as itself. The Qur'an uses the second verb for the human form with evident pleasure: *“He shaped you in the womb, perfecting your form”* (40:64); *“He created the heavens and the earth for a purpose. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form.”* (64:3); *“Who has perfected everything He created”* (32:7); and the summary statement of Sūrat al-Tīn, *“Indeed, We created humans in the best form”* (95:4).

The plural address — *you* — has been explained in two ways. Al-Ṭabarī prefers that it addresses humanity as a whole in Adam: you were created in him, and decreed in him, and then brought into existence from him. Others read the sequence as stages of the species: created as matter, formed as a body, then animated. Either reading carries the same theological point, which the next clauses make explicit: the human being did not design himself, and his form is not an accident of chemistry but the product of an intention.

**The Prostration and What It Confers**

Then God addressed the angels: *“Prostrate before Adam.”* The angels obeyed, and the Qur'an states their obedience without qualification. The command requires theological care, because prostration appears to be an act of worship and worship belongs to God alone. The classical commentators resolve this by distinguishing the *act* from its *object of worship*: the prostration was commanded by God, performed for God, and directed at Adam as a *qiblah* of honor — a salute, in the manner of a subject greeting a king. Al-Qurṭubī cites the analogy of Jacob and his sons prostrating before Joseph (12:100), which the Qur'an records without censure: the prostration of greeting was a known courtly form, and its permissibility or prohibition is set by the divine command. What the angels performed was obedience to God expressed in the direction He chose.

That the direction was a human being is the astonishing part. The angels are described elsewhere as creatures of uninterrupted worship — *“who never disobey whatever Allah orders—always doing as commanded”* (66:6) — and here they are told to bow to dust that has been shaped and animated by God. The honor of humanity, in this scene, is not intrinsic but *conferred*, and it is conferred by the very act that Iblīs will refuse. Dignity, in the Qur'an's account, is always a grant; the moment it is treated as a personal possession, it becomes the occasion of a fall.

**Iblīs and the Grammar of the Exception**

*Illā Iblīs* — except Iblīs. The verse's final clause is unusual: *but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others* — the Arabic (*lam yakun min al-sājidīn*) states the refusal as an absence, *he was not among those who prostrated*. The Qur'an distributes the facets of his act across sūrahs: he *refused and was arrogant* (2:34); he *was one of the jinn, but he rebelled* (18:50); he *protested* (17:61); he *said, “It is not for me to prostrate to a human You created from sounding clay”* (15:33). Each wording adds a detail. From 18:50 we learn that he was not an angel at all but a jinn, whose free will was the very test the command was designed to exercise. From 2:34 we learn that the refusal was accompanied by *istikbār* — the attribution of greatness to oneself. And from this verse we learn that his non-prostration was a settled state: he did not merely miss the moment; he placed himself outside the ranks of the obedient and remained there.

**The Warning Stored in the Honor**

The sūrah's first audience was a proud merchant leadership, and this narrative was addressed to them. The first rebellion in creation was not caused by disbelief in God's existence; Iblīs believed, and even invoked God's act of creation as his proof. It was caused by a ranking instinct — the conviction that a position undeserved by another belonged properly to oneself. The Prophet ﷺ stated the danger in a single hadith: *“No one who has an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise.”* When a man asked how one could like his clothes and his shoes to be good, the Prophet ﷺ clarified the definition: *“Arrogance is rejecting the truth and belittling people.”* (Muslim 91, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd). Both halves of that definition are present in the verses that follow — and both were present in the court of the angels, where a creature with free will was shown what his freedom was for.


**The Order of the Two Verbs**

The verse opens on two acts in sequence — We created you, then We shaped you — and the Book keeps that sequence wherever it states it. Sūrah al-Muʾmin lists the same pair among the grounds of gratitude: *“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form. And He has provided you with what is good and lawful.”* (40:64). Sūrah al-Infiṭār compresses it into a question addressed to the human being: *“Who created you, fashioned you, and perfected your design, moulding you in whatever form He willed?”* (82:7–8).

The root behind the second verb, *ṣ-w-r*, gives the word for a form or an image, and its use here is what makes the verse’s honour a statement about shape rather than about material. Clay is the substance and it is shared with the rest of the earth; the form is what was given to this creature and to none of the others in the scene. The sūrah’s argument with Iblīs turns on exactly this: he compares substances, and the verse has already placed the difference somewhere else.


**The Plural Address and the Single Scene**

The verse speaks to a plural audience about a single event. *We created you, then We shaped you* is addressed to all who hear it, and the prostration that follows is narrated as an event in the life of one man. The commentators note the shift and read it as deliberate: the shaping is not something that happened once to Adam and then stopped, and the honour conferred in the scene is conferred on the species whose head was standing there.

That is why the sūrah can address the children of Adam four times in the verses that follow and speak to them of a temptation that reached their father. The plural of this opening verse and the vocative of those later ones are the same device: the reader is placed inside the story rather than opposite it. The refusal recorded at the end of the verse is likewise not only a report about Iblīs. It is the first instance of a choice the sūrah will present to its hearers two hundred times over, and the warning stored in the honour is that an honour conferred can be declined by the one who receives it.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:12

> **Allah asked, “What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?” He replied, “I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Put to the Accused**

The scene turns to the interrogation, and its form repeats the pattern established in verses 6 and 7: God asks, and the answer exposes. The question is *mā manaʿaka* — literally, *what prevented you?* The verb *manaʿa* is the vocabulary of withholding and of barriers; a *māniʿ* is a thing that stands in the way. The question is therefore not a request for information. It puts before the accused the one thing he must now name: the obstacle. And since the command had come from God and nothing external had blocked the way, the only possible answer was the barrier he had built inside himself. The Qur'an's question strips away every third-party explanation before Iblīs speaks a word.

His answer does not name that barrier. It supplies, instead, an argument.

**The First Analogy in the Tradition's Telling**

*“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* The classical scholars read these words as the first act of reasoning by analogy (*qiyās*) in the history of the creation, and they examined its form with the care of logicians. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī set out the objections in sequence.

First, the premise is asserted, not established. Iblīs claims a nobility of fire above clay as though the proposition were self-evident. It is not; it is a claim about material substances whose ranking Iblīs had no revelation to support. The Qur'an, for its part, treats the composition of both as dust-bound and God-given: *“He created humankind from ˹sounding˺ clay like pottery, and created jinn from a ˹smokeless˺ flame of fire”* (55:14–15), and the human being is *“We created man from sounding clay moulded from black mud”* (15:26). Arranging these ingredients in a hierarchy of superiority is a human projection, not a scriptural datum.

Second, even a true premise could not have produced that conclusion. The value of a thing before God is not set by what it is made of, but by its obedience and its reverence: *“Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you.”* (49:13). Iblīs reasoned from origin to rank, and the Qur'an's entire moral architecture refuses that move. A creature of fire and a creature of clay stand equally as creatures; only the command of God differentiates their duties.

Third, and decisively, the argument was raised against a direct command. Theologians of every school drew the line here: no demonstration — even a sound one — abrogates an explicit divine obligation. A person's reasoning is authorized to conclude that God is one, that the Messenger speaks for Him, that the prayer is due; it is not authorized to override what is thus concluded. To reason so is not to reason, but to use reasoning as an alibi.

**When Intelligence Goes to Work for Desire**

The most instructive feature of the answer is that it is *articulate*. Iblīs does not say “I did not want to.” He constructs a case. The Qur'an thus presents, at the first moral crisis of the created order, the psychology that will recur in every subsequent one: the mind's capacity to convert a preferred outcome into a reasoned position. Al-Rāzī notes that this is why the lesson of the verse is not confined to Iblīs. Any argument can be assembled backward from the conclusion one is unwilling to surrender; and the sharper the intelligence, the more respectable the assembly looks.

The criterion that separates sound reasoning from this corruption is stated by the angels in the parallel scene of al-Baqarah. When God announced the creation of a deputy on earth and the angels asked their question, the answer given for them — and given by them — was: *“Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise”* (2:32). The angels also reasoned — but they closed their reasoning with submission, whereas Iblīs closed his with a verdict. That is the whole difference, and the sūrah intends it to be remembered.

**The Lie in the Phrase “I Am Better”**

The comparative carries its own refutation. Iblīs accepted God's act of creation and even cited it as an argument; what he refused was God's authority to command. He was, in effect, a theist in metaphysics and an atheist in ethics, dividing lordship into departments so that the department that inconvenienced him could be reserved for himself. The Qur'an will answer the posture directly in another sūrah: *“Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60).

And the final irony is the criterion he chose. *“I am better than he is”* (7:12) — better in substance, by a material comparison. The Book's answer is that the creature he despised would receive what he lost: *“Indeed, We have dignified the children of Adam”* (17:70). Rank in the divine court is not a property of matter; it is a matter of response. It is the one measurement Iblīs never applied, because applying it would have cost him the argument — and it is the same measurement this sūrah put before its readers four verses earlier, when it asked who among the settled, provided, and shaped would give thanks.


**The Same Question in Three Other Places**

The interrogation is not told once. Sūrah al-Ḥijr records it with the addressee named: *“O Iblîs! What is the matter with you that you did not join others in prostration?”* (15:32), and the answer given there omits the comparison and states the refusal as a matter of what is fitting: *“It is not for me to prostrate to a human You created from sounding clay moulded from black mud.”* (15:33). Sūrah Ṣād gives the answer in the words this sūrah gives it: *“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* (38:76). Sūrah al-Isrāʾ compresses the protest into a question: *“Should I prostrate to the one You have created from mud?”* (17:61).

The four accounts differ in one respect worth holding. In al-Ḥijr the reply is a statement of unfitness — it is not for me — which is a claim about the order of things. In al-Aʿrāf and in Ṣād it is a statement of superiority, and superiority is a claim about a ranking. In al-Isrāʾ it takes the form of a question, and the question is the most revealing of the three, because it asks God to look again at the object of His own command. This sūrah’s version is the middle term: the ranking asserted flatly, without the hesitation of a question and without the appeal to fitness. That is why the reply it receives in the next verse is not a counter-argument but a dismissal.


**The Command as a Test of Obedience**

The tradition reads Iblīs’s answer as the first instance of a reasoning that runs against a command, and the reading is not a moral verdict added to the story but a statement about its logic. The command to prostrate was issued without a reason attached. Iblīs supplied a reason of his own — the nobility of the element — and used it to overrule what had been said. In the vocabulary the jurists later developed, that is analogy set against an explicit text, and the tradition treats the case as its archetype: a measurement invented at the point where a command had already spoken.

This is why the question in the verse is not asked for information. It asks the accused to state his own ground, and the ground he states is the whole of his case — an origin, a comparison, and a preference. The response does not dispute the chemistry. Fire is not argued to be worse than clay, and Adam is not argued to be composed of nobler stuff; the response is that the ranking belonged to the one who issued the command, and that the creature who had just been shown his place among those commanded had no standing to revise it. On this reading the honour Adam received was not in his substance at all. It was in being chosen, and being chosen is not a property of clay.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:13

> **Allah said, “Then get down from Paradise! It is not for you to be arrogant here. So get out! You are truly one of the disgraced.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict and Its Exact Fit**

Iblīs had offered an argument; the verse answers with a sentence. *Fa-hbiṭ* — get down. The command is abrupt, and its brevity is part of its meaning: the case is closed, and no further exchange is permitted. What precedes it in the sūrah is now visible as a whole: a command was given, a creature measured himself against another, a rationale was produced, and the answer is a two-word eviction.

The proportionality is worth pausing over. The punishment is not an arbitrary penalty attached to a rule; it is the *reversal* of the thing he did. He placed himself above his station, so his station is lowered. He judged himself great, so he is told he is small — *min al-ṣāghirīn*, of the humbled, the reduced. The Qur'an states this correspondence elsewhere as a settled law: *“Is Hell not a fitting home for the arrogant?”* (39:60), and *“Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60). The grammar of the hereafter is the grammar of a mirror.

**A Dwelling That Cannot Hold Arrogance**

The verse states the reason for the expulsion with precision: *lā yakūnu laka an tatakabbara fīhā* — it is not for you to be arrogant *in it*. The pronoun has been discussed by the commentators: the Garden, or the exalted assembly, or the presence in which the command was given. Whichever is intended, the clause carries a principle that runs through the whole Book. There are places and states that exclude self-exaltation not by legislation but by nature. Paradise is one of them: it is the house of those who submitted. The Prophet ﷺ described its inhabitants as *“the humble”* and said that its gates are entered by the one who acknowledges; in another report, the poor and the meek enter it before the wealthy and the proud.

This is why the verse says *it is not for you* rather than merely *you are not allowed*. The wording is ontological before it is legal: arrogance is not an offense that may be committed in that house and then repented of there; it is a condition incompatible with residence. The person who insists on being above others is not being denied a room; he is being told that he is asking for the wrong building.

The sūrah contains two removal commands, and the commentators distinguished them. The first is here — *ihbiṭ*, get down — and the second comes at verse 18: *ukhruj*, go forth, with the added description *madhʾūman madḥūran*, disgraced and banished. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr read the two as stages of a single sentence: the first removes him from the place in which the transgression occurred; the second confirms the state of ruin, the permanent expulsion from mercy. Others observe that the first descent precedes his request for respite (vv. 14–15) and his vow to mislead (vv. 16–17), and that the second expulsion follows those words — the sentence deepening with each further act of defiance. On either reading, the structure teaches something the reader of this sūrah needs: the fall was not a single slip followed by a settled punishment, but a path he continued to walk, one hardened statement at a time.

**ṣāghirīn: The Weight of Smallness**

The final word of the verse, *al-ṣāghirīn*, comes from *ṣ-gh-r*, the root of smallness and of willing submission. It is the direct antonym of *kibr* — the very thing that caused the fall. Arabic makes the reversal audible: the one who claimed *kabīr* (great) is made *ṣāghir* (small). The Qur'an does not use the language of size casually. In its idiom, greatness belongs to God alone — *al-Kabīr*, *al-Mutakabbir* — and any creature who appropriates the attribute contracts an absurdity that the moral order must eventually correct. The correction is rarely instantaneous in this life, which is precisely what makes this verse's placement instructive: the correction in the story is immediate, before the eyes of the angels, while in the reader's experience it is usually deferred, and the deferral is the space in which repentance is still possible.

That last point is the mercy hidden inside a verse of punishment. Iblīs' sentence was pronounced and stood; there was no door of return opened for him, because his refusal was not a lapse but a position. For human beings the Qur'an keeps the door open to the very end, and it does so explicitly: the same Adam who will slip in the verses that follow receives words from his Lord and is forgiven (2:37). The sūrah's first fall is therefore a warning and not a template. It teaches what arrogance costs and how it is answered, and it leaves the reader standing where Iblīs no longer stood — in the time when the correction can still be made by choice rather than by sentence.

**The Vocabulary of the Expulsion**

The two words that close the sentence — *madhʾūman madḥūran*, disgraced and rejected — are a fixed pair in the Qur'an, and the reader who notices where else the Book uses them will hear the sūrah's alarm more clearly. *Dh-ʾ-m* is the root of blame and disgrace; *d-ḥ-r* is the root of driving a thing away from oneself, of putting it out of reach. The pair describes a condition in which both the judgment and the separation are final.

That last verse is the one that gives 7:13 its pastoral weight. What happened to Iblīs is not presented as a unique event in the biography of a jinn; it is the template of a verdict that human beings can reach by the same route. The sūrah has already shown its readers the mechanism — the refusal to bow, performed as a matter of dignity — and it will spend the next forty verses showing the human versions of the same posture, ending with the gates that do not open. The word *disgraced* in verse 13 is spoken to a creature who thought he was maintaining his rank.


**Get Down: One Verb, Three Addressees**

The command is *ihbiṭ*, from *h-b-ṭ*, to descend or to go down. The sūrah uses it three times and to three different addressees: to Iblīs here (7:13), to the pair later in the same narrative (7:24), and — in the Book’s other account — to the two together with their enemy. Al-Baqarah records the third: *“Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other.”* (2:36)

The verb is therefore not a punishment addressed to one party but a relocation addressed to all of them. The descent is common, and the enmity is what distinguishes the parties inside it. 7:13 states the descent and the disgrace; 2:36 and 20:123 state the descent and the enmity; and 20:123 adds the condition that follows — guidance will come, and whoever follows it will not go astray

This is why the expulsion in the sūrah is stated twice rather than once. The first expulsion removes Iblīs from a rank (7:13); the second fills a place with him and with his followers (7:18)


**Disgraced Here, Rejected There**

The verdict ends with a single word: *“You are truly one of the disgraced.”* (7:13). Five verses later the same case is closed with two: *“Get out of Paradise! You are disgraced and rejected!”* (7:18). The second expulsion adds the rejection and the oath about Hell, and the first states the rank that has been lost.

*Ṣāghir* is the one who has become small — the word the Book uses of a humiliation that is felt as well as imposed. The two passives of 7:18 describe what is said of him; the word of 7:13 describes what he has become. The exegetes note the sequence: a dwelling that cannot hold arrogance (7:13), then a dismissal that cannot be reversed (7:18).

The two verses also differ in what they name. 7:13 names the place — it is not for you to be arrogant *here* — and makes the incompatibility the ground of the expulsion. 7:18 names the consequence: Hell filled with him and whoever follows. The sūrah therefore states the verdict and then the sentence, and between them the descent that puts both into effect.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:14

> **He appealed, “Then delay my end until the Day of their resurrection.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Request That Reveals the Man**

Iblīs has been sentenced and evicted, and this is the first thing he says afterward. He does not ask for pardon. He does not ask to be returned. He does not ask a question about the judgment that has just passed over him. He asks for *time*. The request is the clearest window the sūrah offers into what had happened inside him: the verdict fell, and nothing in him bent.

The comparison with the story's other fall is exact and deliberate. When Adam and his wife ate from the tree, the first words they spoke were a petition of a different kind: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers”* (7:23). Two creatures broke a command in the same narrative; one asks for mercy, the other asks for a longer rope. The sūrah places them side by side to make the distinction visible: what makes a fall fatal is not the fall itself but what the fallen one says next.

**anẓirnī: The Language of a Debtor**

The verb *anẓirnī* comes from *n-ẓ-r* in its second form, *inẓār*: to grant a delay, to let a term run on. It is the vocabulary of the creditor who gives a debtor more time, and the Qur'an uses it precisely there: *“If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew” (2:280)* (2:280). Iblīs, then, phrases his demand in the technical language of a man who owes and asks for an extension.

The wording exposes him. He has just been sentenced as the wrongdoer; he speaks as though he were a debtor with a claim to accommodation. And the extension he requests is not for the purpose a debtor asks for time — to gather means and repay. It is time to work against the creditors. The vocabulary of the verse is therefore doing two things at once: it shows the formal courtesy of the request, and it shows that the courtesy is the outer layer of a plan he will announce in two verses.

**The Day He Believes In**

The most unsettling phrase in the sentence is its endpoint: *until the Day of their resurrection.* Iblīs is the arch-rebel of the Qur'an, and he asks to be kept alive until the Resurrection — which means he does not doubt it. There will be a raising, he accepts it, and he asks for his term to stretch all the way to it.

The sūrah's lesson is embedded in that detail. Iblīs was never an atheist. He spoke with God, heard the command, and reasoned about creation; his rebellion was not a denial of God's existence but a refusal of God's authority over him. The Qur'an's own diagnosis in another sūrah names this posture exactly: *“When it is said to them, ‘Fear Allah,’ pride carries them off to sin.”* (2:206). Disbelief in practice is a different thing from disbelief in theory, and it is far more common. A person may affirm the Resurrection in his creed, and still conduct his life as if the Day were a rumor — and this verse puts that inconsistency in the mouth of the first rebel in the universe. He did not argue that the Day was unreal. He asked for a schedule that would let him keep working until it came.

**The Respite as a Workshop**

The request is granted — the next verse is the answer — and the granting is not a concession to his will but the opening of the test. That is the pattern the Qur'an states as law: *“Do not think ˹O Prophet˺ that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them until a Day when ˹their˺ eyes will stare in horror”* (14:42), and *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them; they are only given more time to increase in sin”* (3:178). The same delay that is a workshop of repentance for one person is a workshop of accumulation for another; the clock itself is neutral, and time is what the human being is made of.

There is a mercy folded into this verse that its words do not advertise. Al-Ḥijr and Ṣād report the same exchange, and there the answer adds a refinement: the respite runs *“until the appointed Day”* (15:38; 38:81) — the known time whose knowledge belongs to God alone, not the Day of Resurrection as such. The Qur'an leaves that ambiguity in place, and the effect is instructive. No one — not the believer, not the rebel, not the one who asks for time — ever knows how much time he has. Every term is fixed, as the sūrah itself will state later: *“For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it”* (7:34; see also 10:49; 63:11).

The verse thus hands the reader the one thing that no creature can negotiate. Iblīs was given his extension because the trial required it; the human being is given his days for the same reason. The difference is what the two build with them.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:15

> **Allah said, “You are delayed ˹until the appointed Day˺.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Bare Answer to a Large Request**

The answer is a single sentence, without a rebuke attached and without a condition: *innaka min al-munẓarīn* — you are delayed ˹until the appointed Day˺, one of those granted respite. In the other accounts of this exchange the granting is given with the same economy, and in al-Ḥijr and Ṣād it is completed by the clause *“until the appointed Day”* (15:37–38; 38:80–81).

The brevity deserves attention because of what it does not contain. No lecture follows, no warning, no invitation to reconsider. The request is granted as stated. This is the Qur'an's way of teaching the difference between guidance and coercion: God's will is that creatures act freely, and freedom has a cost that the divine government does not suppress. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the respite was granted because the trial of humanity required a tempter who is present — the human being is being tested with his eyes open, not trapped.

**"Delayed Until the Appointed Day"**

The phrasing is partitive: *min al-munẓarīn*, *among* the deferred, a member of a class. Iblīs is not handed a unique exemption; he is enrolled in a standing law. Everything mortal lives on borrowed time: *“No soul can ever die without Allah's Will at the destined time”* (3:145); *“For each community there is an appointed term”* (7:34); *“Allah never delays a soul when its appointed time comes”* (63:11). The indefinite plural is the point. He had asked to be made an exception to the general rule of ends; the answer tells him that he has been given a longer rope, not a different rope.

It is worth pausing on the subtlety the grammarians saw in the construction. Had the verse said *you are deferred* without the partitive, the sentence would still have been true; the addition of *min* places him inside a category shared by all creatures whose terms are set. The proudest being in the story is told, in the very sentence that grants his wish, that he is one of a crowd.

**The Delay That Builds Two Different Men**

The Qur'an treats delay as a moral substance, and it divides its users. For the wrongdoer it is accumulation: *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin”* (3:178). For the rebellious community it is a trap that feels like kindness: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise”* (6:44). And against that, the same delay is the space in which a person returns: *“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ ‘O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy”* (39:53).

The three verses describe one clock with three faces. Iblīs' respite produced a strategy against humanity (vv. 16–17). A human being's respite can produce either the same ruthless accumulation or the quiet correction of a life. Nothing in the calendar tells the difference; only the use does.

**istidrāj: The Respite That Looks Like Generosity**

Arabic gives this delay a technical name, and the Qur'an builds a doctrine on it. *Istidrāj* is the drawing-on of a person stage by stage, so that he is led further while believing he is being blessed. *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend.”* (68:44), and the verse that follows seals it: *“I only delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”* (68:45). The sūrah of the Heights says the same thing in its own voice: *“I only delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”* (7:183), immediately after describing those who reject the signs and are given increase.

The psychological mechanism is what makes the doctrine so uncomfortable, and the Qur'an states it without softening: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired”* (6:44). The gifts keep arriving; the warnings stop feeling urgent; the recipient concludes that the silence of heaven is approval. This is why the Qur'an repeatedly forbids the interpretation of prosperity as a verdict — the wealthy denier's comfort is not a certificate, and the sufferer's hardship is not a sentence. The delay granted to Iblīs, extended to the end of time, is the purest case of *istidrāj* in the Book: an unlimited opportunity, mistaken for an endorsement.

**The Appointed Day and the Hidden Hour**

The specification in the parallel accounts — *“until the appointed Day”* — has occupied the commentators. Some take it as the Day of Resurrection, which is what Iblīs had asked for in 7:14; others read it as the end of the world as it is known, the first blast at which all things die, the moment after which only God remains. Al-Ṭabarī records both positions and their chains. What the disagreement reveals is a deliberate silence in the text: the term is *known* — fixed, recorded, unpostponable — and *unknown* to the creature who holds it. That combination is the structure of human responsibility. If the hour were known, the life before it would become a countdown, and virtue would be arithmetic; if no hour existed, nothing would carry consequence.

The verse therefore does two things at once. It answers Iblīs with a grant, and it answers every reader with a warning, using the same words. Whatever one is building, the permission to keep building has a ceiling. The creature who asked for the extension believed he had obtained a room to work in; the sūrah's later verses will show what he built in it — an ambush on the road to God — and will also show, in the same sūrah, what the refuge from that ambush is: *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”* (7:200).

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:16

> **He said, “For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Causal Clause: "For Leaving Me to Stray"**

Iblīs' first act with his new lease is to file an appeal, and its argument is that the fault is God's. *Bi-mā aghwaytanī* — *for leaving me to stray*. The Arabic causal *mā* makes the sentence a claim of cause and effect: my deviation is traced to its author, and the sentence that follows is presented as the natural consequence of it.

Two things must be said about this clause, and the sūrah says both by placing it as it does. The first is that the Qur'an reports the words of its characters without adopting them. Iblīs' theology is his own, and the Book records it as evidence against him, not as doctrine. The second is that the Qur'an elsewhere defines what God's *causing to stray* means, and it never means what Iblīs wants it to mean. *“He leaves none to stray except the rebellious”* (2:26) — the straying is the consequence of a settled character, not an injection into an innocent one. *“So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate”* (61:5) — the deviation of the heart follows a prior deviation of the will. The Book's law of recompense runs in kind: a person who leans away is let lean.

Al-Rāzī draws out the difference with care. There is a *straying* that God decrees as a trial and a *straying* that He decrees as a punishment, and both are consequences interior to a path the creature has chosen, not replacements for the creature's choice. Iblīs, facing the results of his own refusal, describes them in the passive voice of another's agency. The sūrah lets the reader see the maneuver for what it is: the first blame-shift in the moral history of the universe.

**The Two Who Took the Blame**

The counter-text sits a few verses away. When Adam and Eve broke the command, they said: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves”* (7:23). Two creatures, two falls, two grammars: one sentence pushes the fault upward and outward, the other keeps it where the act was performed.

This is why the Adam narrative in the Qur'an is a story about hope and the Iblīs narrative is a story about ruin — not because their acts differed in magnitude, but because their confessions differed in direction. Islam's whole science of repentance is built on the second grammar. The Prophet ﷺ described the returning servant in the terms of that sentence: a man who says, *My Lord, forgive me my sin*, and is answered by a God who says, *My servant committed a sin and then came to know that he has a Lord who forgives the sin and takes account of it* — and at the third turning, *do what you like, I have forgiven you* (Muslim 2758, from Abū Hurayrah). The clause in this verse is the anti-model of every such prayer.

**The Ambush on the Road**

Then the vow: *la-aqʿudanna lahum ṣirāṭaka al-mustaqīm* — I shall surely *sit* for them on Your straight path. The verb *qaʿada* gives the picture of a seated watcher, a highwayman at his post; the emphatic *nūn* of *la-aqʿudanna* matches the certainty of the divine oaths, as though the creature were claiming the same decisiveness for his vendetta. The translations render it "lie in wait," and that is the sense: not a direct assault but an interception.

The target he names is startling. He does not say "the path of the believers" or "their road"; he says *Your* straight path — the road God made, claimed, and commanded. The audacity is the doctrine. The enemy of humanity does not deny that the road exists or that it leads to God; he stations himself on it, because that is where the travelers are. The sūrah's image of the road recurs throughout the Book — *“Indeed, that is My Path — perfectly straight. So follow it”* (6:153); the Fātiḥah's central petition — and the ambush explains why the petition asks not only for the road but for guidance upon it, in the company of those who walked it.

**The Exception He Cannot Breach**

The other accounts complete the vow with a limit Iblīs was forced to concede: *“except Your chosen servants among them”* (15:40; 38:83). And the Qur'an states the boundary as a standing law: *“you will certainly have no authority over My servants, except the deviant who follow you”* (15:42); *“He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord”* (16:99); *“You will truly have no authority over My faithful servants”* (17:65). Even the permission given to the tester is bounded by the freedom of the tested. His weapon is suggestion (*waswasah*), and suggestion works only on a will that agrees with it.

That is why the sūrah's own remedy is not a wall or a weapon but a turning: *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah”* (7:200); and the verse that follows it describes the escape precisely — *“when Satan whispers to those mindful of Allah, they remember their Lord, then they start to see things clearly”* (7:201). The ambush in 7:16 is real. So is the road's protection, and the protection is that the traveler keeps looking at where he is going.

The Book's readers are meant to notice the difference between the two confessions: Iblīs attributes his ruin to God, while Adam and Eve attribute theirs to themselves. The sūrah places the two sentences a few verses apart, and the contrast is the whole doctrine of responsibility in miniature.

The sūrah's reader is thus given the sequence in its true order: the sign is presented, the heart turns, and the turning is then confirmed in the heart's own condition. The Book's narratives of the towns and of Israel all illustrate the same progression, and the verse's statement about deviating first and being made to deviate afterwards is its clearest formulation.


**My Path, Perfectly Straight**

The verse names the object of the ambush: *“For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”* (7:16). The path is described as God’s, and al-Anʿām describes the same path as a single one against many: *“Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight. So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”* (6:153).

The verse supplies what makes the ambush intelligible. A single path can be watched; many cannot. 6:153’s warning about other ways is therefore not a warning about alternatives to a road but about leaving the one road on which a person can be stopped. The enemy’s position is described in the same terms as the command to the believer — a path, and a direction.

The exegetes read 7:16 as the reason the path is named straight. Straightness here is not simplicity but singularity: there is one, it is identifiable, and it is where the ambush is set. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the sūrah forbids the same practice to people two thirds of the way through, at 7:86, using the image of sitting on a road.


**Trust as the Ground of the Exception**

The verse states an intention; an-Naḥl states its limit. *“He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.”* (16:99). The next verse defines the authority that remains: *“His authority is only over those who take him as a patron and who—under his influence—associate ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺.”* (16:100).

The two verses make authority depend on a relation rather than on strength. The enemy has no standing over the believer who relies on God, and his standing over others is described as patronage accepted — *yatawallawnahu*, taking him as a protector. What he can do is what a patron is allowed to do by the one who takes him.

This is the ground on which 7:16 can be read as a declaration rather than as a threat. The ambush is set on the path, and the sūrah’s answer is not that the path is cleared but that the one who walks it in reliance is outside the ambusher’s jurisdiction. 7:200 states the same position as an instruction to the individual: seek refuge when the goading touches you.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:17

> **I will approach them from their front, their back, their right, their left, and then You will find most of them ungrateful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Four Approaches and One Road**

The vow begun in the previous verse is now diagrammed. Iblīs announces that he will come at humanity from four quarters: *min bayni aydīhim* — from their front; *wa-min khalfihim* — their back; *wa-ʿan aymānihim* — their right; *wa-ʿan shamāʾilihim* — their left. The picture is of encirclement. He is not promising a single temptation but a surrounding, an approach from whichever side the traveler leaves unguarded.

The verse therefore explains the practical shape of the trial that the previous verses set up. A test conducted by frontal assault would be easy to recognize and easy to repel; a test that arrives from four directions at once means that the danger is rarely where a person is looking. The sūrah's later remedy fits this image exactly — the refuge is not a fortification on one flank but a turning to God from any flank: *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah”* (7:200).

**What the Commentators Read into the Directions**

The classical exegetes, beginning with reports traced to Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ṭabarī, treated the four directions as a map of the ways a person is assailed, and their readings are worth recording because they have worn well.

From *in front*, they said, comes the temptation of the future: doubt about what lies ahead, the promise that there will be time later, the fear of what one may lose by obeying now. From *behind* comes the weight of what is past: inherited custom, the practice of ancestors, the argument that no one in one's family ever did this, the guilt that says the record is already too spoiled to repair. From the *right* comes corruption of religion itself: excess, self-satisfaction, the transformation of worship into display, the confidence of the person who is certain he is among the saved. From the *left* comes the pull of appetite: the open sins, the small indulgences, the countless daily permissions.

The classifications differ between al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and Ibn Kathīr in their details, and the differences are useful. They show that the exegetes did not treat the four directions as a code to be decoded but as a comprehensive figure: the whole perimeter of a human life. The enemy's claim is total, and the commentators' fourfold reading is simply an acknowledgment that the claim is not obviously false.

**The Directions He Did Not Name**

A widely transmitted observation, reported from Ibn ʿAbbās in the commentary literature, notes that Iblīs named four directions and left out two: he did not say he would come from above or from below. The explanation offered is that from above comes mercy, and from below comes the humility of the servant in prostration — the two postures the rebel cannot occupy.

The point should be held with a light hand. It is an exegetical insight rather than a revealed datum; the verse says what it says, and its silence about two directions is suggestive rather than dogmatic. But the suggestion is consistent with everything else the sūrah has established. The arrogant creature was ruined by refusing to lower himself, and the remedy for those he attacks is the very thing he would not do: to bow. The unguarded quadrant of the human being is not a blind spot in space but a missing posture in the soul.

**The Siege and Its Psychology**

The Prophet ﷺ described the siege from the inside, as a condition of every human life: *“Each one of you has a devil-companion from the jinn over him.”* When the companions asked whether this included him, he answered: *“Even me, yet Allah helped me against him until he submitted; he does not order me to do anything but good.”* (Muslim 2814, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd).

Two lessons follow from that report, and both answer this verse. The first is that the presence of the whisperer is not a sign of divine abandonment; it is the human condition, the same condition under which the Prophet ﷺ lived. The second is that the companion can be reduced to a whisperer who no longer commands — *“he does not order me to do anything but good”* — by help that comes from God. The four-sided approach of Iblīs is real; so is the possibility that a man reaches a state in which the approaches no longer find an entrance.

**His Verdict on Humanity — and the Remnant**

The verse closes with the enemy's own summary of the human race: *“and then You will find most of them ungrateful.”* The clause is an echo, and the sūrah intends it. Verse 10 had already told humanity the same thing in God's own words — *˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks!* — and there the diagnosis stood as a charge against the ungrateful. Here the same charge appears in the mouth of the accuser, which is the sharpest possible way of stating it: the ingratitude is the entry point he is counting on.

The Qur'an confirms the statistic without confirming his conclusion. *“Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most of them are ungrateful”* (10:60; see also 27:73; 16:83) — and the same Book says of the divine bounty that it reaches the grateful and the ungrateful alike, since *“He has granted you all that you asked Him for”* (14:34). The word *most* is where the hope lives. The enemy's sentence leaves a remainder, and the remainder is the company he himself was forced to acknowledge and exclude from his reach: *“except Your chosen servants among them”* (15:40; 38:83). Gratitude, in this sūrah's architecture, is not a virtue added to faith. It is the door the ambush was designed to block, and the shield that shuts it is a single remembered favour at the right moment.


**Sitting in Wait on the Straight Path**

The verse before this one contains Iblīs’s first declaration: *“For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”* (7:16). 7:17 then lists four directions from which he will come. The two verses describe the same operation from two positions — stationary and mobile — and the sūrah’s own prohibition names the first of them.

For the sūrah has already forbidden exactly this practice, in its account of Shuʿayb: *“And do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked.”* (7:86). The same phrase — lying in ambush on a road — is used of the enemy at 7:16 and of the corrupters of Midian at 7:86. The Book thus reports the practice as both the method of Iblīs and the method of the men who cut the roads, and forbids it to the believers in the same sūrah.


**The Proclamation That Answers the Forecast**

The verse ends with Iblīs’s forecast: *“and then You will find most of them ungrateful.”* (7:17). It is a prediction about *shukr*, from the root *sh-k-r*, which means to acknowledge a favour by using it as it was given and by naming the giver. Ingratitude in the Qurʾān is not primarily a feeling but a use: the favour received and then spent against its giver, or spent without his name.

The sūrah tests the prediction in its own histories, and the test is documented rather than asserted. Every town given a sign responds with denial; every people given respite responds with security; the sūrah’s summary of the pattern is that the few who were grateful were the remnant (7:10). Sabaʾ records the same estimate inside God’s charge to the family of David — *“˹Only˺ a few of My servants are ˹truly˺ grateful.”* (34:13) — and it is the reason the prediction is not treated as a boast in the exegetical tradition but as a statement of fact.

The counter-statement is also in the sūrah. *“And remember when your Lord proclaimed, ‘If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.’”* (14:7). The proclamation answers the prediction by making gratitude a matter of increase rather than of numbers: what Iblīs forecast about the majority is true, and what the proclamation offers is available to anyone who performs it. 7:17 therefore states the enemy’s expectation and leaves the sūrah’s readers with the verse that defeats it.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:18

> **Allah said, “Get out of Paradise! You are disgraced and rejected! I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Expulsion, Sharper Than the First**

The sūrah contains two removal commands addressed to Iblīs, and the commentators read them as the two halves of one sentence. The first was *ihbiṭ* — get down (7:13), spoken in answer to his arrogance; the second is *ukhruj* — go forth (here), spoken after he has declared his plan to besiege humanity. The first removed him from the place in which the transgression occurred. The second confirms the state: *ukhruj minhā* — out of it, and out of the rank that went with it.

Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr note the deepening: in the first command he is told to descend; in the second, after the vow of verse 16 and the four-sided siege of verse 17, he is told to leave and is given two descriptions that settle what he now is. The sentence does not grow because God's anger grows — the divine judgment does not fluctuate — but because the accused has now declared himself. He was given the chance to say nothing further; he used the opportunity to pronounce a war.

**madhʾūman and madḥūran: Two Roots, One Verdict**

The two words are precise, and the older commentary in this file garbled them; stated correctly, they are *madhʾūman* and *madḥūran*.

*Madhʾūm* comes from the root *dh-ʾ-m*, which carries the sense of a driven-away disgrace, the foul reproach that attaches to one who has forfeited standing. *Madḥūr* comes from *d-ḥ-r*, to repel with force, to drive off violently — the root used of scattering an enemy. Together they describe an inside and an outside: the honor is stripped, and the person is expelled. Because both words are passive participles, the construction also says who did it. He is not merely disgraced as a condition and banished as an event; he is disgraced and banished *by the sentence of another*. The creature who claimed autonomous greatness ends the exchange as the object of two verbs he did not choose.

The mirror with his own crime is exact. He had made himself great in his own estimation (*ana khayrun minhu*, 7:12) and had refused to be moved by a command; the sentence accordingly reduces him and moves him by force. The rule the sūrah keeps demonstrating is that God answers self-exaltation with reduction, and refusal with expulsion.

**The Oath of the Filling**

*La-amlaʾanna jahannama minkum ajmaʿīn* — I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together. The first-person oath-pronoun is God's, and the same declaration is repeated at three other places in the Book: *“I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together”* (11:119); *“My Word will come to pass: I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together”* (32:13); and the address to Iblīs, *“I will surely fill up Hell with you and whoever follows you from among them, all together”* (38:85).

The repetition has drawn theological commentary for centuries, and the commentators have been careful about what it does and does not mean. It does not describe a deficiency that creatures must supply, as though the Fire were a container awaiting its quota. Sūrat al-Sajdah states the logic explicitly: *“Had We willed, We could have easily imposed guidance on every soul. But My Word will come to pass”* (32:13). The filling is the consequence of a world created with genuine choice — a world in which guidance is offered and can be refused. The declaration is therefore a statement about the realism of the test: God does not pretend that everyone will pass.

The sūrah also states the population of that sentence with precision in the verse following al-Ḥijr's parallel: *“and surely Hell is their destined place, all together. It has seven gates, to each a group of them is designated”* (15:43–44). The imagery of gates and groups is not a decoration of the threat; it is a refusal to describe the Fire as a mass. Those who enter are not a crowd but named categories of a chosen road.

**"Whoever Follows You" — the Condition That Keeps It Just**

The threat is conditional, and the condition is doing the work: *man ittabaʿaka minhum* — literally, *whoever among them follows you*; the translation names them simply as *your followers*. What is threatened is not humanity but the *following*. The Qur'an states the same boundary as a law of the enemy's power: he has *no authority* over the sincere (15:42; 16:99; 17:65), and his capacity to lead is itself part of the test — *“He does not have any authority over them, but Our Will is only to distinguish those who believe in the Hereafter from those who are in doubt about it”* (34:21). The tempter tempts; he does not compel. A man who enters the Fire has walked there, however subtly the walking was arranged.

**Mercy Standing at the Door of the Next Verse**

It is important to notice the sequence of the sūrah after this sentence. The very next verses return to Adam, and they end with forgiveness: *“Then Adam was inspired with words of prayer by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”* (2:37; see also 7:23). The banishment of Iblīs is followed immediately by the pardon of the human being, and the juxtaposition is the sūrah's message in miniature. The same mercy that God declared to Moses in this very sūrah — *“But My mercy encompasses everything.”* (7:156) — stands open to the descendants of Adam, while the one who refused to ask for it stands outside. The chapter that begins its narrative with the most final-sounding verdict in the Book ends its narrative with a returning man forgiven, and the reader is placed between the two doors.


**The Word That Fills: Hell and Its Two Sources**

The verse’s threat is an oath in the emphatic form: *la-amlaʾanna jahannam* — *“I will certainly fill up Hell”* (7:18). The verb *malaʾa* means to fill a vessel to capacity, and the noun of the oath carries the doubled emphasis of the *nūn* of confirmation. What is sworn is not a punishment but a fullness: the vessel will not be left partly empty.

Alif-Lām-Mīm as-Sajdah gives the same oath with its sources named: *“Had We willed, We could have easily imposed guidance on every soul. But My Word will come to pass: I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together.”* (32:13). The verse adds the clause that 7:18 leaves implicit — that the filling is compatible with a guidance God could have imposed on everyone — and it names both orders of creature, the jinn to whom Iblīs belongs and the humans who follow him.

Read with 32:13 the oath at 7:18 is not a threat against a particular group but a statement about the outcome of a choice that both orders share


**Disgraced and Rejected, and the Followers Named**

The two passives describe a status: *madhʾūman*, blamed and held in contempt, from *dhaʾama*; *madḥūran*, banished and driven away, from *daḥara*. Neither is a description of feeling. The sūrah has already recorded the reason — the refusal to prostrate and the claim of superiority (7:12) — and the two words are its consequence stated as a condition.

The verse then names who shares it: *“I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together.”* (7:18). The Book describes those followers elsewhere as more than human: *“And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception.”* (6:112). The verse explains the mechanism by which a refusal becomes a following — decorative speech passed between two kinds of creature — and it makes the same point 32:13 makes by naming both orders.

The sūrah’s own account of the following is more precise still: at 7:20 it records that the whispering was addressed to a pair, and at 7:27 that the devils see the people from where they cannot be seen. 7:18 therefore states the end of a chain the sūrah describes link by link — a refusal, a whisper, a following, and a filling that includes both.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:19

> **˹Allah said,˺ “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat from wherever you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Generosity of the Command**

The narrative returns to Adam with a command that is almost all permission. *Uskun* — dwell, take up residence — and then *fa-kulā min ḥaythu shiʾtumā*: eat from wherever the two of you wish. The Qur'an's fuller account in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā fills in what the permission covers: *“Here it is guaranteed that you will never go hungry or unclothed, nor will you ˹ever˺ suffer from thirst or ˹the sun's˺ heat”* (20:118–119). Food, clothing, water, shade — the four anxieties that organize most human labor — are declared settled in advance. The Garden is presented not as a reward to be earned but as a home to be inhabited, and the single prohibition is set inside a field of open permissions.

**One Tree, Deliberately Unnamed**

*Wa-lā taqrabā hādhihi al-shajarah* — and do not come near this tree. Two details of the wording carry the teaching. The first is *lā taqrabā*, do not approach, rather than *lā taʾkulā*, do not eat. The Qur'an uses the same construction for adultery — *“Do not go near adultery”* (17:32) — and for the orphan's property — *“do not come near the wealth of the orphan”* (6:152). The prohibition is a fence placed around the act, not merely a line at the act itself, and the jurisprudence of *sadd al-dharāʾiʿ* — blocking the pathways to what is forbidden — is read by the jurists out of exactly this idiom.

The second detail is that the tree is never identified. The commentators hold that God withheld the name deliberately. Al-Ṭabarī records statements to the effect that it was a fig or a vine or another fruit, and then notes that no report is authoritative and none is needed; Ibn Kathīr draws the conclusion that disputing about the species is time spent on what the verse chose to leave open. The purpose of the prohibition was never information about botany. It was obedience: a single, unmistakable boundary in the middle of an unlimited gift, so that the creature's freedom would have somewhere to be exercised.

**Both of Them, and the Silence About Hawwāʾ**

The verse addresses the pair: *dwell, you and your wife* — and the wife is not named anywhere in the Qur'an. The Book has kept her identity from the text, though the commentators transmit the name Hawwāʾ from the older reports.

That silence is worth noticing, because of what the surrounding verses do with the pair. In 7:20–22 the tempter addresses *them*, both of them act, and both are exposed together. The Qur'an never assigns the first initiative to the woman. Where the older scriptural narrative presents a sequence in which the woman is deceived and then leads the man, this sūrah presents a single act of two people, and the responsibility is shared and equal: *“Then their Lord called out to them, ‘Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?’”* The point matters because a long tradition of misogynist preaching has drawn from the story a doctrine of female culpability for the first sin. The Qur'an's own text does not support it, and the careful reader of this verse has already been given the corrective: the warning was addressed to both, the command was given to both, and the failure was theirs together.

**The Anatomy of a Test**

Set within the sūrah's architecture, the verse completes the scene the reader has been prepared for. Verses 11 to 18 showed a creature who refused a command and lost everything by refusing it. Here a different creature receives a command to hold the boundary, and inside the permission there is freedom to move, to eat, to enjoy. What is being tested is not appetite — the appetite is licensed — but trust: whether the word of God about a tree will be believed over the apparent silence of everything else.

The final clause names the cost of the failure before it happens: *fa-takūnā min al-ẓālimīn* — lest you two become of the wrongdoers. It is the same word the townspeople of verse 5 used of themselves at the moment of destruction, and the same word that will reappear in Adam's own confession at verse 23. The sūrah is teaching its vocabulary as it goes: the *ẓulm* of the first verses is a misplacement, and a creature who places his own judgment above a command has displaced himself from where he was put.

**Law and Mercy in One Verse**

The theological weight of the passage sits in the coexistence of the two facts it announces at once. There is a command that must be obeyed, and there is a garden wide enough that disobeying it is never necessary. The boundary is narrow; the room around it is vast. Rabbinic and Christian traditions later built elaborate doctrines of a fallen nature on the first act; the Islamic reading, formed by these verses, insists on something more precise. The human being was created with a real capacity to obey — the permission was genuine, and no one was placed in a trap — and the same human being was created with a real capacity to fall, because a creature whose obedience was automatic would not be a moral being at all.

The rest of the sūrah will show what happens when the boundary is crossed — the exposure, the shame, the sewing of leaves, the searching call of God in the Garden — and how a creature who has fallen is to answer. But the verse's own balance should be preserved before the story moves on: the command that will be broken was given by a Lord who had first spread a table.


**The Command in al-Baqarah and Ṭā Hā**

The command is given twice elsewhere with different emphases. Sūrah al-Baqarah states it in almost the same words: *“O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”* (2:35). Sūrah Ṭā Hā states the provision in terms of the four needs it meets: *“Here it is guaranteed that you will never go hungry or unclothed,”* (20:118), *“nor will you ˹ever˺ suffer from thirst or ˹the sun’s˺ heat.”* (20:119).

The three accounts agree on the shape of the arrangement: a residence, an unrestricted permission, and one prohibition. They differ in what they enumerate. Al-Baqarah names the permission to eat; Ṭā Hā itemises the guarantee against hunger, nakedness, thirst and exposure; this verse combines residence and eating and adds the phrase *wherever you please*, which is the widest form of the permission in the three. The sūrah is therefore the most generous of the accounts in its statement of what was allowed, and that generosity is what makes the single prohibition legible as a test rather than as a restriction.


**Approach, Not Eating**

The prohibition is on approaching the tree rather than on eating from it, and the verb is the Book’s standard verb for fencing a matter off. The same verb prohibits the act the sūrah will later name among the forbidden things: *“Do not go near adultery. It is truly a shameful deed and an evil way.”* (17:32). The prohibition of adultery is not phrased as a prohibition of the act but of the road to it.

That phrasing is what makes the command in this verse a discipline rather than a rule. The tree is one object among an unrestricted permission, and the forbidden thing is the movement toward it — the approach, which begins long before the eating. The commentators read the sūrah’s account of the fall in that light: the tempter works on the approach, offering a name for the tree and a reason to draw near, and the eating is the last step in a sequence the prohibition had already addressed. The verse that follows this one in the sūrah reports what the whisper did, and it reports it as a sequence of approaches rather than as a single act.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:20

> **Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, “Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Whisper: A Method, Not an Announcement**

The previous episode showed the tempter declaring war openly — the vow to sit in ambush on the straight path (7:16), the four-sided approach (7:17). Here he changes his register entirely. *Fa-waswasa lahumā al-shayṭān*: he whispered to them. The Arabic *waswasah* names a sound at the edge of hearing — the rustle of a garment, a step half-made, the murmur that a person cannot quite attribute to anyone. The word is used in the Qur'an for the work of *al-waswās al-khannās*, the retreating whisperer who works in the breast (114:4–5).

The choice of verb is diagnostic. The enemy who has been defeated in argument does not return with a better argument; he returns with a method that does not require an audience. He does not say, "I am the one who refused to prostrate." He speaks in the mode of an inner suggestion, so that the thought can be mistaken for the person's own.

**The Aim: Exposure**

The verse names the tempter's objective with uncomfortable precision: *li-yubdiya lahumā mā wūriya ʿanhumā min sawʾātihimā* — in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. The purpose was not the fruit. The fruit was the instrument; the exposure was the goal.

The psychology here has been noted by the commentators, and it is the reason this verse functions as a warning rather than a chronicle. Shame in the Qur'an's account is not a moral invention imposed from outside; it is the response of a creature to a covering that has been withdrawn. The covering in the Garden — before any transgression — was *wūriya*, hidden and concealed, a condition of dignity given rather than created. What the whisperer wants is the collapse of that condition, and he is willing to use anything at hand to bring it about. Whatever the particular tree was, the mechanism was the same as it is in every generation: a lawful thing in itself, offered on a condition that only God has the authority to require.

**Two Promises: Transcendence and Permanence**

His argument is preserved in the fuller account: *“Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?”* (20:120). Here it is given in its compressed form: your Lord has forbidden you this tree *“Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, ‘Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.’”* (7:20).

The two lures are chosen with a craftsman's knowledge of the human interior. The first appeals to the desire to rise — to be more than one is, to occupy a larger station. That is the hunger that destroyed Iblīs himself in verse 12, and it is now offered to Adam as the reason for the prohibition. The second appeals to the desire not to lose — immortality, *khuld*, the refusal of the horizon that makes a creature a creature. Between them, they cover the two directions in which human longing runs: upward, and backward from death.

The claim about God is its own offense. *Mā naha-kumā rabbukumā ʿan hādhihi al-shajarah illā an takūnā malakayn* — the prohibition is made to appear a restriction on human advancement, an act of divine jealousy rather than of care. This is the tempter's oldest strategy and his most durable one: not "God has forbidden nothing," but "God has forbidden this for a reason that is not to your advantage." The sūrah will deal with that accusation directly in the next verses, and the answer is not a rebuttal but an outcome.

**Suggestion and Consent**

The Islamic account of temptation that this verse anchors was given its classic shape in a single image from the Prophet ﷺ, recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: *“Satan circulates in the body of man like the circulation of blood”* (Muslim 2175; the same report appears in al-Bukhārī 3281, both from Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy). The image is precise in what it does and does not claim. It claims nearness and passage — the whisper has no distance to cross. It does not claim compulsion.

The Qur'an's distribution of responsibility follows the image exactly. Adam is blamed for his act and named as the one who forgot (20:115) and disobeyed (20:121). Satan is blamed for the deception. No verse of the Book permits a human being to say that the whisperer is the reason he fell. The whisper is not obedience; it borrows a voice that sounds like one's own, and the sūrah teaches its reader to recognize the accent now, before the story reaches the exposure, because after the exposure it is always too late to say that the suggestion was never recognized as foreign.

**The First Crack in the Cover**

The verse's final clause is where Christian and Islamic readings part, and the parting deserves to be stated plainly. What the Qur'an records is an act, its motive, and its loss — not a transmitted condition that propagates through the species. The Book will say in Sūrah al-Zumar that *no soul bears the burden of another* (6:164; 39:7), and in al-Najm that *the human being has only what he strives for* (53:39). Adam's descendants inherit the circumstances of his life — the earth, the term, the enemy — but not his guilt.

What the verse does hand on, though, is the outline of a permanent risk. The whisper comes to a creature who is already provided for, already clothed, already placed; the suggestion is not hunger, but ambition; the weapon is not the fruit but a claim about the One who prohibited it. Every later verse of this sūrah about eating and drinking, about clothing and about the temptation of excess (vv. 26–32) is a reworking of the same scene, because the sūrah's original audience knew precisely the danger: a litany of permissions, one unidentified boundary, and a voice suggesting that the boundary was never meant for their good.


**Clothing Provided Before the Whisper**

The whisper’s aim is stated in the verse’s first clause: to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. The sūrah has already described what covered it: *“O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness.”* (7:26).

The verse distinguishes two functions of clothing — covering and adornment — and then names a third thing that deserves the word better. Read against 7:20, the exposure the enemy intends is the removal of the first function, and the sūrah’s own answer is that the covering that matters is not the one that can be removed.

The placement of 7:26 is deliberate. It stands inside the sūrah’s address to the children of Ādam, before the histories begin, and it describes a provision already made. The whisper at 7:20 therefore operates against a background of provision, which is why the sūrah can describe its aim as exposure of something hidden rather than as the creation of a new shame.


**The Garden’s Terms**

The verse reports a prohibition attributed to a motive. Al-Baqarah records the terms as they were given: *“O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”* (2:35).

The three terms are a dwelling, an open permission, and one exception with its consequence named. Nothing in them suggests a motive for the exception beyond the warning attached to it — *fa-takūnā min al-ẓālimīn*, or else you will be wrongdoers. The whisper at 7:20 supplies the missing motive by inventing one: that the tree was withheld in order to withhold something else.

This is the shape of the deception and the reason the sūrah reports it in the enemy’s own words. The permission was general and the exception was single; the whisper reverses the proportion, presenting the prohibition as the substance of the arrangement and the permission as incidental. 2:35 stands as the record against which the reversal can be seen.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:21

> **And he swore to them, “I am truly your sincere advisor.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Perjured Oath**

*Wa-qāsamahumā* — and he swore to them. The verb is from *qasam*, the oath, and it is chosen for its weight in a society where an oath was the ultimate instrument of trust. The tempter had no standing to be believed on his word, so he manufactured standing by appealing to the one thing the Arabs of the sūrah's audience treated as beyond manipulation: the sworn word.

The commentators note the formal completeness of the deception. He did not assert; he promised. He did not persuade with evidence; he offered a guarantee. And in doing so he produced the first false oath in the moral history of the creation — a detail the sūrah does not dwell on but the reader should notice, because the Book will later make oath-taking by the divine name a matter of severe account: *“Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good”* (2:224), and *“those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter”* (3:77). The ancestor of all swearing-away of the truth is the oath of Iblīs.

**The Theft of a Religious Word**

The claim itself is a single phrase: *innī lakumā la-min al-nāṣiḥīn* — surely I am to you two among the sincere advisers. *Nāṣiḥ* comes from *n-ṣ-ḥ*, the root of purity and of counsel: the sincere advice that seeks the good of the one advised and nothing else. The emphasis is piled on, with both the *inna* and the *lām* of asseveration.

The word is not accidental; the sūrah has been using it of the prophets. Each of the five messengers of Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ opens with the same claim: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you”* (26:107; 26:125; 26:143; 26:162; 26:178), and the sūrah's own messengers speak in the same register: *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor”* (7:68), *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice”* (7:62), and the farewell Shuʿayb addresses to his people, *“I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”* (7:93). The tempter takes the signature phrase of the prophetic office and wears it. This is a deliberate arrangement by the sūrah: it teaches the reader that the counterfeit of a category is not the absence of that category but its imitation, and that the imitation will sound exactly like the original.

**Why the Voice Cannot Be the Criterion**

The verse's practical force lies here. A person cannot verify sincerity by tone; the perjurer is often warmer than the truthful man, and the Qur'an says so of the very people who oppose religion: *“When you see them, their appearance impresses you. And when they speak, you listen to their ˹impressive˺ speech.”* (63:4). The Book, therefore, refuses to make sincerity self-authenticating. It gives criteria outside the speaker's delivery.

The first criterion is verification. *“O believers, if an evildoer brings you any news, verify ˹it˺ so you do not harm people unknowingly, becoming regretful for what you have done.”* (49:6). The instruction is general and applies to counsel as much as to news: the weight of a claim is not established by the confidence of the claimant. The second criterion is the content's relation to God's command. The tempter's speech was sweet and its content was permission to cross a boundary. Where counsel trends toward the loosening of what God has legislated, the *nāṣiḥ* label becomes evidence against the speaker, whatever the timbre of his concern. The third criterion is outcome, which is precisely what the next verses provide — and the sūrah intends that the lesson be learned from the outcome rather than repeated.

**The Guardian's Warning Against Words Alone**

The Prophet ﷺ trained his community to distinguish the surface from the substance in this very area.
