He warned of those whose speech would be more pleasing than it deserved and whose piety would be of the tongue; he described a people who would recite the Qur'an but whose recitation would not pass their throats (al-Bukhārī 3344; Muslim 1064, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, of the Khawārij). The warning is about sincerity of a specific kind: words that borrow the authority of religion while serving something other than God.

There is a further layer for the reader of this sūrah. The oath of 7:21 was sworn to two people who had no reason to distrust the speaker, because they had never met a lie. The human race has no such excuse. We have the record of the first deception, and the record of every deception it fathered. The verse therefore functions as a vaccination: it introduces the pattern of the counterfeit adviser early, at the first opportunity, so that a person encountering the same voice in a marketplace, a classroom, a screen, or his own private reasoning will recognize what he is hearing before he acts on it.

**The Sincerity That Keeps Its Address**

One further note belongs here, because it is the difference between the tempter's *nāṣiḥ* and the prophets' *nāṣiḥ*. The messengers of this sūrah never demand to be trusted for their own sake; each of them says, in the same breath, *“I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:109; 26:127; 26:145; 26:164; 26:180). Sincere counsel in the Qur'anic sense is counsel that can name where it is going — to the commanded good, and to God. The oath of the tempter names nothing beyond itself. The safest question a person can put to any adviser, including the advice that rises inside his own chest, is the one this verse leaves unspoken but answers: toward whose good does this counsel actually point?

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:22

> **So he brought about their fall through deception. And when they tasted of the tree, their nakedness was exposed to them, prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise. Then their Lord called out to them, “Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Descent into Delusion**

*Fa-dallāhumā bi-ghurūr* — so he brought them down by delusion. The verb *dallā* is the transitive of *tadallā*, to hang down, to let a cord out gradually; the picture is of lowering something by degrees. Beside it stands *ghurūr*, the noun of deception, formed from the same root the Qur'an uses for the deceitful world (*al-ghurūr*) and for the delusion of the one who trusts it — *“So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah.”* (31:33; 35:5).

The two words together describe a mechanism rather than a moment. Adam and his wife were not struck down; they were let down, step by step, with the road appearing to run upward the whole way. That is the anatomy of the first temptation, and it is the one the reader of the sūrah will meet again in the surah's own warnings about wealth, adornment, and appetite (7:26–32): a slow gradualism in which each step is justified by the promise of the next.

**"When They Tasted"**

Then the act itself: *fa-lammā dhāqā al-shajarah*. The verb is *dhāqa*, to taste — not *akala*, to eat a meal; not *shabiʿa*, to be filled. Even in the telling of the disobedience, the Qur'an does not describe the couple as banqueting. A taste was enough.

The choice of verb has been read in every generation as the sharpest possible comment on the act. The offense was minimal in quantity and total in kind. Nothing was gained — a taste — and everything given was jeopardized: residence, covering, dignity, ease. The reason the sūrah does not need to harangue its reader about the gravity of small sins is that it has already staged the demonstration: the measurement of a transgression is the One against whose command it was committed, not the size of the object taken. The Prophet ﷺ stated the principle in a hadith that has been memorized in the same spirit — *“Beware of minor sins; they pile upon a man until they ruin him”* (Musnad Aḥmad 3808, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, graded ṣaḥīḥ by Aḥmad Shākir). The imagery the tradition drew from it — a people who each bring a twig until they have gathered enough to bake their bread — is in the report of Sahl ibn Saʿd (Musnad Aḥmad 22808, graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Arnaʾūṭ).

**The Exposure and the First Kind of Work**

*Badat lahumā sawʾātuhumā* — their nakedness became plain to them. Then the sūrah's most human detail: *wa-ṭafiqā yakhṣifāni ʿalayhimā min waraq al-jannah* — they began to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise, literally "patching together" upon themselves. The verb *yakhṣifāni* is the vocabulary of stitching and of mending, and it is, in the whole Book, the first recorded human labor after the fall.

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī both note the poignancy of the moment: the covering they were given by God is gone, and what they can assemble with their own hands is leaves. This is the precise condition of a fallen creature that the sūrah's later verse will describe directly — *“O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness. This is one of Allah’s bounties, so perhaps you will be mindful.”* (7:26). The leaves are the first attempt at a covering that will not hold; the *taqwā* named two verses later is the covering that will.

**The Call in the Garden**

Then comes the divine address, and its shape is a lesson in how God deals with a fallen creature: *“Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?”* (7:22) The construction is interrogative but the content is a reminder. Two things are called back to mind: the command that was given, and the warning that had accompanied it.

The sūrah has, in fact, already delivered that warning to the reader — *“Do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise”* (7:27). Sūrat Ṭāhā records the warning given to Adam himself: *“O Adam! This is surely an enemy to you and to your wife.”* (20:117). The call therefore closes no gap of information. It exposes a gap of attention: the enemy was named in advance, the boundary was pointed out in advance, and both were held in the same hand. The wording *ʿaduww mubīn* — an open, manifest enemy — is one of the Qur'an's recurring formulas about Satan, and it recurs so often (2:168; 2:208; 6:142; 7:22; 12:5; 17:53; 28:15; 36:60; 43:62) because the Book is teaching a single habit of mind: whereas a person's dealings with enemies in the visible world are conducted with caution, the enemy who works through the inner suggestion is regularly treated as a friend.

**The Excuse That Was Not Offered**

One negative observation is worth making, because it is what the sūrah's next verse will make positive. When God calls them out, Adam and his wife do not say: the tempter swore to us. They do not say: the whisper sounded like our own thought. They do not say: the tree was unmarked, or the prohibition was ambiguous. The silence of the narrative is complete on this point, and it is deliberate — because the very next verse gives the answer they did make, and it contains no third party at all.

That is the difference between the fall of 7:22 and the fall of 7:12. Both creatures broke a command after being warned. One produced an argument against the command and never returned from it; the others are about to produce a sentence against themselves. The sūrah's placement of the two falls side by side, in a single continuous narrative, is the whole moral of the passage: what happens after the act is what determines where the act will end.


**Deceived and Made to Fall: The Other Account**

The verse names the instrument: *“So he brought about their fall through deception.”* (7:22). Al-Baqarah describes the same act with its result: *“But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in”* (2:36). The two verses agree on the deception and on the fall, and al-Baqarah adds the state they were left.

The noun the sūrah uses for the deception is *ghurūr*, from a root meaning to make a thing appear other than it is. The exegetes note that *ghurūr* is not lying but misleading by appearance, which is what the whisper at 7:20 consisted of — a prohibition given a motive it did not have, and two benefits promised that the tree could not contain.

2:36’s addition matters for the sūrah’s argument. The fall is from a state of bliss, and the descent that follows is into a place of residence and provision for a term. The sūrah’s own account of the descent (7:24–25) adds the enmity and the guidance that will come, so that the fall is never described as the last term of the narrative.


**Enemies to Each Other: What the Descent Establishes**

The verse’s second half describes the exposure and the first covering; the command that follows establishes a relation. Ṭāhā states it: *“Descend, both of you, from here together ˹with Satan˺ as enemies to each other. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺ nor suffer ˹in the next˺.”* (20:123).

The verse makes two things permanent and one conditional. The descent and the enmity are stated as accomplished; the guidance is stated as coming, and its effect is made dependent on following. This is the position the sūrah’s readers occupy, and 7:22 is the verse that puts them there.

The enmity is what makes the sūrah’s later instructions intelligible. Refuge is commanded at the moment of provocation (7:200), reliance is described as the ground on which the enemy has no authority (16:99), and the histories report town after town taking him as a patron instead. The first narrative in the sūrah establishes the relation that all of them assume.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:23

> **They replied, “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Words That Were Given**

This verse is the turning point of the entire narrative, and the Qur'an tells us where the words came from. *“Then Adam was inspired with words of prayer by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance”* (2:37). The sentence in al-Baqarah uses *talaqqā*, to receive — the words were not composed by the fallen man in the Garden; they were given to him. The tradition's commentators read a mercy in that grammar. A creature who had just broken a command does not know what to say; the Book's answer is that the formula of return is itself supplied from above, which is why the Prophet ﷺ taught his community to ask God to teach them how to ask Him.

**"Our Lord" — The Address That Survives the Fall**

The sentence opens with *rabbanā*. It would have been possible for a shame-stricken creature to address God by the Name of power, of judgment, of wrath; the pairing chosen is the Name of nurture and cultivation. The first word after the failure is therefore a claim on the relationship, not a renunciation of it. The Qur'an's model of repentance begins here, and this is why the same opening recurs on the lips of the returning: *“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves”* (7:23), *“Our Lord! We have believed, so forgive our sins and protect us”* (3:16), *“Our Lord! Forgive our sins”* (3:193).

**"We Have Wronged Ourselves"**

*Ẓalamnā anfusanā.* Three words, and the whole architecture of Islamic accountability is inside them. The object of the wrong is the self — *anfusanā* — not the majesty of God in the abstract, and not another party. The verse thus contains a diagnosis before it contains a request: sin is first of all an injury to the one who commits it, and the Qur'an uses this self-directed language consistently. *“And whoever commits a sin—it is only to their own loss. Allah is AllKnowing, All-Wise.”* (4:111); *“Indeed, whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has clearly gone ˹far˺ astray”* (33:36); *“Surely you have wronged yourselves”* (2:54).

The verb is in the perfect tense, with the *nā* of the first person plural. It reports a finished act and accepts it as one's own. Now compare it with the sentence spoken by Iblīs eleven verses earlier — *“He said, ‘For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”* (7:16) — and the contrast the sūrah has built becomes unavoidable. One creature files the blame upward; the other files the blame inward. The Book does not present both as mistakes with different flavors. It presents one as a position from which no return was ever sought, and the other as the exact posture from which return always begins.

**The Two Requests and Their Precision**

*In lam taghfir lanā wa tarḥamnā* — if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us. The two verbs cover the two halves of what a wrongdoer needs. *Ghufrān* is covering and cancellation: the record erased, the debt discharged. *Raḥmah* is positive: the gift, the restoration, the good supplied where nothing was owed. The pair runs through the Book's prayers — *“My Lord! Forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of those who show mercy.”* (23:118) — and its order is significant. Forgiveness comes first because mercy has nothing to land on until the account is cleared.

The conditional formulation is worth a moment. *If You do not forgive us…* is not doubt; the Arabic conditional here expresses surrender rather than uncertainty, a placing of the matter entirely in God's hand. The servant does not argue his entitlement to pardon. He does not present the balance of his good deeds, or the extenuation of a tempter's oath. He states the consequence of not being forgiven — *we will certainly be losers* — and leaves the decision where it belongs.

**The Same Words from a Different People**

The sūrah does something remarkable with this formula: it puts the identical sentence in the mouths of a later generation. When the Children of Israel repent of the calf, the Qur'an reports: *“Later, when they were filled with remorse and realized they had gone astray, they cried, ‘If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers.’”* (7:149). The parallel is deliberately exact, and it makes a doctrinal point that the sūrah wants carried forward through its long history of Israelite failure: the *mechanism* of return never changes. It is not a Christian or a Jewish rite, not a particular shrine, not an intercession purchased from a priest. It is the acknowledgment of self-inflicted harm, addressed by a creature to his Lord, without a mediator and without an excuse.

**The Master Formula**

The Prophet ﷺ gave this pattern its most complete written form in the *sayyid al-istighfār*, the master supplication: *“O God, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant, and I abide by Your covenant and promise as much as I am able. I seek refuge with You from the evil I have done. I acknowledge before You Your favour upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.”* (al-Bukhārī 6306, from Shaddād ibn Aws). The components are exactly those of 7:23 — lordship addressed, fault owned, mercy requested, credit given to God alone — and the hadith adds the detail that makes the earlier scene intelligible: the one who says this in the morning and dies that day enters the Garden.

The verse therefore closes the first fall with hope rather than condemnation, and the sūrah's readers should note carefully what is *not* in the sentence. No protest of manipulation, no appeal to the tempter's oath, no minimizing of the act. Adam and his wife do the one thing the previous episode established as decisive: they speak to God, and they tell the truth about themselves. The Book's verdict on that turning is given in the verse that follows in Sūrah al-Baqarah — *“Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”* — and the sūrah of the Heights will spend the rest of its length teaching the children of Adam to use the same door.


The Same Confession From a Different Servant

The words of 7:23 are a confession with two requests attached, and the Book records the same confession from a servant in a different situation. Mūsā, after the blow that killed, pleads: *“My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me.”* (28:16), and the verse reports the outcome in three words: *“So He forgave him”* (28:16). The structure is the one 7:23 uses — an address, an admission in the first person, a request — and the admission in both cases is placed on the speaker rather than on a circumstance.

The difference between the two passages is instructive. Mūsā's wrong was a single act with a body left in the sand; the wrong of 7:23 was an act of obedience to a prohibition, committed by two people together, and followed by an expulsion. Both confessions name the self as the object of the wrong: I have wronged my soul, and we have wronged ourselves. Neither blames the other party, the occasion, or the whisperer, and in both cases the admission precedes the request rather than following it. The order is what makes the request intelligible.

The sūrah places these words at the point where they become a formula. 7:23 is spoken once, in the garden, and the Book reports that the same words return in the mouths of later peoples; the sūrah's own account of the towns shows communities that never said them, and the absence is what their destruction reports


Words Given: The Confession as a Thing Received

7:23 begins with the fact that the words were supplied, and al-Baqarah states the same fact in a single clause: *“Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance”* (2:37)

What this adds to the sūrah's account is the direction of the movement. The people of 7:23 do not invent an apology and offer it upward; they receive words and speak them

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:24

> **Allah said, “Descend as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Descent: A Sentence That Is Also a Grant**

*Qāla ihbiṭū* — Allah said, descend. The command is plural, and the Qur'an's parallel accounts specify who is included. In al-Baqarah the instruction is to the pair, *“Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other.”* (2:36); in Ṭā-Hā it is expanded to include the tempter, *“Descend, both of you, from here together with Satan as enemies to each other”* (20:123). The sūrah of the Heights does not need the fuller statement; its readers have just watched the whole exchange.

The wording deserves attention because of what it does *not* say. There is no mention of a punishment being imposed. What is announced is a condition — the earth, a dwelling, a provision, a term — and everything inside that announcement is a good. The same verse that marks the end of the Garden records the beginning of the human world as the Qur'an will treat it in verse 10 above: a place made habitable, supplied, and governed by a schedule known to God. The fall is real; so is the provision that immediately accompanies it.

**"Descend as Enemies to Each Other"**

*Baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ʿaduww* — some of you are enemies to others. The plural is broad and the commentators read it widely: Iblīs and the human race; the human being and his own kind; the human being and the demons; and, in the reading al-Qurṭubī reports, the two members of the couple with respect to a domestic strife the temptation had opened. The Book returns to this condition repeatedly, because it is the structure of life in the world the descent created: *“But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, ‘Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.’”* (2:36); *“Surely Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy”* (35:6); *“Do not follow Satan's footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy”* (2:168).

The verse therefore supplies the realistic premise for everything the sūrah will legislate afterwards. The Qur'an does not describe the earth as neutral ground. It describes it as a contested one, in which the human being lives with a declared opponent and his own appetites, and in which the guidance that arrives from God is the map. The sūrah's later chapters on food, clothing, worship and wealth make sense only against this premise.

**mustaqarr and matāʿ: Dwelling and Provision**

Two nouns are given for the earthly condition. *Mustaqarr* — a place of settlement, from the root *qarra*, to settle, to remain still — is the word the Qur'an uses elsewhere for the stability of created things: *“The sun travels for its fixed term”* (36:38); *“And He is the One Who created the day and the night, the sun and the moon—each travelling in an orbit”* (21:33). The earth is given to the human being as something firm enough to build a life on. Beside it stands *matāʿ*, provision or enjoyment — with the nuance of a thing borrowed and used for a while, since the same word describes the goods of this life generally: *“Know that this worldly life is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children.”* (57:20).

The pairing is the sūrah's doctrine of the world in two words. It is a home and it is not a permanent one. Read without the second term, the verse produces worldliness; read without the first, it produces the kind of contempt for the earth that makes the human vocation unintelligible. The Book holds both: a place to settle, and a limit on the settlement.

**"Until a Time"**

*Ilā ḥīn* — until a time. The phrase is deliberately indefinite, and the indefiniteness is one of the Book's recurring devices: the term is fixed *“When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it”* (7:34) and unknown, and it is the unknown part that produces the moral seriousness of a life. The same phrase appears at the end of Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's account of the people of Jonah: *“who then believed ˹in him˺, so We allowed them enjoyment for a while.”* (37:148; see also 2:36).

The verse thus hands the reader the three coordinates within which everything in this sūrah will happen: *where* — a settled earth; *with what* — provision that can be received with gratitude or with greed; *for how long* — a term no one knows. It is the same framework verse 10 laid out at the beginning of the sūrah — *“We have established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood”* — now restated after the fall, which is to say: the fall did not withdraw the earlier gift.

**The Silence About the Garden**

One theological observation belongs at the end of this scene, and the commentators draw it out. The Qur'an never says that Adam and his wife were expelled from the Garden and forbidden to return. What it says is that they descended into a different mode of existence — that of testing — and that the guidance they were promised in the next verse (7:35) would determine where they ended. Sūrat al-Baqarah states the same sequence with an explicit promise attached: *“Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”* (2:38).

The world, in other words, is not the wreckage of the Garden; it is the arena of the return. The sūrah's opening beats — the towns destroyed at night (vv. 4–5), the question and the weighing (vv. 6–9), the provision of verse 10 — have already laid out the terms, and the Adam narrative has now embedded them in the story of the first human beings. Every reader who continues into the sūrah's long confrontation with the Children of Israel is reading, in a sense, an extended commentary on this verse: what a settled creature does with a provision, in the time remaining, before the term arrives.


The Earth Laid Out: A Residence Described as a Place

The sentence at 7:24 gives the pair a place to go and a thing to live on, and it does both in one breath: descend as enemies, and find in the earth a residence and a provision for an appointed stay. The two nouns the verse supplies are the ground of the whole human story that follows in the sūrah, and the Book describes that ground elsewhere in language that is almost administrative. *“Who has laid out the earth for ˹all of˺ you, and set in it pathways for you”* (20:53), and *“We made in it means of sustenance for you and others, who you do not provide for”* (15:20)

Read together with 7:24, the two passages settle a question the verse raises by its wording. A *mustaqarr* is a place of settling, a fixed abode, and the verse pairs it with *matāʿ*, the enjoyment of a term. The pairing is deliberate: the earth is a settled place, and the settling is bounded

The enmity named in the same sentence is therefore set inside a provisioned place. This is why the human story in al-Aʿrāf is a story of towns rather than of individuals: the earth given to the pair is the earth the towns inhabit, the earth whose blessings the sūrah enumerates at 7:10 and whose destruction it reports at 7:4 and 7:97–99


Enemies to Each Other: The Enmity and the Term That Bounds It

The command to descend as enemies is stated as a fact about the pair's relation rather than as a curse, and the Book treats enmity in the same register elsewhere. What distinguishes 7:24 is that the enmity is named at the moment of the grant, not after a transgression in the new place; it belongs to the descent itself

The term attached to the provision does the work the enmity cannot. An appointed stay means that the residence has a date, and the Book's repeated insistence on that date is what keeps the enmity from being the last word about the pair

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:25

> **He added, “There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Clauses, One Place**

The verse is built on a single repeated pronoun. *Fīhā* — "therein", "in it", the "there" of the translation — governs all three clauses, and the antecedent is the earth named in the command to descend that precedes it. Life is in it, death is in it, and the coming forth is from it. Nothing in the sequence happens anywhere else.

That is the whole force of the construction, and it is easy to read past. The verse does not say that man will live, die and be raised; it says that all three will happen *in relation to one place*, and that the place is the same. The earth is not a corridor the human being passes through on the way to somewhere more important. It is the location of the beginning, the location of the end, and the location of the return.

> *He added, “There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.”*

The third clause changes its preposition deliberately. The first two use *fīhā*, in it; the third uses *minhā*, from it. Life and death are contained by the earth; the rising is an emergence out of it. The same ground that closes over a body is the ground that gives it back.

**Who Is Being Addressed**

The command to descend in verse 24 is plural — *ihbiṭū*, "descend", all of you — and al-Ṭabarī reads it as addressed to Adam and Eve, to their future progeny, and to Iblīs together. The enmity named in the same breath, *as enemies to each other*, is therefore not only a statement about the human being and the tempter but about human beings among themselves.

The scope matters for what follows. Verse 13 had banished Iblīs from the Garden specifically: *Get down from it.* This command is wider — a descent from the celestial realm altogether — and it carries the whole human race with it. Verse 25 is what the descent leads to, and it is addressed to everyone who descended.

The verse is also a statement of the terms. Nothing is negotiated; nothing is offered back. The three clauses are declarative, and the human being is told where his life will run and where it will end before he has taken a step.

**A Fall Read as Mercy**

Some Sufi commentators read the whole sequence providentially, and even mercifully. Al-Jīlī and those who follow him note that the act of disobedience led to Adam's assumption of the vicegerency on earth, and that it opened a way of drawing near to God which is only available after distance has been experienced. Proximity that has never been lost is not the same thing as proximity recovered.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh, the eighth-/fourteenth-century Shādhilī master, put the principle in a single line of his *Ḥikam*:

> *"An act of disobedience that bequeaths humility and need is better than an act of obedience that bequeaths might and pride."* (Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh, al-Ḥikam 96)

The comparison is not between disobedience and obedience but between two outcomes. What is being weighed is what the act leaves in the soul. An obedience that produces self-sufficiency has lost the thing worship exists for; a fall that produces need has found it. On this reading the descent is not only a punishment but the condition of a perfection that was not reachable otherwise — because it requires repentance, and repentance requires something to return from.

The same reading gives the fall a second consequence, on God's side rather than man's. It occasions the manifestation of an attribute that innocence would never have disclosed. Forgiveness is only manifest where there is something to forgive.

**The Second Account**

This verse closes the second telling of the Adam narrative in the order of the muṣḥaf. The first is at 2:30–39; later accounts run at 17:61–65 and 20:115–24, and at 15:28–43 and 38:71–85 the same story is told of the first human being without naming him.

The repetition is not redundancy, and the differences are where the meaning lies. Each account closes differently, and this one closes on the earth: on where the story's descendants will actually live, die and rise. The telling in Sūrah Ṭā Hā closes on the warning not to forget; this one closes on a geography.

That is why the three clauses are worth taking as a unit rather than as a summary. The verse is the Qur'an's most compressed statement of the human condition — one place, three events, no exit from the sequence and no alternative venue for any of them.

**What the Sequence Forecloses**

The order is fixed and no stage can be skipped. The man who hopes to arrive at the being-brought-forth without passing through the dying has misunderstood the verse; the one who hopes to live somewhere other than the earth has misunderstood it too.

The practical weight of that is not morbid. A life lived on the assumption that it will end in the same ground it began in is a life in which the ground has a claim. The verse makes the earth a witness to the whole of a human career — present at the living, present at the dying, and the thing that hands the person back. It is not scenery.


**The Verb That Both Sends and Raises**

The third clause turns on a single verb, *tubʿathūn*, from the root *b-ʿ-th*. That root holds two offices in the Qurʾān, and this verse uses the one that belongs to the end of the world. God *baʿatha* messengers to their peoples, and God *baʿatha* the dead from their graves; the same act of dispatch runs toward history in the first case and away from it in the second. The human being described here is spoken of in the vocabulary of revelation — not merely returned, but sent.

That is why the clause stands as the Book’s answer to an objection it records in the objector’s own words: *“Who will give life to decayed bones?”* (36:78). The question assumes that what has decayed is finished; the verse assumes that the same ground is the instrument of the return. Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt gives the objection in fuller form — *“Will we really be restored to our former state, even after we have been reduced to decayed bones?”* (79:10–11) — and adds the objector’s own conclusion, *“Then such a return would be a ˹total˺ loss ˹for us˺!”* (79:12). Verse 25 does not argue with that conclusion. It states the itinerary, and leaves the loss to be calculated by whoever walks it.


**The Same Three Prepositions in Ṭā Hā and Nūḥ**

Two other passages lay out the same itinerary, and both bind it to the same ground. In the address that follows Mūsā’s commissioning, Sūrah Ṭā Hā says: *“From the earth We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you back again.”* (20:55). Nūḥ preaches it to his people in the language of cultivation: *“Allah ˹alone˺ caused you to grow from the earth like a plant.”* (71:17), *“Then He will return you to it, and then simply bring you forth ˹again˺.”* (71:18).


**The Earth as the Place of Return in Law**

The jurists read the third clause as the ground of burial. If the coming forth is *from* the earth, the staying is *in* it, and the return of a body to the soil is not a local custom but the shape the verse describes. Sūrah al-Mursalāt states the arrangement as a provision made for the creature: *“Have We not made the earth a lodging for the living and the dead”* (77:25–26). Sūrah ʿAbasa puts the two acts in a single line — God *“then causes them to die and be buried”* (80:21) — the verb *qabara*, from which the word for grave derives.

Hence the practice the tradition settled on: burial promptly, in the earth, with the body laid on its side toward the qiblah, and the mound raised only enough for the grave to be recognised. The martyrs of Uḥud were buried where they fell, which is the verse’s principle applied without amendment: a man stays in the ground where he died. What this verse adds is the third term. The grave is not a disposal but a deposit, held in the same ground that will be asked for it back.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:26

> **O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness. This is one of Allah’s bounties, so perhaps you will be mindful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Garments in One Verse**

The verse that follows the fall turns immediately to clothing, and it does so with a wordplay only Arabic can carry. *Libās* is any covering worn on the body; *rīsh* is the plumage of a bird — the feathers that make a creature not merely covered but beautiful; and *libās al-taqwā* is a third garment, made of neither cloth nor skin. Human beings, in this verse, are given three layers: a cover for the body, an adornment for the eye, and a covering for the soul.

The sequence deserves to be read slowly, because the sūrah has just left a scene of leaves stitched together in panic (7:22). The first garment given to the first couple was God's; the leaves were their own attempt at replacement; and this verse announces that the original arrangement stands — covering itself is from God, *anzalnā*, We sent down.

**"Sent Down": Clothing as a Divine Gift**

The verb *anzalnā* is the same verb the Qur'an uses for rain, for the Book, and for iron (*“We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people”*, 57:25). Clothing is placed in that company deliberately. The wool of sheep, the strength of flax, the growth of cotton, the shade of a tree — none of these were manufactured by the human being who wears them; what the human being contributes is knowledge of how to use what was supplied. The same point is made in Sūrah al-Naḥl, where garments and their purposes are traced to the Creator: *“He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle” (16:81)* (16:81). For the mercantile Makkans, whose cloth trade was a livelihood, the verse quietly relocates the origin of their merchandise: the wealth of their caravans was borrowed.

**rīsh: The Case for Beauty**

The second garment is not a concession; it is named with affection. *Rīsh* is plumage, and the commentators record two overlapping readings. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as the adornment of this world — the fine clothing and the beauty that makes a person pleasing to look at. Others, following a lexically attested sense of the root *r-y-sh* (prosperity, the means by which one lives at ease), read it as provision and sufficiency. The two readings converge: God is not embarrassed by beauty, and He supplies the conditions for it.

This is the verse that Muslim tradition cites against a spirituality of self-neglect. The Prophet ﷺ, when a man came to him looking disheveled, remarked that God is beautiful and loves beauty, and that the display of God's favour upon a servant is part of what is due to Him. The Qur'an's own term for the good things of life is *ṭayyibāt*, and it treats their enjoyment as worship when gratitude accompanies it (2:172; 7:32). *rīsh* is the licence for that enjoyment, written into the earliest instruction given to the human race after the fall.

**libās al-taqwā: The Garment That Cannot Be Bought**

Then the verse introduces its comparative: *wa-libāsu al-taqwā dhālika khayr* — the best clothing is righteousness. The *khayr* is not a dismissal of the earlier garments; it is a ranking. Cloth covers a body that will decay; *taqwā* covers a soul that will be presented to God. The Qur'an elsewhere names *taqwā* as the thing that survives when all provisions are counted: *“Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness.”* (2:197). The metaphor works because it shares the function of clothing exactly. Taqwā hides what ought not to be seen — the faults, the appetite that has not yet been disciplined — and it protects its wearer from exposure. In the sūrah's own story, the first thing sin produced was exposure; the remedy offered to the children of Adam is a covering that cannot be lost by taste or theft.

**A Sign to Be Remembered**

The verse closes by naming itself a sign: *so perhaps you will be mindful*. And the reason clothing functions as a sign is anthropological. Human beings are the only creatures in the world whose dignity depends on covering; a horse needs no garment, a bird is already dressed. The nakedness that shamed Adam and his wife was not a bodily defect but a moral fact — the loss of the covering that God had given. Every garment a person puts on is therefore a reminder, whether he notices or not, that he is a being with a shame to guard and a Lord who provided for it.

That is why the verse ends with memory rather than command. The argument is not that clothing is obligatory; it is that clothing is evidence. A person who sees the evidence will not spend the rest of his life treating his outer covering as though it were the whole story, or (as the next passage will warn) treating the loss of God's command as a small thing because the world is warm and there are leaves enough.

The verse's sequence is therefore itself an argument: the fall is mentioned, and the clothing is named immediately afterwards, as though the Book wanted the reader to see that the provision for the body and the provision for the soul were given together and never revoked.


**How Clothing Is Sent Down**

The verse says that clothing was sent down — *anzalnā lakum libāsā* — and the commentators have always had to meet the obvious objection, since garments are woven rather than revealed. Their answers are levels rather than alternatives. At the first level the material is literally sent down: nothing reaches the loom that did not begin as water, and the water falls. Sūrah al-Naḥl lists the finished products in the same register of provision: *“And out of their wool, fur, and hair He has given you furnishings and goods for a while.”* (16:80), *“He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle.”* (16:81).

At the second level what is sent down is the knowledge, since the covering that distinguishes the human being is a practice that had to be taught — and the sūrah’s own narrative has just shown the first couple learning it under the compulsion of shame (7:22). At the third level the phrase belongs to the Book’s habit of tracing every provision to its source rather than to its manufacturer, which is why the verse closes by calling the whole arrangement one of God’s bounties. The three readings agree on what the verse is making of a garment: not a possession but a provision. It is under that heading that the sūrah will shortly forbid anyone to declare provision unlawful (7:32).


**The Variant Reading and the Ruling It Supports**

The word for the second of the three garments, *rīsh*, is read by some of the reciters as *riyāsh*, and the two forms are cognate. The lexicons take both to mean what adorns — plumage in the literal sense, outward means and wealth in the derived one — while several commentators distinguish them finely, reading *rīsh* as what beautifies a person and *riyāsh* as the possessions that make the beautifying possible. The variant therefore widens the sense rather than changing it, and it was the widening the jurists put to use.

From this verse and the command at 7:31 they drew the rulings on covering: the obligation to cover the *ʿawrah* in prayer, the recommendation of the best of one’s clothing at the places of worship, and the rejection of the ascetic who declares adornment forbidden in order to be more devout than the law requires. The sūrah’s argument is not that beauty distracts from mindfulness. It ranks the three garments — covering, adornment, and the clothing of mindfulness — and sets the third above the first two without abolishing them. What is refused is not adornment but anyone’s claim to forbid it, which is why the verse ends on bounty rather than on restriction.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:27

> **O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise and caused their cover to be removed in order to expose their nakedness. Surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them. We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning Repeated to the Children**

The verse opens with the same address as the one before it — *O children of Adam* — and it is not a repetition of the earlier instruction but a repetition of the earlier *danger*. God had warned Adam directly: *“This is surely an enemy to you and to your wife”* (20:117). Now the warning passes to the sons: *do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise.*

The structure is the Book's model of education. Information is not the shortage; the shortage is attention. The Qur'an therefore tells the story of the first fall not once but many times, from different angles, in different sūrahs, and returns to it here immediately after clothing and reverence have been discussed. The sūrah's reader has just been told what the best garment is; he is now told who is most interested in removing it.

**"Causing Their Cover to Be Removed"**

*Yanziʿu ʿanhumā libāsahumā* — he strips them of their garment, in order to expose their nakedness. The verb *nazaʿa* is the vocabulary of forcible removal: to pull off, to take away, to dispossess. The Qur'an's account is unsparing about the aim of the enemy. He does not merely want a particular act performed; he wants the removal of protection, so that the shame can be displayed.

That aim has not changed in the slightest. The temptations of every generation are refinements of the same project: to get a person to loosen the covering of reverence — one verse, one appetite, one compromise at a time — and then to leave him standing exposed in the middle of his own garden, sewing whatever there is at hand. The Arabic word for the result, *sawʾāt*, is the same in this verse and in 7:20 and 7:22, tying the earlier scene to this warning as a single, repeated phenomenon.

**The Asymmetry of Vision**

Then comes the sentence that makes the whole passage practical: *innahu yarākum huwa wa-qabīluhu min ḥaythu lā tarawanahum* — surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them. The word *qabīl*, rendered here "his soldiers", is kinship language: a clan, a tribe, an organized body. The jinn are described as a community with forces, and the Qur'an elsewhere names their orders and ranks — infantry and cavalry, incursion and collaboration (17:64) — and the four-sided approach of 7:17.

The verse thus removes from the reader the comfort of an even fight. The opponent can observe the human being's movements and habits; the human being cannot observe him. And this is precisely why the sūrah's remedy for the ambush is not intelligence-gathering but refuge — *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah”* (7:200) — and why the Book supplies the missing visibility by naming the enemy's techniques in advance. What the human being cannot see, God has described.

The hadith tradition handles the same reality with a metaphor that has stayed in the Muslim imagination: *“Satan circulates in the human being as blood circulates in him”* (al-Bukhārī 3281, from Ṣafiyyah). The Prophet ﷺ said it while warning one of his wives that the enemy might throw a suggestion into her heart — a remark that tells the reader this is not a subject for those who consider themselves immune. The nearness is the point: no wall, no distance, no rank provides separation. What protects is not insulation but vigilance, and beside it, the divine word that names the danger.

**"We Have Made the Devils Allies of Those Who Disbelieve"**

The final clause is the verse's theology. *Innā jaʿalnā al-shayāṭīn awliyāʾa li-lladhīna lā yuʾminūn* — We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve. *Walī* is the nearest of relations: protector, patron, the one to whom loyalty is given and from whom protection is expected. The Qur'an uses the term for the divine guardianship over the believers (*“Allah is the Protector of those who believe”*, 2:257) and here for its inversion.

The construction *jaʿalnā*, We made, has drawn the attention of theologians: is this a decree or a consequence? The Book's usage answers by holding the two together. The alliance is a settlement that the person's own movement has produced — the same law stated in Sūrah al-Zukhruf, *“And whoever turns a blind eye to the Reminder of the Most Compassionate, We place at the disposal of each a devilish one as their close associate”* (43:36) — and once settled, it is administered by God's decree. Responsibility is not dissolved by the fact that the outcome was decreed; the human being, not God, chose the road that led to the companion.

The verse therefore closes with the plainest of statements. There are two guardianships available to a human being, and to choose the first is to accept the terms set by the enemy of the second. Everything else in the sūrah's long confrontation with its two audiences happens inside that framework.

The verse's readers are meant to carry the asymmetry into their own lives: the enemy sees what they do not, and the remedy the Book prescribes is not greater confidence in oneself but constant recourse to the One who sees.


**The Word for Garment, and What Else It Covers**

The covering the verse says was stripped is *libās*, the ordinary word for a garment — but the Book uses it of persons as well as cloth. Of spouses it says: *“Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them.”* (2:187). The word therefore carries both senses at once in this verse: something worn, and something that protects by being near. What is removed in the Garden is not only fabric but a covering in the second sense, and the warning to the children of Adam is that the tempter still works by stripping coverings rather than by adding them.

The root *l-b-s* splits into two verbs, and the split is worth holding. *Labisa* is to wear; *labasa* is to confound, to mix a matter until it can no longer be read. From the first comes *libās*, garment; from the second comes *labs*, the confusion of a thing with what it is not. The temptation in this verse does both at once: it uncovers the body and it obscures the case. That is why the sūrah’s next addresses to the children of Adam concern dress at the places of worship (7:31) and the refusal to let anyone declare forbidden what God has produced for them (7:32–33). Clarity about what covers a person and clarity about what is permitted to him are the same discipline.


**The Vocative of the Children of Adam**

This verse opens with a call the sūrah keeps to itself. *Yā banī Ādam* — O children of Adam — occurs four times in the Qurʾān, and all four are here (7:26, 27, 31, 35); each introduces either a ruling about dress and provision or a warning about being turned aside. Elsewhere the phrase appears only descriptively, in the statement of the honour conferred on the species: *“Indeed, We have dignified the children of Adam, carried them on land and sea, granted them good and lawful provisions, and privileged them far above many of Our creatures.”* (17:70).


**Seeing Without Being Seen**

The clause that the tempter and his tribe see you from where you do not see them fixes an asymmetry, and the commentators drew a practical rule from it. A maxim attributed to al-Shāfiʿī and quoted in the exegetical literature on this verse holds that whoever claims to see the jinn is not to be believed on his claim — because the verse has already stated that the seeing runs one way. The rule is not a denial that the jinn exist; it is a refusal to let an unverifiable assertion carry weight in a matter where other people’s conduct depends on the answer.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:28

> **Whenever they commit a shameful deed, they say, “We found our forefathers doing it and Allah has commanded us to do it.” Say, “No! Allah never commands what is shameful. How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Argument from the Fathers**

*Wa-idhā faʿalū fāḥishatan qālū wajadnā ʿalayhā ābāʾanā* — whenever they commit a shameful deed, they say, we found our forefathers doing it. The verse is a portrait of a religious mentality, drawn from life. The people in question are not denying the practice; they are defending it, and their defense rests on inheritance. The practice is old, the ancestors did it, therefore it stands.

The commentators record the occasion the first audience would have recognized. Reports transmitted by al-Ṭabarī and repeated by Ibn Kathīr describe the pre-Islamic Arabs circumambulating the House naked — men by day and women by night — and describing their nakedness as a religious act, on the reasoning that one should not perform the circuit in clothes in which one had sinned. Other reports attach the verse to particular customs of the tribes. Whichever specific practice is intended, the sūrah is addressing a general habit of mind, and it names it with precision: an act that is objectively shameful, defended by the fact that it is customary.

**Taqlīd: The Qur'an's Sustained Objection**

This is not an isolated complaint. The Qur'an returns to the ancestral argument again and again and rejects it in nearly identical words: *“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they reply, ‘No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.’ ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance?”* (2:170; see also 5:104; 31:21; 43:22–24). The rejoinder in al-Baqarah is the sūrah's own rejoinder here, sharpened into a question about the competence of the ancestors to be followed.

The point is not hostility to tradition. Islam is, in its own self-description, the religion of Abraham and of the prophets before Muhammad ﷺ, and the sūrah will spend a great part of its length appealing to the inheritance of the Children of Israel. What the Book rejects is not inherited practice but inherited practice used *as a proof*. A custom can be a legitimate vehicle of a genuine command, but its antiquity is not the reason the command binds; the command binds because God commanded it, and the command must be traceable to Him. The moment a practice is defended by the fact that it is ancestral, it has been removed from the jurisdiction of revelation altogether.

**The Worse Claim: "Allah Has Commanded Us to Do It"**

The verse's second clause escalates the error. *Wa-llāhu amaranā bihā* — and Allah has commanded us to do it. To follow one's fathers is a mistake; to attribute the following to a divine command is a fabrication about God. The distinction is one the sūrah will make explicit three verses later, when it lists what God has actually forbidden (7:33), and it explains why this verse's answer is framed as a flat denial: *qul inna Allāha lā yaʾmuru bi-l-faḥshāʾ* — say, God does not command indecency.

The principle underneath is fundamental to Islamic theology. God's commands are not arbitrary; they are consistent with His names and His revealed law. A command to commit what revelation names *fāḥishah* — an obscenity, a thing the sound conscience recoils from — cannot come from God, because God has already declared such things forbidden in the Book and in the innate disposition He created (7:157; 16:90; 30:30). Any claim of a divine command that contradicts the divine law has just refuted itself. This is the criterion the tradition later used to sift an enormous body of purported reports and rulings, and it begins here.

**The Epistemic Sins**

The verse closes with the question that gives the passage its teeth: *a-taqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn* — how can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?

Speaking about God without knowledge is treated in this sūrah as a distinct and grave category of offense. Verse 33 will list it among the four things God has forbidden — indecencies, sin, wrongful aggression, and *“associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized—and attributing to Allah what you do not know”* (7:33) Sūrah al-Baqarah warns that the same enemy who incites indecency also urges *“to claim against Allah what you do not know”* (2:169), and Sūrah al-Naḥl condemns the fabrication of permissions and prohibitions by the tongue alone: *“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, ‘This is lawful, and that is unlawful,’ ˹only˺ fabricating lies against Allah.”* (16:116).

The reason for the severity is that this particular error cannot be corrected by information. A person who follows an inherited custom can be shown the text; a person who reports God's own opinion on the matter has placed himself beyond the reach of correction, because he has made his claim unimpeachable by construction. The verse therefore asks the one question that can reopen the case: *how do you know?* It is a question the Muslim tradition turned into a discipline — the science of *isnād*, of chains of transmission, of the scrutiny of claims attributed to God and His Prophet — and the chapter that legislates it is this one.

The verse's question is therefore an examination rather than a rhetorical flourish, and the sūrah's readers are included in it: every claim made on God's behalf is to be measured by what has actually been revealed and by what can actually be known.


**Two Excuses, and the Reply That Takes Them in Reverse**

The verse reports two defences, and the answer addresses them in the reverse of the order in which they were offered. The first is inheritance — *we found our forefathers doing it*. The second is revelation — *Allah has commanded us to do it*. The reply opens on the second: no, God does not command the shameful. Only then does it reach the ground beneath both, in the question that closes the verse: how can you attribute to God what you do not know?

The order is deliberate, because the two claims do not stand or fall together. An appeal to the fathers is an argument from history, which can be reported and disputed; an appeal to a command is a claim about God, which is either warranted or it is not. Taking the second first withdraws the authority the first was borrowing, and what remains of the custom is a practice with no ground at all. The Book reports the same exchange wherever the appeal to the fathers appears — *“No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.”* (2:170) — and its polemic is always aimed at the warrant, never at the character of the ancestors.


**Attributing to God What One Does Not Know**

The final clause names the underlying offence as epistemic rather than moral, and the same act is forbidden in the register of law. The tongue that declares *“This is lawful, and that is unlawful”* without warrant is *“fabricating lies against Allah”*, and the verdict on it is flat: *“Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will never succeed.”* (16:116).

The pairing gives the reader a test with two limbs. A practice defended by custom needs a history; a practice defended by command needs a warrant. Where neither is produced, what remains is a statement about God made without knowledge — the one charge in this verse that the answer does not argue with, but denies the possibility of. The question the sūrah puts to the town is left standing over its readers, and it applies to every ruling a person attributes to God without having been given it.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:29

> **Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord has commanded uprightness and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship, calling upon Him with sincere devotion. Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer in Four Movements**

After refuting the argument from the fathers, the sūrah gives the answer: *qul amara rabbī bi-l-qisṭ* — say, my Lord has commanded uprightness, *qisṭ* being the justice that gives each its due. The command to answer is itself significant. Verse 28 ended with a lie about God; verse 29 begins with a command to speak, and what is put in the Prophet's mouth is not a counter-argument but a summary of what God actually requires. The refutation of a fabricated law is the real law, stated plainly.

The verse then unfolds in four movements, and each deserves its own attention: justice, orientation in worship, sincerity, and the return.

**Justice First**

The first item is *qisṭ*, and the choice of the word is deliberate. Arabic has several words for justice — *ʿadl* for balance and equity, *ḥukm* for judgment, *qisṭ* for the fair share that is due. *Qisṭ* is the word of the scale, and its use here, in a sūrah that has just placed a balance on the Day of Judgment (7:8–9), ties the ethics of this life to the accounting of the next. Justice is not one virtue among many in the Qur'an; it is the first thing named when a prophet is asked to describe what his Lord commands. The Book reinforces this repeatedly: *“Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as courtesy to close relatives.”* (16:90); *“when you judge between people, judge with fairness”* (4:58); *“Be just — that is closer to righteousness”* (5:8), the verse that commands justice even toward those one hates.

The placement matters for the sūrah's argument. Its audience was a trading city whose religious life had been handed down by custom, and the Qur'an's first answer to inherited religion is not a ritual but a moral standard. God commands what is fair. Any tradition, however venerable, that has licensed unfairness has failed the first test of revelation.

**Faces Set Toward Him**

*Wa-aqīmū wujūhakum ʿinda kulli masjid* — literally, "set your faces at every place of worship"; the translation carries the clause as *dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship*. The verb *aqāma* is from *q-w-m*, the root of standing upright, and the Qur'an uses it for establishing prayer (*aqāma al-ṣalāh*) throughout. The commentators give several readings of the phrase. Al-Ṭabarī takes it as a command to direct oneself wholly to God in every act of worship, whatever place one is in. Others read it as a statement about consistency: at every mosque, in every prayer, in every gathering, let the face be set — not turned now to one loyalty and now to another. The word *wajh*, face, in the Qur'an's idiom carries the sense of the whole directed self, which is why *aslamtu wajhī* is not to be rendered word-for-word as *I have turned my face* but carries the sense *“I have submitted myself to Allah”* (3:20; see also 2:112).

The instruction answers the polytheist practice of the previous verse with an argument by contrast. They came to the House in a manner that was neither dignified nor directed; the command is to arrive with the whole person oriented to God. The place of prayer is not a stage for performance but a point of alignment.

**Sincerity as the Definition of Religion**

*Wa-dʿūhu mukhliṣīna lahu al-dīn* — and call upon Him with sincere devotion. The phrase *mukhliṣīn lahu al-dīn* recurs through the Book as the definition of the religion Abraham founded — in the call of 10:22 and 29:65, in the supplication of 31:32, and in the two addresses of 40:14 and 40:65 — and it is given its final summary in Sūrat al-Bayyinah: *“even though they were only commanded to worship Allah ˹alone˺ with sincere devotion to Him in all uprightness, establish prayer, and pay almstax. That is the upright Way”* (98:5).

The doctrine of *ikhlāṣ* rests on this phrase. The Arabic root *kh-l-ṣ* carries the sense of being free of mixture, and in the terminology of the tradition it means that an act has been purified of every motive except the pleasure of God. The Qur'an's own definition of the failure is instructive: a person who prays to God in difficulty and forgets Him in ease has not purified anything (10:22). The command therefore polices the interior of worship — the very thing a religion of inherited custom never examined, because custom can be performed without any interior at all.

**"Just as He First Brought You into Being, You Will Be Brought to Life Again"**

The verse closes with the resurrection, and the argument it uses is one of the Qur'an's most persistent: the appeal to the beginning as proof of the return. *Kamā badaʾakum taʿūdūn.* Sūrat al-Rūm states it with the reasoning spelled out — *“And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him.”* (30:27) — and the same proof is pressed in 21:104, 29:19, 27:64, and 10:4. Al-Anbiyāʾ puts it as a promise: *“Just as We produced the first creation, so shall We reproduce it”* (21:104). And when the Makkans posed the challenge in its hardest form, asking who would restore bones to life, the answer given was the same: *“The One Who created you the first time.”* (17:51).

There is a second layer in the phrase, and the sūrah exploits it immediately. *Just as He first brought you into being* — the human being began as nothing, without property, without name, without a tribe. The verse is a reminder that this is also how the account will be resumed: as the Qur'an says elsewhere, *“˹Today˺ you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time”* (6:94), and *“You have surely returned to Us ˹all alone˺ as We created you the first time”* (18:48). Justice in this life, worship in this life, sincerity in this life — and then a return to the condition in which one began, where all that will distinguish a person is what he earned by those three things and not what his fathers did before him.


Every Place of Worship: The Locations Named and Their Owner

7:29 issues four commands in a single sentence, and the second of them fixes a location: set your faces at every place of worship. The Book states elsewhere who owns those locations, in a verse that reads as a rule rather than a description: *“The places of worship are ˹only˺ for Allah, so do not invoke anyone besides Him.”* (72:18)

The phrase *ʿinda kulli masjid* is worth noting for its breadth. Every place of prostration, without qualification of city or community, receives the same command; the faces are to be set toward Him in all of them. This is the same breadth the sūrah shows in its addresses, where the command to worship is put to every people in turn, and it is what allows the verse to be read as a rule for the worship of the believers rather than as an instruction to a particular congregation

The remaining three commands of 7:29 order the worship that takes place in those locations. Justice is commanded first, which places a social obligation before a ritual one; then the faces are set, which fixes the posture; then the call upon Him is qualified by sincere devotion, which fixes the interior state


Sincere Devotion: The Definition of the Upright Way

The verse's final command is to call upon Him with sincere devotion, and the Book states the same requirement as the content of a command given to others before. *“To worship Allah ˹alone˺ with sincere devotion to Him in all uprightness, establish prayer, and pay almstax”* (98:5), and the verse then names what has been listed: that is the upright way

The definition bears directly on the sūrah's account of the towns. Their failure was not a failure of observance but of direction; they called on others beside Him, and 72:18 forbids exactly that inside the places of worship. A religion defined by sincere devotion is a religion in which the site and the posture are necessary but not sufficient, and the sūrah's destruction of communities that had both is the demonstration of that insufficiency

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:30

> **He has guided some, while others are destined to stray. They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah— thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Parties on One Road**

*Farīqan hadā wa-farīqan ḥaqqat ʿalayhimu al-ḍalālah.* The verse divides humanity into two groups, and the two verbs are not symmetrical. For the first, guidance is something done *to* them — *hadā*, He guided, with God as the subject. For the second, straying is something that has *settled upon* them — *ḥaqqat*, from a root meaning to be due, to fall upon a person as a right or a consequence.

The asymmetry is the Qur'an's careful position on one of its most discussed questions. Guidance is an act of God's grace; misguidance is a settled consequence. The Book never says that God *made a party stray* in the way it says He guided a party; at most it says He *left* them, *turned away* from them, or *did not guide* them — and it never allows these statements to be detached from the condition of those concerned. Sūrat al-Ṣaff states the sequence explicitly: *“So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”* (61:5). The deviation of the heart is a recompense, not a cause. The same law appears in 2:26, where straying happens to *“the rebellious”*; in 6:125, where the chest of the one left astray is constricted because of what he chose; and in 42:44, where the one left astray has no protector after Him.

The sūrah's readers are not being told that God arbitrarily assigns fates. They are being told that after a certain point, a direction hardens into a destiny. The verse states it in the past tense of a settled condition, and the whole of the passage that surrounds it — the ancestral argument, the lie against God, the warning about the enemy — is a description of how the settlement is reached.

**"They Took Devils as Their Masters Instead of Allah"**

The cause is then named: *ittakhadhū al-shayāṭīn awliyāʾa min dūni Allāh*. The construction *min dūni Allāh* — apart from, to the exclusion of God — is the Qur'an's standard formula for the displaced loyalty that constitutes *shirk*. The verse is not speaking of a formal cult of the jinn, though such cults existed and are addressed elsewhere (72:6; 6:100). It is speaking of the appointment of a guardian: the habit of turning to something other than God for protection, validation, and direction — an appetite, a patron, a custom, an ideology, an inner voice.

The commentators note how this connects to the verse two lines earlier. There the divine act was named — *We made the satans the friends of those who disbelieve* (7:27) — and here the human act is named: *they took* them as protectors. The two are one event seen from the two sides of the same covenant, and the Book keeps both because neither alone tells the truth about responsibility. God's decree and the human being's choice meet in the same act, and the person's accountability survives the encounter.

The second sūrah of the Qur'an states the outcome of the two guardianships in one verse: *“Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”* (2:257). The guidance of verse 30 is simply the first half of that verse in practice.

**"And They Think They Are Guided"**

Then the clause that makes the verse frightening: *wa-hum yaḥsabūna annahum muhtadūn*. Not merely lost — lost while convinced of the opposite. The Qur'an treats this as a distinct condition with its own vocabulary. Sūrat al-Kahf describes people *“whose efforts are in vain in this worldly life, while they think they are doing good”* (18:104). Sūrat Fāṭir asks the question the sūrah of the Heights has been building toward: *“Are those whose evil-doing is made so appealing to them that they deem it good like those who are rightly guided?”* (35:8). And Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn shows it operating at the social level: a group swearing oaths of loyalty while the Qur'an names them liars (63:1; 58:18).

The psychology of this sentence is the reason the verse pairs it with the ancestral argument of 7:28 and the enemy of 7:27. There are three roads into the same ditch: blaming one's failure on God, as Iblīs did; defending a practice because one's fathers did it; and taking the enemy as a protector while believing one has taken God. The common feature of all three is that none of them feels like error from inside. It is the settled condition, not the momentary sin, that the verse describes — and it is why the sūrah keeps returning to the criterion of revelation rather than the criterion of feeling.

**The Reflection That Is Owed**

The verse's placement at the end of the sūrah's opening argument gives it a pastoral function. Having just described the two parties, the Qur'an does not tell the reader which one he is in; it hands him the instruments to find out. The rest of the sūrah — the answer of verse 29, the prohibition of verse 33, the stories of the nations that follow — is the criterion applied.

The third sūrah of the Qur'an states the point about misguidance and its victims in one line that preserves hope: *“Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us”* (3:8). The Prophet ﷺ taught the same supplication in his own practice: *“O Turner of hearts, keep my heart firm upon Your religion.”* The verse before us explains why such a prayer is necessary. Certainty is not the same as guidance, and the person who has never asked God to keep his heart has no guarantee that his own confidence is anything more than the settled state of a misdirected road.


**Deserving to Stray: The Verb of Entitlement**

The verse divides people into two parties with two verbs: some He guided, and some *ḥaqqat ʿalayhim al-ḍalālah* — *“others are destined to stray”* (7:30). The verb is form X of *ḥ-q-q*, the root of truth and of what is due. In this form it means to deserve, to have a claim established against one. Straying here is not merely what happens to a party; it is what has become due to them.

An-Nisāʾ describes the same movement as a consequence of a prior choice: *“And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell—what an evil end!”* (4:115)

This is the grammar 7:30 depends on. The party that deserved to stray is not a party selected before its acts; the entitlement was established by what it did with guidance that had become clear


**An Enemy to Be Taken as an Enemy**

The verse’s second sentence reports an exchange that did not happen: people took devils as protectors *besides* Allah while supposing themselves guided. Fāṭir states what the exchange actually is: *“Surely Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his followers to become inmates of the Blaze.”* (35:6).

The verse is built as an instruction rather than a warning. Enmity is not denied or explained; it is to be adopted as a posture. The second clause gives the reason in the shortest possible form — the invitation has one destination — and the first clause follows from it: a party whose host intends your ruin is not a party to take as a protector.

7:30 supplies the case the instruction is aimed at. The sūrah has already described the mechanism: the devils see people from where they cannot be seen (7:27), the whisper is answered by a remembrance (7:201), and refuge is commanded at the moment of provocation (7:200). What 7:30 adds is the state of mind in which all of this is accepted as guidance — which is why the verse ends where it does, with the supposition rather than with the punishment.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:31

> **O Children of Adam! Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat and drink, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command to Be Beautiful in Worship**

*Khudhū zīnatakum ʿinda kulli masjid* — dress properly whenever you are at worship, literally "take your adornment at every mosque". The verse answers the previous two by legislation. Verse 28 had condemned an act defended as ancestral; verse 29 had stated what God actually commands; now this verse supplies the practice that fills the gap. The sūrah turns what the polytheists had inverted into a command: they came to the House stripped, and the Qur'an instructs the believers to come dressed, deliberately and well.

The commentators record the occasions this addresses. Al-Ṭabarī transmits reports that the pre-Islamic Arabs would circumambulate the Kaʿbah naked — men by day, women by night — with a rationale drawn from the world of the jinn and from the idea that one should not circle the House in garments in which one had sinned. Other reports attach the verse to the Jews and Christians, who had forbidden themselves certain good food and certain clothing in ascetic observance, and to those among the Arabs who had dedicated certain of their livestock and crops and would not eat or wear them. The command answers all of them at once: what God has made lawful is lawful, and the place of worship is precisely where the gifts of God should be brought into view.

**Worship and Dignity**

The word *zīnah* is the same word used in 7:32, where God defends the adornments He has brought forth for His servants — the two verses are a pair, one granting and one commanding. Taken together they form the Qur'an's refusal of two opposite errors. The first is the ascetic error: the notion that God is honored by the rejection of the good things He gave, that piety is measured in shabbiness and self-denial. The second is the error of the naked circumambulation, where religion was used to strip away the very covering God provided.

The Prophet ﷺ embodied the middle path. He wore clean clothes, disliked disorder in appearance, and told a man who came looking unkempt that God loves to see the traces of His favour upon His servants. His guidance on arriving for prayer was cleanliness of body and garment, the use of scent for the assembly, and a deliberate attention to appearance that distinguished the Muslim gathering from a performance of poverty. That is the practice this verse legislates: the place of worship is where a human being presents himself before his Lord, and the presentation is part of the worship.

**"Eat and Drink, But Do Not Be Prodigal"**

The second half of the verse turns from dress to appetite, and it does so with the same reasoning. *Kulū wa-shrabū wa-lā tusrifū* — eat and drink, and do not exceed. The permission comes first, in the imperative, and it is not qualified by any condition of poverty of spirit. The prohibition that follows is not against enjoyment but against excess, and the Qur'an's term for that excess is *isrāf*, from the root *s-r-f*: to go beyond the limit, to pour water past the brim.

The Book repeats the prohibition as a settled principle: *“Eat from the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful.”* (6:141); *“Do not spend wastefully; surely the wasteful are like brothers to the devils, and the Devil is ever ungrateful to his Lord”* (17:26–27); *“They are those who spend neither wastefully nor stingily, but moderately in between”* (25:67). The last verse describes the servants of the All-Merciful, and the standard it gives — neither the open hand of the wastrel nor the clenched fist of the miser — is the balance this sūrah has been teaching since it placed a scale on the Day of Judgment.

**The Hadith of the Stomach**

The Prophet ﷺ gave the ethic of 7:31 its most concrete expression. From Miqdām ibn Maʿdī Karib, he said: *“The human being does not fill any vessel worse than his stomach. It is enough for the son of Adam to eat a few morsels to keep his back straight. But if he must eat more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath.”* (al-Tirmidhī 2380, from al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by al-Tirmidhī and ṣaḥīḥ by Dār al-Salām). The tradition read this hadith as a rule of bodily discipline with spiritual consequences: the full stomach produces a sluggish heart, and the appetite that is never denied becomes the door through which every other appetite enters.

The verse's final clause makes the prohibition theological rather than hygienic: *innahu lā yuḥibbu al-musrifīn* — He does not love the extravagant. The Quranic formula of God's love and its absence is the Book's way of ranking conduct on the scale of relationship rather than of legality. Extravagance is not merely unwise; it is the kind of conduct a person engages in when he has stopped seeing the One who provided. That is why the verse appears where it does, after a chapter on provisioning (7:10), a chapter on covering (7:26), and a chapter on the enemy who strips cover away (7:27). Ingratitude, exposure, excess — three names for the same misplacement — and the remedy offered is one: to take, deliberately and gratefully, what God has sent down, and not one measure more.


**The Occasion Reported for the Command**

The commentators report an occasion for these verses in a practice of the pre-Islamic pilgrimage: certain tribes went round the Kaʿbah unclothed, some defending the practice as inherited rite and others as renunciation, and the command to take one’s adornment at every place of worship is read as addressed to it. The occasion matters because it fixes the direction of the argument. The prohibition here is not against excess of dress but against its absence in worship; the deficiency was the offence, and the deficiency was being defended as piety.

That is why the command about clothing is paired with the command about food and drink. Both are permissions with a limit attached — dress, eat, drink, and do not exceed — and the jurists took from the pairing a rule about worship generally: the beauty of the outward state belongs to the act rather than being added to it as an ornament, and a person who strips himself of what God permitted has not become more devout but less obedient. The sūrah will state the same rule as a question in the verse that follows this one.
