**Isrāf and Tabdhīr**

The word for the excess forbidden here is *isrāf*, and the Book distinguishes it from a second word for waste, *tabdhīr*. The commentators draw the line by direction: *isrāf* is excess in what is itself permitted, spending past the measure on a lawful thing, while *tabdhīr* is spending on what ought not to be spent on at all — the word used where the wasteful are assigned a company: *“Surely the wasteful are ˹like˺ brothers to the devils. And the Devil is ever ungrateful to his Lord.”* (17:27).

The same prohibition is attached elsewhere to a specific act of worship, which shows how the limit works in practice: *“Eat from the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful.”* (6:141). There the excess is measured against a due already owed — the harvest has a claim on the crop, and consuming past what remains once the claim is discharged is the *isrāf* named here. Verse 31 states the rule for the table and the wardrobe; 6:141 states it for the field.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:32

> **Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?” Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life, but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment. This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question That Indicts the Questioner**

*Man ḥarrama zīnata Allāh* — who has forbidden the adornment Allah has brought forth for His servants? The construction is a question, but its force is that of a challenge, because the answer it invites is silence. No one in the sūrah's audience could claim a divine warrant for the prohibitions they had invented, and the verse makes the absence of a warrant visible by asking for it in public.

The Qur'an is careful with what follows. The adornment is not described as a human possession; it is *Allāh's* adornment, *allatī akhraja li-ʿibādihi* — which He brought out for His servants. The possessive construction repeats in two directions: the beauty belongs to God, and its purpose is the welfare of the people who serve Him. To forbid it is not austerity but expropriation — the removal of a gift from the beneficiaries God Himself designated.

**The Long History of Pious Prohibition**

The verse is addressing a pattern, not a single practice. The commentators attach it to several: the Arabs who set aside certain livestock and crops as *baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*, and *waṣīlah*, declaring them forbidden by religious vow (5:103; 6:138–139); the People of the Book who forbade themselves foods that God had never forbidden (3:93; 4:160; 6:146); and the ascetics, referred to in the Qur'an's own words about monasticism: *“As for monasticism, they made it up — We never ordained it for them — only seeking to please Allah…” (57:27)* (57:27).

The Book's attitude to all of them is consistent. Self-denial is not a virtue in itself, and legislation that God did not issue is not worship but a claim upon His authority. The Prophet ﷺ made the principle explicit when he heard that some of his companions had resolved to fast continuously, to stand all night in prayer, and to abstain from marriage: he refused to have anything to do with such a discipline and said, *“But I fast and break the fast, I pray and sleep, and I marry — so whoever turns away from my practice is not of me”* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401). The response is not a rebuke of devotion; it is the rejection of devotion conducted by a law that God did not write.

**"For the Enjoyment of the Believers in This Worldly Life, and Exclusively Theirs on the Day of Judgment"**

The verse's second half is a statement about ownership, and it answers a question the first audience disputed. Some had argued that the good things of the world were destined for the believers alone, or that non-Muslims enjoyed them illegitimately; others held the opposite, that the Hereafter offered something thinner than the pleasures of the present life. The verse settles both: *khāliṣatan lahum yawma al-qiyāmah* — they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment.

Al-Ṭabarī records the readings. The dominant one is that in this world the good things are shared — the rain falls on everyone, the fields of the ungrateful yield as well as those of the grateful — and in the Hereafter the good things will be pure, reserved, and without the mixing that characterizes a world in which the righteous and the wicked live side by side. This is what the Book means elsewhere when it says of the Garden that its reward is past imagining — *“No soul can imagine what delights are kept in store for them”* (32:17) — and that its people *“will have whatever they desire”* (50:35; 16:31; 39:34; 42:22; see also 41:31, *“There you will have whatever your souls desire”*). The promise is not that the believer will be repaid in kind; it is that the enjoyment of the good will finally be untroubled.

The verse closes: *This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge.* The phrase is not decorative. The dispute about permitted and forbidden is, in the Qur'an's analysis, an epistemic dispute: it arises where knowledge has been replaced by custom, fear, or self-importance. Al-Rāzī makes the point sharply: the question of what God has permitted is answered by revelation, and where revelation has spoken, no further authority may add to it.

**Two Pieties the Verse Rejects by Name**

The question *who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought out for His servants?* answers two opposite errors, and the Book answers each of them elsewhere in its own terms. The first is the piety that treats the good things of the world as inherently defiling: Sūrat al-Māʾidah commands, *“Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors”* (5:87), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf itself had laid the foundation two verses earlier: *“Eat and drink, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful”* (7:31). The second error is the licence that reads the verse as permission for excess, and the same clause rules it out: the lawful is *ṭayyib*, good, and the Book's command is to eat it with gratitude (2:172; 16:114), not to gorge on it.

The Prophet ﷺ settled the first error with a scene that has become the standard commentary on this verse. Anas ibn Mālik reports that three men came to the houses of the Prophet's wives asking about his worship; when it was described to them, they treated it as insufficient and each vowed an extreme: prayer all night, fasting without a break, and celibacy. The Prophet came out and said, *“Are you the ones who said such and such? By Allah, I am the most God-fearing and pious among you, yet I fast and I break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me”* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401).

The sūrah's case is doctrinal rather than merely disciplinary, and its final clause states it: the good things of God are *for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life*, and *exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment*. The believer's enjoyment of what God permits is not a concession to weakness, and it is not shared with the Hereafter, where it becomes his alone — a reallocation that quietly reverses the whole economy of Makkah, whose notables had assumed that the pleasant things of God were theirs in this world and would remain theirs in the next.


Adornment Provided: Clothes and Armour Among the Gifts

The question at 7:32 asks who has forbidden the adornment Allah has brought out for His servants, and the Book describes the bringing out in concrete terms: *“He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle.”* (16:81)

The sūrah's own account of clothing makes the same point from the other direction. At 7:26 clothing is given to cover and as adornment, and the verse adds that the clothing of mindfulness is better. The two verses of al-Aʿrāf are therefore not in tension: the adornment is provided, and a better covering is named beside it

The verse's answer is given in the same form as its question: say that the adornments are for those who believe in this life, and exclusively theirs on the Day of Resurrection. The restriction is temporal rather than moral. A thing enjoyed by believers and unbelievers alike in this life becomes the property of the believers alone in the next, and the sūrah's accounts show the enjoyment continuing in the towns right up to the destruction


Eat and Be Grateful: The Lawful and Its Use

The permission of 7:32 is matched by a command about its use: *“So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you”* (16:114). The verse of an-Naḥl joins the eating to gratitude and to worship, which is the use the sūrah's verse assumes

What this adds to 7:32 is the ground of the prohibition the verse rejects. A thing forbidden by human decree is not received with gratitude, since the gratitude would be directed at a permission no one gave. The verse of an-Naḥl places gratitude inside worship, and the verse of al-Aʿrāf places the adornments inside a provision brought out by Allah

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:33

> **Say, “My Lord has only forbidden open and secret indecencies, sinfulness, unjust aggression, associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized—and attributing to Allah what you do not know.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-List**

Verse 33 answers the question of verse 32 by supplying the actual prohibitions: *qul innamā ḥarrama rabbī* — say, my Lord has only forbidden. The *innamā* is a tool of restriction: this list, and nothing but this list, is what the divine prohibition contains. The verse is therefore simultaneously a prohibition and a defence of liberty — an authoritative statement that whatever lies outside these categories has not been forbidden, and that no one may place it under interdict on God's behalf.

**The Five Forbidden Things**

The list that follows has a considered order.

*Al-fawāḥish* — indecencies, *mā ẓahara minhā wa-mā baṭan*: what is open of them and what is hidden. The word *fāḥishah* covers sexual immorality in the broadest Qur'anic sense — the act that is shameful by nature and that every sound tradition has recognized as such. The phrase *outward and inward* is the verse's own insistence that the prohibition is not merely about conduct. It reaches the intention, the imagination, the private arrangement, and the intention that never reaches conduct. The Book repeats the same pairing elsewhere — *“Shun all sin—open and secret”* (6:120) — and the Prophet ﷺ summarized the whole doctrine in a single sentence: *“Verily, Allah does not look at your faces or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.”* (Muslim 2564, from Abū Hurayrah).

*Wa-l-ithm* — and sin. Commentators differ on the specific extension: some read it as the class of sins generally, others as intoxicants by a well-attested usage of *ithm* in the Arabic of the Qur'an (2:219; see also 5:90), others as the inward malice that leads to wrong. The placement between indecency and aggression is instructive, because it is the middle term: an act whose harm is not bodily, whose shame may be unacknowledged, and which lies between the violation of the self and the violation of others.

*Wa-l-baghy bi-ghayr al-ḥaqq* — and wrongful aggression, transgression without right. *Baghy* is the overstepping of a boundary against another person: the seizure of what is not one's own, the abuse of power, the arrogant exercise of superiority. The qualifier *without right* is a reminder that not every use of force is aggression; the verse acknowledges a legitimate claim without defining it here, and the sūrah's later legal passages will. The Qur'an ranks *baghy* among the most serious of social sins, and the Islamic tradition identified it as the characteristic sin of the powerful.

*Wa-an tushrikū bi-Allāh mā lam yunazzil bihi sulṭānā* — and that you associate others with Allah, a practice He has never authorized. The word is *sulṭān*: evidence, warrant, authorization. The Qur'an does not merely say that idolatry is incomplete; it says that the classes of things worshiped besides God are, without exception, unsupported by any evidence. This is a challenge to produce a warrant, and it is issued repeatedly in the Book with the same confidence (10:68; 16:116; 34:22; 46:4).

*Wa-an taqūlū ʿalā Allāh mā lā taʿlamūn* — and that you say of God what you do not know. The list closes with the offense the sūrah has already met: the invented religious claim of verse 28. Its placement last, after the great sins, is a deliberate ranking. Speech about God without knowledge is the root from which fabricated laws, corrupted religion, and misdirected worship grow; it is the sin that makes all the others possible to legislate.

**The Parallel Lists**

This verse sits inside one of the Qur'an's most systematic treatments of the divine moral law. Sūrat al-Anʿām gives the longer version: *“Come! Let me recite to you what your Lord has forbidden to you: do not associate others with Him ˹in worship˺. ˹Do not fail to˺ honour your parents. Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for you and for them. Do not come near indecencies, openly or secretly. Do not take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right. This is what He has commanded you, so perhaps you will understand.”* (6:151), continuing through the orphan's property, honest measure, and truthful speech (6:152). Sūrat al-Isrāʾ gives a third version in a passage of some thirty verses (17:22–39). The three passages are usually read together by scholars, who observe that the Qur'an restates the same moral core in different contexts — which itself tells the reader that the essentials of the divine law are stable, known, and not adaptable by the preferences of a generation.

**What the Verse Does with Guilt**

One practical effect of the list deserves to be named. By restricting the divine prohibition to named categories, the verse liberates the conscience from invented burden. People who live under a religion of unnumbered prohibitions — the anxious, the scrupulous, those who fear that pleasure itself is a trespass — are given here an authoritative short list and told that the graces God brought out for His servants are theirs to enjoy.

But the list also closes a door in the other direction. A person may not conclude that the moral life is exhausted by avoiding the five categories; the same sūrah is full of commands, and the Book contains hundreds of others. What the verse establishes is a jurisdictional limit: the right to declare a thing forbidden belongs to God, exercised through revelation; and the one who exercises it in God's name without knowledge has placed himself, by this verse's own account, inside the list.


**No Authority Sent Down**

The fourth item in the list carries a clause of its own: associating others with God, *a practice He has never authorized*. The qualification states the ground of the prohibition — not the practice’s offensiveness but the absence of warrant — and the Book puts the same criterion to work in its polemic: *“Or do they have associate-gods who have ordained for them some ˹polytheistic˺ beliefs, which Allah has not authorized?”* (42:21).

The word behind the clause is *sulṭān*, an authority that can be produced, and this sūrah has already used it of the names given to idols (7:71). Its appearance inside the list is what makes the list a legal text rather than a moral one. A prohibition stated with its ground can be tested: produce the warrant and the practice stands, fail to produce it and the practice falls, whatever its antiquity or its popularity. The fifth item names the same failure from the other direction — attributing to God what one does not know — so the last two enclose the first three with the condition under which anything may be required of a person.


**The Default the Pair of Verses Establishes**

This verse is preceded by a question that carries as much of a ruling as the list does: *“Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?”* (7:32). The two together give the jurists the principle they state as the default: things are permitted until a prohibition is established, and prohibitions are established by warrant rather than by preference.

The Book states the principle from inside a ruling on food, where the list is explicitly closed: *“I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah.”* (6:145). The form of that sentence is the point — a search of what has been revealed, an exception, and nothing beyond it. Verse 33 belongs to the same discipline. Its five items enumerate what has been forbidden, and the enumeration is the reason a sixth may not be added by anyone who has not been given it.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:34

> **For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Law Written into History**

*Wa-li-kulli ummatin ajal* — for each community there is an appointed term. Having closed the list of what God has forbidden, the sūrah returns to the theme it opened with: the destroyed towns of verses 4 and 5, the account of verses 6 and 9. The verse supplies the principle behind those scenes. The nations of the past were not struck at random; each had a span, and each span ended.

The pairing of the two nouns deserves attention. *Ummah* is not merely a political unit; the word comes from *amm*, to head toward, and it names a body of people oriented by a shared direction — a community following a way. *Ajal* is the term set for a debt, the moment at which a thing's time has run out. The two together describe something the Qur'an treats as a fixed feature of the created order: communities have a lifetime as surely as individuals do, and their orientation determines what fills it.

**The Same Sentence, Repeated in the Book**

The verse's second half is one of the most repeated formulas in the Qur'an: *lā yastaʾkhirūna sāʿatan wa-lā yastaqdimūn*. It appears in the sūrah of Yūnus, in Sūrat al-Naḥl, in al-Muʾminūn, and elsewhere with the same insistence (10:49; 16:61; 23:43; 7:34; 34:30). The repetition is not a stylistic habit; the Book repeats what its audience is most inclined to forget.

*Sāʿah* means an hour, and the verse's point is its smallness: not that a community may not receive an extension of years, but that not even an hour can be negotiated. The two verbs are the crucial ones — *yastaʾkhirūn*, to put off, and *yastaqdimūn*, to bring forward. The first closes the hope of the procrastinator, who assumes that the deadline can be renegotiated. The second closes the door on the anxious, who fears that his hour may come too soon and who tries to make his arrangements as though he could hurry or delay the decree. Neither is possible, and the verse's grammar states the symmetry exactly: the term can neither be delayed for a moment nor advanced.

Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn restates the law at the level of the individual soul: *“Allah never delays a soul when its appointed time comes”* (63:11). And Sūrat Āl ʿImrān says the same thing from the opposite angle, as a comfort: *“No soul can ever die without Allah's Will at the destined time”* (3:145) — no one dies early, no one is cheated of a moment that was his.

**What the Verse Is Doing in This Place**

The placement is deliberate. The preceding verses listed the forbidden things; the verses that follow describe the messengers who come to warn and the fate of those who deny them (7:35–36). Between the law and the warning, the sūrah inserts the fact of the term. The logic is the logic of the whole chapter: the warning is urgent because the time in which it can be answered is not unlimited.

Al-Ṭabarī notes a second function of the verse here. The sūrah's original audience was watching the Prophet's community grow and calculating its odds in the terms of Quraysh's own experience — a new movement in a city of established powers. The verse tells them what the history of the nations of the Book had already demonstrated: no community is destroyed before its term, and no community survives past it. The Qurayshi leaders who dismissed Muhammad ﷺ as a passing fever were themselves a community with a term, and so, for that matter, was the community of the believers.

**The Use of the Doctrine**

The Islamic tradition drew two practical conclusions from this verse and its parallels. The first is that urgency belongs to the individual and not to the world. A person cannot know whether his own term will end today; the Book's counsel is that this uncertainty is the structure of moral seriousness, which is why it says that *no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow* (31:34) and *no soul knows in what land it will die* (31:34). The Prophet ﷺ reinforced it with an instruction reported from Ibn ʿUmar: *“Be in this world as a stranger or a traveler”* (al-Bukhārī 6416, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar) — a saying that turns the doctrine of the term into a way of carrying one's possessions.

The second conclusion is the patience it produces in communal life. A fixed term means that the rise and fall of nations is administered by a decree rather than by the maneuverings that seem to decide events. The sūrah's readers were told, in effect, that they did not need to worry about the calendar of history — only about what they did inside the hours assigned to them. The whole of the Book's attitude toward political defeat, economic decline, and the appearance of the enemies' triumph rests on this verse's arithmetic. There is no hour to be regained from the past and none to be borrowed from the future. What exists is the present term, and the account that will be taken when it closes.

The sūrah's placement of the doctrine in the middle of its prohibitions gives it a practical edge: a community that knows its term is being addressed is a community that cannot pretend its choices are weightless, and the Book's address to the Prophet's city works exactly that way.


**The Term in the Book’s Vocabulary**

The word for the appointed term is *ajal*, and the Book distinguishes two terms under that name: *“He is the One Who created you from clay, then appointed a term ˹for your death˺ and another known only to Him ˹for your resurrection˺”* (6:2). The bracketed glosses are the translators’, and they record the commentators’ reading — one *ajal* expires at a death, the other at the Hour, and the second is known to God alone.

Verse 34 applies the first kind of term to communities rather than to persons, and that extension is the verse’s real claim: a town has a term the way a body does. It is what allows the sūrah’s histories to be told as a sequence of completed periods instead of moral examples floating outside time. Each town arrives, is addressed, refuses or accepts, and ends, and the ending is dated. The doctrine is also what lets the sūrah speak of its own audience’s moment as a moment — with a term attached — rather than as an open field in which nothing is ever settled.


**Neither Delayed nor Advanced**

The clause is echoed almost word for word in Sūrah al-Naḥl, where the same rule is given first as a mercy and then as a limit: *“If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for their wrongdoing, He would not have left a single living being on earth. But He delays them for an appointed term. And when their time arrives, they cannot delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it.”* (16:61).

Read together, the two verses give the doctrine its full shape. The delay is the mercy, and it is why every town in this sūrah had time to be warned and why its hearers still have time. The immovability is the guarantee that the delay is not indefinite. The verse’s placement between the histories and the sūrah’s closing addresses makes it operate as a rule rather than a comment: each town the reader has just passed through had a term, and the term’s arrival is described in language admitting no negotiation, no extension and no appeal.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:35

> **O children of Adam! When messengers from among yourselves come to you reciting My revelations—whoever shuns evil and mends their ways, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Messengers From Among You**

The verse returns to the address that has organized this whole passage: *O children of Adam.* And this time the subject is the arrival of revelation in human form: *immā yaʾtiyannakum rusulun minkum* — should there come to you messengers from among yourselves. The phrase *min anfusikum*, from your own selves, is the sūrah's standing answer to the Makkans' most persistent objection.

That objection is recorded in the Qur'an's own words in at least four places. The Makkans said, *“What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places?”* (25:7). They said that a messenger should be accompanied by an angel (17:92–93). They asked why the Qur'an had not been given to some great man of influence (43:31). The Book's answer is consistent and this verse is part of it: the messenger is *from among you*, because a revelation addressed to human beings must reach them through a channel that shares their condition. The Book states the underlying principle more than once: *“We did not send ˹messengers˺ before you ˹O Prophet˺ except mere men inspired by Us”* (16:43; 21:7; see also 12:109, *“We only sent before you ˹O Prophet˺ men inspired by Us”*).

The wisdom is worth spelling out. A messenger who was not one of us could not demonstrate that the life he demands is livable; his purity would be a fact about a different kind of being. A messenger who is one of us can be scrutinized, followed, touched, and copied — and the Qur'an's insistence on the humanness of its messengers is precisely the Islamic answer to every later doctrine that made a mediator of another nature. Islam's Prophet is a man who ate in the marketplace, whose wives and neighbors knew him, and whose conduct has been transmitted with a biographical precision unmatched in the history of religion.

**"Reciting My Revelations to You"**

The message is described with the verb *yaquṣṣūna*, from the same root as *qiṣṣah* — the step-by-step recounting. Revelation in this verse is not a formula to be accepted but a narrative to be followed: the messengers *recount* the signs, one after another, so that the hearer can see the pattern. It is the same verb the sūrah used in verse 7 for the divine recounting on the Day of Judgment, and the echo is intended: what is recounted here in warning will be recited there in judgment.

**The Two Conditions**

The promise that follows has two conditions: *fa-mani ittaqā wa-aṣlaḥa* — then whoever shuns evil and mends their ways. The pair deserves to be examined, because it is the sūrah's summary of what is demanded of the hearer of a prophet, and it names the two dimensions of a life that is being renewed.

*Ittaqā* is the verbal form of *taqwā* — the reverent caution that guards against the divine displeasure, the inward disposition the sūrah named two verses ago as the best of all garments (7:26). It is the vertical axis, and it comes first, because the horizontals of religion are parasitic on it.

*Wa-aṣlaḥa* is the form of *iṣlāḥ*, to repair. Its object is deliberately unspecified, and the commentators have drawn the silence out: the person who is reverent repairs whatever in his condition needs repair — the wrong he has done, the harm he has caused, the property he has taken, the relationship he has broken. The Qur'an uses the word for the making of peace between people (49:9–10), for the improvement of one's own conduct (4:128), and in the mouth of Shuʿayb as the banner of his mission: *“I only intend reform to the best of my ability”* (11:88).

The order matters. Reverence without repair produces a piety that leaves its damages in place; repair without reverence produces an ethics with no anchor. The verse asks for both, and it puts the fear of God first for the reason the whole sūrah has been demonstrating: a person who does not measure himself against the command will never quite see what needs repairing.

**The Formula of Security**

The verse closes with a phrase that recurs in the Qur'an in almost identical form: *fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn* — there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve. It appears in al-Baqarah for the followers of guidance (2:38), for the believers in the broadest sense (2:62; 5:69), for those who reform (6:48), for the friends of God (10:62), and for those who remain steadfast (46:13). The tradition's commentators found a distinction in its two halves: no fear for what lies ahead, and no grief for what is behind — the two directions in which human anxiety runs, closed by one clause.

The word *khawf* means fear of a coming evil; *ḥuzn* means sorrow for something lost. Between them they cover the whole of what unsettles a human life. And the verse locates their removal not in external security but in the two conditions it has just named. The reverent and repairing person has nothing to fear from the future, because his account is in order, and nothing to grieve over in the past, because what was amiss he has mended. That is the promise held out to the children of Adam at the end of the passage that began with a whisper in a garden.


**The Formula of Security**

The promise closing the verse — no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve — is a fixed formula in the Book, and its repetition states what the two conditions buy. Sūrah al-Baqarah gives the same formula with its own condition attached: *“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.”* (2:112). The condition there, submitting and doing good, is the condition here in other words: shunning evil and mending.

The commentators read the two halves of the formula as covering the two directions in which a person is exposed. Fear belongs to what is coming and grief to what has passed; a promise removing both takes the future and the past away as objects of distress and leaves the present, which is where the conditions are performed. That is why the formula is attached to a conditional sentence rather than to a name or a lineage: the security is not inherited, and it is not forfeited by a past that has been mended.


**Messengers From Among Yourselves**

The opening clause states the form guidance will take — messengers from among you, reciting My revelations — and the Book defends that form against the demand for another: *“Had there been angels walking the earth, well settled, We would have surely sent down for them an angel from heaven as a messenger.”* (17:95). A human messenger is not a concession to human weakness. On the Book’s own reasoning he is the only kind of messenger a human community could take instruction from, because the instruction includes how to live in a body, in a town and in a market.

That is the weight of *from among yourselves* here. The sūrah has just put the same phrase in the reminder given to ʿĀd (7:69) and uses it again of the towns it surveys; in this verse it is addressed to the whole species, in the last of the four calls to the children of Adam. The recitation named in the clause is a second guarantee: the messenger not only arrives from among you, he brings something that can be heard, repeated and checked — which is what makes the two conditions that follow possible to perform at all.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:36

> **But those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Rejection With Contempt**

The previous verse described the reverent who mend; this one describes the opposite, and it does not simply say that they disbelieved. The Arabic is *alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā wa-stakbarū ʿanhā* — those who denied Our signs *and treated them with disdain*. Two acts, joined by *wa*: denial, and then the arrogance that refuses to take them seriously.

The distinction is not a redundancy. A person may deny a claim and still treat it with the respect due to a serious proposition; he may weigh it, reject it on grounds, and remain answerable for his reasoning. What this verse names is the other posture: the refusal to grant the claim a hearing, the turning away of the proud man who is offended by the thought that he might be addressed. Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn's image of the arrogant is that they turn their heads aside (63:5); Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own image, six verses later, will be the camel and the needle's eye.

**The Echo of Iblīs**

The word *istakbara* is the same word the sūrah used for Iblīs in verse 12 — *abā wa-stakbara*, he refused and was arrogant — and in al-Baqarah's account of the same scene, *“who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful”* (2:34). The echo is structural. The sūrah opened its narrative with a creature destroyed by arrogance against a command; here, at the end of the passage addressed to the children of Adam, the same word describes the fate of those who meet the signs of God with disdain. The chapter's answer to its own opening story is that arrogance is not a historical curiosity in the biography of one jinn. It is the recurring disposition that turns rejection into final loss.

Narrative aside, the Book treats *istikbār* as a category of its own with a specific destination. *“Your Lord has proclaimed: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60). *“On the Day of Judgment you will see those who lied about Allah with their faces gloomy. Is Hell not a fitting home for the arrogant?”* (39:60). *“The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels nearest to Allah. Those who are too proud and arrogant to worship Him will be brought before Him all together.”* (4:172). The last verse is notable for who is included: even the highest created beings are said never to be too proud, which leaves the human arrogance of 7:36 with no model to imitate and no company.

**The Definition the Prophet Gave**

The sūrah's readers would have understood the word, but the Prophet ﷺ defined it, and the definition is a small masterpiece of precision: *“Arrogance is rejecting the truth and belittling people”* (Muslim 91, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd). A single sentence, two halves, and both are present in this verse.

*Rejecting the truth* is the denial: *kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā*. *Belittling people* is what the arrogant posture does to the messenger and to the community of the weak whom the message gathers — and the sūrah's own account of the Makkan leadership is a study in exactly that (see 7:75–76, where the proud ask whether they should believe as the poor do). The Prophet's definition leaves no room for the self-flattering interpretation of arrogance as dignity. In his sentence, it is not a feeling about oneself at all; it is a pair of actions, one toward God's truth and one toward His creatures.

He also stated the consequence in a form this verse's audience would have grasped immediately: *“No one who has an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise”* (Muslim 91, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd). The sūrah will shortly translate the same verdict into the image of the gates and the needle.

**"The Residents of the Fire"**

The sentence is stated flatly: *fa-ulāʾika aṣḥāb al-nār*, they are the companions of the Fire; *hum fīhā khālidūn*, they will abide there. Two words carry the theology.

*Aṣḥāb* is the vocabulary of companionship and ownership — the term Arabic uses for the owner of a thing, the companion of a person, the people of a place. The Qur'an could have said, "they will be put in the fire"; it says they are *its people*. The relationship is one of settled residence, which is what the word *khālidūn*, abiding forever, then states explicitly.

The Messenger of God's description of the same place preserves the sūrah's insistence that what ends there began as a manner of dealing with the truth. The Prophet ﷺ said that the Fire will be brought forward on the Day with seventy thousand bridles, each held by seventy thousand angels, and that it will arrive with its people. What the verse establishes is not an arbitrary sentence but the completion of a relationship: the servant who despised the signs spent his life elsewhere, and is placed with the objects of his attention.

**The Contempt That Costs Nothing Until It Costs Everything**

One final observation belongs to the psychology of the verse, and the sūrah has prepared for it. *Istikbār* was the cheapest option available to Iblīs: a feeling, requiring no act, expressed in nothing but a refusal to bend. It was, by any worldly measure, a low-cost choice. That is what makes it so dangerous, because it is the reason the proud do not recognize the moment of their loss. Nothing happened; no deed was performed; no harm was done to another; and a creature's destiny quietly closed the other way.

The children of Adam are warned at the end of a passage about clothing, food, and worship — all of it tangible, all of it actionable — and this verse names the one thing an otherwise decent life can carry into damnation. Disdain does not look like sin. It looks like standards.


**Residents of the Fire: The Same Sentence in al-Baqarah**

Al-Baqarah states the verse’s sentence almost word for word: *“But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”* (2:39). The two verses differ in one term — 7:36 adds arrogance to denial — and agree in everything else, including the closing clause of permanence.

The addition is the verse’s own contribution. Denial alone describes a judgment about the signs; arrogance describes a posture toward them. The sūrah has just given the posture its archetype in Iblīs, whose refusal was stated as a claim of superiority (7:12), and 2:39 is therefore the general rule of which 7:36 is the qualified case.

The exegetes read the qualification as decisive. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the verse is placed before the description of the parties at the Heights (7:46–49), so that the reader knows what separates them: not the record of deeds alone but the manner in which the signs were received.


**Endless Ages**

The verse’s final clause states the duration. An-Nabaʾ states it in the terms of the Fire’s own inhabitants: *“where they will remain for ˹endless˺ ages.”* (78:23). The noun is *aḥqāb*, the plural of *ḥuqub*, a long stretch of time, and the verse describes remaining inside it rather than passing through it.

The two verses belong together because neither is a threat addressed to an opponent. 7:36 is a description of a class, given before the histories begin; 78:23 is part of a description of the Day. Both state permanence as a property of the place rather than as a sentence pronounced on an individual, which is why the sūrah can use the statement to frame its narratives.

This is the function of the verse in the sūrah’s architecture. The five towns that follow it are destroyed inside time, with terms appointed and signs given; the class described here is placed outside time. The reader is told at the outset what the histories are leading to, and the histories themselves are then free to be about the interval.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:37

> **Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations? They will receive what is destined for them, until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls, asking them, “Where are those ˹false gods˺ you used to invoke besides Allah?” They will cry, “They have failed us,” and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Crimes That Head the List**

*Fa-man aẓlamu mimman iftarā ʿalā Allāh kadhiban aw kadhdhaba bi-āyātihi* — who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations? The interrogative is rhetorical in form and absolute in force: the question has no answer other than the one the verse has just named. The sūrah has been circling this pair for ten verses. The lie against God was committed by those who said *God has commanded us thus* (7:28) and by those who forbade what God had made lawful (7:32). The denial of the signs was the disdain of verse 36.

The Book repeats this superlative with striking consistency. *“Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed”* (6:21). *“Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah or claims, ‘I have received revelations!’—although nothing was revealed to them”* (6:93). *“Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah? They will be brought before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, ‘These are the ones who lied against their Lord’”* (11:18). *“Who then does more wrong than those who lie about Allah and reject the truth after it has reached them?”* (39:32). The cumulative effect of the repetition is to establish a hierarchy in the Qur'anic understanding of sin: the gravest wrong is not violence but the corruption of the channel through which God is known — either by inventing a message in His name or by refusing the message He sent.

**"They Will Receive What Is Destined for Them"**

The next clause has been read in two ways by the commentators, and both readings are instructive. *Fa-ulāʾika yanāluhum naṣībuhum min al-kitāb* — they will receive what is destined for them.

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī record the first reading: the *kitāb* is the decree, the record of what has been written for each soul, and the verse states that whatever share of provision or punishment has been apportioned will be delivered in full — nothing withheld, nothing adrift. The second reading takes *kitāb* as the scripture itself: their portion of what was revealed will reach them, whether they receive it as guidance and reject it, or hear it only as a testimony against them at the reckoning.

The two readings converge on a single idea that the sūrah has been building since its first verses. Nothing owed to a person fails to arrive. The record of verses 6 to 9 — the question, the recounting, the weighing — is a description of an accounting that cannot lose any part of its data. The phrase *will reach them* is the Book's reassurance that the encounter with the truth is not optional and not avoidable: a message that has been delivered is delivered, and the one who walks away from it has not escaped the meeting, only deferred it.

**The Messenger-Angels Who Arrive to Take Their Souls**

*Ḥattā idhā jāʾathum rusulunā yatawaffawnahum* — until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls. The messengers here are the angels of death, and the Qur'an gives their work a vocabulary of precision. Sūrat al-Sajdah names the office: *“Your soul will be taken by the Angel of Death, who is in charge of you. Then to your Lord you will ˹all˺ be returned.”* (32:11). Sūrat al-Anʿām describes the process of the *tawaffī*, the taking of the soul: *“He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you. When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul, never neglecting this duty.”* (6:61). And where the death is a punishment, the account is harsher: *“If only you could see when the angels take the souls of the disbelievers, beating their faces and backs”* (8:50; see also 47:27).

There is a deep congruence between the sūrah's structure and this verse. Its first scene was a courtroom — the question, the book, the scale. The same court is now shown convening at the bedside of a single person, and the questions are asked in the past tense of a life that has just closed.

**The Question and Its Answer**

*Ayna mā kuntum tadʿūna min dūni Allāh* — where are those ˹false gods˺ you used to invoke besides Allah? The interrogation is the exact fulfillment of what the sūrah warned in verse 30: the patrons who were taken as protectors instead of God are now the objects of a demand. And the answer the dying person gives is the shortest sentence in the verse: *qālū ḍallū ʿannā* — they said, they have failed us.

**"They Will Confess Against Themselves"**

The verse closes with self-condemnation: *wa-shahidū ʿalā anfusihim annahum kānū kāfirīn* — and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers. The courtroom that has stamped the whole sūrah now gets its confession, and it is not extracted by the prosecutor. Sūrat al-Anʿām has the same formula: *“˹Today˺ you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time”* (6:94), and the interrogation of the jinn and humans ends with their own admission — *“We confess against ourselves!”* (6:130; see also 41:21, where the skin itself testifies). Sūrat al-Qiyāmah puts the principle as a general law of the human constitution: *“In fact, people will testify against their own souls, despite the excuses they come up with”* (75:14–15).

The verse thus ends with the last form of the argument this sūrah has been making since verse 16. Iblīs blamed God; the townspeople of verse 5 confessed too late; the fabricators of verse 28 denied knowing better. This verse shows the door closed on every one of those positions at the hour of death, when the excuses have run out because the memory that produced them is intact and its owner is the one reading it aloud to himself. The passage began with the children of Adam and a whisper in a garden; it ends with their descendants bearing witness against themselves, and no one in the room to blame.


The Messenger-Angels Who Arrive: The Same Scene in an-Naḥl

7:37 moves from a charge to a scene. Those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations receive what is destined for them, and then the messenger-angels arrive to take their souls. The arrival is described in al-Anʿām's account of the same moment, with a detail 7:37 leaves out: *“Those whose souls the angels seize while they wrong themselves will then offer ˹full˺ submission”* (16:28). The submission offered at the gate is the confession that 7:37 reports a few words later, and the two verses describe one event from two angles. Al-Aʿrāf gives the charge that precedes the arrival; an-Naḥl gives the words spoken at it.

The wording of the charge is what makes the scene intelligible. Fabricating a lie against Allah and denying His revelations are the two crimes the sūrah returns to at every turn, and the verse treats them as a pair because they are two forms of one act: saying about Allah what is not so. The people of the towns do both

The arrival is at the soul rather than at the body, and the verse closes with the same framing: they will confess against themselves that they were disbelievers. The confession is made by those who denied, and it is made when denial is no longer possible


Where Are Those You Called: The Question Put at the Gate

The question the angels ask in 7:37 has a parallel in al-Qaṣaṣ, where it is put by Allah Himself on the Day: *“Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”* (28:62). The answer given there is the same in substance as the confession in 7:37, and the verse that follows it records the disowning that the sūrah describes from the other side: *“Those ˹misleaders˺ against whom the decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will cry”* (28:63) that they led their followers astray and disassociate themselves from them

The two questions establish what is being examined. The angels ask where the claimed gods are, and the answer is that they are not there; Allah asks the same question on the Day, and the answer is a confession of disbelief

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:38

> **Allah will say, “Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.” Whenever a group enters Hell, it will curse the preceding one until they are all gathered inside, the followers will say about their leaders, “Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.” He will answer, “It has already been multiplied for all, but you do not know.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence at the Gate**

The sūrah's court has reached the stage of execution. *Qāla dkhulū fī umamin qad khalat min qablikum mina al-jinni wa-l-ins* — enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you. The wording is careful in two respects. The condemned do not enter alone; they enter *among* communities, as members of a company. And the company is not a single nation but the whole accumulated population of the two kinds — jinn and human beings — that preceded them. The last generation is not judged in isolation; it is inserted into a procession.

The commentators read the verse as the answer to a specific hope, one the Makkan leadership entertained and which the Qur'an records elsewhere. Sūrah al-Aḥqāf has the leaders of the people saying, *“We found our forefathers following a particular way, and we are following in their footsteps”* (43:22), and Sūrat al-Zukhruf has the warners anticipate the objection (43:24). The verse before us closes that door at the last moment: the ancestors are not an alibi. They are the front of the line.

**"Whenever a Group Enters, It Curses the Preceding One"**

*Kullamā dakhalat ummatun laʿanat ukhtahā.* The word *ukht* — sister — is doing something remarkable in this sentence. The Qur'an's ordinary vocabulary for a doomed nation is *ummah*, a group defined by its direction. Here the same groups are given a family relation: they are sisters, and the relation survives into the Fire. The curse that a community pronounces on the one before it is, in the Qur'an's image, the continuation of a quarrel between relatives.

That is the point of the clause, and it is one of the sharpest psychological observations in the Book. In this world, the relationships among the nations that reject revelation are presented as alliances: shared economy, shared ancestry, shared opposition. The verse shows what is underneath the alliance. Every newcomer to the Fire curses the one who preceded it — the generation that modelled the practice, the teachers who taught the doctrine, the fathers who made the religion of custom look like religion. The solidarities that held them together dissolve on contact with the consequence, and what is left is blame.

**The Plea of the Last for the First**

*Ḥattā idhā iddārakū fīhā jamīʿan qālat ukhrāhum li-ūlāhum* — until they are all gathered inside, the followers will say about their leaders: *“Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.”* (7:38) The plea is precisely the one the Qur'an records in four other passages, in almost identical words. Sūrat al-Aḥzāb has the condemned in the Fire saying, *“Our Lord! We obeyed our leaders and elite, but they led us astray from the Right Way. Our Lord! Give them double our punishment, and condemn them tremendously”* (33:67–68). Sūrat Ṣād has the same petition (38:61). Sūrat Sabaʾ records the exchange in full (34:31–33). And Sūrat al-Baqarah states the outcome: those who misled others disown their followers, the bonds between them are cut, and the followers cry out for a second chance (2:166–167).

The pattern is so consistently repeated that it must be read as a deliberate teaching device. The Book is telling its readers, in advance, what the social architecture of religious error looks like when the scaffolding is removed: the influential and the dependent, the eloquent and the persuaded, the ones who commanded and the ones who obeyed — each standing where he placed himself, each blaming the other, and neither able to produce the other as a defense.

**"For Each Is Double"**

The divine answer is a single line: *qāla li-kullin diʿf* — He will answer, it has already been multiplied for all, *wa-lākin lā taʿlamūn* — but you do not know. The answer does not accept the plea's allocation while granting its principle. It affirms that responsibility is real for every party — the leaders for the invitation, the followers for the acceptance — and it refuses to let either shift the burden.

The "double" is not a doubling of torture; it is the doubling that the Book attaches to whoever combines two offenses. The leader who sinned *and* caused others to sin carries both; the follower who sinned and who imitated another's authority carries what he earned. The same arithmetic is stated as a law of the Book: *“Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear!”* (16:25). And it is balanced by the verse of the same Book that says every soul will receive only what it earned: *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”* (35:18; 53:38).

**What the Verse Is For**

Read at the level of the sūrah's argument, the verse is a preemptive dismantling of the single most common alibi for inherited religion: that one was following one's betters. This is the same objection that verse 28 recorded in its polite form — *we found our fathers doing it* — now answered in its final form, when the fathers are in the same fire and the daughter-community has nothing to say except a curse.

The passage ends on a note that is easy to overrun: *but you do not know*. The clause is not mercy and not sarcasm; it is the closing of the epistemic door the sūrah has been walking through since verse 28. There are facts about the consequence of leading others astray that no human being can calculate — which is exactly why the Qur'an does not encourage the game of distributing blame and does encourage the single question the reader can answer: what am I teaching, by my words, my practice, and my silence? The cursed sister-communities of this verse never had a chance to discuss it afterwards.


**An Assembly of Jinn and Men**

The verse’s company is mixed: *“Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.”* (7:38). Al-Anʿām describes the same mixed assembly at the gathering: *“˹Consider˺ the Day He will gather them ˹all˺ together and say, ‘O assembly of jinn! You misled humans in great numbers.’”* (6:128).

The charge in 6:128 is addressed to the jinn first and names the number of those misled as great. The reply that follows in that verse is the one 7:38 dramatises: the human associates say that they benefited from one another’s company and have now reached their term. The two verses describe the same relation from the two sides — leading and benefiting — and both end inside the Fire.

7:38 adds what neither of them states: the sequence. Each group curses the one that preceded it, so the company that entered together is arranged in an order of blame. The verse therefore reports a society preserved in the structure it had in life, with the followers addressing their leaders and the request for a doubled portion made on their behalf (7:38).


**The Acknowledgement Inside the Fire**

Fāṭir records the speech of the same place: *“There they will be ˹fervently˺ screaming, ‘Our Lord! Take us out ˹and send us back˺. We will do good, unlike what we used to do.’”* (35:37). The plea is answered with the reason it cannot be granted: *“Did We not give you lives long enough so that whoever wanted to be mindful could have done so?”* (35:37).

The reply fixes what 7:38 assumes. The cursing, the plea and the request for a doubled punishment all occur after the term has been reached, and the sūrah has already stated that no soul is asked to make amends once its term is up (7:53). 35:37 supplies the missing premise in the form of a question: a life long enough had been given, and a warner had come.

This is why the verse reports speech rather than torment. What the Fire contains, in the sūrah’s account, is a conversation between people who shared a road and now share an outcome — the followers cursing the leaders, the leaders asking that the punishment be doubled for both (7:38), and the whole exchange conducted in the terms the Book uses of a case already closed.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:39

> **Then the leaders will say to their followers, “You were no better than us! So taste the torment for what you used to commit.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reply of the First to the Last**

*Wa-qālat ūlāhum li-ukhrāhum* — then the leaders will say to their followers. The exchange of the previous verse is now answered, and the direction of the address is reversed. There, the later community cursed the earlier; here, the earlier turns on the later. The commentators differ on which group is which: al-Ṭabarī records readings in which *ūlāhum* means the leaders, the predecessors in time, or the predecessors in rank, and the same for *ukhrā*. What is not in dispute is the content of the reply, and it is a single sentence that dismantles every hierarchy the condemned had been relying on.

**"You Have No Favour Over Us"**

*Fa-mā kāna lakum ʿalaynā min faḍl* — you have no superiority over us. The word *faḍl* is the vocabulary of rank, merit, and advantage; it is the same word the Qur'an uses for God's bounty and for the distinctions He grants among people. The first community's reply is a claim of strict equality: whatever we did, you did; whatever we taught, you accepted; the ledger carries no favour of yours over ours.

The sentence is the reversal of the whole social logic of the world. In the marketplace of Makkah, *faḍl* was the measure of a man: lineage, wealth, the size of a following, the weight of a name. The Qur'an's earlier verses in this sūrah had shown the same logic operating in religion and being applied to the believers — the arrogant chiefs asking, *“Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”* while the lowly answered, *“We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”* (7:75–76). Here, in the Fire, the question of *faḍl* is raised one last time, and the answer is the same for everyone: none of you is any better than the others in the only ranking that survived.

The Book pronounces the same verdict as a general law of the Hereafter. *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”* (35:18; 53:38; 6:164). *“Whoever chooses to be guided, it is only for their own good; and whoever chooses to stray, it is only to their own loss. No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”* (17:15). The plain meaning of the doctrine is that the moral architecture of this life — rank, influence, dependency, the ability to make others carry one's cost — does not extend across the threshold, and every one of those arrangements which the previous verse showed collapsing is here denied the last consolation it might have claimed.

**"Taste the Torment for What You Used to Commit"**

*Fa-dhūqū al-ʿadhāb bimā kuntum taksibūn* — so taste the torment for what you used to commit. Two features of the clause are worth noting. The verb *dhūqū*, taste, is the same verb the sūrah used for Adam and his wife's act in the Garden — *“when they tasted of the tree”* (7:22). The Book has a vocabulary of tasting that runs from the first forbidden mouthful to the last consequence of a life; the same faculty that was designed to sample the good provision of God is now the faculty being addressed with the payment. The second feature is *kuntum taksibūn*, you used to earn: *kasb*, earning, is the Qur'an's commercial word for action. An act is a wage. The sūrah has already put a scale on the Day and called it *ḥaqq* (7:8); this verse names the currency.

**The Argument That Fails Everywhere**

The exchange between the leaders and the followers belongs to a family of scenes in which the Qur'an rehearses, in advance, every alibi a human being might carry into the reckoning. What emerges from the whole set is that the argument of *following* never works, and the Book itself gives the reason. Sūrat al-Baqarah's account of the same dispute ends with the followers saying, *“If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us”* (2:167) — that is, the regret is not that they were misled but that they obeyed. Sūrat Sabaʾ puts the rebuttal in the mouths of the leaders: *“Did we ever hinder you from guidance after it came to you? In fact, you were wicked on your own”* (34:32).

And the reason the argument fails is that the guidance was never held hostage by any human being. The Qur'an describes the obligation of the follower and the obligation of the leader as two separate accounts, and it states that the message reaches both: *“O assembly of jinn and humans! Did messengers not come from among you, proclaiming My revelations and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?”* (6:130). Between the two groups stands a criterion the followers possessed all along — the ability to check, to ask, to refuse, to seek — and the verse's refusal of their plea is the refusal to let a person hand back the faculty with which he was created.

**The Mercy Hidden in a Verse of Blame**

It is worth pausing, finally, on what this refusal protects. A world in which the follower could transfer responsibility to the leader would be a world in which the powerful could not be blamed for anything and the weak would be blamed for everything. The Qur'an's insistence on individual accountability is the only arrangement in which each person has something to answer for that is genuinely his, and in which the imposing of authority — a teacher's, a parent's, a ruler's, a movement's — remains subject to a standard no human authority can override.

The Prophet ﷺ summarized the resulting posture in a hadith that the sūrah's own readers kept on their tongues: *“No obedience in disobedience to Allah; obedience is only in what is right”* (al-Bukhārī 7257; Muslim 1840, from ʿAlī). The verse of the Heights supplies the reason: the day is coming when the first will turn on the last and nobody's rank will count. Between now and then, there is one relation whose rank holds, and the book of this sūrah has already named it: *“He has guided some, while others are destined to stray.”* (7:30).


No Advantage Over Us: The Bonds Cut Off

The leaders' reply at 7:39 is a denial of superiority, and the Book records the same denial in a verse that describes what happens to the relation between the two parties, beginning from the Day *“when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off”* (2:166). The disowning and the cutting are two descriptions of one event, and 7:39 gives the words spoken inside it: you were no better than us, so taste the torment for what you used to commit. The followers had expected the leaders to carry something into the Fire on their behalf, and the leaders' answer removes that expectation by placing both parties on the same level.

The verse that follows in al-Baqarah records the wish that the level produces: *“If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.”* (2:167). The wish is not for a different act in the world but for a second act in the Fire, which is precisely what 7:53 denies when it asks whether there is any intercessor. The leaders at 7:39 are not offering a defence; they are refusing one

The equality asserted in the Fire is the sūrah's own standard applied to the leaders. The weighing at 7:8–9 measures what each person carried, and no one's record can be transferred to another; the verse at 7:39 is the leaders' acknowledgement of that rule at the moment it operates against them


For What You Used to Commit: Each Soul's Own Earning

The second half of the leaders' reply states the ground of the torment, and the Book states that ground as a rule of the Day: *“Today every soul will be rewarded for what it has done. No injustice Today!”* (40:17)

The rule has a consequence for the sūrah's account of leadership. Leaders are held for their own misleading and followers for their own following; neither carries the other's record, and neither is excused by the other's presence

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:40

> **Surely those who receive our revelations with denial and arrogance, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle. This is how We reward the wicked.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Gates That Do Not Open**

*Inna alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā wa-stakbarū ʿanhā lā tufattaḥu lahum abwāb al-samāʾ* — surely those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them. The verse is a mirror of the one before it, with a single phrase exchanged: where verse 36 said *they are the inhabitants of the Fire*, this verse says what the Fire means in architectural terms. The gates do not open.

The image of the gates of heaven is a Qur'anic constant, and its use here is precise. In Sūrat al-Zumar, the gates are opened for the blessed: *“And those who were mindful of their Lord will be led to Paradise in ˹successive˺ groups. When they arrive at its ˹already˺ open gates, its keepers will say, ‘Peace be upon you! You have done well, so come in, to stay forever.’”* (39:73) — while the disbelievers, driven in groups to the Fire, also find gates, and are told: *“Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. What an evil home for the arrogant!”* (39:72). The Book's heavens are gate-able: Sūrat al-Nabaʾ describes the sky split open, *becoming many gates* (78:19), and Sūrat al-Qamar records the opening of the gates of the sky with pouring rain (54:11). To say that the gates will not be opened for this group is therefore to say that the entire architecture of access — ascent, acceptance, entry — is closed to them, and the reason given is the one this sūrah has been developing since its first narrative: *disdain*.

**"Until the Camel Passes Through the Eye of the Needle"**

*Wa-lā yadkhulūna al-jannata ḥattā yalija al-jamalu fī sammi al-khiyāṭ* — nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle. The Arabic of the clause has been the subject of one of the most careful philological discussions in the tradition, and the discussion is instructive.

The word read *jamal* means camel. A second reading, well attested in the qirāʾāt and defended by lexicographers, is *jummal*: a thick ship's cable, a hawser. Al-Ṭabarī reports both and notes that under either reading the sentence's force is identical, because both images describe the impossible: a large body passing through a small aperture. The camel is the largest animal in the everyday experience of the sūrah's first audience; the cable is the largest cord in the experience of a port. The proverb's power lies in being stated as a *condition*: they will not enter *until* this happens — and the "until" is the grammatical form of an impossibility dressed as a waiting.

The Prophet ﷺ used the same register for the destination this verse denies, describing the entry of the blessed in terms no camel could satisfy: *“The first group to enter Paradise will be like the full moon”* (al-Bukhārī 3245, from Abū Hurayrah; Muslim 2834 records the same in fuller form). The tradition of commentary drew the specific application from the verse itself: *those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance*. It is not the possession of wealth that bars the gate — the sūrah's own verses on lawful enjoyment (7:31–32) forbid that reading — but the swelling self that makes a person's entry physically impossible. Al-Rāzī puts it in a sentence worth keeping: pride is a size, and the gate does not change.

**What the Verse Says About Divine Exclusion**

Read together with the garden imagery of the whole Book, the verse makes a claim that many modern readers find startling: heaven has a policy. The Qur'an is not vague about who is inside. It names the qualities that enter — reverence and reform in verse 35, faith and right action throughout — and it names the qualities that do not. The early sūrahs of the Makkan period repeat the point in dozens of images, from the balance of al-Qāriʿah (101:6–9) to the books handed right and left (69:19–25).

And yet the Book is careful not to make the gate a function of a single category of person. The verse's own clause requires two acts — denial *and* disdain — and the two together describe a settled character rather than a momentary lapse. The distinction has practical consequences, and the tradition drew them. It is the difference between the person who sins and the person who has decided; between the soul that falls and the soul that has taken up a position against the signs. The sūrah's earlier verses about repentance (7:23) and divine acceptance (2:37) remain available to everyone whose disdain has not become a permanent structure. What the camel-and-needle proverb states is what happens when it has.

**The Final Clause**

*Wa-kadhālika najzī al-mujrimīn* — this is how We reward the wicked. The word *mujrim* is from *j-r-m*, the root of cutting off and of earning guilt; the Qur'an uses it for the one whose conduct has severed him. The phrase "this is how We reward" is the sūrah's returning formula of proportion: the punishment is not arbitrary, it is the fitting end of what the person built.

The verse's placement closes the unit that began in verse 32 and gives it its final shape. The sūrah asked who had forbidden God's adornment, and answered by naming what is truly forbidden (32–33); it announced a term for every community (34); it promised security to the reverent and reformer (35); it described the disdainful (36); it followed them to the moment of death (37); and it has now followed them past the gates. In between, it left one door conspicuously open, and the next two verses will show the faces of the people walking through it.


**The Needle’s Eye and the Reading of the Rope**

The image is built on two words worth separating: the camel, the largest animal the sūrah’s audience handled daily, and the eye of the needle, the smallest aperture they threaded. The impossibility is stated as a physical one and is therefore measurable by anyone present, which is what allows it to function as an exclusion rather than as a threat. Nothing is promised or withheld; a condition is named that will not be met.

The tradition preserves a reading in which the first word is not the animal but a thick rope or cable, and the sense survives the change while the register shifts: a twisted hawser against the eye of a needle is a craftsman’s impossibility rather than a herdsman’s. The commentators handle both, and the handling is itself evidence — the phrase is being treated as a fixed expression rather than as a description of an animal. Either way the verse does what the sūrah’s other impossibilities do. It takes a thing no one has seen happen and states it as the condition of a thing no one will see happen.


**The Gates in Their Other Uses**

The gates named here do not open, and the Book uses the same image of gates that do. On the Day: *“The sky will be ˹split˺ open, becoming ˹many˺ gates,”* (78:19). And of the other company: *“And those who were mindful of their Lord will be led to Paradise in ˹successive˺ groups. When they arrive at its ˹already˺ open gates,”* (39:73) — open before the arrival, with keepers who greet rather than bar.

The contrast fixes the meaning of the closure in verse 40. A gate that is not opened is not an obstacle to be overcome by effort, wealth or intercession; it is a state. The sūrah has spent its histories on towns seized while they felt secure, and this verse states the outcome for the individuals inside those towns in the image its audience understood best: a door that does not open, and a passage too narrow for the largest thing they own. The verse’s second clause, denying entry until the impossible occurs, is the same statement in the grammar of a condition.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:41

> **Hell will be their bed; flames will be their cover. This is how We reward the wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Bed Beneath and the Cover Above**

*Lahum min jahannama mihādun wa-min fawqihim ghawāsh* — for them there is a bed of Hell, and above them coverings. The clause arranges the punishment along the axis of the human body, below and above, and in doing so it describes not an event but an environment. Nobody in this verse is being thrown anywhere. The condemned are *installed*: a *mihād* set beneath, *ghawāsh* laid over.

The choice of words is the sūrah's usual economy. *Mihād* is the Qur'an's term for a bed prepared and spread — the cradle of an infant, the resting place made ready by someone who cares about the sleeper. Sūrat al-Nabaʾ uses it for the earth itself: *“Have We not smoothed out the earth like a bed?”* (78:6), and Sūrat al-Baqarah uses its sibling *firāsh* for the same idea: *“˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you”* (2:22). *Ghawāsh*, plural of *ghāshiyah*, is a covering — the counterpane, the thing drawn over a person asleep. The Book has taken the vocabulary of the most ordinary comfort a human being knows and filled it with fire.

**The Same Architecture, Elsewhere in the Book**

The image recurs because the Qur'an wants it to. Sūrat al-Zumar states it to the believers as a threat aimed at their own complacency: *“They will have layers of fire above and below them. That is what Allah warns His servants with. So fear Me, O My servants!”* (39:16). Sūrat al-Kahf encloses the wrongdoer in a *muḥīṭ*, a thing that surrounds and from which there is no direction of escape (18:29). Sūrat Ibrāhīm clothes the rebels in tar and covers their faces with flame (14:50), and Sūrat al-Ḥajj cuts garments of fire for the deniers (22:19). Sūrat al-Raʿd's contrast uses the same logic in the other direction: the good word is a tree whose shade and fruit are available to all (14:24–25).

Read next to the paradise verses of the same sūrah — rivers, garments, thrones (7:43; 18:31) — the point becomes plain. The afterlife in the Qur'an is described as a *place* with furniture, because the human beings it addresses are embodied creatures who understand the moral state of a life through the conditions of a home. The pride of verse 36 chose a posture; this verse gives the posture a room.

**"This Is How We Reward the Wrongdoers"**

*Wa-kadhālika najzī al-ẓālimīn* — and this is how We reward the unjust. The phrase closes the verse on a note of exactness, and the vocabulary carries it. *Jazāʾ*, requital, is the Qur'an's term of payment in kind: the wage returned for work done. *“Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it”* (99:7–8). *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. But whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one. None will be wronged” (6:160)* (6:160). The formula *this is how We reward* appears throughout the sūrahs of warning, and in every appearance it forecloses one specific objection — that the punishment of God is arbitrary, or excessive, or born of wounded pride in the way human punishment so often is.

The sūrah has already given the court where the accounting is done: *“The weighing on that Day will be just”* (7:8). This verse names the currency. What is repaid is what was spent, and the recompense is not a change of direction in God's disposition but the arrival of a bill already written.

**Who the Wrongdoers Are Here**

One word in the closing formula deserves attention: the condemned are called *ẓālimīn*, and this sūrah has been unusually careful about that root. It is the word Adam and his wife use against themselves when they turn back: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves”* (7:23). It is the word the sūrah applies to the fabrication of lies about God (7:37), to those who disbelieve in His signs (7:40), and to the arrogant who despise them (7:36). There is no other vocabulary in the chapter for what went wrong, and the reason is that the chapter is not describing a category of moral opinion but a boundary crossed. *Ẓulm* in the Qur'an is the placing of a thing outside the station God gave it: the sign treated as disposable, the creature placed where the Creator belongs, the capacity of a soul spent against its own interest.

The wrongdoer of this verse is therefore not the person who lost a battle of ideas. He is the one who moved what God had set. The bed of verse 41 is what happens when a man spends a lifetime putting himself in the place of what is above him: he is finally laid down in it.

**A Furnishing That Closes Every Door**

There is a further detail that only becomes visible when the verse is read beside verse 40. There, the gates of heaven *do not open*. Here, the condemned are covered from above and bedded from below. Between the two verses, every aperture of the human body's world has been sealed: no door above, no exit below, and no direction of movement that is not fire.

That is the sūrah's terrifying consistency. It began these verses with a question — who is more wrong than the one who lies about God? — and has answered it with an itinerary whose every stage was described, centuries before, in the architecture of an ordinary room. The men being described would have gone to sleep that night on their own beds, under their own covers, and would have considered the verse a matter of rhetoric. The verse says that from now until then, God has changed one thing only: the material.


**A Covering: The Same Noun at al-Baqarah’s Opening**

The verse furnishes the Fire with two things: a bed beneath and a covering above. The noun for the covering is *ghishāwah*, from *gh-sh-y*, to envelop. Al-Baqarah uses the same noun of the disbelievers in this life: *“Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.”* (2:7).

The two uses describe one covering at two stages. In 2:7 the *ghishāwah* is over the sight and belongs to the present; in 7:41 it is over the body and belongs to the Fire. The exegetes read the pair as the same condition completed — what covered the faculties becomes what covers the person — and al-Ṭabarī notes that the verse’s furnishings are named so that no part of the inhabitant is left outside them.

The verse’s two nouns are therefore not decoration but a claim about enclosure. A bed is what one lies on and a covering is what lies on top; between them nothing is exposed. The same completeness is stated in 2:7 by the organs listed — heart, hearing, sight — and the sūrah’s summary sentence at the end of 7:41 reports it as a reward, using the Book’s ordinary word for what is given in return.


**The Wrongdoers and the Rule That Spares No One**

The verse ends: *“This is how We reward the wrongdoers.”* (7:41). *Ẓālim* is the sūrah’s standing term, and its uses mark the shape of the argument: the first confession admits it of itself (7:23), the gate of heaven is closed to those who deny and are *ẓālimūn* (7:40), the calf-worshippers are named by their invention (7:152), and the towns are destroyed under the same word.

Yūnus states the rule that governs all of them: *“Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves.”* (10:44).
