The verse removes the only available objection to a reward of this kind — that it exceeds what was done — by locating the wrong in the one who suffers it.

7:41 therefore reports a furnishing and a verdict in the same breath. The verdict is not that the wrongdoers have been treated harshly but that they have been treated exactly, and 10:44 explains why exactness here is not severity: the wrong was self-inflicted, so the return is a measurement rather than an addition.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:42

> **As for those who believe and do good—We never require of any soul more than what it can afford—it is they who will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence That Turns the Page**

Verse 41 ended with a formula: *and thus do We recompense the wrongdoers* (7:41). Verse 42 opens with the same construction and the opposite content: *wa-lladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti* — and those who believed and did righteous deeds. The sūrah does this repeatedly, and the repetition is the point: the same court, the same scale, the same verb of requital, and the difference is what a person brought to it.

The closing clause returns the vocabulary of verse 36 to its rightful owners: where the arrogant were *aṣḥāb al-nār*, the residents of the Fire, these are *aṣḥāb al-jannah*, the residents of Paradise, and the abiding is stated in the identical word — *khālidūn*, there forever. In a sūrah that has arranged its arguments in pairs since the first page — the guided and the misguided (7:30), the reverent and the disdainful (7:35–36), the bed of fire and the rivers of the garden — this symmetry is not ornament. It tells the reader that the two destinies are being described on a single map, and that the road to either is built one deed at a time.

**"Those Who Believed and Did Righteous Deeds"**

The pair *āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* is the Qur'an's most frequent description of the saved, occurring more than fifty times. Its two halves are constructed so that neither can stand alone. *Īmān* is trust — the interior act by which a person accepts what God has said — and *ʿamal ṣāliḥ* is the outward act that trust produces. The Book does not separate them anywhere: not grace without the act, and not act without the trust. The pairing is itself a commentary on the sūrah's quarrel with the Makkan leadership, who were not short of deeds and were short of nothing but trust, and on the people of the sabbath of 7:163 whom the sūrah will shortly describe — a community that possessed the form of religion and lost its substance.

The adjective *ṣāliḥ* comes from the root *ṣ-l-ḥ*, which in Arabic is the vocabulary of repair — the opposite of *fasād*, corruption. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf has already used the contrast in the call of its prophets: the messenger of this sūrah comes *commanding what is right and forbidding what is wrong* (7:157), and verse 35 described the saved as those who *reform* themselves. The Qur'an's concept of good work is thus not merely legal compliance but correction: the setting right of what has been bent, beginning with oneself.

**The Parenthesis That Answers Two Questions**

Dropped into the middle of the promise is a clause that does not appear to belong there: *lā nukallifu nafsan illā wusʿahā* — We never require of any soul more than what it can afford. It is a complete principle of obligation standing between the conditions and the reward, and its placement is deliberate.

The Qur'an states it three times in this form and several more in substance: *“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford”* (2:286), *“We never require of any soul more than what it can afford”* (23:62), *“Allah does not require of any soul beyond what He has given it”* (65:7), and it is embedded in the practical legislation of the Book — in the concession for the traveller who cannot fast (2:184–185), in the prohibitions against burdening the nursing mother or the father beyond means (2:233), in the declaration, *“He deserves, for ˹it is˺ He ˹Who˺ has chosen you, and laid upon you no hardship in the religion—the way of your forefather Abraham”* (22:78). The tradition drew from it the whole discipline of *taklīf*, the assignment of obligation according to ability, and the jurists built on it the principle that no duty is imposed where it cannot be performed.

But the clause answers two readers, not one. The soul tempted to despair at the standard reads that faith and right action are required, measures the height of the demand, and stops. The clause tells that soul that the demand was measured before it was made. And the soul tempted to make a system of excuses reads the same clause as permission, and is answered by the exact wording — not, "we never require of any soul", but *we never require of any soul more than what it can afford*. Grace does not abolish the order; it sets its size.

The Prophet ﷺ gave the doctrine its practical shape in a hadith the sūrah's readers have always paired with this verse: *“The deeds of any one of you will not save him” — they said, “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?” — he said, “Not even me, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy. So be moderate and do what you can”* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816, from Abū Hurayrah — the clause *and give glad tidings* belongs to the report of ʿĀʾishah at al-Bukhārī 6099 and Muslim 2818). Neither the despair nor the presumption survives that sentence.

**The People of the Garden**

The verse then states the destination with a possessive that the sūrah has already used twice: *ulāʾika aṣḥāb al-jannah*. *Aṣḥāb* is the vocabulary of belonging and company — the owner of a house, the companion of a road. The Qur'an does not say the righteous will be admitted to the Garden, though it says that too elsewhere (16:32; 39:73); here it says they *are its people*, and the clause *hum fīhā khālidūn* settles the tenure.

There is a pastoral reason the sūrah repeats the abiding so insistently in this short stretch. The community receiving these verses knew loss as a daily condition: the exile of the early Muslims from Makkah, the death of children, the confiscation of property, the long patience of people who had no reason to expect that anything in their circumstances would hold. Against that experience, the Book places a possession that cannot be taken, in a place whose gates — unlike those of verse 40 — are open.

The arrangement of the three verses is worth seeing whole. Verse 41 furnishes the Fire. Verse 42 furnishes the Garden with the simplest inventory the Qur'an possesses: belief, action, and a measure that fits the soul. Verse 43 will give the Garden its voice. Between the two descriptions, the sūrah leaves only one thing for the reader to decide, and it is not hidden in either of them.


No Soul Required Beyond Its Capacity: The Rule and Its Record

The parenthesis of 7:42 states a rule in the middle of a promise, and the Book states the same rule with its two consequences: *“We never require of any soul more than what it can afford. And with Us is a record which speaks the truth. None will be wronged.”* (23:62)

The rule's position inside 7:42 is what makes it doctrinally useful. It is placed between the description of the believers and the promise of the Garden, which means it governs the relation between the two. The people promised Paradise are not people who exceeded a capacity; they are people who performed within one

What the record adds is the guarantee that the capacity was not exceeded in the accounting either. A soul required to do what it can afford, and then weighed by a record that speaks the truth, is a soul whose outcome is neither arbitrary nor disproportionate


Residents Forever: The Same Sentence in al-Baqarah

The promise of 7:42 is stated in al-Baqarah in almost identical words: *“And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.”* (2:82). The two verses share their subject, their predicate, and their duration, and the difference between them is the parenthesis that al-Aʿrāf inserts

The pairing of belief and good works is the sūrah's standard formula, and it appears at 7:42 in the position the formula always occupies — before the outcome rather than after it. What follows from the pairing is that the residence is not a reward for belief alone or for conduct alone; the two are named as one subject

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:43

> **We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. Rivers will flow under their feet. And they will say, “Praise be to Allah for guiding us to this. We would have never been guided if Allah had not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth.” It will be announced to them, “This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"We Will Remove Whatever Bitterness They Had in Their Hearts"**

*Wa-nazaʿnā mā fī ṣudūrihim min ghill* — and We shall strip out whatever rancour was in their hearts. The verb *nazaʿa* is the verb of drawing a thing out that has sunk in: a nail from wood, a spear from a wound, a root from soil. *Ghill* is the particular vice it removes — not anger of the moment but the sediment of old grievance, the grudge that has been carried so long it has become part of a person's furniture.

The promise is repeated almost word for word in Sūrat al-Ḥijr, and the following clause there explains the purpose: *“We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. In a friendly manner, they will be on thrones, facing one another”* (15:47). Facing one another. The Qur'an's Garden is a place where assembly is possible without the history that makes assembly dangerous, and the Book has prepared the reader for why this matters. The sūrah's own account of Ṣāliḥ's people (7:75–76) was a scene of division: the arrogant chiefs on one side, the lowly believers on the other, and a social order in which one group's rank was the other group's humiliation. The Muslim community receiving these verses had come out of a tribal world in which a man's grievance against a clan could last three generations.

What the verse promises is not amnesia but surgery. The memory stays; the poison is extracted. And the phrase is only one of several in which the Book describes the moral hygiene of the Garden: purified spouses (2:25), speech in which no idle talk or falsehood is heard (56:25), a place whose only sound is peace (19:62). The world to come is drawn not as a bigger version of this world's societies but as one whose members have had the thing removed that made society a contest.

**The Rivers Beneath Their Feet**

**The First Words of the Saved**

The verse now records what its inhabitants say, and the first sound of the Garden is gratitude: *al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī hadānā li-hādhā* — praise belongs to Allah, who guided us to this. The opening of the Book's first sūrah is placed in the mouths of the saved in the last sūrah's communities; the doxology of the servant at the beginning of the Qur'an becomes the language of the reward at the end.

The confession continues with a sentence that carries the weight of the chapter's whole argument about guidance: *wa-mā kunnā li-nahtadiya lawlā an hadānā Allāh* — and we would never have been guided had Allah not guided us. The construction is one of total dependence: *lawlā* — were it not for — introduces a counterfactual the speaker knows to be true. These are the people who did the deeds of verse 42, and their first act in the Garden is to deny that the deeds were self-generated. The sūrah has already stated the doctrine from the other side: *“He has guided some, while others are destined to stray”* (7:30). Here the guided state the same fact from inside their own biography.

**"It Will Be Announced: This Is Paradise Awarded to You"**

*Wa-nūdū an tilkumu al-jannatu ūrithtumūhā bimā kuntum taʿmalūn* — and it will be announced to them: "This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do." Two grammatical details carry the theology.

The first is the passive *nūdū*: it is announced, and the announcer is unnamed. The sūrah used the same device four verses later, where a nameless caller pronounces condemnation on the wrongdoers (7:44). The message is what matters; the voice belongs to the place.

The second is the verb *ūrithtumūhā*, you have been made its heirs. The Book could have said you have been paid it, or awarded it, or admitted to it. It says inherited — the term of a transfer that no one earns in the ordinary sense. The clause continues *bimā kuntum taʿmalūn*, for what you used to do, and both halves are necessary. The sūrah's parenthetical in verse 42 insisted that no soul is burdened beyond capacity; this clause insists that the Garden is not the wage a soul's capacity could ever produce. Sūrat al-Zukhruf speaks of the same place in the same register: *“That is the Paradise which you will be awarded for what you used to do”* (43:72), and Sūrat Āl ʿImrān calls the whole arrangement *an accommodation from Allah* (3:198). The Prophet ﷺ stated the balance in one sentence: the deeds do not entitle anyone, and the deeds are the road. What the verse establishes is that the road and the destination have the same owner.

**Why the Verse Is Sung**

The sūrah has moved from court to gate to settlement, and now it records music. It is a deliberate choice of the Book of the Heights: the description of Paradise is not concluded with an inventory of its wealth but with a confession of its cause. The people of the Garden have no boast about their own performance, no lineage to recite, no list of merits; they have a Lord who guided them, a truth they can now confirm from the inside, and an inheritance they did nothing to earn and everything to reach.

The reader of the sūrah is meant to notice what is missing from the sentence: no one in the Garden says "I". The pronouns are all "we", and every "we" is the object of a divine verb. That is the last word of the sūrah's passage on the two destinies, and it is the exact opposite of the single word the sūrah's narrative placed at the beginning — the one spoken by a creature who refused, and said nothing else.


**Ghill: Fever and Collar in the Breast**

The noun translated *bitterness* is *ghill*, from the root *gh-l-l*. The root carries heat in the chest: *ghalla* means to be parched with thirst, and *ghull* is the shackle worn on the neck. A *ghill* is what sits in the breast like a fever and what binds a man like a collar — rancour held against a brother. Al-Zajjāj defines it as concealed enmity, and the commentators add that it includes envy, resentment over an old injury and the wish to see another diminished. The word is therefore not a general term for bad feeling; it names the particular heat that survives between people who ought to be at peace.

The same removal is promised in al-Ḥijr: *“We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. In a friendly manner, they will be on thrones, facing one another.”* (15:47). The first sentence is identical to the first sentence of 7:43, and the second sentence supplies what the removal makes possible: sitting face to face. A man who carries *ghill* turns away from the one he resents; the two thrones set opposite each other are the outward form of its absence. That is the point of the verse’s word order — the clearing of the breasts is mentioned before the rivers and before the praise, because the first gift of the garden is the end of what people carried against one another.


**Grace and Desert Inside One Verse**

The verse holds two statements that pull in opposite directions. Its people say, *“Praise be to Allah for guiding us to this. We would have never been guided if Allah had not guided us.”* (7:43) — an acknowledgement that nothing in their arrival was their own doing. Then the call announces, *“This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do”* (7:43) — an award measured against their deeds. Grace and desert, stated within a few words of each other.

The commentators reconcile the two in the only way the verse allows: the deeds were themselves part of the guidance. A man who is guided is guided to believe and to act, so that what he did is both the fruit of grace and the ground of the award. Neither clause is cancelled by the other — the award is real, and it is not self-generated. The verse therefore states the position the Book takes everywhere: reward is promised for deeds, and the capacity to do them is given.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:44

> **The residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire, “We have certainly found our Lord’s promise to be true. Have you too found your Lord’s promise to be true?” They will reply, “Yes, we have!” Then a caller will announce to both, “May Allah’s condemnation be upon the wrongdoers,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Call Across the Divide**

*Wa-nādā aṣḥābu al-jannati aṣḥāba al-nār* — and the residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire. The sūrah's next six verses are built on the verb *nādā*, to call from a distance: here, and again at 7:48, and again at 7:50 where the residents of the Fire cry out to the residents of the Garden. The Book is describing a landscape in which the two populations are within sight and voice of one another, and in which nothing can be exchanged between them but words.

That is a deliberate design, and the sūrah has prepared the reader for it. In this world, the two groups are intermingled and indistinguishable to the outer eye; the sūrah's earlier narratives showed them arguing across a social distance that could still be crossed — the proud chiefs and the lowly believers of Ṣāliḥ's town (7:75–76). After death, the crossing is over, and all that remains of the relationship is the call. The voice carries. Nothing else does. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf will make that plain three verses later, when the condemned beg for a drop of water and receive a doctrinal answer instead (7:50).

**The Question That Is the Punishment**

*Innā wajadnā mā waʿadanā rabbunā ḥaqqan* — we have certainly found our Lord’s promise to be true — *fa-hal wajadtum mā waʿada rabbukum ḥaqqan* — have you too found your Lord’s promise to be true? *Qālū naʿam* — they said, yes.

The interrogative is the most economical instrument of punishment in the entire Book. The blessed do not gloat, and the Book does not put a taunt in their mouths; they ask a question whose answer is already experienced by everyone present. The verb *wajada*, to find, is a verb of discovery in the concrete world — the verb of a man who finds water in a well or a coin in the road. It states that revelation turned out to be *there*, like a thing you can put your hand on. The sentence is thus the last form of the sūrah's central argument, made by two communities at once and answered with a single word from the condemned.

Sūrat al-Aʿrāf records the same admission in another key seven verses later: the day the warning is fulfilled, those who ignored it will say, *“The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth”* (7:53). Sūrat al-Anʿām closes the door on its usefulness: *“On the Day your Lord’s signs arrive, belief will not benefit those who did not believe earlier or those who did no good through their faith”* (6:158). The exchange of verse 44 is the moment when the whole vocabulary of the Book's warnings becomes a physical fact, and, crucially, it is the blessed who pose the question and the damned who supply the confession.

**The Herald Between Them**

*Fa-adhdhana muʾadhdhinun baynahum* — and a herald called out between them. The word is the ancestor of *adhān*, the call to prayer: a public announcement made in a raised voice for a gathered crowd. In this world the phrase *the call between them* has a mundane history — the muezzin of Madinah calling across the rows — and the sūrah borrows the image for the last announcement that will ever be made in that landscape.

The content of the herald's cry is a sentence from the vocabulary of exclusion: *laʿnatu Allāh ʿalā al-ẓālimīn* — the curse of Allah is upon the unjust. *Laʿna* in the Qur'an is not profanity but the opposite of mercy: the expulsion of a creature from the radius within which God's special favour operates (2:161; 4:52). It is the same fate the sūrah announced for Iblīs in the first narrative of the chapter, when he was driven out for his arrogance (7:13), and the reader is expected to hear the echo. The announcement is made *between* the two populations, which is to say in the hearing of both: the blessed are told what they were saved from, and the condemned what they chose.

**The Hope That Lives Inside the Verdict**

The curse of verse 44 is stated in the absolute, and the tradition of the Prophet ﷺ read it within a larger mercy that the Book states in a hundred places. The Messenger of God described what will happen after the reckoning in a report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: when the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire have entered their homes, God will say, *“Take out whoever has faith equal to a mustard seed in his heart”* — and they will come out blackened like coal, and they will be cast into the river of al-Ḥayyāt, and they will sprout green as a seed does on the bank of a torrent (al-Bukhārī 6560, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī). The smoke-blackened figures in that hadith are people whose heart contained something the fire could not consume.

The verse of the Heights and that hadith are not in tension; they are describing different levels of the same verdict. The curse falls on the *ẓālimīn* as those who are defined by the injustice they settled in — the fixed posture, the chosen identity, the disdain of verse 36. The mustard seed is what remains of a creature who was better than the label. The sūrah's own reader is asked to check which of the two sentences describes the direction he is walking, and the question of verse 44 is the one he will be asked by voices that were once his neighbours.

**Why the Wrongdoers Are Defined Now**

Before the hasher's voice fades, the very next verse turns to define the word *ẓālimīn* — those who have just been cursed. It is the sūrah's most characteristic habit, and one of its most humane: whenever it pronounces a sentence, it immediately tells the reader what the sentence is for, so that the reader may measure himself instead of guessing. Verse 36 named disdain; verse 40 named denial; verse 41 named the crossing of a boundary. Verse 45 will name an act that can be seen in a human life today, and the reader who finds it there has been given the warning early enough to act on it.


The Promise Found True: The Words the Saved Had Prayed

The call across the divide at 7:44 opens with a report rather than a taunt: we have found the promise of our Lord to be true. The Book records the same finding as a prayer made before it, in the words of those who ask for what was promised: *“Grant us what You have promised us through Your messengers and do not put us to shame on Judgment Day—for certainly You never fail in Your promise.”* (3:194)

The question put to the residents of the Fire is what makes the report a punishment. Have you found the promise of your Lord to be true: the answer is yes, and the yes is the whole of it. Nothing else is said, no excuse is offered, and the sūrah's herald then announces the curse on the wrongdoers. The structure shows that the punishment at this point is not additional suffering but recognition — the knowledge, stated aloud to the party that was warned, that the warning was accurate.

The verse's own term for the wrongdoers is defined by the acts listed at 7:45: hindering from the way, seeking to make it crooked, and disbelieving in the Hereafter. The herald's announcement therefore falls on a described group rather than on a general category, and the description is the same one the sūrah applies throughout its account of the towns


Two Promises and the One That Failed

The truth of the promise reported at 7:44 has a counterpart in the Book's account of the other promise that was made to the same people. Satan addresses his followers after the judgment: *“Indeed, Allah has made you a true promise. I too made you a promise, but I failed you.”* (14:22)

What the two passages share is the timing. Both reports come after the judgment rather than before it, and both are addressed to people who had chosen between the promises while the choice still seemed costless

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:45

> **those who hindered ˹others˺ from Allah’s Way, strived to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, and disbelieved in the Hereafter.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Catalogue, Not an Insult**

The herald of verse 44 has just pronounced the curse of God upon the unjust. Verse 45 tells the reader whom the word describes: *alladhīna yaṣuddūna ʿan sabīli Allāh* — those who hindered others from Allah’s Way — *wa-yabghūnahā ʿiwajan* — strived to make it appear crooked — *wa-hum bi-l-ākhirati kāfirūn* — and disbelieved in the Hereafter.

The sentence is a three-part diagnosis, and the order of the parts is the order of a process. First a person is turned away from a road. Then the road itself is misrepresented — the seeker is told that it bends this way and does not reach where it claims to reach. Then, at the root, the one who does the misrepresenting has already decided that the destination does not exist. The Qur'an repeats the trio almost verbatim in four other places, and the repetition establishes it as a definition rather than a description of a particular historical group: *“who hinder ˹others˺ from Allah’s Path, striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, and disbelieve in the Hereafter”* (11:19); *“Why do you turn the believers away from the Way of Allah—striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, while you are witnesses ˹to its truth˺?”* (3:99); *“˹They are˺ the ones who favour the life of this world over the Hereafter and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked”* (14:3; see also 16:88, where added punishment is promised because of the corruption they spread).

**The Verb That Presupposes a Traveller**

*Ṣadda ʿan* is one of the Qur'an's most sociable verbs: it cannot be used without a second person. You cannot *block* in the abstract; the grammatical form of the sin requires somebody who was walking and was turned back. This is the crime that the sūrah's Makkan leadership is, in the reading of the commentators, most directly charged with: barring the way to the Sacred Mosque, pressuring the new believers of the town, forbidding access to the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ. The Book states that charge at length elsewhere: *“they hinder pilgrims from the Sacred Mosque”* (8:34); *“They are the ones who persisted in disbelief and hindered you from the Sacred Mosque”* (48:25); *“But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque”* (2:217). The Makkan leadership's real offense, on this reading, was not merely unbelief but blockade.

And the verse's principle reaches further than Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ stated the two directions of the traffic in a hadith from Abū Hurayrah: *“Whoever calls others to guidance will have a reward equal to that of those who follow, without anything being diminished from their reward”* — and its mirror, the one who calls to misguidance, carries the load of those who follow (Muslim 2674, from Abū Hurayrah). The verse of the Heights supplies the reason: the path is not a private opinion. It is a public road, and there is a crime in standing on it and telling travelers it goes nowhere.

**"Seeking to Make It Crooked"**

The Arabic of the next clause is a small masterpiece of precision. *Yabghūnahā ʿiwajan*: *baghā*, to seek or to covet, and *ʿiwaj*, crookedness. The lexicographers distinguish *ʿiwaj*, which Arabic uses for the crookedness of things — a road, a wall, a staff — from *ʿawaj*, which Arabic uses for the crookedness of conduct or judgment. The Qur'an chooses the first word, and the choice sharpens the charge. The accusation is not that these people behaved wickedly; it is that they *bent the road*. The path of God is described by the Book's own opening prayer as *al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*, the straight way (1:6). A straight line can only be opposed in two ways: by denying that it exists, or by representing it as something other than straight. The verse names the second, which is always the more sophisticated attack, and the one that requires a public relations campaign.

Sūrat Āl ʿImrān adds the detail that makes this clause especially severe: the People of the Book who do this do it *while you are witnesses to its truth* (3:99). The one who bends the road bends it in the full knowledge of where it led.

**The Engine Underneath**

The last clause supplies the motive: *wa-hum bi-l-ākhirati kāfirūn*. The denial of the Hereafter is not tacked onto the verse as an unrelated item of unbelief; it is offered as the reason the rest of the sentence is possible. This is one of the Qur'an's most consistent psychological claims: a person who is certain that no account will be demanded has no motive to keep the road clear for others and no reason to be careful about what he tells them. The Book says as much in its portraits of the heedless: *“But no! In fact, you love this fleeting world, and neglect the Hereafter”* (75:20–21), and it puts the same confession about the Fire in the mouth of the deniers themselves (74:42–46).

The verse therefore closes the circle opened at 7:8, where the scale of the Day was described as just. The people who are cursed in verse 44 are, at bottom, people who removed the scale from their world. They then removed the road, and then the travelers.

**The Reader's Place in the Sentence**

There remains one application of the verse that any honest reader has to make before he makes any other. It is not only tyrants who are addressed by *yaṣuddūna ʿan sabīli Allāh*. A parent, a teacher, a friend, an elder, a movement, a writer — anyone with a voice and a following who makes the religion look like something it is not, or who makes the straight road seem impassable, stands inside the category the verse has drawn.

The sūrah will spend its next verses on the people who stand on the heights and on the ones who cry out from below them. Before the reader arrives at that scene, the definition of verse 45 sits in his way as the sūrah's own mirror. It is not difficult to walk a crooked road; the verse says so. What it takes is somebody to make it crooked first — and the Book, characteristically, offers no third option between calling and blocking.


Ambush on Every Road: The Sūrah's Own Parallel

The description at 7:45 is a catalogue of three acts, and the sūrah states the same acts as a prohibition addressed to a living community. Shuʿayb tells the people of Midian: *“do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked”* (7:86)

The shift from description to prohibition is what gives the catalogue its force. A hindrance from the way is not a private disbelief but a public act performed on a road, and the road in 7:86 is every road. The sūrah's towns are destroyed for conduct of this kind, and the verse at 7:45 explains why the conduct is listed rather than merely condemned: it has a shape, it has a location, and it can be recognised in a community before the community is destroyed

The third item in the catalogue, disbelief in the Hereafter, is the ground of the first two. A path can be obstructed without cost only if there is no accounting for the obstruction, and the sūrah's insistence on the meeting with Allah throughout its towns' accounts is an insistence on the thing that makes obstruction expensive


Turning Believers Away: The Same Charge in Āl ʿImrān

The charge of 7:45 is put to another group in the same terms: *“Why do you turn the believers away from the Way of Allah—striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, while you are witnesses ˹to its truth˺?”* (3:99)

The two verbs of the charge describe one operation from two sides. Turning away is an act on the traveller; making crooked is an act on the path. The first removes a person from the way, and the second makes the way itself unusable for those who remain, which is why the sūrah treats it as the more serious of the two

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:46

> **There will be a barrier between Paradise and Hell. And on the heights ˹of that barrier˺ will be people who will recognize ˹the residents of˺ both by their appearance. They will call out to the residents of Paradise, “Peace be upon you!” They will have not yet entered Paradise, but eagerly hope to.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Barrier**

*Wa-baynahumā ḥijāb* — and between them a barrier. The word *ḥijāb* is the Qur'an's term for a screen that divides while allowing perception through or across it: the partition that shielded Maryam from her people (19:17), the barrier God placed before the disbelievers so that they cannot grasp the revelation while it is being recited (17:45), the veil that belongs to God's own transcendence (42:51). Here it is a physical feature of the Hereafter, and the Book describes it in another sūrah with a detail this one assumes: *“Then a ˹separating˺ wall with a gate will be erected between them. On the near side will be grace…” (57:13)* (57:13).

The geography is important and easy to skim past. The Qur'an's Hereafter is not a moral abstraction; it has structure. There is a Garden, there is a Fire, and between them there is a construction. The people of this verse stand on that construction, and everything the verse says about them follows from the fact that they are *in between* — neither inside nor excluded, and able to see both directions.

**The Heights**

The Arabic word for what they stand on gives the sūrah its name: *al-aʿrāf*, the plural of *ʿurf*, the elevated part of a thing — the crest of a wall, the ridge of a dune, the high ground from which a whole valley can be seen. Just as the Book's sky has gates, its separation has high places, and the exegetes took the word literally: a wall with a top, and people on top of it.

Who they are has been a subject of discussion since the earliest generations. Al-Ṭabarī records a range of views and reports the opinion attributed to more than one of the Companions, including the reading associated with Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, that the people of the Heights are those whose scales balance — whose good deeds and bad deeds are exactly equal, so that neither the Garden nor the Fire claims them, and they wait on the ridge while the reckoning runs its course. Other reports identify them as angels watching over the crowd, or as the most honoured of the believers who have been granted a view first. The verse itself declines to name them, and this reticence is itself instructive: it fixes the reader's attention on what they are doing rather than whose identity documents they carry.

That is the sūrah's constant method. Its long narratives do not answer the question "which historical group produced this detail?" until the lesson has landed.

**"They Will Recognize Both by Their Appearance"**

*Yaʿrifūna kullan bi-sīmāhum* — they recognize each group by their marks. The word *sīmā* is the brand a man puts on his cattle, the characteristic by which a tribe is identified in the dark. The Qur'an uses it three times for the Hereafter and the world, and in each place it makes the same claim: the moral quality of a person becomes visible. *“The wicked will be recognized by their appearance, then will be seized by their forelocks and feet”* (55:41). In this world the mark is often invisible — the Book tells the Prophet that he will know the hypocrites *by the tone of their speech* (47:30), and it tells him that the impoverished believers who give in secret are known only *by their mark* to those who look carefully (2:273). On the Day, the recognition becomes the universal reading of a face.

There is a further resonance to the word choice. The place is *al-aʿrāf*; the people there *yaʿrifūn*, they know. The root is the same: *ʿ-r-f*. The ones who possessed knowledge in this world — of God's signs, of the difference between the mark of the faithful and the mark of the proud — are given the station of recognition. The Book's doctrine that knowledge is a trust now becomes a vantage point.

**"Peace Be Upon You"**

*Wa-nādaw aṣḥāba al-jannati an salāmun ʿalaykum.* The verb of the previous verse returns: they call out, and the content of the call is the greeting of Paradise itself. *Salām* is the first word the Book's own liturgy places in the mouths of the redeemed — *“in which their prayer will be, ‘Glory be to You, O Allah!’ and their greeting will be, ‘Peace!’”* (10:10) — and the greeting the angels will give the blessed at the gates: *“Peace be upon you! Enter Paradise for what you used to do”* (16:32; 39:73).

What makes this a moment of high composition is that the greeting is offered by people who have not yet entered. They stand on the wall, they see the gardens, they salute their inhabitants, and their own case is still pending. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of the community's faces being bright with the marks of the worship they performed in the world — *“My community will be called on the Day of Resurrection al-ghurr al-muḥajjalūn, radiant from the traces of ablution”* (al-Bukhārī 136; Muslim 246, from Abū Hurayrah) — and the verse of the Heights shows a group identified by marks and greeting those who have arrived.

**"And They Have Not Entered It, Yet They Hope"**

The verse's last clause is the hinge of the whole scene: *lā yadkhulūnahā wa-hum yaṭmaʿūn* — they have not entered it, but they are eager in hope. The Arabic *ṭamaʿa* denotes desire tinged with confidence, and the Qur'an uses it for the hope a believer has of forgiveness: Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ places in Ibrāhīm's prayer the words, *“And He is ˹the One˺ Who, I hope, will forgive my flaws on Judgment Day.”* (26:82).

Everything in the Book's vocabulary of salvation is present in that clause. Faith is not certainty of outcome; it is hope anchored in the mercy of God and worked out in conduct. A person standing on the wall between the Garden and the Fire, having seen the faces of both populations and registered their marks, does not recite doctrine. He hopes. The sūrah leaves its readers in exactly that posture — which is to say, in the place where the Qur'an normally leaves a human being: certain of what he has done, uncertain of what he has not yet been forgiven, and asking.


A Barrier They Never Cross

7:46 opens with a barrier between the two abodes, and the Book describes a barrier of the same kind in the created world: *“between them is a barrier they never cross”* (55:20), said of the two seas whose waters meet without mixing. The parallel is structural rather than merely verbal. In both cases two things that touch are kept distinct by a limit neither can pass, and in both cases the limit is stated as a fact about the arrangement rather than as an act of enforcement. The barrier of 7:46 has people standing on it, which the barrier of ar-Raḥmān does not, and that addition is the verse's own contribution.

The people on the heights are described by what they can do from there: they recognise the residents of both by their marks. Recognition across a barrier is the position the verse gives them, and it is a position of knowledge without membership

The barrier is what makes the recognition possible. Without it the two abodes would be one place and the marks would not be distinguishable; with it the marks are visible from a third position that belongs to neither


Peace Given and Peace Earned

The greeting of 7:46 is spoken before entry, and the Book records the same greeting at the moment of arrival: *“Peace be upon you for your perseverance. How excellent is the ultimate abode!”* (13:24). The verse of ar-Raʿd attaches a ground to the greeting, since the peace is given for perseverance, while the greeting of al-Aʿrāf is given to people whose entry has not yet happened

What the comparison settles is the status of the hope named at the end of 7:46. Hope without entry is not a suspended verdict but a position with a greeting attached to it; the people of the heights are addressed in the language of the saved before they are admitted, and the verse of ar-Raʿd shows what the same language means when the admission has taken place

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:47

> **When their eyes will turn towards the residents of Hell, they will pray, “Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn of the Eye**

*Wa-idhā ṣurifat abṣāruhum tilqāʾa aṣḥābi al-nār* — and when their eyes will turn towards the residents of Hell. The syntax deserves the attention it takes. Their gaze is not described as wandering or as choosing; the verb is passive, *ṣurifat*, they are turned. Something or someone directs the sight of the people on the Heights when the moment comes, and the Qur'an leaves the agent unnamed, as it leaves the announcer of 7:44 unnamed and the speaker of the final command of 7:49 unnamed. The Book's Hereafter is full of arrangements made by an authority that never identifies itself, and the effect is the sense of a reality governed from behind the scenes.

The image itself is one of the Book's most affecting small scenes. These are people who have just saluted the inhabitants of Paradise, who stand close enough to see the gardens and their residents. Then their eyes are turned the other way, to the other population, and the greeting gives way to a prayer.

**The Prayer of the Almost-Saved**

*Rabbanā lā tajʿalnā maʿa al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — “Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.” The petition is not for a rank and not for a gift. It is a request to be kept out of a *company*. *Lā tajʿalnā maʿa* — do not make us *with* — is the vocabulary of placement, and the Book uses it consistently in the mouth of those who understand that the company is the consequence.

The Qur'an's most exact rendering of the sentiment appears in the prayer of the family of ʿImrān, which the sūrah of Āl ʿImrān reports in full: *“Our Lord! We have heard the caller to ˹true˺ belief, ˹proclaiming,˺ ‘Believe in your Lord ˹alone˺,’ so we believed. Our Lord! Forgive our sins, absolve us of our misdeeds, and allow us ˹each˺ to die as one of the virtuous.”* (3:193), preceded by the plea *“Our Lord! Indeed, those You commit to the Fire will be ˹completely˺ disgraced!”* (3:192). Sūrat al-Furqān attributes to the servants of the Merciful the habit of praying, *“Our Lord! Keep the punishment of Hell away from us, for its punishment is indeed unrelenting” (25:65)* (25:65), and Sūrat al-Muʾminūn teaches the same petition in the present life: *“My Lord! I seek refuge in You from the temptations of the devils, and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, that they even come near me”* (23:97–98).

Two features of these prayers recur wherever the Book records them. The first is that they address God as *rabbanā*, "our Lord" — the possessive of devotion, the invocation of the servant who has a claim of kinship with his Maker through dependence. The second is that they ask for the avoidance of a destination rather than for the enjoyment of a reward.

**Why the Fear Is of Company, Not of Pain**

Modern readers often read the Hereafter as a payments system: quantities of pain, quantities of pleasure, each matched to a ledger. The sūrah's imagery has been pointing somewhere else, and this verse states it plainly. The thing the people of the Heights fear is not fire. It is being *with* the wrongdoers — of finding themselves in the company of the people whose lives they watched in the world.

That is the sūrah's consistent teaching about the two destinies. Verse 38 described the communities entering the fire and cursing one another; verse 39 had the first saying to the last, *you have no superiority over us*; verse 40 closed the gates; verse 44 recorded the accusation; verse 45 defined the accused. Every one of those scenes is about association — who is gathered with whom, and what follows from it. Sūrat al-Zukhruf states the principle for the whole Day: *“Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous”* (43:67). Sūrat al-Furqān records the regret of the one who took a bad companion: *“I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend.”* (25:28). And Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt tells the story of a man in the Garden who looks down and sees his old comrade in the Fire (37:51–57).

The Book is not squeamish about the point. What a person tolerates in his friendships, his reading, his company, and his teachers is not a detail of his morals but the shape of his end, and the Hereafter assembles people accordingly. The people on the Heights pray to be excluded from the assembly, and the prayer is the most intelligent one ever uttered in the Book's scenes.

**The Sūrah's Teaching for the Present**

There is a reason the Qur'an records these prayers in the afterlife rather than only in the world. The reader is being taught the vocabulary of the saved before he needs it. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to ask for refuge in nearly identical terms, and the tradition carried the practice into the daily liturgies: the supplication to be spared the Fire appears in the night prayer, in the prayer for the mosque, and in the brief duas the Prophet recommended to his Companions. The line the sūrah draws is direct: whoever learns the prayer of the Heights now will not need to learn it in the hour when it must be answered immediately.

And the verse's fear has a diagnostic value for anyone who prays it honestly. It sits uncomfortably with a life built around the approval of crowds, the company of the influential, the borrowed authority of fashionable opinion. The prayer asks God to keep the speaker out of *that* company, and the man who seriously prays it will find the same request shaping his choice of whom he sits with, listens to, and answers to.


**Do Not Place Us With Them: The Verb of Making**

The prayer is *lā tajʿalnā maʿa al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — *“Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.”* (7:47). The verb is *jaʿala*, from *j-ʿ-l*, the Book’s general verb for making and placing: it makes the night and the day, makes the earth a resting place, and here is asked not to make a placement

The same verb and the same construction appear in the prayer al-Baqarah records for the believers: *“Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us.”* (2:286)

The exegetes note that *jaʿala* takes two objects, so the prayer asks about an assignment that has a subject and a place. Al-Rāzī reads this as evidence that the people on the Heights understand their own position as undetermined in a way they cannot settle themselves, which is why the prayer is addressed rather than resolved


**Three Groups and Their Three Calls**

7:47 sits inside a scene the sūrah divides into three parties, each of which speaks. The people of Paradise call to the people of the Fire: *“We have certainly found our Lord’s promise to be true. Have you too found your Lord’s promise to be true?”* (7:44). The people of the Heights call to men they recognise by their marks: *“Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺!”* (7:48).

7:47 is the third call, and it is the only one addressed upward. The saved speak across to the damned; the people of the Heights speak down to men they knew; and in 7:47 the eyes turn toward the Fire and the speech goes to God. That is the structural point of the verse: it marks the moment at which the party in the middle stops looking sideways and asks. The sūrah gives no other instance of a scene in the hereafter in which a party’s words are addressed to its Lord rather than to another party.

The three calls also carry three different tenses of knowledge. 7:44 reports a promise found true, in the past perfect of a completed discovery; 7:48 reports a reckoning already known to the speakers, who recognise the men they address; 7:47 reports nothing known, only a fear about company. The people of the Heights are therefore described as the party that has found and the party that recognises, while the speakers of 7:47 are described by the direction of their eyes.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:48

> **Those on the heights will call out to some ˹tyrants in the Fire˺, who they will recognize by their appearance, saying, “Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Call to Particular Men**

*Wa-nādā aṣḥābu al-aʿrāfi rijālan* — and the people of the Heights called out to certain men. The verb of the previous two verses returns for the third time: the Hereafter of this sūrah is a scene of speaking across distances. What is new is the object of the address. The blessed were addressed as a community (*aṣḥāba al-jannati*), the cursed as a community (*aṣḥāba al-nār*), but here the call goes out to *rijāl* — men, individuals, identifiable persons whose faces the callers know. The Qur'an uses the plural *rijāl* for grown men in their public capacity, and its appearance here says something the larger scene would have blurred: the leaders are not swallowed by the crowd they led. They are each still themselves, on show.

*Alladhīna yaʿrifūnahum bi-sīmāhum* — whom they recognize by their marks. The third occurrence of this phrase in three verses takes on a sharper edge now, because the marks in question belong to tyrants whose faces the world knew from coins and speeches. Sūrat al-Raḥmān describes the same reversal: *“The wicked will be recognized by their appearance, then will be seized by their forelocks and feet”* (55:41). The Book's claim is not that God needs identifying marks — it is that character, which in this world is hidden under clothing, reputation, and public relations, will end up written on the body.

**"Your Numbers Have Availed You Nothing"**

*Mā aghnā ʿankum jamʿukum* — your multitude has not enriched you in anything. *Aghnā* is the verb of sufficiency: to make someone need nothing more. *Jamʿ* is the mass — the assembled following, the party, the coalition, the mob, the congregation of clients and dependents, the crowd a man can produce when he wants to demonstrate that he matters. The sentence declares that the entire apparatus has been weighed and found to have no purchasing power.

This is one of the Book's most persistent themes and one of its least welcome. *“If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah's way”* (6:116). *“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him in worship”* (12:106). *“Competition for more ˹gains˺ diverts you ˹from Allah˺, until you end up in ˹your˺ graves.”* (102:1–2). *“We are far superior ˹to the believers˺ in wealth and children, and we will never be punished.”* — this is the speech of the affluent of Sabaʾ (34:35), and the answer comes in the next verses: *“It is not your wealth or children that bring you closer to Us”* (34:37). Sūrat al-Baqarah records an army that fled its homes in the thousands for fear of death and was told to die (2:243). The Qur'an mentions the size of the crowds that followed the truth and the size of the crowds that opposed it, and it refuses, in either case, to treat the number as an argument.

The wording *your multitude* also carries a sting that a Makkan audience would have felt precisely. The chiefs of the town had dependents, allies, clients, slaves, and the moral weight of clan solidarity behind them; their confidence in the outcome of the coming judgment was indistinguishable from their confidence in the size of their following. Verse 48 tells them the following has been left on the other side of the fire.

**"Nor What You Used to Be Arrogant About"**

*Wa-mā kuntum tastakbirūn* — and neither has the arrogance you used to practise. The phrase returns to the sūrah's single diagnosis. Verse 36 described those who *denied Our signs and treated them with disdain*; verse 40 closed the gates of heaven against the same people; verse 48 now names what the disdain was, and whom it was for. The arrogant elite of the sūrah's narratives had defined themselves by the lowliness of the people who believed: the chiefs of Ṣāliḥ's town asking *“Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”* while the lowly answered, *“We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”* (7:75–76); the disbelieving chiefs of Noah's people telling him that only *the lowliest* follow him (11:27); the people of Shuʿayb lying in ambush on the road to turn back those who believed (7:86).

The Prophet ﷺ gave the two populations their portraits in a single hadith, and no commentary improves on it. Harithah ibn Wahb heard the Messenger of God say: *“Shall I tell you of the people of Paradise? They comprise every poor humble person, and if he swears by Allah to do something, Allah will fulfil it; while the people of the fire comprise every violent, cruel, arrogant person”* (al-Bukhārī 6657, from Ḥārithah ibn Wahb). The verse of the Heights has staged that hadith as a conversation between two populations who can see one another.

**The Failure of Social Capital**

Read economically, verse 48 is a statement about currency. Arrogance is a form of capital in this world: it purchases obedience, deference, precedence in a queue, the last word in a meeting, the silence of the people who would otherwise object. The verse declares the exchange rate on the Day: zero. There is no market in the Hereafter for any of the transactions the tyrannical elite spent a lifetime perfecting.

And the alternative assets are the ones the sūrah has already named, in the plainest language it possesses. Verse 35 defined salvation as *reform* and reverence; verse 42 as belief and right action; verse 43 as an inheritance granted for what one did and a guidance that came from God. Against the tyrants' *jamʿ* — the crowd — the sūrah files the *ṣālihāt* — the deeds — and its verdict on the comparison is the single sentence being shouted across the barrier in this verse.

**The Question That Follows**

The scene is not finished with the tyrants. Verse 49 will put a question to them in the same voices, and the question will be the last word of the passage: *Are these the ones you swore would never be shown Allah's mercy?* — pointing, in the manner of the sūrah, at the poor and lowly who followed the messengers and who stand at that moment inside the Garden while the men who mocked them watch from the Fire. The people of the Heights do not answer their own question. The next verse answers it with a command, and the command is not addressed to the tyrants.


Recognized by Their Appearance: The Marks in ar-Raḥmān

The call at 7:48 is made to particular men, and the callers know them by their marks. The Book states the same recognition in ar-Raḥmān: *“The wicked will be recognized by their appearance, then will be seized by ˹their˺ forelocks and feet.”* (55:41)

The marks are what the two abodes have in common. The people of the heights recognise the residents of both by their appearance at 7:46, and at 7:48 they recognise particular men among the residents of the Fire

What the recognition removes is anonymity. The men addressed at 7:48 are known by their marks, and the things that distinguished them in the world are named in the call itself — their numbers and their arrogance. The sūrah's account of the chiefs throughout its towns describes the same distinguishing features in life, and the call at the heights reports them as recognised after death


Wealth and Children Do Not Bring Nearness

The two things named in the call at 7:48 are the things the Book elsewhere removes from the scale: *“It is not your wealth or children that bring you closer to Us.”* (34:37). The verse of Sabaʾ states the removal and then states what remains: *“But those who believe and do good—it is they who will have a multiplied reward for what they did, and they will be secure in ˹elevated˺ mansions”* (34:37)

What this adds to 7:48 is the measure that replaces the removed one. Numbers avail nothing, and belief joined to good works is multiplied; the arithmetic of the world is replaced by an arithmetic of the record. The sūrah states the same replacement at 7:8–9, where the weighing decides and no soul is wronged, and the verse at 7:48 reports the replacement from inside the Fire, addressed to men whose numbers had been their argument in life

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:49

> **Are these ˹humble believers˺ the ones you swore would never be shown Allah’s mercy?” ˹Finally, those on the heights will be told:˺ “Enter Paradise! There will be no fear for you, nor will you grieve.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question That Names the Mockery**

*A-hāʾulāʾi alladhīna aqsamtum lā yanāluhum Allāh bi-raḥma* — are these the ones you swore would never be shown Allah’s mercy? The verse is a question addressed to the tyrants of verse 48, and it closes the longest single argument the sūrah has constructed: the exchange between the proud and the lowly that began, in the world, with a sneer and now ends in the Hereafter with a demonstration.

The oath in the question is the point of it. *Aqsamtum* is the verb of a solemn sworn claim, and the claim is a denial of God's mercy to specific people — the poor, the dependent, the unimpressive believers who had attached themselves to the messengers. The sūrah's own account of that sneer has already appeared: the arrogant chiefs asking the lowly whether they were sure their prophet was really from God (7:75–76). The Qur'an preserves the same scene in the histories of other prophets. The chiefs of Noah's people said, *“We see you only as a human being like ourselves, and we see that no one follows you except the lowliest among us”* (11:27). The people of Shuʿayb's town asked the prophet, *“How can we believe in you, when you are followed only by the lowest of the low?”* (26:111). And the sūrah of the Cave records the instruction given to the Prophet in the middle of a Makkah that made precisely this calculation: *“And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not let your eyes look beyond them, desiring the luxuries of this worldly life”* (18:28; see also 6:52).

**What Is Actually Being Denied**

The statement that the poor will never be shown mercy is not simply a rude opinion about the weak. It is a claim about God — an assertion that the divine decision has been settled in advance by the social order, that the gates of Paradise are staffed like the gates of a Makkan house, and that the meritoriousness of a person can be read off his standing in the world. That presumption is what makes the verse a scene of judgment rather than a scene of embarrassment.

The Book states the correction in the imperative, and it does so in the sharpest available form: *“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ ‘O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins. He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”* (39:53). The verse does not qualify the offer by class, lineage, learning, or the approval of the notable. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf itself has already stated the theology that the tyrants' oath denied: *“But My mercy encompasses everything.”* (7:156), and its own definition of who inherits the Garden — belief and right action, no inventory of titles (7:42).

**The Answer Nobody in the Verse Gives**

The question is asked and left unanswered in the mouths of those who greeted the Garden with *Peace*, and the silence is the composition. The people of the Heights cannot admit the mockers into the Garden and cannot promise them anything; they can only ask the question whose answer is visible to everyone standing on the wall. It is answered a line later, by an authority that has been operating throughout these verses without ever introducing itself: *udkhulū al-jannata* — enter the Garden.

*Lā khawfun ʿalaykum wa-lā antum taḥzanūn* — no fear will be upon you, and you will not grieve. The formula is one of the most repeated promises in the Book: it is given to the followers of guidance in the first descent from the Garden (2:38), to all who believe in God and the Last Day and do good (2:62; 5:69), to those who submit themselves to God (2:112), to the friends of God (10:62), and to those who say, *Our Lord is Allah*, and remain steadfast (46:13). Its two halves are exhaustive by design. *Lā khawfun ʿalaykum* — nothing to fear ahead, no threat still in the pipeline, no sentence pending, no loss still possible. *Wa-lā antum taḥzanūn* — nothing to grieve behind, no ache for what was lost, no regret for the years, no memory doing damage. Sūrat Fāṭir gives the residents of the Garden the same sentiment in their own words: *“Praise be to Allah, Who has kept away from us all causes of sorrow”* (35:34), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own verse 43 will say that God has removed what was bitter in their hearts.

**The Vindication of the Lowly**

The command to enter is issued to the people on the Heights. The verse's structure is thus complete, and it is a structure the sūrah has been building since its first pages: the believers who were too insignificant to be counted in the world are the first to be told to go in, and the elites who mocked them watch from across the barrier.

**The Sūrah's Last Word on the Two Crowds**

The passage ends, as it began in verse 36, on the question of who gets in. It began with a word — *istakbarū*, they disdained — and it ends with a door. Along the way, the sūrah showed the dishonest question (7:37), the community cursing its sister (7:38), the leaders and followers trading blame (7:39), the camel and the needle (7:40), the bed and its covers (7:41), the capacity of the soul (7:42), the song of the grateful (7:43), the call and its answer (7:44), the definition of the unjust (7:45), the people who recognize (7:46), the prayer of the almost-saved (7:47), the useless crowd (7:48), and this command. Every one of those verses made the same distinction in a different register, and the last of them makes it by pointing: these, whom you discounted, are told to enter.

The verse that follows will show the men left behind asking for a mouthful of water. The Book places them next to each other deliberately, because the sūrah's audience in Makkah was made up of people who had to choose that day — with their families, their clans, their businesses, and the opinion of everyone who mattered watching them decide.


No Fear and No Grief: The Two Negations at the Gate

The sentence given to the people of the heights at 7:49 removes two things rather than granting one: enter Paradise, and there will be no fear upon you nor will you grieve. The Book states the same pair as the condition of following guidance, in the address given at the descent: *“when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”* (2:38)

The pairing of fear and grief covers the two directions in which a life can be unsettled. Fear is about what is coming and grief about what has passed, and their removal is therefore a removal of the whole range rather than of one anxiety. The sūrah's own account of the towns describes communities living inside both: afraid of what a messenger threatens and grieving what a punishment has taken. The two negations at 7:49 are the reversal of that condition, stated as the terms of entry.

What precedes the entry in the verse is the question that names the mockery. The people addressed are described as those about whom an oath had been sworn, that Allah would not show them mercy, and the question is put by the party that had taken the oath


Mercy Sworn Against and Mercy Given

The oath reported at 7:49 is a claim about the extent of mercy, and the Book answers such claims in the plainest terms: *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls!”* (39:53) — and then, *“for Allah certainly forgives all sins”* (39:53)

What the two passages establish is that mercy is not distributed by human estimates. The people of the heights were judged by their appearance in the world and found wanting; the servants of az-Zumar were judged by their own account and found exceeding the limits

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:50

> **The residents of the Fire will then cry out to the residents of Paradise, “Aid us with some water or any provision Allah has granted you.” They will reply, “Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fourth Call**

*Wa-nādā aṣḥābu al-nāri aṣḥāba al-jannati* — and the residents of the Fire will cry out to the residents of Paradise. The verb *nādā* has now been used four times in seven verses: the Garden calls to the Fire (7:44), the Heights call to the Garden (7:46), the Heights call to the tyrants (7:48), and now the Fire calls to the Garden. The sūrah has constructed a complete traffic of voices across the barrier, and it is worth noticing what the traffic never carries: any movement of goods, any answer that changes a condition, any transfer at all. The only exchange between the two populations in the Hereafter is speech, and speech has become a spectator sport.

**What the Condemned Ask For**

*Afīḍū ʿalaynā mina al-māʾi aw mimmā razaqakum Allāh* — pour out on us some water, or any of what Allah has provided you. The request is remarkable for how little it asks. These are the residents of the Fire, and they do not ask to be released, nor to have their punishment reduced, nor even to enter the Garden. They ask for water — for a share of the *provision* of the Garden, in whatever amount, in whatever form. The Book's portrait of damnation at its most concrete is a request for a mouthful.

The Qur'an's other accounts of the condemned in the Hereafter insist on the same modesty of demand. Sūrat al-Sajdah describes them saying, *“Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good.”* (32:12). Sūrat Fāṭir has them crying, *“Our Lord! Take us out ˹and send us back˺. We will do good, unlike what we used to do. ˹They will be told,˺ ‘Did’”* (35:37). And the sūrah's own verse 53 will record the same plea. But this verse is unique in the Book for asking nothing more than a drink, which is exactly why it lands. Everything the Fire's inhabitants once possessed has been reduced to one wish, and the wish is for water.

The Gospel gives the same scene in its own idiom: the rich man in torment looks across the chasm and begs that Lazarus might dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue (Luke 16:24). The Books of revelation agree on the architecture of the Hereafter to a degree that has struck every reader who has put the two passages side by side: a fixed separation, a vision of the other side, and a request that cannot be answered.

**The Reply: "It Is Forbidden"**

*Qālū inna Allāha ḥarramahumā ʿalā al-kāfirīn* — they replied: Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers. The answer is not delivered as a taunt and not as a punishment; it is delivered as information. The people of the Garden state a fact about the order of things, which is the consistent register of the saved in this sūrah: verse 44's blessed asked a question already answered, and here they supply a prohibition.

The verb is the one the sūrah has already put on trial. At verse 32 the sūrah demanded, *“Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?”* — and the answer then was that false prohibitions belong to the fabricators, not to God. Here the same verb returns as a verdict: those who spent their lives forbidding what God made lawful now find their own share of water forbidden by God. The symmetry is not a coincidence of vocabulary; the sūrah has been building to it since verse 32, and the point is the doctrine of requital in kind that the Book states repeatedly: *“Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it”* (99:8); *“This is the reward for what your hands have done, and Allah is never unjust to His creation”* (3:182).

**Why Water?**

The choice of water as the subject of this final deprivation is not incidental to the sūrah. Water is the Book's standing emblem of mercy and of life: *“We split them apart? And We created from water every living thing.”* (21:30); *“Have you considered the water you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so?”* (56:68–69); *“Say, ‘Consider this: if your water were to sink ˹into the earth˺, then who ˹else˺ could bring you flowing water?’”* (67:30). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf itself had opened its meditation on God's provision with the rain: *“He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land”* (7:57).

To deny a person water is, in the Book's vocabulary, to deny him the created symbol of God's care — and the men being denied spent their lives turning away from the source of that care. The verse's theology is therefore tighter than a picture of thirst. The Garden's rivers are not a beverage; they are what flows from the mercy of the One who made them flow. A man who refused the mercy will not be able to drink its sign, and the reply of verse 50 is simply the announcement that the connection is closed.

**The Silence of the Garden**

It matters that the residents of the Garden do not say *we will not give you*. Their answer names God as the one who forbade, and their sentence therefore contains no private refusal — no revenge, no satisfaction, no gloating. The saved of this sūrah have already asked and received; their concern in these scenes is not the fate of the condemned but the accuracy of the account. Verse 44: have you found your Lord's promise true? Verse 50: Allah has forbidden it.

That is a deliberate composition, and it is the sūrah's answer to the charge that religion is a system of tribal resentment. The Book refuses to let the saved enjoy the punishment of the damned. It has them state a fact about the order of the world, ask their question, offer their greeting of peace, and then — as verse 49 did with a command that mentioned nobody left behind — move on. Whatever the reader has been imagining about the satisfaction of the righteous over their enemies, the sūrah replaces it with a watering request and an answer from the Book of decrees.


Water in the Fire: The Same Element in al-Ḥajj

The request at 7:50 is for water or for any provision, and the reply forbids both to the disbelievers. The Book describes water inside the Fire in terms that explain why the request is refused rather than merely denied: *“garments of Fire will be cut out for them and boiling water will be poured over their heads”* (22:19), *“melting whatever is in their bellies, along with their skin”* (22:20)

The verse of al-Ḥajj sets this scene inside a dispute: two opposing groups that disagree about their Lord. The request at 7:50 is made across the same divide as the call at 7:44, and it is the fourth of the sūrah's calls between the two abodes

The specificity of water is what makes the scene intelligible to the sūrah's reader. The towns of al-Aʿrāf are destroyed in part by water — the flood at 7:133, the rain at 7:84 — and the deliverance of the believers is also by water at 7:160


What Landed You: The Category Answer

The reply at 7:50 names a category rather than the persons asking, and the Book records the same kind of answer given by the condemned themselves. They are asked *“What has landed you in Hell?”* (74:42) and they answer in terms of what they were not: *“We were not of those who prayed”* (74:43), *“nor did we feed the poor.”* (74:44)

What this adds to the scene is the reason the request cannot be granted. Provision at the gate is distributed by belonging, and the speakers at 7:50 are outside the belonging that carries it. The verses of al-Muddaththir show the condemned understanding this in their own terms, listing the practices they did not perform rather than the punishment they received

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:51

> **those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life.” ˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs and for rejecting Our revelations.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Religion Taken as a Hobby**

*Alladhīna ittakhadhū dīnahum lahwan wa-laʿiban* — those who took this faith as mere amusement and play. The construction is worth pausing on. The object of the taking is *dīnuhum* — their own religion, the thing that should have been the organizing axis of their days, the affair to which they belonged. What they made of it was *lahw*, distraction, and *laʿib*, game. The two nouns are the Qur'an's standard pair for whatever occupies a person while having no consequence: the entertainment and the sport, the pastime and the joke.

The Qur'an repeats the accusation against the same category of people in three other places, and in each case the phrase sits at the end of a catalogue of serious failures. *“And leave those who take this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere play and amusement and are deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life”* (6:70). *“those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. ˹Allah will say,˺ ‘Today We will ignore them’”* (7:51). And in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd, the divine description of the world's own texture: *“Know that this worldly life is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children.”* (57:20).

It is important not to misread the charge as an attack on pleasure. The sūrah itself forbade the men who banned God's adornments (7:32) and defended the lawful enjoyment of food, drink, and clothing (7:31). The Book's objection is never to delight; it is to the *demotion* of the highest concern to the level of a trifle. A religion held as a hobby cannot command a person at the moment of a real decision. That is the whole of the indictment, and the sūrah's Makkan audience knew exactly what it meant: they had gods, ceremonies, pilgrimage, poetry, and ancestral custom, and they held none of it as an obligation capable of costing them anything.

**The Mockery Behind the Description**

The verse's phrase has a second edge, and history sharpens it. The Aʿrāf's Makkah was a place where the Prophet's recitation was treated as an entertainment: *“The disbelievers say, ‘This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication which he made up with the help of others.’”* (25:4); *“they hear ˹you recite˺ the Reminder, and say, ‘He is certainly a madman.’”* (68:51); *“Indeed, the wicked used to laugh at the believers”* (83:29–30). The Book records the mockery as a social technology, not a private opinion: it was how the strong kept the weak from listening, and how the notables of the town made the act of belief look embarrassing.

**"Deluded by ˹Their˺ Worldly Life"**

*Wa-gharrat-humu al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* — and they were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. The verb *gharra* is the verb of the mirage: to make a thing look like what it is not, to promise what it will not deliver. The Book uses it constantly and always with the same target: *“So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah”* (31:33; 35:5); *“the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”* (3:185, 57:20).

The mechanism of the deception is worth naming, because the Book names it. The *dunyā* — from *danā*, nearness — is the near, the available, the immediately rewarding. It does not deceive by being evil at every turn; it deceives by occupying the whole of a person's attention with things that are true and good and near, so that the far and greater thing is never attended to at all. The Makkan merchants of the sūrah were not, for the most part, monsters. They were busy, successful, generous within their circles, proud of their city, and convinced that the world had always been as they knew it. The delusion is that a man can be absorbed by what he can see and still keep his bearings about what he cannot.

**"Today We Will Forget Them"**

The verse passes from description to sentence: *fa-l-yawma nansāhum kamā nasū liqāʾa yawmihim hādhā* — so today We will ignore them, just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs. The idiom of God "forgetting" is one the Book uses with care, and it never means a lapse of knowledge — the Qur'an's God is the One from whom nothing is hidden (40:16; 2:284). *Nisyān* here is the vocabulary of abandonment: the withdrawal of attention, the cancellation of the relationship. Sūrat al-Sajdah states the same sentence in the same words: *“So taste ˹the punishment˺ for neglecting the meeting of this Day of yours. We ˹too˺ will certainly neglect you.”* (32:14); Sūrat al-Jāthiyah repeats it (45:34); and Sūrat al-Tawbah applies it to the hypocrites who forgot God and were forgotten in turn (9:67).

Behind the idiom stands one of the Book's most consistent laws: the punishment is the thing itself, returned. Those who treated the meeting with their Lord as unworthy of attention are given the attention they gave. It is the exact form of the requital described in verse 41 — the bed of Hell for the man who set himself above God — and the exact form the sūrah will name at the end of the verse: *wa-mā kānū bi-āyātinā yajḥadūn* — and for rejecting Our revelations.

The word *yajḥadūn* is not the general verb for disbelief. *Juḥūd* is denial of what one knows to be true — the refusal to acknowledge a thing whose evidence is already in hand. Sūrat al-Naml describes the people of the signs as rejecting them *“And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly.”* (27:14), and the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf's own account of Iblīs's fall supplies the pattern: he did not doubt God's existence; he declined to obey. The men of verse 51 are not being condemned for an intellectual failure. They are being condemned for a habit of ignoring what they had already been shown — which is precisely why the verse says *they forgot*, and not *they never heard*.


Deluded by the Life of This World: The Instrument of the Delusion

7:51 describes two things done to those at the gate: a religion taken as amusement and play, and a delusion produced by the life of this world. The second is stated in al-Ḥadīd as an instrument with an operation of its own: *“You chose to be tempted ˹by hypocrisy˺, ˹eagerly˺ awaited ˹our demise˺, doubted ˹the truth˺, and were deluded by false hopes”* (57:14). The verse of al-Aʿrāf names the deluder, and al-Ḥadīd names the thing that does the deluding, namely hopes that were false. Both verses place the delusion inside the world's life rather than in an external temptation, and both make it the ground of a refusal that was freely made.

The two nouns of 7:51, amusement and play, describe the manner in which the religion was held. A thing taken as amusement is held without consequence, and a thing taken as play is held without a claim on the holder. The sūrah's account of the towns shows the same manner: worship performed, signs requested, promises made under torment and broken when the torment lifted

The verse's own sentence about forgetting follows from this. Those who ignored the meeting of the Day are ignored on the Day, and the correspondence is exact in form: the same act, returned.
