The sūrah states the meeting as a thing that can be ignored, which means it is a thing that can be attended to, and the ignoring is a choice made inside a life that seemed to require no such attendance


The Meeting Ignored: What the Book Says of Its Rejection

The rejection named at 7:51 has a consequence stated elsewhere in terms of weight: *“It is they who reject the signs of their Lord and their meeting with Him, rendering their deeds void, so We will not give their deeds any weight on Judgment Day”* (18:105)

What this adds to 7:51 is the measure of the loss. The verse of al-Aʿrāf reports the forgetting; the verse of al-Kahf reports the void. A religion taken as amusement produces deeds that are performed and then found to weigh nothing, and the finding happens on the Day whose meeting was ignored

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:52

> **We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained with knowledge—a guide and mercy for those who believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**After the Verdict, the Evidence**

The sūrah has just shown the condemned asking for water and listening to a prohibition. It now steps out of the Hereafter and back to the thing that decided the case: *wa-laqad jiʾnāhum bi-kitābin faṣṣalnāhu ʿalā ʿilmin* — and We brought them a Book which We explained in detail, with knowledge.

The placement is the argument. The Book is not introduced as a book that *should* have been followed; it is introduced as the exhibit filed after the sentence has been pronounced and the reason the sentence is just. The Qur'an's habit throughout is to state its own nature as a response to the accusations brought against it, and this verse summarizes the response in four words: *brought*, *explained*, *with knowledge*, and — further on — *guidance and mercy*.

**"We Explained It in Detail"**

The verb *faṣṣala* means to separate a thing into its parts so that each one is distinct: the cutting of a text into clear statements, the articulation of a body of teaching into chapters, commands, stories, warnings, and promises. The Qur'an uses it to describe its own composition at its opening pages: *“a Book whose verses are well perfected and then fully explained. It is from the One Who is All-Wise, All-Aware”* (11:1); *“a Book whose verses are perfectly explained”* (41:3). And it uses the same verb for what the Book's opponents demand: *“If only its verses were made clear ˹in our language˺”* — the sūrah of Fuṣṣilat records the objection and answers it (41:44).

The claim *ʿalā ʿilm*, with knowledge, is the one that distinguishes this Book from the other things the Makkans classed it with. The audience of 7:52 had poets, soothsayers, genealogists, and story-tellers, and all of them produced texts out of talent and memory. The Qur'an asserts a different provenance: what is in it was put there knowingly, by the One who knows the human being from the inside. Sūrat Yā-Sīn denies the poet label outright — *“We have not taught him poetry, nor is it fitting for him.”* (36:69) — and Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah lists the alternatives and rejects them one by one: it is not the word of a poet, not the word of a soothsayer, not the word of a soothsayer-like jinn (69:40–42).

**"A Guide and Mercy for Those Who Believe"**

*Hudan wa-raḥmatun li-qawmin yuʾminūn* — guidance and mercy for those who have faith. The pair is one of the Book's standing self-descriptions: *“O humanity! Indeed, there has come to you a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers.”* (10:57). *“We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss.”* (17:82). *“And it is truly a guide and mercy for the believers”* (27:77). *“˹It is˺ a guide and mercy for the good-doers”* (31:3).

The promise is generous and the qualifier is exact. The Book is not described as a source of mercy in the abstract; it is *a guide and mercy for those who believe*, and Sūrat Fuṣṣilat explains what it does to those who will not: *“As for those who disbelieve, there is deafness in their ears and blindness to it ˹in their hearts˺”* (41:44). The same revelation, in the same words, is a cure for one listener and an aggravation for another, and the difference is described by the Book as a condition of the heart rather than a quality of the text. The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf states the law bluntly a few verses later: God will turn away from His signs those who treat them with arrogance (7:146).

**The Explanation Requires Students**

If a Book is explained in detail, its hearers have an obligation that those who receive oracles do not have: the obligation to study. The Qur'an expects its audience to look things up — *“Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it.”* (4:83) — and the sūrah of Muḥammad instructs them to reflect on it directly: *“Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Or are there locks upon their hearts?”* (47:24). Sūrat al-Nisāʾ goes further and makes recitation, memorization, and teaching the identifying work of a community (4:82; 9:122).

The Prophet ﷺ summarized the resulting status in a sentence the tradition has never stopped repeating: *“The best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it”* (al-Bukhārī 5027, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān). Verse 52 is the doctrinal ground under that hadith. The Book that was explained in detail can only accomplish what it was sent to accomplish through people who take the explanation seriously enough to pass it on.

**What the Sūrah Does With the Book**

It is worth noting how consistently al-Aʿrāf returns to revelation as its anchor. It opened with the letters *alif lām mīm ṣād* and the announcement of a Book revealed so that its Prophet might warn (7:2). It told its readers, *“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him”* (7:3). It will say of itself that it is *“˹This is˺ a Book which We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ so that you may lead people out of darkness and into light”* (14:1), and it will close the section on the people of the Heights with the reminder that those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer are not forgotten (7:170).

Verse 52 therefore sits in the sūrah as the answer to every scene that has preceded it. The mockers of 7:51 treated the revelation as entertainment; the condemned of 7:50 had nothing to drink; the people of the Heights recognized everyone by their marks. And the reason none of that had to happen — the whole weight of the sūrah's grief — is contained in the phrase *We brought them a Book*. It was not hidden, not withheld, and not vague. It was explained, in detail, with knowledge, and it was offered as mercy to whoever would believe.


Verses Perfectly Explained: The Same Claim in Fuṣṣilat

7:52 describes a Book brought with knowledge, and the description has a close parallel at the opening of Fuṣṣilat: *“a revelation from the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”* (41:2), *“a Book whose verses are perfectly explained—a Quran in Arabic for people who know”* (41:3). The two verses state the same three things: a source in mercy, an explanation carried into the verses themselves, and an audience described by knowledge

The explanation described in both is internal to the Book rather than supplied from outside it. The verses are explained, and the explaining is done with knowledge, which means the detail is not an ornament but the form the knowledge takes. This is why the sūrah can present its own long accounts of the towns as part of the explanation: the histories are the detail, and the detail is what makes the guidance usable. A book explained in general terms would require an interpreter; a book whose verses are explained requires a reader.

The audience named in 41:3 is a people who know, and the audience named in 7:52 is those who believe. The two descriptions are not alternatives but the same readers from two sides, and the sūrah's own account shows what happens to those who are neither: the Book is brought, and the bringing is reported as evidence at the moment of the verdict


A Healing and Mercy, and an Increase in Loss

The mercy of 7:52 is specified for the believers, and the Book states the same specification with its consequence: *“We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss.”* (17:82)

This is the answer to the question the sūrah raises throughout its towns' accounts. Why does a messenger's evidence fail to persuade? The verse of al-Isrāʾ states that the evidence operates in both directions, and the sūrah's histories are the demonstration: signs given in detail, a refusal sustained, and a loss increased by each additional sign

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:53

> **Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺? The Day it will be fulfilled, those who ignored it before will say, “The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth. Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf? Or can we be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?” They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of the Waiting**

*Hal yanẓurūna illā taʾwīlahu* — do they only await its fulfilment? The verb *yanẓurūn* here is not the word for looking but the word for waiting in suspense, and the noun is one of the Qur'an's most interesting technical terms. *Taʾwīl* is the coming-to-be of a statement: the point at which a proclamation stops being a prediction and becomes a fact. Sūrat Yūsuf uses it for the fulfilment of the dream (12:100); Sūrat Yūnus uses it for the fulfilment of a warning that the mockers had asked to be hurried (10:39).

The question is thus a rebuke in the form of an observation. Everyone alive is waiting for something; the sūrah asks what else these particular people could be waiting for, given that the thing they deny is the only thing on the horizon. Sūrat al-Zukhruf puts the same question to the mockers — *“Are they waiting for the Hour to take them by surprise when they least expect ˹it˺?”* (43:66) — and Sūrat al-Anʿām adds the warning that belief on the morning of arrival will be of no use (6:158).

**"Those Who Ignored It Before"**

*Yaqūlu alladhīna nasūhu min qabul* — those who ignored it before will say. The verb is the same one used in verse 51, where God says He will ignore them as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs. The sūrah's argument is now complete and it circles: their forgetting was the offense; God's forgetting was the requital; and the Day itself is the memory that cannot be suppressed. The men who "forgot" were not people with a defective memory. The verse immediately preceding described them as those who had denied the signs they knew — a deliberate forgetting, maintained until the moment it could no longer be maintained.

**The Confession the Sūrah Extracts**

*Laqad jāʾat rusulu rabbinā bi-l-ḥaqq* — the messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth. This is the fourth time the sūrah has placed a confession in the mouth of the condemned. Verse 37 had the dying say that their patrons had forsaken them; verse 39 had the leaders and followers abolish each other's rank; verse 44 had the population of the Fire answer the Garden's question with a single *yes*; verse 53 has them affirm the truth of the messengers whose coming they spent a lifetime denying.

**"Are There Any Intercessors Who Can Plead for Us?"**

*Fa-hal lanā min shufaʿāʾa fa-yashfaʿū lanā* — is there anyone to intercede for us? The plea is the one the Qur'an deals with most thoroughly, because it was the central hope of the Makkan religion. Its gods were intercessors; its ancestors were intercessors; the pilgrimage was made in their names. The Book answers the hope on the highest theological level and refuses the version of it the sūrah's audience was banking on.

**"Or We Could Be Sent Back"**

*Aw nuraddu fa-naʿmala ghayra alladhī kunnā naʿmal* — or be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do. The request for return is the Book's most repeated final plea: *“Our Lord! Take us out ˹and send us back˺. We will do good, unlike what we used to do. ˹They will be told,˺ ‘Did’”* (35:37); *“My Lord! Let me go back, so I may do good in what I left behind.”* (23:99–100); *“If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us”* (2:167); *“Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good.”* (32:12). Sūrat al-Zumar records the same request in the first person: *“If only I had a second chance, I would have been one of the good-doers”* (39:58) — and the Book states elsewhere the ransom such a speaker would offer: *“Even if the wrongdoers were to possess everything in the world twice over, they would certainly offer it to ransom themselves”* (39:47; see also 13:18; 3:91).

And the Book's refusal is equally consistent, and it is not cruelty. Sūrat al-Anʿām has already given the reason with a precision that makes the plea collapse: if they were returned they would return to exactly what was forbidden them (6:28). The request is not a change of will; it is a change of circumstances. What they want is not to become different but to have another opportunity to be the same with better odds. The sūrah of Yūnus puts the same anatomy of repentance on record: the repentance of the drowning is not counted as faith (10:90–91).

**"They Have Ruined Themselves"**

The verse's last sentence ends the scene with an accounting: *qad khasirū anfusuhum* — they will have certainly ruined themselves — *wa-ḍalla ʿanhum mā kānū yaftarūn* — and whatever they fabricated will fail them. The word *khasira* is the trader's word for losing his capital, and the Book uses it for those whose capital was the self: *“But those whose scale is light, they have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs.”* (7:9); *“The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day. That is indeed the clearest loss.”* (39:15). The parable is exact. Investment is what a person does with a life; the profit and loss statement is the balance of the Day; and the people in this verse have lost the principal.

The passage that began with a question about what the mockers were waiting for ends with the answer: they were waiting to discover that nothing they had built existed, and that they had spent an entire life on the only available opportunity to build something that did.


**The Request to Be Sent Back, Elsewhere**

The request the verse records is made in the same words at two different moments, and the Book reports both. At death: *“My Lord! Let me go back,”* (23:99), and the answer is immediate — *“It is only a ˹useless˺ appeal they make. And there is a barrier behind them until the Day they are resurrected.”* (23:100). At the judgment the request returns with the same two grounds, sight and hearing: *“Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good. We truly have sure faith ˹now˺!”* (32:12).

The three passages agree on what the request contains and on what it lacks. In each case the petitioner offers future conduct in exchange for a return, and in each case the exchange is refused because the thing offered was available earlier and was not used. This verse places the request inside a confession arriving at the same moment, so the reader sees both halves of one case: the truth acknowledged, and the remedy asked for after the term.


**Intercession Asked Where There Is None**

The second of the verse’s two wishes asks for intercessors, and the Book has already told its readers what the Day will contain in that respect: *“before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession”* (2:254). The three items named are the three ordinary ways a person is helped — by trade, by relationship, by a spokesman — and the verse removes all three at once.

That is why the wish is not a hope but a diagnostic. Asking for an intercessor on that Day is asking for the machinery of this one, and the sūrah’s histories have been an account of exactly that machinery failing: chiefs unable to protect their followers, fathers whose practice was cited as a warrant, wealth that could not be carried. The verse leaves its speakers with a confession and two impossible wishes, which is the sūrah’s way of saying that on that Day nothing remains except what a person did while the term was running.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:54

> **Indeed your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then established Himself on the Throne. He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession. He created the sun, the moon, and the stars—all subjected by His command. The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺. Blessed is Allah—Lord of all worlds!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Hereafter to the Maker**

The sūrah has spent a long stretch among the last things: the gates, the bed and its coverings, the wall, the calls across it, the request for water, the confession of the lost. At verse 54 it turns to the first things — *inna rabbakumu Allāh alladhī khalaqa al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa fī sittati ayyām* — and the effect is deliberate. The Hereafter has just been shown to be an established order with gates and barriers and accounts; verse 54 names the One who established it, and does so with the vocabulary of creation rather than of judgment.

**"In Six Days"**

The phrase *sittati ayyām* has drawn the attention of every commentator, and two lines of reading are worth preserving. The first concerns the measure: a "day" in the Qur'an's own usage is not necessarily a solar day. Sūrat al-Ḥajj states that *“But a day with your Lord is indeed like a thousand years by your counting.”* (22:47), and Sūrat al-Maʿārij gives the measure of a day as fifty thousand years (70:4). What the verse tells the reader, therefore, is not a schedule but a manner: the creation was brought about in ordered stages, not in a single stroke.

The second line concerns the purpose of the number. Sūrat Hūd's version of the verse continues, *“in order to test which of you is best in deeds”* (11:7), connecting the six days to a moral project rather than to a mechanics. And the Book is emphatic about one implication the number has been misused to draw: *“We created the heavens and the earth and everything in between in six Days, and We were not even touched with fatigue”* (50:38). The verse is placed directly against the claim, current among the sūrah's audience's neighbours, that God rested on the seventh day. In the Qur'an, the completion of creation in six days demonstrates deliberateness; it does not imply exhaustion, and it does not establish a sabbath of divine recuperation.

**"Then He Rose over the Throne"**

*Thumma istawā ʿalā al-ʿarsh.* The Throne — *al-ʿarsh* — is the Book's image of the seat of universal authority: the angels carry it (69:17), circle it (39:75), and glorify God around it (40:7); God's All-Encompassing Seat, the *Kursī*, extends over the heavens and the earth (2:255). The verse's claim is that the One who made the world governs it from that authority, and the sūrah later adds its practical consequence: *“Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly.”* (7:55) — the God being addressed is the owner, not a distant first cause.

What is not disputed is the point being made. The Prophet ﷺ tested the belief of a slave girl whom her master intended to free, asking her, *“Where is Allah?”* She answered, *“In the heaven,”* and he ruled that she was a believing woman and ordered her freed (Muslim 537, from Muʿāwiyah ibn al-Ḥakam). The verse of the Heights belongs to the same plain doctrinal grammar: God is above His creation, the Throne is His, and the affairs of the world are run from there.

**"The Night Covers the Day; It Pursues It Relentlessly"**

*Yughshī al-layl al-nahār yaṭlubuhu ḥathīthan* — He covers the night with the day, and it pursues it unceasingly. The verb *yughshī* is a word for throwing a covering over something — the same root that supplied *ghawāsh*, the coverings of fire in verse 41. It is worth noticing the sūrah's reuse of it: the same image of a cover is used for the punishment of the arrogant and for the mercy of the alternation of night and day, because the Book is consistent about the fact that God is the author of both conditions.

**The Sun, the Moon, the Stars Under Command**

*Wa-l-shamsa wa-l-qamara wa-l-nujūma musakhkharātin bi-amrih* — and the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command. The word *musakhkhar* is the term for a thing compelled into service, and the Book uses it of everything in the natural order that serves human life: the day and the night, the sun and the moon, the ships at sea, the rivers, the winds, the clouds (16:12; 14:33; 45:13).

**"His Is the Creation and the Command"**

*Alā lahu al-khalqu wa-l-amr* — surely His are the creation and the command. The pairing is one the later scholars made into a technical distinction: the bringing of a thing into being and the directing of it once it exists both belong to God, and no created power holds either. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's next verses will draw the practical consequences — prayer, supplication, and hope (7:55–56) — and the sūrah's argument has been building to precisely this.

*Tabāraka Allāh rabbu al-ʿālamīn* — blessed is Allah, Lord of all worlds. *Tabāraka* is the Book's formula of exalted generosity, used at the openings of Sūrat al-Furqān and Sūrat al-Mulk over precisely the same doctrine — the One who sent the Criterion, the One in whose hand is dominion (25:1; 67:1). *Rabb al-ʿālamīn*, the Lord of all worlds, is the appellation with which the Book's own opening sūrah names Him (1:2), and the phrase *al-ʿālamīn* includes every order of creation — the angels, the jinn, humanity, and every species and system the reader does not know.

The verse's function in the sūrah is to convert the whole preceding passage into a claim on the present. The gates, the scale, the wall, the requests, the confessions, and the two crowds all belong to the One who made the heaven and the earth in six days and covers the night with the day. The next verses will explain what a person is supposed to do about that: call on Him, in humility, in secret, with hope and fear, and not corrupt the earth after it has been set right (7:55–56).


**The Bearers of the Throne**

The verse reports an establishment on the Throne. Ghāfir describes what surrounds it: *“Those ˹angels˺ who carry the Throne and those around it glorify the praises of their Lord, have faith in Him, and seek forgiveness for the believers”* (40:7). The verse names two groups — the carriers and those around them — and gives each an act: glorification, faith, and intercession for the believers.

The connection to 7:54 is one of rank. The sūrah has just described creation in six days and the establishment on the Throne, and the Book’s fullest description of that Throne’s attendants belongs to the same scene. 7:206 closes the sūrah with those nearest to God not too proud to worship Him; 40:7 describes them at the Throne, glorifying and asking forgiveness for people on the earth.

The exegetes read the mention of the Throne in 7:54 as a statement of dominion rather than of location, and cite the attendant verses as evidence that the Throne is described in the Book only in connection with worship — carried by beings who glorify, surrounded by beings who believe. That is the same point the sūrah makes at its end, where the last act reported is prostration.


**Creation and Command, Then Supplication**

The verse closes with a division: *“The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺.”* (7:54). The two nouns separate what God makes from what God orders, and the sūrah’s next verse turns the second of them into an instruction: *“Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Surely He does not like the transgressors.”* (7:55).

The sequence is the exegetes’ ground for reading the two verses together. A dominion that issues command is one that can be addressed, and the address it accepts is stated in the terms of 7:55 — humility and secrecy. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the sūrah moves here from its cosmology to its practice without a transition, because the practice follows from the cosmology: the one who holds both creation and command is the one to be called on.

This is also why the verse is placed where the sūrah places it. The preceding section has described the Day and its parties (7:36–53); 7:54 turns from the hereafter to its Maker, and 7:55 turns from the Maker to the act by which a person addresses Him. The sūrah’s argument about the towns resumes immediately afterwards, but it resumes with the ground stated.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:55

> **Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Surely He does not like the transgressors.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Throne to the Supplication**

Verse 54 ended with the claim that the creation and the command belong to God, and the next two verses explain what a creature is supposed to do about that claim. The doctrine moves immediately into practice: the One who made the heavens and the earth is the One who is asked. Sūrat al-Baqarah states the same proximity in its own way — *“When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me”* (2:186) — and Sūrat Ghāfir supplies the command with a warning attached: *“Your Lord has proclaimed: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60).

**Teacharrruʿan wa-Khufyatan: The Two Adverbs**

The Qur'an does not only command supplication; it prescribes its manner. *Taḍarruʿan wa-khufyatan* — humbly and quietly. The first word names the posture of a person who is visibly in need: the root carries the sense of abasement, of showing one's weakness, and it is used of the suppliant who approaches without a claim. The second describes the voice: *khufya* is secrecy and silence, the opposite of performance. What the verse rules out on both ends is theatrical religion — the wailing of the mourners of the age and the loud bargaining of a man who thinks his voice is leverage.

The sūrah returns to the same instruction in its own later verse, in a line that is the practical commentary on this one: *“Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless.”* (7:205) — that is, the same two adverbs, applied to remembrance rather than request. Sūrat al-Isrāʾ takes the pulse of the regulation from the other side, in the middle of an argument with the pagans about the manner of their prayer: *“Do not recite your prayers too loudly or silently, but seek a way between.”* (17:110).

The Qur'an's most complete portrait of a supplicant resembles this verse's two adverbs and adds a third detail: Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ describes the prophets as those who *“Indeed, they used to race in doing good, and call upon Us with hope and fear, totally humbling themselves before Us.”* (21:90), and Sūrat al-Sajdah describes the believers by their nights: *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them.”* (32:16).

**"He Does Not Like the Transgressors"**

The prohibition's object — *al-muʿtadīn*, the transgressors — is the sūrah's key moral word, and its placement here tells the reader what kind of supplication exceeds the limit. The exegetes listed the forms: asking for what is forbidden, asking with an air of demand rather than need, invoking God by names He has not given Himself, and — in the general sense the sūrah prefers — the transgression that consists in turning worship into a display. The same root names the boundary-crossers of verse 55's legal context throughout the Book: *“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder— a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then bloodmoney should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously.”* (2:178), *“do not exceed the limits. Surely Allah does not like transgressors.”* (2:190).

The sentence therefore does double duty. It forbids the manner of supplication that treats God as a functionary — the loud, the convenient, the transactional — and it reminds the reader that the One being called is also the One who set the limits the suppliant is asking Him to work within. The Book's ritual instructions are frequently delivered in this key: the command and the constraint arrive together, because the Book is not teaching people to influence a power but to stand in the right relationship to their Maker.

**The Three Modes the Verse Excludes**

Putting the two adverbs beside the prohibition yields a short list of the modes of prayer this verse is correcting. First, the prayer of the claimant: the person who states a case, as if he were owed. Second, the prayer of the performer: the person whose devotion requires an audience, whether an earthly one or the self-satisfied one inside. Third, the prayer of the transgressor: the person who wants God's aid inside a project God has forbidden.

Against all three, the verse sets the two conditions that the tradition kept repeating in its instruction of children: *humbly* — without status, and *quietly* — without posturing. The Book's prayer is a private transaction between a creature and his Creator who is closer to him than the vein in his neck (50:16), and the silence the verse recommends is less an acoustic requirement than a statement about who is listening.

**A Practice With a Door**

The verses that follow continue the same practical thread — do not corrupt the earth, call with hope and fear — and the sūrah is arranging the life of its reader around the doctrine of verse 54. The God whose Throne is above the waters and who covers the night with the day is available to the quiet voice of a person who has nothing to offer and nowhere else to go. Sūrat al-Furqān puts the last piece in place: it is not the volume of the prayer or the standing of the suppliant that determines the answer, but the fact that the one calling is calling the One who responds — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘You ˹all˺ would not ˹even˺ matter to my Lord were it not for your faith ˹in Him˺. But now you ˹disbelievers˺ have denied ˹the truth˺, so the torment is bound to come.’”* (25:77).


**Call Upon Me, I Will Respond**

The verse commands a manner of calling; Ghāfir states the exchange itself: *“Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled.”* (40:60). The two clauses answer the two clauses of 7:55 — an invitation with a promised response, and a fate for those too proud to accept it.

The pairing defines the transgression 7:55 excludes. *Muʿtadūn*, the transgressors, are those who exceed a limit; in the context of a call whose response is guaranteed, the excess is in the calling itself. The commentators name the forms it takes: asking for what is not God’s to give, asking in a voice raised for display, and asking while the heart is elsewhere. 40:60 supplies the reason these are transgressions — the response has already been promised, so what is left to negotiate is only the posture.

The verse is therefore an instruction about how to be a caller rather than about what to ask. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said that the believers’ supplication was accompanied by humility in the voice and in the limbs, and the exegetes cite this verse as the ground of both.


**Hope and Fear: The Posture Named in al-Anbiyāʾ**

The two adverbs of 7:55 — humbly and secretly — describe a posture the Book names elsewhere in a pair of its own: *“Indeed, they used to race in doing good, and call upon Us with hope and fear, totally humbling themselves before Us.”* (21:90). As-Sajdah describes the same posture in a single image: *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them.”* (32:16).

The three verses agree on the components: a call, two motives held together, and a humility stated in the body — humbling before God, abandoning the bed. 7:55 supplies the manner of the voice; 21:90 and 32:16 supply the manner of the heart and of the limbs. Read together they describe the act the sūrah commands as a whole.

The exegetes note that hope and fear are named together everywhere the Book describes an accepted call, because either alone distorts it: hope without fear is the transgression of presumption, fear without hope is the transgression of despair. That is the same balance the sūrah states at 7:56, where the two terms appear again in the verse that follows this one.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:56

> **Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. And call upon Him with hope and fear. Indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command to Repair What Is Set Right**

*Wa-lā tufsidū fī al-arḍ baʿda iṣlāḥihā* — and do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. The verse sits immediately after the command to call upon God humbly, and its placement makes a theological point that the Qur'an never leaves in doubt: the disorder that the Book calls *fasād* is not merely a civic nuisance. It is damage done inside a repair.

The word *iṣlāḥ* — the setting right — is the sūrah's own term for what the messengers came to do. Verse 35 described the saved as those who *reform*; the first command of the sūrah's opening address was to follow what has been sent down (7:3), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's prophets are consistently described as *nāṣiḥ* — sincere, repairing counsellors (7:62, 7:68, 7:79). *Fasād*, its opposite, covers the whole field of ruin: the destruction of crops and livestock (2:205), the breaking of treaties, the exploitation of the weak, and the corruption of religion, which the sūrah has been cataloguing since verse 28. The verse's premise is that the world arrived ordered — that the earth was established by its Maker in a condition suited to human life — and that the human being's job description is maintenance, not demolition.

**Corruption With a History**

The Book uses this verse's vocabulary consistently in its accounts of ruined nations. Sūrat al-Baqarah describes the mischief-maker who is told not to corrupt the earth and answers that he is merely a reformer: *“Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.”* (2:11–12). Sūrat al-Rūm states the general law: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺”* (30:41). And Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records Shuʿayb's prohibition in the same terms: *“And do not follow the command of the transgressors — who spread corruption throughout the land, never setting things right”* (26:151–152).

The sūrah's own use of the verb will arrive twice within a few verses: once in Hūd's reminder to ʿĀd (7:74) and once in Shuʿayb's to his people (7:85). Its presence here, before the first prophet appears, makes it a footnote under the whole succeeding narrative: the towns the sūrah is about to describe did not fall for a single crime, they fell for the systematic undoing of what had been set in place.

**"Call Upon Him With Hope and Fear"**

*Wa-dʿūhu khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan.* The verse returns to supplication and now gives it its emotional content. *Khawf* is fear of the consequence and the judgment; *ṭamaʿ* is the eager hope of recompense and forgiveness. The pairing is one of the Qur'an's favourite descriptions of the believer's inner register, and the Book rarely mentions one without the other. Sūrat al-Sajdah describes the believing worshippers as *“invoking their Lord with hope and fear”* (32:16); Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ states that the prophets *“in doing good, and call upon Us with hope and fear”* (21:90); Sūrat al-Zumar asks, with a touch of rebuke, whether the one who *“hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of their Lord?”* is equal to the heedless (39:9), and Sūrat al-Isrāʾ places the same fear in the prayer of every sincere suppliant (17:57).

The doctrinal effect of the pair is a balanced religion. Fear without hope curdles into despair, and the Book condemns it explicitly (12:87; 39:53); hope without fear curdles into presumption, and the Book condemns that too — *“Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers.”* (7:99). The one supplication that is forbidden by 7:55 is the one that has lost the fear; the one that is sterile is the one that has lost the hope.

**"Mercy Is Near"**

The verse closes: *inna raḥmata Allāhi qarībun mina al-muḥsinīn* — indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers. The predication has been noticed by every commentator: mercy is not called *close* in any limiting sense — it is not said that mercy is near a place or a moment — but *near*. Sūrat al-Baqarah's verse about the divine response says simply, *“I am near”* (2:186), and the Qur'an speaks of God's help in the same idiom when it reassures a besieged community: *“Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy”* (39:53).

The qualifier concentrates the promise on conduct. *Muḥsinūn* — those who do good, who do a thing well — carries in the Book the sense of a life with quality in it: the Book's first mention of the term at 2:195 attaches it to generous spending, and 4:125 to the religion of Abraham. The connection being drawn is precise: the person who calls with hope and fear does not receive the mercy because the prayer was loud or the formalities correct, but because the caller's life has been aiming at the good. The verse therefore links the practical instruction at its beginning with the practical standard at its end: worship is not a substitute for integrity, and the sūrah will not let its reader think that the cultivation of the earth is a side issue in the religion of its Creator.


**Corruption After Order**

The prohibition is qualified in a way that changes its sense: do not corrupt the land *after it has been set in order*. The commentators read the ordering as the establishment of law through the messengers, so the corruption forbidden is not the disorder of a wilderness but the undoing of a settlement. The Book reports how that undoing presents itself. Those told *“Do not spread corruption in the land”* reply *“We are only peace-makers!”*, and the answer is given without qualification: *“Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.”* (2:11–12).

Verse 56 therefore carries a claim about history as well as a command. Every town this sūrah surveys had been set in order before it was corrupted: messengers came, a law was given, favours were enumerated. The corruption is a second act, and that is what makes it culpable in the way the closing clause requires — mercy is near the good-doers, and the good-doing in view here is the maintenance of an order someone else established.


**Hope and Fear**

The command to call on God with hope and fear names the two dispositions the tradition treats as the wings of supplication, and the Book pairs them wherever it describes the people it praises. Of those whose prayer was answered: *“Indeed, they used to race in doing good, and call upon Us with hope and fear, totally humbling themselves before Us.”* (21:90). Of believers at prayer: *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them.”* (32:16).

The pairing disciplines in both directions. Hope without fear becomes presumption, and presumption is what produces the corruption this verse forbids when it stops taking the settlement seriously. Fear without hope becomes despair, the state the sūrah diagnoses in towns that stopped expecting anything from their warnings. Hope is named first here, and the clause that follows explains why: the mercy is near. Its nearness is stated as a fact about God’s mercy rather than as a reward for the supplicant’s feeling, and that is what makes the hope rational instead of merely comfortable.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:57

> **He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit. Similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Winds That Herald the Mercy**

*Huwa alladhī yursilu al-riyāḥa bushrā bayna yaday raḥmatihi* — He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. The sūrah has just asked its reader to call upon God with hope, and it now supplies one of the Book's most repeated arguments for hope: the ordinary weather. The winds go before the rain the way a messenger goes before a king, and the Book adopts the imagery in several places with the same term: *“And He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy, and We send down pure rain from the sky”* (25:48); *“And one of His signs is that He sends the winds, ushering in good news ˹of rain˺ so that He may give you a taste of His mercy”* (30:46); *“He is the One Who shows you lightning, inspiring ˹you with˺ hope and fear, and produces heavy clouds”* (13:12).

The vocabulary is deliberately administrative. *Bushrā* is the announcement given to a person awaiting news; *raḥma* here is specifically rain, the sustenance that keeps a desert population alive from one season to the next. The verse is telling its reader that the mercy he is asking for in hidden, quiet prayer is the same thing he watches arrive overhead every winter with a herder's anxiety — the Book is not introducing a new category of event, only naming the author of a familiar one.

**The Argument From the Dead Land**

*Ḥattā idhā aqallat saḥāban thiqālan suqnāhu li-baladin mayyitin* — until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land. The progression is careful: the winds, the clouds, the journey of the clouds by a movement the verse attributes to God (*suqnāhu*, We drove it), the rainfall, and then the fruit. What is emphasized is the destination. The clouds are not sent to the sea, where the rain would be wasted, or to the fertile mountains; they are driven to the *mayyit* — the corpse-land, the dust that has no green on it.

Then comes the application: *kadhālika nukhriju al-mawtā laʿallakum tadhakkarūn* — similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful. The comparison is drawn in the Book repeatedly and with a consistent structure: rain revives a dead land, and that revival is the closest thing in the experience of the Book's audience to the resurrection. *“And We send down blessed rain from the sky, bringing forth gardens and grains for harvest”* (50:9), followed a verse later by *“˹as˺ a provision for ˹Our˺ servants. And with this ˹rain˺ We revive a lifeless land. Similar is the emergence ˹from the graves˺.”* (50:11). Sūrat al-Rūm makes the inference explicit: *“See then the impact of Allah’s mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same Creator˺ can raise the dead” (30:50)* (30:50; 16:65; 45:5; 22:5).

The argument works because it is inductive, and the sūrah trusts its audience to complete it. Nobody in the audience doubted that last year's rain produced last year's pasture; the only question the verse asks them to face is whether the power that did that is short of the power required for a different kind of spring.

**The Resurrection Argument in Its Own Register**

The Book's readers have often noted that its proofs of the resurrection are drawn overwhelmingly from agriculture and gestation rather than from philosophy. *“You sow? Is it you who cause it to grow, or is it We Who do so?”* (56:63–64). *“O humanity! If you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then ˹know that˺ We did create you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then ˹developed you into˺ a clinging clot ˹of blood˺, then a lump of flesh —fully formed or unformed—in order to demonstrate ˹Our power˺ to you.”* (22:5). *“And it is Allah Who sends the winds, which then stir up ˹vapour, forming˺ clouds, and then We drive them to a lifeless land, giving life to the earth after its death. Similar is the Resurrection.”* (35:9).

The choice is a claim about accessibility. Arguments from first principles require learning, and the Book is addressed to shepherds and weavers as much as to the learned; its demonstration is a process every farmer performs annually without noticing that he is performing it. The dead land, the rain, the green shoot, and the fruit are, in the logic of these verses, a rehearsal of the Day performed in front of the whole human race on an annual basis — and the final phrase of verse 57, *laʿallakum tadhakkarūn*, is the Book's sigh at the fact that they still forget.

**Who Is Being Addressed**

The verse's closing words matter: *so that you may remember*. The Qur'an's reminders are always aimed at a faculty rather than at an ignorance, and the here-and-now setting of the sūrah — its Makkan audience watching the winter rains and the caravans — makes verse 57 one of the most concrete verses in the chapter. The Book does not tell them that they have never encountered mercy; it tells them that they have encountered it every year under a different name and have not drawn the conclusion. The cultivation of the earth that verse 56 commanded and the rain that verse 57 describes are the same story told twice: the world is maintained by a mercy that keeps arriving, and the religion being preached in Makkah is the act of noticing where it comes from.


**The Winds Described by Their Function**

The word describing the winds is read in several ways in the recitation tradition, and the readings converge on a function rather than a direction: they are sent *before* the mercy, as heralds of it. The verse’s syntax makes the relation temporal — the winds are between the hands of the mercy, an idiom for what immediately precedes a thing — so the wind is not the mercy but its announcement.

The idiom matters for the argument the verse goes on to make. What arrives first is not itself the gift, and a reader who mistakes the herald for the thing heralded will misjudge both. The sūrah applies the same structure to its messengers throughout: they come before the mercy, they are not the mercy, and the towns that mistook the herald for an intruder lost the thing he was announcing. The wind is therefore the verse’s first lesson in how to read a sign that arrives early.


**The Same Argument in Its Other Forms**

The dead land revived by rain is the Book’s standing evidence for the rising of the dead, and it is stated elsewhere with the inference drawn openly. Sūrah Yā Sīn: *“There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life, producing grain from it for them to eat.”* (36:33). Sūrah al-Rūm makes the second step explicit: *“See then the impact of Allah’s mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same Creator˺ can raise the dead. For He is Most Capable of everything.”* (30:50).

Verse 57 states the same movement in the same order — winds, clouds, water, a dead land, fruit — and then attaches the conclusion in a single phrase: thus do We bring out the dead. The comparison with the other two passages shows what this verse adds. Yā Sīn names the sign and leaves the inference; al-Rūm names the inference and names the mercy that produces it; al-Aʿrāf narrates the whole mechanism from the wind onward, so that the reader watches the resurrection being prepared in the weather before being told that this is how the dead are brought out.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:58

> **The fertile land produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord, whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything. This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Parable of Two Soils**

*Wa-l-baladu al-ṭayyibu yakhruju nabātuhu bi-idhni rabbihi* — the good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord — *wa-lladhī khabutha lā yakhruju illā nakidan* — and the land that is bad brings forth nothing but with difficulty. The verse applies the rain of verse 57, and it is stated as an observation of nature that any farmer in the audience could test. Two plots of ground receive the same rain. The good soil answers with a crop; the exhausted, salty or stony ground, though it receives the same water, gives back little.

The Qur'an builds a whole doctrine on this image, and the sūrah of Ibrāhīm has the most developed version: *“Do you not see how Allah compares a good word to a good tree? Its root is firm and its branches reach the sky, ˹always˺ yielding its fruit in every season by the Will of its Lord.”* — and immediately, the bad counterpart: *“And the parable of an evil word is that of an evil tree, uprooted from the earth, having no stability.”* (14:24–26). Sūrat al-Raʿd adds the element of foam: the torrent carries away the dross while the water that is useful stays for people, and the Book concludes the image with a sentence that reads like an exegetical note: *“This is how Allah sets forth parables.”* (13:17).

**What the Soil Stands For**

The classical commentary is practically unanimous on the referent: the land is the human heart, and the rain is revelation. The good land gives its crop *by the permission of its Lord* — the phrase is important because it keeps the comparison from becoming a doctrine of self-cultivation. Even the productive soil does not manufacture the harvest; it responds, and the fruit comes by God's permission. The bad land's failure is described with a word — *nakid*, scant, bitter, hard-won — that sounds like the complaint of an exhausted farmer: the plot that requires enormous labour and returns almost nothing.

The image aligns with the sūrah's own anatomy of its audience. Verse 52 described the Book as a guidance and mercy for people who believe; verse 146 will describe God turning away from His signs those who behave with arrogance; and the sūrah's whole narrative section — the prophets and the towns — is an exhibit of two soils receiving identical messengers. Noah's town and the ark; Ḥūd's people and the remnant saved with him; Ṣāliḥ's lowly believers and the arrogant chiefs of verse 75: the same rain fell in each case and the same split appeared.

**"This Is How We Vary ˹Our˺ Lessons"**

*Kadhālika nuṣarrifu al-āyāt li-qawmin yashkurūn* — this is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful. The verb *ṣarrafa* is the Book's word for turning a thing through its aspects: to put a subject in different lights so that each angle is exhausted, to rotate an argument. The Qur'an uses it repeatedly as a description of its own method: *“And so We vary our signs to the extent that they will say, ‘You have studied ˹previous scriptures˺,” and We make this ˹Quran˺ clear for people who know.’* (6:105); *“We have surely varied ˹the signs˺ in this Quran so perhaps they may be mindful, but it only drives them farther away. Other Gods?”* (17:41).

The Book's self-description is a claim about redundancy by design. The same lesson arrives as a prophet narrative, a courtroom scene, a weather report, a soil sample, and a scale; the reader who misses the agricultural version will meet a military version, and the reader who misses both will meet it in the fire of the Hereafter. What the variety presupposes is a reader who is still able to perceive — and the qualifying phrase of the verse, *a people who are thankful*, names the faculty. *Shukr* in the Qur'an is not politeness about goods received; it is the recognition of the giver that turns a recipient into a student.

**Why the Parable Matters Here**

It is worth noticing where the sūrah places this parable. It has just argued from rain and dead ground to the resurrection; it is about to begin the long sequence of prophets, in which the pattern of acceptance and rejection will repeat through five towns in the next forty verses. The soil verse stands at the seam and explains the mechanics of both: why the same message produces a garden in one heart and nothing in another, and why the Book keeps ploughing ground it has already sown.

The verse's theology also protects the sūrah's later judgment scenes. When the people of ʿĀd, Thamūd, Sodom, and Madyan are destroyed in the coming narratives, the reader has already been told the principle: the rain fell on all of them. The Book's retribution in the sūrah's narratives is consistently the consequence that follows the refusal of a mercy already given — which is why the whole section ends with the resurrection argument of verse 57 and the farmer's observation of verse 58. Nothing in it is arbitrary and nothing is secret.


**The Word for a Grudging Yield**

The second half of the verse turns on a word that appears nowhere else in the Qurʾān. The bad land’s produce is *nakid* — rendered here as hardly producing anything — and the lexicons gloss it as a giving that comes with difficulty: a well that yields little after effort, a man who gives grudgingly and only when pressed. The word is not about quantity alone. It describes a yield that has to be extracted, and so it names the moral character of the second soil and not merely its agronomy.

The contrast with the first soil is exact. The good land’s vegetation comes forth *bi-idhn rabbihī*, by its Lord’s permission, and permission is the opposite of extraction. What grows there grows because it is allowed to, and the verse credits the abundance to the permission rather than to the soil’s own power. The same formula runs through the Book wherever an effect is traced to its Lord: nothing falls, grows or happens except by His *idhn*. A thankful land is one whose yield is understood as permission granted; the unthankful land is the one whose yield is wrested, late, and resented by the one who pulls it out.


**The Rain Parables Elsewhere in the Book**

This parable belongs to a family, and the family is worth reading together because each member varies a different term. Sūrah al-Raʿd makes the water the variable: *“He sends down rain from the sky, causing the valleys to flow, each according to its capacity.”* (13:17). Sūrah al-Zumar makes time the variable: *“then produces with it crops of various colours, then they dry up and you see them wither, and then He reduces them to chaff”* (39:21). Sūrah al-Baqarah makes the giver’s intention the variable, in the image of the garden on the height: *“when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient.”* (2:265).


**The Prophet’s Own Parable of Three Grounds**

The commentators set beside this verse a parable the Prophet ﷺ gave of his own mission, and the comparison is instructive because it adds a third ground. *“The example of guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me is like abundant rain falling on the earth, some of which was fertile soil that absorbed rain water and brought forth vegetation and grass in abundance”* (al-Bukhārī 79, from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, in the Book of Knowledge). The report continues with a second portion that is hard and holds the water for people to drink and irrigate from, and a third that is barren, holding nothing and growing nothing; the first ground is the one who understands the religion and teaches it, the last the one who takes no notice of it at all.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:59

> **Indeed, We sent Noah to his people. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First of the Five Towns**

*Laqad arsalnā Nūḥan ilā qawmihi* — indeed We sent Noah to his people. With this verse the sūrah begins the longest sequence of prophetic narratives in the Qur'an: Noah (7:59–64), Ḥūd and ʿĀd (7:65–72), Ṣāliḥ and Thamūd (7:73–79), Lot (7:80–84), Shuʿayb and Madyan (7:85–93), followed by Moses and the children of Israel in the longest installment of all (7:103–171). Each of the five pre-Mosaic accounts follows a recognizable architecture: the calling, the accusation by the town's elite, the messenger's defense, the warning, and the end. The reader who has received the parable of the two soils in verse 58 is now shown the same rain falling five times on the same kind of ground.

**"Worship Allah; You Have No God Besides Him"**

The sūrah gives each prophet the same sentence, and the repetition is the point: *“O my people! Worship Allah — you have no other god except Him.”* The message of the entire sequence is thus placed under one heading. The towns being described were not atheistic; they had gods, sanctuaries, liturgies, and inherited customs, and the Qur'an never accuses them of doubting that a divine existed. What the messengers attack is the plurality: the assignment of divine prerogatives to created things — stone, star, ancestor, king — and, behind that assignment, the assumption that worship can be distributed the way power is distributed.

Sūrat al-Naḥl states the principle the messengers were enforcing: *“And Allah has said, ‘Do not take two gods. There is only One God.’”* (16:51), and Sūrat al-Zumar puts it in the first person with a rhetorical question that dismantles the position: *“Are you urging me to worship ˹anyone˺ other than Allah, O ignorant ones?”* (39:64). The sūrah's own first narrative had already staged the same issue from the other direction: Iblīs's refusal was the refusal of a creature to accept the ordering God had given his kind. The five towns commit the same error at collective scale.

**"I Fear for You the Torment of a Tremendous Day"**

*Innī akhāfu ʿalaykum ʿadhāba yawmin ʿaẓīm* — I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day. The formula is the sūrah's own and its speakers' — Ḥūd and Ṣāliḥ will speak in the same register, and Sūrat al-Zumar's prophet uses the identical phrase (39:13). The *tremendous Day* is the Day of Judgment, and the sūrah has already defined it three times in its own voice (7:14, 7:51, 7:53). What is distinctive in Noah's sentence is the verb: *I fear for you*, not *I warn you of what is about to happen to you*. The messenger places himself inside the anxiety; the sūrah's prophets are not prosecutors but men burdened with an outcome they would prefer not to see.

That tone is worth noticing, because the sūrah's audience is about to meet it five times and it will always be followed by the same response. The pastoral vocabulary of the messengers — *my people*, *I fear for you*, *sincere advice* — is set against the vocabulary of the towns — *misguided*, *fool*, *liar* — and the sūrah's reader is invited to compare the two dictionaries at his leisure.

**Noah in the Book's Larger Portrait**

The Qur'an gives Noah the longest continuous treatment of any pre-Mosaic prophet, and the details of the other passages fill out what the sūrah assumes. Sūrat Nūḥ preserves his private reasoning with his Lord over the centuries of his calling: *“My Lord! I have surely called my people day and night, but my calls only”* (71:5–6). Sūrat Hūd records the elite's argument that he is merely a man like themselves and that only the lowest follow him (11:27), and Noah's response that he will not drive the believers away (11:29–30). Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt gives the duration: *“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them for a thousand years, less fifty.”* (29:14).

The significance of the narrative in this sūrah's arrangement is its function as the paradigm. Every subsequent messenger in the sequence will be accused as Noah was accused, will be rejected as Noah was rejected, and will see the rescue of a remnant as Noah saw it. The ark of verse 64 will become the sūrah's image of the one security available in a drowning world, and the towns that follow will keep failing to build one.

**The Great Day, Named Early**

Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt records the duration of that mission in a single clause — *“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them for a thousand years, less fifty”* (29:14) — and Sūrat Nūḥ preserves the messenger's own report of what the years produced: *“My Lord! I have surely called my people day and night, but my calls only made them run farther away”* (71:5–6). Verse 59's brevity compresses one of the longest ministries in the Book's history, and the compression is the sūrah's method: five towns, five speeches, one message, and a reader invited to notice that the outcome was never in doubt.

The sūrah has not yet told its reader what will happen to Noah's people, but the reader of the Book already knows from the other accounts: the flood, the ark, the people who called Noah a liar and drowned. Verse 59 works as an overture precisely because it says so little about the outcome and so much about the message. The reader who has followed the sūrah's first fifty-eight verses has already seen the courtroom, the scales, the gates, the wall, and the two crowds; he knows what a *tremendous Day* means, and he knows that the towns currently holding their breath in the narrative are walking toward it with their gods in their arms.


**Sent in the Language of His People**

The verse opens the sūrah’s cycle of towns with a single verb: *arsalnā* — “We sent.” The object is Nūḥ, and the destination is *ilā qawmihī*, to his people. *Qawm* is from *q-w-m*, to stand; a *qawm* is a group that stands together, and the word implies a bond of kinship or of shared standing rather than a mere crowd

Ibrāhīm states the rule that governs the sending: *“We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them. Then Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills.”* (14:4)

The pairing explains what the five towns’ cycle is for. The message is delivered in terms the hearers cannot claim to have misunderstood, which is why each refusal in the sūrah is a refusal of something understood. 14:4’s second sentence removes the last available excuse, and the sūrah’s refrain — *fa-kayfa kāna ʿāqibat al-mukadhdhibīn* — is the demonstration of it town by town


**A Thousand Years Less Fifty**

The sūrah compresses Nūḥ’s mission into a few verses. Al-ʿAnkabūt gives its length: *“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them for a thousand years, less fifty. Then the Flood overtook them, while they persisted in wrongdoing.”* (29:14). The verse states the duration in an arithmetic form — a thousand less fifty — and then the outcome, with the people’s persistence named as the thing that filled the interval.

The ninety-fifty formulation is read by the exegetes as a way of stating a long period exactly without stating it roundly: nine hundred and fifty years expressed as a subtraction from a thousand. Al-Ṭabarī reports the reading and notes that the verse is the Book’s only statement of a prophet’s tenure in years, and al-Qurṭubī cites it in his discussion of patience under a mission that does not succeed. Read against 7:59, the length changes the weight of the sūrah’s opening: the fear Nūḥ names for his people is a fear sustained over nine and a half centuries.

Both verses name the Day early. 7:59 has it as *“the torment of a tremendous Day”* (7:59); Shuʿayb’s address in Hūd has the same structure: *“I truly fear for you the torment of an overwhelming Day.”* (11:84). The formula belongs to the messengers rather than to the narrators, and it appears in the mouth of the first and of the last of this sūrah’s five.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:60

> **But the chiefs of his people said, “We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict of the Elite**

*Qāla al-malaʾu min qawmihi innā la-narāka fī ḍalālin mubīn* — the chiefs of his people said: we surely see you in clear misguidance. The sentence is short and it does three things at once, and all three are the standard operating procedure of the sūrah's towns.

First, it identifies the speakers: *al-malaʾ*, the assembled notables — the men whose standing gives them the authority to pronounce. The Qur'an uses this term for the elite of every ruined city in this sūrah, and it uses it as a diagnosis. Noah's town (7:60), ʿĀd (7:66), the court of Pharaoh (7:103), Madyan's affluent leaders (7:88) — in each case the first voice raised against the messenger is the voice of established power. The ordinary people of the towns are not the ones who speak; the sūrah will later show them believing (7:75) and being silenced.

Second, the sentence is not an argument but a classification. Noah has just delivered a message about the worship of the One God and a warning about the Day; the response says nothing about either. What the chiefs supply instead is a label, *ḍalāl mubīn*, clear misguidance — one of the two verdicts the sūrah's narratives will trade in, the other being *liar*, which ʿĀd will use of Ḥūd (7:66) and Thamūd of Ṣāliḥ (7:77). The Qur'an's actors prefer the label because the label requires no reasoning: it moves the discussion from what was said to who is saying it.

Third, the plural is important. *We see you* — the claim is corporate. The chiefs are speaking for the town, and behind the grammar is the oldest argument in religious history: the weight of numbers and respectability. The verse's audience already knows how the Book answers that argument, because verse 48 placed a crowd of tyrants in the Fire being told that their multitude had availed them nothing.

**The Word Turned Around**

The label's irony is the sūrah's own. *Ḍalāl* — misguidance, straying — is the Qur'an's technical term for the condition of those who reject revelation, and the sūrah's earlier verse 30 had already used it in the divine voice: *“He has guided some, while others are destined to stray”* (7:30). From the chiefs' mouths, the word is a verdict on Noah; from the Book's, it is a verdict on them. Sūrat al-Naḥl records the same inversion at the Day of Judgment, where the followers of the misleaders say, *“For those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, We will add more punishment to their punishment for all the corruption they spread.”* (16:88; see also 33:67–68).

The Qur'an's habit of returning the accusers' vocabulary is not rhetorical flourish but the doctrine of requital in kind that the sūrah has been stating since the scale of verse 8. Every label the towns apply to the messengers in the following verses — misguided, fool, liar, sorcerer, bewitched — is used by the Book, later, of the towns.

**The Elite as a Category in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an's analysis of the *malaʾ* deserves attention because it is one of the Book's most consistent social observations. Sūrat al-Muʾminūn's version of Noah's narrative has the chiefs say, *“But the disbelieving chiefs of his people said ˹to the masses˺, ‘This is only a human like you, who wants to be superior to you. Had Allah willed, He could have easily sent down angels ˹instead˺. We have never heard of this in ˹the history of˺ our forefathers.”* (23:24). Sūrat Hūd's has them argue that only *the lowliest* follow him (11:27). Sūrat Sabaʾ has the affluent of a town explain their superiority in wealth and children (34:35). Sūrat al-Zukhruf has the Makkans object that the Qur'an should have been sent to *a great man of the two cities* (43:31).

The common structure is the identification of truth with status. What makes the messengers unbearable to the elite is not usually the theology in the abstract but its consequence: if the message is true, the elders of the town have been wrong for a lifetime, and the poor who believed them first are ahead of them. The sūrah shows that reflex operating five times, and it does not let its reader forget that its own first audience, in Makkah, was reading the story of its own chiefs.

**What Noah Does Not Do**

The last thing worth noticing in verse 60 is what it does not contain. Noah is called clearly misguided by men with the power to ruin him, and the sūrah does not record that he answered with equivalent language. His response, in the next verse, begins with the address *O my people* and immediately denies the charge in the plainest terms while retaining the relationship, and then answers with the thing he actually is: a messenger conveying the messages of the Lord of all worlds. The Book's prophets are always more interested in the message than in their reputations.

The verse that follows the accusation is thus a small manual for anyone who has been publicly mislabelled for religious reasons: state the case, refuse the label, keep the address, and let the outcome be God's. The sūrah's coming narratives will supply the outcome five times over, and in each case the town's elite will have disappeared before the verdict, which is itself a comment on how much their consensus was worth.


**The Chiefs Speak in Every History**

The verse introduces its speakers as the chiefs of his people, *al-malaʾ*, and the same group speaks in each of the sūrah’s histories, with the same three moves: an attack on the messenger’s judgment, an attack on the standing of his followers, and a threat. The attack on the followers is stated most openly in the Thamūd account, where the chiefs address the believers rather than the prophet: *“Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”* (7:75) — and receive the answer that ends the argument, *“We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”* (7:75)

The division is the sūrah’s anatomy of a town. The chiefs are not described as its wisest or its strongest, only as its *malaʾ* — the group whose standing depends on the arrangement the messenger is questioning. Their verdict on Nūḥ here is a verdict on their own position, and the sūrah marks that by reporting the charge in the same register in every history: never an argument about the message, always a statement about the man who brought it and the people who followed him.


**Nūḥ’s Reply and the Office It States**

The answer comes in the next two verses, in the form this sūrah will reuse for Hūd: *“O my people! I am not misguided! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds,”* (7:61), *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know.”* (7:62). The denial answers the charge in the charge’s own terms. The statement of office replaces the terms.

The third clause carries the difference between the two parties. *I know from God what you do not know* is not a claim to superior intelligence but a report about where the messenger’s knowledge comes from, which is why an assessment of the man cannot reach it. The sūrah’s argument about the elite is complete in that clause: a verdict delivered by people who do not know what the messenger knows is not a verdict on the message. The verses that follow put the message’s content in his mouth with no further reference to their opinion of him.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:61

> **He replied, “O my people! I am not misguided! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"You Are No Fool; You Are a Messenger"**

*Qāla yā qawmi laysa bī ḍalālatun wa-lākinnī rasūlun min rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — he replied: “O my people! I am not misguided! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds.” The reply is a model of economy, and its two halves correspond exactly to the two halves of the accusation.

Against the charge of misguidance, Noah states a bare negation: there is no error in me. He does not argue, does not produce proofs, and does not return the insult by calling the chiefs misguided, though the sūrah's reader knows they are. Instead he states the positive content of his position: *I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds*. The claim is the answer to the charge. A man whose commission comes from the Lord of all worlds cannot be at the same time a man in clear misguidance; the two descriptions are mutually exclusive, and the fact that the chiefs cannot see this is the real subject of the passage.

**"Lord of All Worlds"**

The title Noah uses is the one the sūrah used a few verses earlier in its own voice: *Tabāraka Allāh rabbu al-ʿālamīn* (7:54). The echo is deliberate. The chiefs of the town have just measured a man by the standards of their settlement; the man has just named the authority he represents as the Lord of every world. Makkah, for all its importance as a sanctuary, was one town among thousands; the message being proclaimed in it belonged to a jurisdiction that has no boundary.

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ puts this contrast at the head of every one of its prophets' speeches: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah, and obey me. I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:107–109; 26:127; 26:145; 26:164; 26:180). The phrase is the Qur'an's shorthand for the universality of the prophetic claim and the total absence of a local interest in it. Noah is not asking for the ḥimā of a clan or a share of the caravan traffic; he is announcing a message that has no patrons.

**"I Am Not Misguided" — Prophetic Self-Definition**

The Books of the prophets in the Qur'an show a consistent reticence: the messenger never defends his own spiritual attainment, and he never claims personal authority. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's Shuʿayb answers a similar charge by pointing to what is *with Allah* (7:89); Hūd says less than Noah does here (7:67); and Ṣāliḥ's rebuke of his people in verse 79 places the whole affair in the category of *counsel delivered*. The Book's only claim on behalf of its messengers is the message: *“Your fellow man is neither misguided nor astray. Nor does he speak of his own whims.”* (53:2–3), and *“Say, ‘I am not the first messenger ever sent, nor do I know what will happen to me or you. I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.’”* (46:9).

The reticence is doctrinal, not modest. A messenger whose authority was personal would be replaceable; a messenger whose authority is the words given to him is not the point at all. Sūrat Fuṣṣilat states the same position in the Prophet's own voice: *“I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God”* (41:6).

**The Familiar Address**

The verse's opening words are worth keeping in view: *yā qawmi*, O my people. Noah has been pronounced misguided, and he answers by calling the accusers his own. The Book's prophets never sever the relationship while the argument continues, and the sūrah's five narratives show this address surviving every stage short of the destruction: Noah uses it here, Hūd in his replies (7:65, 7:68), Ṣāliḥ at the end of his town's history, when he turns away saying, *“O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice”* (7:79), and Shuʿayb in the last speech of the sequence (7:89).

This vocabulary places the sūrah's prophets in the lineage of the Qur'an's pastoral language: a messenger is not an officer sent to a district, and his warnings are not a state's verdicts. The word *qawmī* — my people — carries an admission that the speaker belongs to the same community in every sense except the one that matters, which is precisely what makes the message credible and the rejection tragic. Noah's century of rain and ridicule, described elsewhere in the Book, happens inside that pronoun.

**The Pattern the Sūrah Is Building**

The answer in verse 61 establishes the template that the rest of the sequence will follow. Each prophet will be accused; each prophet will deny the charge with the same economy; each will then identify himself by his commission, and each will defend the towns' right to hear the truth even as the towns take away their right to speak. What changes from town to town is only the specific charge — ʿĀd prefers the word *fool*, Thamūd prefers *sorcerer* and *liar*, the people of Lot prefer *expulsion* — and the sūrah's reader is meant to notice that the dictionary of abuse is the towns' only real contribution. The messengers' vocabulary is the same in every case, and it is the vocabulary of the object being announced.


**A Denial Tailored to the Charge**

Nūḥ’s first sentence answers his people in the exact term they used. They said they saw him clearly misguided (7:60); he says *I am not misguided*. Hūd, charged with foolishness, answers *I am no fool* (7:67); Shuʿayb, told he is bewitched, answers that he is not bewitched but a messenger with a clear command. The sūrah gives each prophet a denial shaped by the accusation he received, which is a rhetorical device with a purpose: the reply engages the charge rather than substituting a better one.

The device also fixes the level of the dispute. Each charge was about the man — his judgment, his honesty, his sanity — and each denial is about the man too. Nothing is conceded by answering at that level, because the denial is followed immediately by the statement of office, which moves the matter onto ground the accusers have not occupied. The reader is shown that a messenger does not avoid a personal charge; he disposes of it in one clause and then changes the subject to the message.


**Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn**

The title with which the denial is followed is the Book’s first word about God: *“All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds,”* (1:2). The word *ʿālam* is derived by the classical lexicons from the root for a sign or a mark, so the worlds are everything that functions as a sign of its Maker — a derivation that makes the title a claim about evidence as well as about ownership.

The prophets use the title when they state their commission, and Mūsā defines it for a court that has just asked who the Lord of the worlds might be: *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”* (26:24). In this sūrah the same title carries Nūḥ’s reply, Hūd’s, Ṣāliḥ’s and Shuʿayb’s, and it is the first thing the magicians say when they fall down believing (7:121–122). Its repetition across the histories is the sūrah’s way of saying that the case each prophet argues is one case, and that the title names the jurisdiction in which every town’s refusal is being recorded.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:62

> **conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Duties of a Messenger**

*Uballighukum risālāti rabbī wa-anṣaḥu lakum* — conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. The verse names the messenger's work under two headings, and the order is significant. The first is transmission: the message is not his, and his task is not interpretation or improvement. The second is advice: he is a *nāṣiḥ*, a sincere counsellor, and the word carries in Arabic a whole ethic of service without advantage.

The Qur'an's prophets all describe themselves in the same terms, and the sūrah will use *nāṣiḥ* again for Ḥūd (7:68) and twice at the end of Ṣāliḥ's story (7:79), where he repeats it as the summary of his mission. The word's root — *n-ṣ-ḥ* — carries the sense of purity and the sense of stitching: the adviser whose counsel is free of self-interest, and the tailor who mends without leaving a seam.
