The Book uses it for the man of Madyan who warned Moses of a plot against him (28:20) and for the brother of Yūsuf, and it is the standard term for the religious duty of giving good counsel to those who are open to it.

**"And I Know From Allah What You Do Not Know"**

*Wa-aʿlamu mina Allāh mā lā taʿlamūn* — and I know from Allah what you do not know. The sentence is the epistemological edge of the prophetic claim, and the Book's messengers keep it sharp. The knowledge in question is not information about the future or mastery of hidden things; Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own Ḥūd will declare no such possession, and Sūrat Hūd records Noah saying explicitly that he does not claim the treasures of God or knowledge of the unseen (11:31). What the messengers do possess, in the Book's consistent account, is something received: *“Nor does he speak of his own whims. It is only a revelation sent down ˹to him˺.”* (53:3–4).

The verse's audience is being asked to entertain the possibility that a human being might have access to facts about the moral structure of reality that they have not been given — and that this access is not a rank but a burden. The Book ties the burden to the transmission in the same breath. Sūrat al-Anʿām puts it: *“Still your people ˹O Prophet˺ have rejected this ˹Quran˺, although it is the truth. Say, ‘I am not a keeper over you’”* (6:66; see also 6:107). Knowledge of the kind Noah claims does not confer control; it confers responsibility to speak.

**The Two Ways of Hearing the Verse**

The classical commentators read the pair of duties as a division of labour that answers two very different impulses in the messenger's audience. Transmission speaks to the person who wants information: what does God require? The answer is the message, and it is delivered without alteration — the sūrah's Moses will receive the command *“We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything; commandments and explanations of all things. ˹We commanded,˺ ‘Hold to this firmly and ask your people to take the best of it. I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious.”* (7:145), and the Book's final prophet is instructed simply to recite (96:1). Advice speaks to the person who wants a relationship with the messenger: a father, a guide, a man who wants his people's good. The Qur'an's messengers are not allowed to become authorities over conscience — *“You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:22), *“Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists. We have not appointed you as their keeper, nor are you their maintainer.”* (6:107) — but they are required to be sincere.

The combination protects both the message and the messenger's humanity. The message cannot be diluted on the grounds of pastoral cleverness, and the messenger cannot be turned into a machine. Noah's century of calling, in the Book's telling, is filled with both duties: he explains and he pleads (71:5–20).

**What the Chiefs Refuse to Hear**

Read against verse 60, the two headings identify what the chiefs' accusation made impossible. They called Noah misguided, which is a judgment about his person; they did not engage the message, which is a claim about God. The messenger's reply says, in effect: the question was never my competence. It is whether the message I convey came from the Lord of all worlds, and whether the advice I am giving you is sincere. Both of those questions are answered by testing the content, and the towns will not test it.

The other accounts supply what this verse leaves out, and none of them reports a reversal. *“And it was revealed to Noah, ‘None of your people will believe except those who already have. So do not be distressed by what they have been doing’”* (11:36) — the disclosure arrives after the centuries of argument and confirms what the messenger had learned from God rather than from the town. The claim *I know from Allah what you do not know* is therefore not a boast about private information; it is the statement of a man whose knowledge of the outcome came from the One who sent him, and who continued to call anyway.

The sūrah's arrangement will make that refusal the explicit charge against every city in the sequence. In the account of Noah to come, the town's answer to a century of speech is a decision to wait and see: *“O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky”* (8:32 is Makkan rhetoric; Noah's own version is 71:23–24). The Book's presentation is that the refusal is not an intellectual position at all but a social one: the notables could not examine the message without examining themselves.


**Conveying: The Verb of Reaching**

Hūd describes his office with two participles: *uballighukum* — conveying to you — and *anṣaḥu lakum*, advising you. The first is from *b-l-gh*, to reach or arrive at a limit; form II makes it causative, to make something reach. A *balāgh* is a message delivered to the point where nothing remains undelivered, which is why the Book uses the same root for the completion of a term (7:142) and of a life.

Al-Māʾidah states the office in the imperative: *“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware! But if you turn away, then know that Our Messenger’s duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly.”* (5:92). The verse separates obedience from delivery and makes the second the whole of the messenger’s charge — the same separation 13:40 states as delivery on one side and judgment on the other.

7:62 is that office spoken in the first person by a messenger inside a town that is refusing it. The participle is continuous: he is conveying, not he conveyed. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the sūrah’s messengers describe their work in the present tense precisely where their people accuse them of having gone too far, and that the two participles answer the two charges — the message is not his own, and the advice is for them.


**Disclosed Only to a Messenger of His Choice**

The verse’s second clause is a claim about knowledge: *“And I know from Allah what you do not know.”* (7:62). The clause is not a boast but a description of the office, and al-Jinn states its ground: *“˹He is the˺ Knower of the unseen, disclosing none of it to anyone, except messengers of His choice. Then He appoints angel-guards before and behind them.”* (72:26–27).

The two verses answer the charge Hūd’s people have just made — that he is in clear error and foolishness (7:66). A knowledge disclosed only to a chosen messenger and guarded by appointed angels is not a knowledge a man invents, and the sūrah’s formulation is careful: he knows *from Allah*, *min Allāh*, which names the source rather than the extent.

This is why the clause follows the two duties rather than preceding them. The delivery and the advice are what the people can see; the knowledge is what makes them possible and what they cannot check. 72:27 adds the guardians because the disclosure is the point at which the enemy would intervene, and the sūrah has already described that intervention (7:27).

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:63

> **Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own, warning you, so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Do You Wonder?"**

*A-wa-ʿajibtum an jāʾakum dhikrun min rabbikum ʿalā rajulin minkum* — do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own? The question is the sūrah's answer to the towns' real objection, and it is stated with an incredulity that turns the tables. The chiefs find it *astonishing* that God would send a human being; the verse asks what else they expected.

The Qur'an records the objection in several forms and answers it in kind. *“And they say ˹mockingly˺, ‘What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺? If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner,”* (25:7). *“And nothing has prevented people from believing when guidance comes to them except their protest: ‘Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?’”* (17:94). The Book's reply to the last one is the most elegant: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Had there been angels walking the earth, well settled, We would have surely sent down for them an angel from heaven as a messenger.’”* (17:95). The choice of messenger follows the nature of the addressee; revelation comes in the tongue of the people who must receive it, and the Qur'an says so directly elsewhere: *“We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them. Then Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills.”* (14:4).

**The Argument From Human Ordinariness**

Behind the objection sits an assumption the sūrah is dismantling: that divine speech requires a superhuman vehicle, that a creature who eats and sleeps and dies cannot be a conduit for something eternal. The Qur'an's counter-argument is that the supernatural vehicle would defeat the purpose. The messenger's ordinariness is the guarantee of the message's transferability: a man from *among you*, whose honesty you can audit, whose household you know, whose life before the commission you can inspect. Sūrat Yūnus records the Makkan audience being told exactly that: *“Say, ‘Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you. I had lived my whole life among you before this ˹revelation˺. Do you not understand?’”* (10:16).

The Book returns to this protection in its accounts of the messengers' humanity. They are men who eat food (25:20), who marry and have children (13:38), who grieve and get angry, who die. Sūrat al-Kahf instructs the Prophet to declare, *“I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God.”* (18:110). The humanity is not a compromise; it is the design.

**"A Reminder From Your Lord"**

*Dhikr* — the key word of the verse — is the Qur'an's own name for revelation: a reminder, not a new invention. The Book's self-presentation is that it restores what the human being already knows and has let slip. *“It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it.”* (15:9). *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind.”* (88:21). Noah's question to his town is therefore pointed: the thing arriving is not a foreign system but a recollection, and a recollection does not need a supernatural speaker to be credible. It needs a hearer who is willing to remember.

The sūrah's own audience had the same reminder in the same form: *“This is a blessed Book which We have revealed—confirming what came before it—so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it.”* (6:92), and its Prophet was told to say that his message and the earlier ones share a single source (41:43; 46:9). Verse 63's use of the word places Noah's preaching on the same continuum as the Book being recited in Makkah.

**The Purpose in the Last Clauses**

*Wa-lākinnī rasūlun... li-yundhirakum wa-laʿallakum turḥamūn* — the warning and the mercy. The verse ends by naming the two outcomes the reminder is designed to produce: *so that you may beware*, and *so that you may be shown mercy*. The order is the Book's standard soteriology. Awakening precedes mercy; fear is not the opposite of hope but its antechamber, and the sūrah has just told its readers, two verses before its first prophet opened his mouth, to call upon God *with hope and fear* (7:56).

The Book's frequent phrasing — *perhaps you may be shown mercy* — is not a statement of uncertainty about God's willingness but a condition placed on a human variable. The same construction appears throughout the sūrah's warnings: the towns may be shown mercy, and their conduct decides whether the mercy has a landing place. Sūrat al-Anʿām puts the principle in a single line: *“and ‘If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him. And if He intends good for you, none can withhold His bounty. He grants it to whoever He wills of His servants. And He is the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.’”’* (10:107).

**The Wonder That Damns**

The one thing the verse leaves untouched is the chiefs' capacity for wonder. Their question is not *what does the reminder say* but *how did it get here*; their intelligence has been spent on the vehicle rather than the cargo. That reflex is the sūrah's definition of the elite of every town it describes, and it is the reflex the Book repeatedly judges by its fruit. Sūrat al-Mulk's question answers it across the whole world: *“Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Compassionate.”* (67:19). Wonder at the mechanism is available to everyone; attention to the message is the harder discipline, and the sūrah's next verse shows the town declining to attempt it.


**The Same Question Put Twice**

The verse records a question in the mouth of a messenger: *“Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own, warning you, so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy?”* (7:63). Six verses later Hūd puts the same question in the same words: *“Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you?”* (7:69).

The repetition is not a copy. Hūd’s version drops the two final clauses and adds a remembrance in their place — that God made them successors after the people of Nūḥ and increased them in stature (7:69). The argument from ordinariness is the same; the ground on which it is put is different, and the difference is the people’s own history.

The sūrah therefore uses repetition as a method rather than as emphasis. The first instance states the wonder and answers it with the purposes of the message; the second states the wonder and answers it with the position of the people addressed


**A Mercy for the Whole World**

The verse’s last clause is a purpose: perhaps they may be shown mercy. Al-Anbiyāʾ states the same purpose as the whole content of a mission: *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world.”* (21:107). The adverb *illā*, only, restricts the sending to mercy, and the object is the world rather than a people.

Read against 7:63 the verse explains the structure of the question’s clauses. Warning is first, then wariness, then mercy — the order of a process whose end is not the warning. 21:107 states the end without the process, and the two together describe an office whose form is severe and whose content is not.

The sūrah’s own histories test the claim town by town. In each case the warning is delivered, the mercy is offered, and the outcome turns on what the people do with the interval. 21:107 is therefore not a comfort addressed to the reader but a statement about the mission that the towns refused, and the verse of al-Aʿrāf shows that refusal being made in the face of a mercy already named.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:64

> **But they rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the Ark, and drowned those who rejected Our signs. They were certainly a blind people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ending of the First Town**

*Fa-kadhdhabūhu fa-anjaynāhu wa-lladhīna maʿahu fī al-fulki* — but they rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the ark. The sūrah has compressed the entire flood into a single sentence, and the compression is the point. What the town did is stated first and in one word, *kadhdhabūhu*: they declared him a liar. What God did follows immediately: the rescue and the drowning. Between the two clauses stands the whole of a civilization's history, and the sūrah gives it the length of a comma.

The reader of the Qur'an knows the details from the other accounts: the sign given to Noah about the oven (11:40), the pairs of every species loaded into the vessel (11:40), the ark riding on waves like mountains (11:42), the son who would not board (11:42–43), the call from the ship to a world that had mocked it for a century (11:42), the waters that rose until the vessel came to rest on al-Jūdī (11:44), and the command to the sky and the earth, *“O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky!”* (11:44). Sūrat al-Qamar gives the whole event four verses and a purpose: *“We certainly left this as a sign. So is there anyone who will be mindful?”* (54:15).

**The Ark as the Sūrah's Image**

In the architecture of the sūrah, the ark carries more than its cargo. It is the first of the deliverances that will punctuate the sequence of towns, and it establishes the pattern of the Book's narrative logic: the warning is genuine, the delay is generous, and the rescue is a remnant. Ḥūd's people are saved by mercy (7:72), the believers in Thamūd are named as the lowly who spoke up (7:75), and Lot's family leaves in the night (7:83).

The vessel itself is described elsewhere in the Book with a vocabulary that makes it the prototype of the Hereafter's escape routes. *“And it was said, ‘O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky! Withhold ˹your rain˺.’ The floodwater receded and the decree was carried out. The Ark rested on Mount Judi, and it was said, ‘Away with the wrongdoing people!’”* (11:44). Sūrat al-Qamar, as noted, preserves the ship as a permanent sign (54:15), and Sūrat al-Muʾminūn adds the doctrine of *taskhīr*: the ark rides by God's command (23:27). The Book's use of the flood as a model of the resurrection is explicit in Sūrat al-Qamar: *“So We opened the gates of the sky with pouring rain, and caused the earth to burst with springs, so the waters met for a fate already set.”* (54:11–12).

**"A Blind People"**

*Innahum kānū qawman ʿamīn* — they were a blind people. The adjective is the sūrah's final diagnosis of Noah's town, and its choice is deliberate. The Qur'an's vocabulary of blindness is used consistently for the failure of perception rather than of eyesight — *“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return”* (2:18); *“whoever is blind ˹to the truth˺ in this ˹world˺ will be blind in the Hereafter”* (17:72) — and the Book's most complete statement of the doctrine appears in this very sūrah, eleven verses later: *“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with.”* (7:179).

The word closes the account with a verdict that is not moral but perceptual. Noah's town was not condemned for being wicked in the abstract; it was condemned for standing in the sun for a century and refusing to concede that there was light. The rain of verses 57 and 58 had already described the difference between the fertile land and the barren one, and here the sūrah gives the barren land its name.

**The Bodily Waste of a Warning**

There is a heartbreak built into the grammar of the verse that the Book's audiences have always felt: the person saved is *him and those with him*, and the phrase *those with him* includes the tiny remnant attached to one family — the sons who believed, the wives who did not, and, in some traditions, the household members who fit in a boat. The messenger's century produced a fraction of one town.

The Book's other flood narratives fill in the details this verse withholds. Sūrat al-Qamar describes the vessel — *“We carried him on that ˹Ark made˺ of planks and nails”* (54:13) — and states its purpose: *“We certainly left this as a sign. So is there anyone who will be mindful?”* (54:15). Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah addresses the drowned generation directly: *“Indeed, when the floodwater had overflowed, We carried you in the floating Ark ˹with Noah˺, so that We may make this a reminder to you, and that attentive ears may grasp it”* (69:11–12). And Sūrat Hūd ends its account with the Book's command to the creation itself: *“O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky! Withhold ˹your rain˺. The floodwater receded and the decree was carried out. The Ark rested on Mount Judi”* (11:44). Verse 64's single clause — *We saved him and those with him* — is the sūrah's whole account of that event, and the economy is the point: the interest lies in the verdict, not the spectacle.

The sūrah does not linger on the emotion, and this is characteristic of it. What it lingers on is the causal chain: they rejected, therefore He saved and drowned. The sequence is the same one the reader met in the Hereafter scenes: the refrain that began with the question *who is more unjust than the one who invents a lie about God?* (7:37) reaches its first historical instance here, and the next four towns will run the experiment again with different people, different gods, and identical results. The reader who has been paying attention to the pattern knows what will happen to ʿĀd before the sūrah tells him, and the Book's invitation is to notice which of the responses he recognizes as his own.


Saved in the Ark: The Deliverance Made a Sign

7:64 ends the first of the sūrah's towns, and it ends it in two clauses: those with Nūḥ in the ark were saved, and those who denied the signs were drowned. The Book records the same deliverance elsewhere and adds what was made of it: *“But We delivered him and those in the Ark, making it a sign for all people.”* (29:15)

The drowning is described as the fate of those who denied the signs, and the signs in Nūḥ's case were his message and the warning he delivered over a long period. The sūrah states the sending at 7:59 and the persistence of the denial in the verses that follow, so the drowning is not a response to a single refusal but to a denial sustained across generations

The verse's final description of the drowned is a category rather than an insult. They were certainly a blind people, and blindness in the Book's usage is a failure of the faculty by which signs are recognised. The sūrah uses the same language at 7:179, where hearts, eyes, and ears are described as failing to function, and at 7:146, where the signs are turned away from those who are arrogant in the land


Not the Eyes but the Hearts: Blindness Located

The Book locates the blindness that 7:64 reports: *“it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind”* (22:46). The verse of al-Ḥajj sets the location inside a command to travel and observe, which is the same setting as the sūrah's repeated instruction to look at the ends of the destroyed towns

This location explains why the sūrah treats seeing as insufficient. Signs are given to the senses and are recognised by the heart; where the heart is blind, the senses receive and the recognition does not follow. The verse at 7:146 describes the same sequence from the other side, where those who are arrogant are turned away from the signs even when they see every one of them

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:65

> **And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. Will you not then fear Him?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**ʿĀd and Their Brother**

*Wa-ilā ʿĀdin akhāhum Hūdan* — and to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. The sūrah's second city is introduced with a phrase that carries more weight than its brevity suggests. *Akhāhum* — their brother — is the Qur'an's way of locating the messenger inside the community he addresses. Hūd is not a stranger sent from elsewhere with a warrant; he is a man of ʿĀd, known to its families, sharing its water, its grazing, and its ancestors. The Book uses the same word for every pre-Mosaic messenger in this sequence: the brother of ʿĀd, the brother of Thamūd, the brother of Madyan (7:65, 7:73, 7:85).

The effect is an intensification of the towns' responsibility rather than a softening of the message. The Qur'an's classic statement of the point appears in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ, where the townsmen are told that their messenger's credentials are local: *“when their brother Hûd said to them, ‘Will you not fear Allah?’”* (26:124, with the same opening for Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ, and Shuʿayb at 26:142, 26:161, 26:177), and the Prophet's own community is reminded that there *“certainly has come to you a messenger from among yourselves”* (9:128). The Book's summons is never exotic. It arrives in the voice of a neighbour, and the towns' decision to reject it is a decision about someone they could have questioned any day of the week.

**The People of Iram**

ʿĀd is not a footnote in the Qur'an; it is the Book's standing example of a civilization destroyed by strength. Sūrat al-Fajr names their city with a grandeur the Book reserves almost exclusively for it: *“˹the people˺ of Iram—with ˹their˺ great stature, unmatched in any other land;”* (89:7–8). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ lists their monuments and asks whether they built them for eternity: *“˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity, and construct castles, as if you are going to live forever”* (26:128–129). Sūrat Fuṣṣilat records the boast that the sūrah turns into their epitaph: *“As for ’Ȃd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right, boasting, ‘Who is superior to us in might?” Did they not see that Allah ˹Himself˺, Who created them, was far superior to them in might? Still they persisted in denying Our signs.’* (41:15).

The Makkans who first heard this sūrah did not need the identification explained. ʿĀd's territory lay along the southern trade routes, and the ruined towers of the people the Qur'an calls *dhāti al-ʿimād* were the first thing a caravan saw on the road toward Yemen.

**"Worship Allah; You Have No God Besides Him"**

Hūd's message is Noah's message, word for word, and the sūrah does not vary it. This is a deliberate feature of the sequence and it makes a doctrinal claim about prophecy: the messengers were not religious innovators adapting a message to local taste. *“He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding:˺ ‘Uphold the faith, and make no divisions in it.’”* (42:13). The towns' objections differ, their gods differ, their civilizations differ radically; the message does not.

The verse then adds the ending that the sūrah gives to Hūd alone: *a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — will you not then fear Him? The question form is the Book's most common rhetorical instrument, and it calls for a specific kind of answer. It does not ask whether the hearer has understood the argument; it asks whether the hearer is willing to live inside the consequence of a God who is real. The sūrah's own opening used the same construction to open the whole sūrah: *“˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺— do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it—so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺, and as a reminder to the believers. Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him. How seldom are you mindful!”* (7:2–3), and Sūrat al-Naḥl's affirmation of the divine oneness closes with a similar question (16:51–52).

**Why Ḥūd's Address Begins With Worship**

The verse places worship first and ethics nowhere, and a reader might wonder why the sūrah's messengers always begin with ritual. The answer given by the Book's own accounts of ʿĀd is that the town's problem was not confined to its liturgy; it was the confidence of power. Sūrat al-Aḥqāf records the advice they received and refused: they were reminded of the favours of God and answered with the argument of precedent — *“You come to turn us away from our gods? Bring us then whatever you threaten us with, if what you say is true.”* (46:22). The worship of ʿĀd's gods was not devotion to statues in the abstract; it was the sanctification of their own order, the ritual expression of a society that answered to nobody.

Hūd's demand therefore cuts at the root of the town's self-understanding. If the One God is the only God, then the tribe's authority is delegated rather than inherent, the stronghold is a trust rather than a possession, and the pillars of Iram are neither gods nor monuments to one. The verse's single sentence dissolves the architecture of ʿĀd's political theology, and the sūrah's reader is meant to hear in it the same dissolution applied to the merchants and chiefs of Makkah.

**The Question the Town Never Answers**

The verse ends on a question, and the town's answer will come in the next verse as an insult. Between the two lies the whole distance between the sūrah's method and its opponents': Hūd asks a question about accountability, and ʿĀd replies with a description of Hūd's intelligence. The Book notes the exchange without comment, which is its own comment.

The pattern is the same one the reader saw with Noah, and it will repeat three more times before the passage ends. The sūrah's prophet sequence is thus less a set of biographies than a controlled experiment: the same message, the same audience categories, the same escalation, and the same outcome, presented consecutively so that no reader can attribute the result to a quirk of one town or one messenger. The next verse makes the result explicit, and its terms are the terms of the towns, not of the Book.


ʿĀd and Iram: The People Described Elsewhere

7:65 introduces the second of the sūrah's towns, and the Book describes the same people elsewhere with the detail al-Aʿrāf leaves out: *“Did you not see how your Lord dealt with ’Ȃd”* (89:6), the people of Iram, of great stature, unmatched in any other land (89:7–8)

The description matters because it explains the question at the end of 7:65. Will you not then fear: the question is put to a people whose strength was unmatched, and the fear asked for is not fear of a stronger enemy but of the One who made them strong

The brotherhood named at the head of the verse is what makes the address possible. Ḥūd is one of them, speaks their language, and is not a stranger bringing a foreign claim. The sūrah states the same relation for every messenger it sends, and the relation is the ground on which the refusal becomes culpable: a people addressed by their own brother cannot treat the address as an imposition from outside


The Wind That Ended Them

The end of ʿĀd is described in al-Ḥāqqah in terms that complete the sūrah's account: *“as for ’Ȃd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind”* (69:6), *“which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees.”* (69:7)

The image is the counterpart of the stature described in al-Fajr. A people unmatched in the lands are described as uprooted trunks, and the uprooting is performed by wind rather than by an army. The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf reports the same end in its own terms at 7:72, where the people are cut off to the last and the disbelievers are saved from nothing

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:66

> **The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded, “We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Charges From the Chiefs**

*Qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi innā la-narāka fī safāhatin wa-innā la-naẓunnuka mina al-kādhibīn* — the disbelieving chiefs of his people said: we surely see you in foolishness, and we surely think you are one of the liars. The answer to Hūd's question about accountability is a two-part accusation, and both parts are worth examining because they are the two standard defenses of a threatened establishment.

The first is *safāhah*, folly — an assessment of capacity. The word covers lightness of judgment, imprudence, the mind that cannot weigh things properly. Against a prophet whose message is a claim about ultimate reality, the charge says: you are not wicked, you are not dangerous, you are simply not a serious person. The second is *kādhibīn*, liars — an assessment of character, and the two are mutually exclusive in any sane court. A fool cannot be a consistent fraud, and a deliberate liar is by definition not a fool. The chiefs assert both because their purpose is not to describe Hūd but to remove him from consideration, and any two labels will do the job.

**The Grammar of Social Defense**

The verse is careful about who is speaking: *al-malaʾu alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi* — the disbelieving chiefs of his people. The qualifier is doing explicit work. The sūrah has already told its readers, in the account of Ṣāliḥ, that the elite and the ordinary believers were distinct groups (7:75–76); here the particle *alladhīna kafarū* marks off the notables who disbelieved from the town as a whole. The Book does not hold a people responsible for its leadership's unbelief unless the people follow them into it.

And the accusation comes from the establishment because only the establishment had something to lose. Hūd's message did not ask ʿĀd for money or territory; it asked ʿĀd to stop treating its own tribal order as sacred. What the chiefs heard was a threat not to their wealth but to their standing, and the response they produced is the response that the sūrah's readers will have seen in their own town: a decision to attack the messenger's competence rather than the message's content.

**The Qur'an's Reply to Both Charges**

The Book answers the two accusations throughout its narrative sections with weapons it never tires of using. To the charge of folly, it answers with the Criterion itself: a text whose coherence is offered as evidence, recitation whose like no human being has produced (2:23; 10:38; 11:13; 17:88), and the plain fact that the messengers' claims about the natural order — rain, dead land, resurrection — are the claims their audiences already accepted about their own agriculture. To the charge of lying, it answers with the messengers' biographies: the century of Noah's preaching, the decades of Hūd's presence among people who knew his honesty, the disinterestedness of their message. *“I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:109; 26:127; 26:145; 26:164; 26:180). A liar has a motive; the Book repeatedly points out that the messengers had none.

Sūrat Fuṣṣilat renders the whole exchange in a form that strips the charges of their respectability: *“The disbelievers advised ˹one another˺, ‘Do not listen to this Quran but drown it out so that you may prevail.’”* (41:26). That is the same defense in a cruder register, and the sūrah's version — fools and liars — is only the dressed-up form of the same tactic.

**What the Accusation Reveals About ʿĀd**

The chiefs' words also contain the sūrah's analysis of the town's religion. The men who called Hūd foolish were not, by any account in the Book, foolish themselves; they were the engineers of the pillars, the organizers of the caravan routes, the managers of a sophisticated society. What they lacked was a category for obedience. Their world was made up of things they could assess and use, and a summons to submit to an absent authority was, inside that world, indistinguishable from foolishness.

The sūrah's ʿĀd therefore becomes the Book's case study in the confidence of competence: a people so capable that the very idea of accountability looked like an insult, and so successful that the warning of a Day read like bad manners. Sūrat Fuṣṣilat records their boast — *who is stronger than us in might?* (41:15) — and answers it in the next clause: *did they not see that Allah, who created them, is stronger than them in might?* What ʿĀd possessed was real. The question the sūrah keeps putting to them, and to its own listeners, is whether strength is a warrant or a loan.

**The Second Refusal**

The verse ends the town's first exchange, and the sūrah's second cycle is now running exactly as the first did. Noah was told he was misguided; Hūd is told he is a fool and a liar. The escalation in the vocabulary is worth noting, because the sūrah's towns are progressively less courteous as the sequence unfolds. What does not change is the position of the messenger: Hūd will reply in the next verse with the same denial and the same commission, and the sūrah will continue to present the messengers' sentences side by side until their identity of content becomes impossible to miss, and impossible to attribute to invention.


**The Same Two Charges in the Other Histories**

The double accusation is not particular to Hūd. Shuʿayb’s people make it in nearly the same words: *“You are simply bewitched! Also, you are only a human being like us, and we think you are indeed a liar.”* (26:185–186). Nūḥ’s chiefs put one half of it as a verdict on his guidance: *“We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”* (7:60). The Book reports the charge in its most elaborated form in Sūrah Hūd, where the chiefs add the social argument to the personal one: *“We see you only as a human being like ourselves, and we see that no one follows you except the lowliest among us.”* (11:27).

The recurrence is the sūrah’s point rather than a repetition of material. Every town produces the same two charges because they are what a town has available when it cannot answer: an attack on the messenger’s judgment, and an attack on his truthfulness. Neither engages the message. The grammar of both is worth holding — the first is given as a perception, we see you, the second as an opinion, we think you are — and the sūrah answers the first by claiming a different warrant for the man and the second by pointing to his record among the people making the charge.


**What the Charges Assume**

Both charges assume that the messenger is to be assessed by the standards the town already uses. To call a man a fool is to say that he fails the test of practical judgment by which its own leading men are judged; to call him a liar is to say that his word fails the test of reliability by which its merchants are judged. Hūd’s reply accepts the form of the assessment and refuses its jurisdiction: *“O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds,”* (7:67), *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor.”* (7:68).

The two clauses of the reply correspond to the two charges. The denial of foolishness is followed at once by the statement of office, which is a different kind of fact from the one the chiefs were testing. The claim of sincere advice answers the charge of lying in the register the chiefs themselves work in: *naṣīḥah* is the word for a counsellor whose interest runs with the one counselled, and it is the term a trading people would use of a man who tells a buyer the truth about goods he is selling. The sūrah thus makes the town’s own vocabulary the ground of its refutation, and leaves the chiefs holding a charge they cannot support — that a man who never deceived them in trade is deceiving them about God.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:67

> **Hûd replied, “O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Same Answer in the Same Words**

*Qāla yā qawmi laysa bī safāhatun wa-lākinnī rasūlun min rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — Hûd replied: “O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds.” Hūd's reply is Noah's reply transposed by one letter of vocabulary: Noah denied *ḍalālah*, misguidedness; Hūd denies *safāhah*, folly. Everything else is identical, down to the address *yā qawmī* and the title *rabb al-ʿālamīn*.

The repetition is one of the sūrah's boldest compositional decisions, and it is not a stylistic failure. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ, which tells the same five narratives at greater length, organizes itself around a refrain repeated verbatim by each prophet: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah, and obey me. I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds”* (26:107–109, 26:125–127, 26:143–145, 26:162–164, 26:178–180). The Book's audiences were meant to hear the cadence and to draw the inference: the message has one source, and the messengers are its successive carriers rather than its authors.

**The Prophet's Own Commission**

The title *rasūl min rabbi al-ʿālamīn* is also the title the sūrah applied to Muhammad in its opening verses, and the Book links the two missions explicitly. Sūrat al-Aḥqāf instructs the Prophet to say, *“I am not the first messenger ever sent, nor do I know what will happen to me or you. I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.”* (46:9). Sūrat al-Shūrā grounds the unity more deeply: *“He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus”* (42:13).

What the Makkan chiefs were hearing, therefore, when the Prophet recited Hūd's denial, was not a piece of ancient history. It was a mirror held up in their own assembly, in which their own accusations — *a poet, a soothsayer, a man possessed* (69:41–42; 52:29–30) — were shown to be the latest edition of a document that had been in use for millennia. The sūrah's repetition of the messengers' words is designed for precisely this recognition, and the Book has no interest in making the parallels subtle.

**"O My People": The Address as Evidence**

The consistent opening of the reply — *yā qawmī* — deserves its own attention, because it is the one element of the exchange that the towns never imitate. The chiefs refer to Hūd in the third person among themselves (*we see you… we think you…*); the messenger addresses them as his own. The Qur'an's prophets hold the community inside their speech right up to the last verse of their missions, and the sūrah will show Ṣāliḥ doing it after his town is dead: *“O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice”* (7:79).

The Book's later account of the Prophet's own manner repeats the pattern. When his people drove him from al-Ṭāʾif, the tradition reports that he prayed for them rather than against them; and Sūrat al-Qalam, addressing the accusations of the Makkan chiefs point by point, ends with an instruction to patience and a reminder of the man of the whale, who called out in the darkness (68:48). The address *my people* is the sūrah's evidence that the messengers were not combatants in this dispute but kinsmen.

**What Repetition Teaches the Reader**

There is a pedagogical consequence to the sūrah's arrangement that is easy to miss and impossible to overstate. By the time the reader reaches Hūd's reply, he has heard Noah say the same sentence. By the time he reaches Ṣāliḥ, he has heard it three times; Shuʿayb will make it five. The reader's familiarity with the formula becomes, by the end of the passage, a form of knowledge about the shape of religious history: this argument has been conducted before, in the same terms, with the same objections, and the outcome is documented.

That is precisely what the sūrah has been preparing since verse 59, and it explains why the narratives are compressed rather than expanded: the detail is not in the town's collapse but in the messengers' sentences, and the reader is expected to memorize them.

**The Denial That Names the Charge**

The Book's other accounts of ʿĀd give the boast in the town's own words. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ preserves it as a question: *“˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity, and construct castles, as if you are going to live forever?”* (26:128–129). Sūrat Fuṣṣilat records the arrogance and the answer together: *“As for ʿĀd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right, boasting, ‘Who is superior to us in might?’ Did they not see that Allah ˹Himself˺, Who created them, was far superior to them in might?”* (41:15). Hūd's denial of foolishness is thus spoken into a town that had already decided the only argument worth hearing was its own strength.

One detail distinguishes Hūd's denial from Noah's: the form. Noah says, *there is no misguidance in me*; Hūd says, *there is no foolishness in me*. Both negations take the preposition and the indefinite noun, both refuse the label without insulting the labellers, and both then supply the alternative account of the man speaking. The Book's messengers never respond to a personal charge with a personal countercharge. The refusal is total and the alternative is positive: not *I am wise*, but *I am a messenger*. The reader is invited to see that the exchange was never about the speaker's qualities at all, and that only one of the parties to it seems to know that.


**Foolishness as a Charge Running Both Ways**

The charge answered in this verse is *safāhah* — foolishness, from *s-f-h*, the opposite of sound judgment in conduct rather than of intelligence. Hūd denies it of himself: *“O my people! I am no fool!”* (7:67). Al-Jinn uses the same word of speech about God: *“and that the foolish of us used to utter ˹outrageous˺ falsehoods about Allah.”* (72:4).

The two uses sit at opposite ends of the charge. In 7:67 foolishness is alleged against a messenger by his people; in 72:4 it is confessed by jinn against themselves for what they said about God. The word therefore names a defect in judgment about the highest things, not a defect of wit, and that is why the messenger’s denial is followed immediately by his commission (7:67).

The sūrah records the exchange from both sides. The chiefs answer Hūd at 7:66 with a charge of foolishness and a denial of his message; he answers at 7:67 by refusing the charge and stating his office. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the reply is not an argument about his mind but a statement about his source — a messenger from the Lord of all worlds is not the one whose judgment is in question.


**The Lord of All Worlds, Answered**

Hūd names his sender as *rabb al-ʿālamīn* — the Lord of all worlds. Ash-Shuʿarāʾ records what happened when the same title was used before a ruler: Pharaoh asked what the Lord of all worlds was (26:23), and Mūsā answered, *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”* (26:24).

The answer defines the title by its scope. *ʿĀlam* is the collective of all that is other than God — the worlds of men, of jinn, of angels — and 26:24 gives the definition in the terms of creation: heavens, earth, and what is between. That is the same scope 7:54 describes when it lists what God created and what He subjected.

Hūd’s use of the title is therefore not a formula but a claim about jurisdiction. The chiefs who accuse him of foolishness are themselves inside the worlds he names, and the sūrah’s reply to their charge is the title itself. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the messengers of this sūrah all use *rabb al-ʿālamīn* — Nūḥ (7:61), Hūd (7:67), Mūsā (7:104) — and that the repetition is the sūrah’s way of stating that the five towns were addressed by one Lord.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:68

> **conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counsel and the Commission**

*Uballeghukum rasālāti rabbī wa-anā lakum nāṣiḥun amīn* — conveying to you my Lord’s messages, and I am your sincere advisor. Hūd's sentence repeats Noah's double duty with one addition at the end: *amīn*, trustworthy. The word is the crown of the verse, and it belongs to the vocabulary of deposit and return. *Amīn* is the person entrusted with something — a caravan's goods, a household's stores, a secret — who returns it whole. The messenger is a trustee of the message, and the term claims for the transmission the reliability the towns were denying him in the previous verse.

The slogan is the same one that the Qur'an uses for the Prophet himself: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you”* (26:107, 26:125, 26:143, 26:162, 26:178), and the sequence in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ shows it deliberately repeated by each prophet in the sūrah's own cadence. Trustworthiness is the one quality the Book insists on for its messengers: not brilliance, not eloquence, not miracles, but the faithful return of what was entrusted to them.

**What Trustworthiness Is For**

The Qur'an's arguments for revelation lean heavily on this attribute, and the way it uses it is nearly forensic. A message is only as good as its carrier; a messenger who alters the text to suit his audience destroys the evidence he is bringing. Hence the Book's repeated insistence that the Prophet recite without adjustment — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘I do not say to you that I possess Allah’s treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.”* (6:50) — and its equal insistence that the message be delivered whole, including the parts that are inconvenient to its own community: *“What is revealed to me is that I am only sent with a clear warning.’”* (38:70); *“Say, ‘I am not the first messenger ever sent, nor do I know what will happen to me or you. I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.’”* (46:9).

The makings of ʿĀd's refusal become visible under this instruction. The chiefs did not accuse their messenger of incompetence; they accused him of lying. The verse takes that charge and answers it with a claim about the messenger's reliability — which, for the reader, will be tested by whether the message survives the tongue of a man who was going to be killed for it.

**Sincerity Without Return**

*Nāṣiḥ* — the sincere adviser — reappears here, the second use of the word in the sūrah's sequence, after Noah's. It is worth noting what the messengers do not receive for it. Nowhere in the sūrah's narratives does the sincere adviser of a town profit in any way from his counsel; the Qur'an's prophets are poor, mocked, boycotted, and in most cases driven out. Hūd's audience will end the story by asking him to justify himself with a miracle and will then call for the destruction he warned them of (7:70). The Book's prophets are, by design, without leverage.

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ' formula makes this explicit in the messenger's own voice: *“I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:127). The repeated phrase means that any account of religion as a profession of self-interest must fail against the Book's own description of its prophets, and ʿĀd's charges — fool and liar — collapse against a man with nothing to gain.

**The Sūrah's Doctrine of the Messenger**

This verse and its counterpart in Noah's account give the sūrah's fullest summary of what a messenger is, and everything else in the Book's account hangs on it. He does not rule, does not heal at will, does not know the unseen, and does not command obedience for its own sake — Sūrat al-Kahf instructs the Prophet to announce his servitude and mortality in one breath (18:110), and Sūrat al-Naḥl tells him *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:21–22 in its sūrah). What he does is carry a text and give counsel.

The narrowness is the point. The Book is protecting the message from its carrier, and the towns in this sūrah are shown repeatedly trying to turn the argument into a referendum on the prophet's character — the accusation of folly, the charge of lying, the sneer at verse 75 that the believers are following a deluded man. The messenger's reply to all of it in these verses is the same: what he carries is not his, and he will not let the discussion migrate from the text to himself.

**The Two Words the Towns Never Use**

The sūrah's contrast can be stated precisely. The messengers call themselves *transmitters* and *counsellors*; the towns call them *fools*, *liars*, and *misguided*. In the five narratives of this sūrah, the elite never once accuse the messenger of altering the message or of wanting something from them — because the messengers' conduct makes those charges impossible. What remains for the towns to attack is the messenger's person, and the sūrah's readers, watching the exchange from the distance of a few thousand years and a few pages, are being trained to notice when the same substitution happens in their own arguments.


**The Word for Sincere Counsel**

The second clause is built on *naṣīḥah*, which is not a sentiment but an activity. The root *n-ṣ-ḥ* carries the sense of purifying a thing of what adulterates it — honey strained of wax, cloth cleared of a flaw — and the counsellor is the one who hands over something undiluted. The sūrah uses the word of Nūḥ in the same construction: *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know.”* (7:62), and Nūḥ returns to it when the advice has failed: *“My advice will not benefit you—no matter how hard I try—if Allah wills ˹for˺ you to stray.”* (11:34).

Those two occurrences mark the limits of the activity. Counsel can be given, given well and given without payment, and still not be taken; the counsellor’s obligation is discharged in the giving, and 11:34 is what remains to be said when that is all that is left. The placement of the word after the commission is therefore significant — first the messages, then the advice. The office is to convey what was given, and the sincerity describes how it is conveyed, not a guarantee that the hearers will benefit, which is the one thing a messenger cannot promise.


**The Same Sentence in Four Mouths**

The clause is not Hūd’s alone. Nūḥ says it (7:62), Hūd says it here, and the sūrah gives substantially the same self-description to Ṣāliḥ and to Shuʿayb, so that all four speeches share a common core: I convey to you my Lord’s messages, and I am your sincere counsellor. The repetition is a feature of the sūrah’s design rather than a convenience of narration. Its histories are not four separate stories but four instances of one case, and the shared formula is what makes the comparison possible.

What the formula fixes is the messenger’s relation to his town, and it fixes it identically each time: he is one of them, he is paid by none of them, and his interest runs with theirs. The towns’ replies differ in detail — a charge of foolishness to Hūd, of being bewitched to Shuʿayb, of clear error to Nūḥ — but what is refused is the same in all four. The sūrah gives the formula four times so that when the final address arrives, to all humanity (7:158), the office will be recognised before the one who holds it is named.

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:69

> **Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you? Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you greatly in stature. So remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Do You Wonder?" Again**

*A-wa-ʿajibtum an jāʾakum dhikrun min rabbikum ʿalā rajulin minkum* — do you find it astonishing that a reminder from your Lord should come to you through a man among you? Hūd asks Noah's question in Noah's words, and the sūrah's towns give the same non-answer. The Book's repetition is designed to break the objection's credibility: if the wonder at a human messenger is unreasonable in the first town, it is unreasonable in the second and the fifth, and the Qur'an has already supplied the reason — *“Had there been angels walking the earth, well settled, We would have surely sent down for them an angel from heaven as a messenger.”* (17:95).

The additional purpose clause in Hūd's version is *li-yundhirakum* — so that he may warn you. The warning is the message's function, and the Book keeps attention on it because the towns keep trying to move the conversation elsewhere.

**The Argument From Succession: "He Made You Successors After the People of Noah"**

*Udkhurū idh jaʿalakum khulafāʾa min baʿdi qawmi Nūḥ* — remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah. The verse turns from the messenger's credentials to the audience's history, and it uses a word that occurs at several key points in the sūrah: *khulafāʾ*, successors, deputies, the ones who come after. The Qur'an uses it for humanity's viceregency on the earth (2:30), for the generations that inherit a land after its inhabitants (7:74, 7:100, 10:14, 27:62), and for David's succession (38:26).

The claim being made to ʿĀd is that their civilization is a legacy. The town did not create the land it farms or the routes it trades; it occupied a place made empty by a judgment they themselves regarded as history. The verse is thus a direct assault on the false consciousness of the elite, and it corresponds to the sūrah's own earlier argument from the ruins: the towns of the peninsula passed each other's rubble on their caravan routes and drew no conclusions.

**"And Increased You Greatly in Stature"**

*Wa-zādakum fī al-khalqi basṭatan* — and He increased you in the creation, in stature. The phrase has been read as referring to physical size, and the tradition of commentary preserves reports about the height and strength of ʿĀd; it has also been read more broadly as increase in means — the stretch and abundance of their possessions, the grandeur of their buildings. Both readings fit the Book's account of the town, which elsewhere emphasizes their monuments and their boasts. Sūrat al-Fajr's description of the pillar-city, *the like of which was never created in the lands* (89:8), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's reproof about the palaces built as though their makers would live forever (26:129), support the wider sense.

The point either way is the same and it is the core of the verse's argument: the blessing and the test are one thing. The strength that made ʿĀd formidable made their accountability heavier. The sūrah's scale doctrine of verse 8 applies exactly — what is increased in capacity increases the range of what could be done with it, and the Book's consistent view is that capacity is a trust with a report attached.

**"So Remember the Favours of Allah"**

*Fa-dhkurū ālāʾa Allāh laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — so remember the favours of Allah, so that you may succeed. *Ālāʾ* is the Qur'an's word for the successive gifts of God, and the sūrah will use the same instruction in the next narrative, from Ṣāliḥ (7:74). The command to remember is not an invitation to sentimentality; in the Book's usage, remembrance is the act of tracing a good thing back to its source, which is why it is so closely bound up with gratitude — the faculty the sūrah named at the end of the parable of the soils (7:58).

The connection between remembering and success is stated here as a chain: the town's prosperity is a fact, the source of the prosperity is a knowable fact, and the outcome of acknowledging the second depends on what the town does with the first. The sūrah is offering ʿĀd an identity that does not depend on their strength: they are the recipients of gifts, not the authors of them. Whether or not they take the offer, the reader of the sūrah is invited to test the description against his own city and his own account of his own life.

**The Test of Blessing in the Book**

The Qur'an uses prosperity as a trap and as a mercy with a consistency that has always unsettled comfortable readers. Sūrat al-Anʿām describes a people showered with everything they desired until they became proud of what they were given and were cut off (6:44). Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ describes Qārūn, who said his wealth was due to knowledge he possessed, and was swallowed by the earth (28:78–81). And Sūrat al-Aʿrāf itself will shortly tell of the towns whose security was taken from them *while they were sleeping* (7:97–98).

Verse 69 stands at the head of that theme in the sūrah. It is noteworthy that Hūd does not tell ʿĀd that their blessings will be withdrawn; he tells them that the blessings have a name. The disasters that follow in the sūrah's narratives arrive, in every case, at the hands of towns that had been given everything and could not say from whom.


**The Refrain of Wonder**

The question opening this verse — do you find it astonishing — is the sūrah’s refrain, put first to Nūḥ’s people (7:63) and then to ʿĀd here. Outside the sūrah the same wonder is named and answered at the opening of Sūrah Yūnus: *“Is it astonishing to people that We have sent revelation to a man from among themselves?”* (10:2), a verse that goes on to report what the disbelievers called the man who brought it.

The wonder is not about the message but about the messenger’s species, and both tellings expose it as a claim about rank rather than about evidence. A reminder arriving through one of your own is precisely the condition under which it could be checked, since the man’s history, family and truthfulness were known to the people addressed. The sūrah treats the wonder as a refusal dressed as a question, which is why the answer is not an argument but an enumeration of favours: remember that He made you successors, remember that He increased you.


**Increased in Stature**

The increase given to ʿĀd is *basṭah*, a word denoting ampleness or expansion, and the sūrah attaches it here to the body: increased greatly in stature. The same word is used elsewhere of an endowment of another kind, when the prophet of the Banū Isrāʾīl answers the objection to Ṭālūt’s kingship: *“Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature.”* (2:247). There the two terms stand together, and the objectors had raised exactly the point ʿĀd’s chiefs would raise — that the one chosen was not the one with the wealth or the standing.

The pairing fixes what this verse is doing with ʿĀd’s physique. Stature is a gift and is listed among the favours, so the charge against the town is not that it claimed a superiority it lacked. It is that a superiority it had was made self-originating, which is the same move the sūrah refused in the person of Iblīs and the move its towns make every time they are asked to remember. The verse’s imperative — remember the favours — is the antidote offered to a strength that has begun to think of itself as earned.

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:70

> **They said, “Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Demand for the Punishment**

*Qālū a-jiʾtanā li-naʿbuda Allāha waḥdahu wa-nadhara mā kāna yaʿbudu ābāʾunā* — they said: have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone and give up what our fathers used to worship? The response is the sūrah's clearest statement of the towns' real objection, and it is not a theological one. The chiefs of ʿĀd are not denying that a single God might exist; they are objecting to a proposal that would require them to abandon the religion of their ancestors.

The objection is answered in the Book with a consistency that repays attention. Sūrat al-Zukhruf puts it in the words of every town in history: *“We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are following in their footsteps.”* (43:22) — and the Book supplies God's answer to all such claims: *“Even if what I brought you is better guidance than what you found your forefathers practicing?” They said, “Even if what I brought you is better guidance than what you found your forefathers practicing?” They replied, “We totally reject whatever you have been sent with.”* (43:22–24). Sūrat al-Baqarah's account of the same reflex is sharper still: when the people of Israel were told to follow what God had revealed, they answered, *“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.”* — and they too were asked whether their fathers had understood anything at all (2:170).

The sūrah has been preparing for this verse since its beginning. Verse 28 recorded the townspeople's defense that *“we found our fathers doing so”*, and verse 70 shows the same sentence doing the only work it has ever been able to do. The sūrah's God answers it twice in the following verses, and the reader is meant to notice that the answer does not consist of disparaging the fathers; it consists of asking who authorized the practice they handed down.

**"Then Bring Us What You Threaten Us With"**

*Fa-ʾtinā bimā taʿidunā in kunta mina al-ṣādiqīn* — bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true. The challenge converts the argument into a test of strength, and the sūrah's towns use it repeatedly: Thamūd demands the punishment from Ṣāliḥ (7:77), the Makkans demand it of the Prophet (8:32; 46:22), and the Qur'an records the formula on the lips of the impatient in nearly every era: *“Our Lord! Hasten for us our share ˹of the punishment˺ before the Day of Reckoning.”* (38:16).

The Book's answer to the taunt is not a scheduled miracle but a statement about the purpose of delay. *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten is close at hand.’”* (27:72), and Sūrat Yūnus explains why the postponement exists: *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed. But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their defiance.”* (10:11; see also 16:61, 35:45). The towns treat the absence of the penalty as evidence of impunity; the Book treats the gap as the mercy that keeps them alive.

**The Fathers as an Argument**

It is worth isolating the precise role of the ancestors in this verse, because the sūrah's critique is often misunderstood as a rejection of tradition as such. The Book is not against inherited religion; it is against inherited religion held without examination — and it makes the distinction explicitly by counting itself among the things inherited. *“Follow the way of your fathers Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac”* is not the same argument as *“we found our fathers on a way”*, and the difference is whether the tradition has a warrant in revelation.

The sūrah's question at 7:71 will name that warrant with a single word — *sulṭān*, authority — and its absence is the whole case against the gods of ʿĀd. The Book does not say that the ancestors were liars; it says that the practice they handed down has no authorization from God, and that no community can transfer the responsibility for its worship to its forebears. Verse 38 of the sūrah has already staged the end of the argument in the Hereafter, where communities curse their predecessors as they enter the Fire, and where the excuse of following others is refused (7:39).

**The Ask That Would Have Settled It**

Hūd's opponents make a fair point in form: a messenger who warns of a disaster should be able to produce one. The Book's own accounts of the messengers show that this is not how the pattern is designed. The signs that authenticated the prophets appear on God's schedule and in God's kind — a she-camel for Thamūd, a sea for Moses, a flood for Noah, a fire for Ibrāhīm — and they are never delivered as answers to an audience's test paper. The Book states the principle when the Makkans demand signs: *“Signs are only with Allah. And I am only sent with a clear warning”* (29:50), and it points out that the demanders would not believe even after them (6:109; 2:145).

What ʿĀd asked for was not evidence but leverage; the challenge presumes that the messenger's claim depends on the audience's satisfaction rather than on God's authority. The sūrah's next verse records Hūd's answer, and it does not supply a miracle. It supplies a fact about the past tense.

**The Question Behind the Demand**

Read with the sūrah's earlier verses, the exchange is a drama about authority with an unusually complete inventory of positions. Noah's town had answered the message by labelling the messenger; ʿĀd's town answers by relocating the question to the ancestors and then to the schedule of punishment. What is missing from both replies is the one thing the messengers keep asking for: a decision about God.

The verse's form of the demand — *bring us what you threaten us with* — has a theological double edge that the sūrah's next verses bring out. The thing Hūd is threatening them with is not a personalized magic trick; it is the judgment of God, which the Book elsewhere describes as having been earned already. The challenge to produce it is therefore answered, in the sūrah's narrative, by the fact that the delay was the only thing standing between ʿĀd and a verdict that had been accumulating for a generation.


Rain Stones Upon Us: The Demand Elsewhere

The people of ʿĀd answer their messenger with a demand: bring what you threaten, if you are truthful. The Book records the same demand in the words of another people, put as a prayer: *“O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.”* (8:32)

The demand's form is what the sūrah criticises. A punishment requested as a proof treats the messenger's warning as a claim to be falsified, and it assumes that the request can be survived if the claim is false. The verse of al-Anfāl shows the assumption in its plainest shape, since the people ask for stones from the sky as the condition of believing. In al-Aʿrāf the same assumption appears in the demand at 7:70 and in the refusal at 7:132, where the court declares that no sign will move it; both are statements that the evidence offered is not the evidence required.

The demand is also a statement about the fathers. Worship Allah alone and abandon what the forefathers worshipped: the two halves of the question are joined, and the punishment is requested in defence of the second


Worship Me Alone: What the Demand Refuses

The first half of the question at 7:70 restates the call the sūrah puts to every people, and the Book states that call as the content of every message: *“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.”* (21:25)

What the two verses of al-Aʿrāf and al-Anbiyāʾ establish together is the ground of the sūrah's repeated openings. Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, and the messengers of the towns all begin with the same sentence, and the sūrah's variety of settings is a demonstration that the sentence does not change

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:71

> **He said, “You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath. Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up —a practice Allah has never authorized? Then wait! I too am waiting with you.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Wrath and Anger Have Already Fallen"**

*Qāla qad waqaʿa ʿalaykum min rabbikum rijzun wa-ghaḍab* — he said: wrath and anger from your Lord have already descended upon you. The tense is the verse's startling feature. Hūd does not say that punishment *will* come; he says it has *fallen* — a past-tense verdict pronounced on a town that is still standing, still trading, still strong, and still mocking. The sūrah's doctrinal point is that the judgment of a people begins before the sky changes colour: the decision has been made in the record, and ʿĀd's prosperity is the interval between the sentence and its execution.

*Rijz* is the Qur'an's word for the punishment that is also a pollution — the same term the Book uses for the plagues that fell on Egypt (7:133, 2:59), for the filth God casts on those who refuse to use their reason (10:100), and for the torment that follows the unjust. *Ghaḍab*, anger, is God's displeasure stated in the human vocabulary of a personal response; the Book uses it for those who have earned it (2:61; 5:60; 8:16). The combination names both the fact and the response: a penalty that is a defilement, and a judgment that is a relation.

**The Radical Critique of Idols: "Only Names"**

*A-tujādilūnanī fī asmāʾin sammaytumūhā antum wa-ābāʾukum mā nazzala Allāhu bihā min sulṭān* — do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up, a practice Allah has never authorized? The verse is the Qur'an's most complete statement of what idols are, and the Book repeats it in exactly these terms at two other points: *“Whatever ˹idols˺ you worship instead of Him are mere names which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized. It is only Allah Who decides. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright faith, but most people do not know.”* (12:40, spoken by Yūsuf in prison, and 53:23). The word *asmāʾ* — names — is the whole indictment. The gods of ʿĀd are not described as demons, or as false powers, or as frauds practised on the people; they are described as labels without referents.

The second term is *sulṭān*: authority, evidence, a warrant. The Book's argument against the town is not that the practice is old, or unpopular, or socially damaging, but that it can produce no authorization from the one whose prerogative it invades. The same word appears throughout the sūrah at the exact points where the towns' positions are tested — *“He said, ‘You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath. Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up —a practice Allah has never authorized? Then wait! I too am waiting with you.’”* (7:71; see also 3:151, 10:68), *“They follow nothing but assumptions, and do nothing but lie.”* (6:116). In the Book's epistemology, a claim about God without a warrant from God is not a theology; it is a name.

**The Names People Give Their Gods**

The Qur'an's treatment of the pagan pantheon in Makkah follows the same logic. Sūrat al-Najm names al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt and dismisses them in a single clause: *“These ˹idols˺ are mere names that you and your forefathers have made up — a practice Allah has never authorized”* (53:23). The same analysis applies to ʿĀd, and the sūrah's reader notices that what is condemned is not only the carved stone but the practice of assigning the divine to whatever a community names as sacred.

Verses 70 and 71 together thus form a compact critique of inherited religion and the substitution of vocabulary for authority. The fathers handed down the names; the children defend them; God has authorized neither. When the same Book turns to the older Abrahamic traditions and commands their preservation, it does so on the basis of revealed texts and prophetic precedents — which is precisely the basis that the gods of ʿĀd cannot produce.

**"Then Wait; I Am Waiting With You"**

*Fa-intaẓirū innī maʿakum mina al-muntazirīn* — then wait! I too am waiting with you. The sentence ends the exchange by accepting it. Hūd does not insist, does not threaten, and does not call for immediate action; he places himself on the same bench as his accusers and lets the record run. The Book's messengers use this formula when their arguments are exhausted — Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ's Prophet is told to say, *“Say ˹to them, O Prophet˺, ‘Each ˹of us˺ is waiting, so keep waiting! You will soon know who is on the Straight Path and is ˹rightly˺ guided.’”* (20:135), and Sūrat al-Sāffāt records Noah's townsmen being told the same.

The phrase is a disciplined act of faith and a rebuke at once. It says that the outcome of the dispute is not up to either party in the room; it says that the messenger is not going to force the issue, because the arbitration belongs to a court neither side controls. The sūrah's rhetorical achievement in these verses is that the whole exchange — the challenge, the taunt, the answer — has been conducted with no violence on the messenger's side at all, and the destruction, when it arrives in the next verse, arrives from a direction nobody in the dialogue was managing.

**The Pattern of the Deferred Verdict**

The Book keeps this structure across its prophetic narratives because it is arguing about how God deals with the world. Noah was given a century; ʿĀd was given generations of prosperity and repeated warnings; Thamūd would be given a living sign and told to leave it alone. The summons precedes the sentence, and the delay is not indecision but opportunity: *“Be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say”* (38:17) is addressed to the last of the messengers, whose own people were being given exactly the interval the earlier towns had wasted.

Verse 71 therefore records a verdict from the messenger's perspective and abstains from the verdict itself. What Hūd knows is that the case has closed in heaven: the towns' gods have no authority, the towns' ancestors have no exceptional standing, and the warning has been delivered in a language they understood. The remaining question — when the sentence is executed — the verse places entirely in the hands of the One whose commands Hūd was sent to convey.


Mere Names: The Same Charge in an-Najm

The dispute at 7:71 is about names, and the Book states the same charge in an-Najm: *“These ˹idols˺ are mere names that you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized.”* (53:23). The two verses share their object, their agents, and the ground of the objection

The charge is radical in the sense that it does not argue about the properties of the named things. 7:71 does not ask whether the gods can hear or help, though the sūrah asks that elsewhere; it states that the names themselves are the invention

The forefathers appear in the charge as co-inventors rather than as authorities. The practice of naming was performed by both generations, and the authorization was absent in both. The sūrah's accounts treat the appeal to the fathers as the standard defence of a custom, and the verse at 7:71 removes the defence by making the fathers parties to the invention


Beliefs Ordained Without Authorization

The absence of authorization at 7:71 is stated elsewhere as a question about its source: *“do they have associate-gods who have ordained for them some ˹polytheistic˺ beliefs, which Allah has not authorized?”* (42:21). The verse of ash-Shūrā asks where the beliefs came from if not from Allah, and the question implies that an ordaining requires an ordainer with standing

What the two verses establish together is the sūrah's standard for a religious claim. A claim requires authorization, and authorization comes from the One who sent the messengers whose messages the sūrah narrates. The demand at the end of 7:71 — wait, I too am waiting — is a demand made on the ground of that standard: the outcome will show which party had authorization, and the waiting is the form the standard takes in a dispute that cannot be settled by argument alone

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:72

> **So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy and uprooted those who denied Our signs. They were not believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Saved by Mercy, Cut Off for Denial**

*Fa-anjaynāhu wa-lladhīna maʿahu bi-raḥmatin minnā* — so We saved him and those with him by Our mercy. The rescue is attributed, as in Noah's case, to a rescue rather than to merit: *bi-raḥmatin minnā*, by mercy from Us. The sūrah's narrative has thus far shown towns punished and remnants spared, and it takes care each time to name the mechanism. Ḥūd's people are not saved because they had proven their case or exceeded their accusers in virtue they could measure; they are saved because mercy reached them, and the mercy is the reason given.

The point carries weight in the sūrah's overall argument because it is the same doctrine the Book states in its treatment of the Hereafter. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own scene of the entry into Paradise has the saved confess that they would never have been guided had God not guided them (7:43), and the Prophet's hadith places the same fact in a single sentence: *none of you will be saved by his deeds* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816). The narratives of this sūrah and the doctrine of its Hereafter scenes are teaching one thing in two registers.

**"We Uprooted Those Who Denied Our Signs"**

*Wa-qaṭaʿnā dābira alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā* — and We uprooted those who denied Our signs.
