The verb is one of the Book's grimmest images of destruction: *qaṭaʿa dābira* means to cut off the rear, to leave no successor behind, to end a line. The Qur'an uses it for nations (6:45, 8:7, 15:66, 7:72 here) and the image is agricultural in origin — the cutting of a stem so that nothing regrows from the base.

What makes the phrase pointed in ʿĀd's case is the Book's account of their civilization elsewhere. This is the town of the lofty pillars, of the buildings that imitated eternity (26:129), of the boast *who is stronger than us in might?* (41:15). Their destruction in the sūrah's narrative is the demolition of a legacy: not merely the death of persons but the end of a name that no one could rebuild. Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah's description of the wind makes the physical shape of the sentence explicit: *“a furious, bitter wind which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees.”* (69:6–7). Sūrat al-Qamar adds the morning-after detail: *“Indeed, We sent against them ˹only˺ one ˹mighty˺ blast, leaving them like the twigs of fencebuilders.”* (54:31).

**The Irony of the Delivered Form**

The most remarkable detail of ʿĀd's destruction in the Book appears in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf, where the punishment arrives in the form of what they had been waiting for all along: *“Then when they saw the torment as a ˹dense˺ cloud approaching their valleys, they said ˹happily˺, ‘This is a cloud bringing us rain.’ ˹But Hûd replied,˺ ‘No, it is what you sought to hasten: a ˹fierce˺ wind carrying a painful punishment!’ It destroyed everything by the command of its Lord, leaving nothing visible except their ruins.”* (46:24–25). The Book's composition has the towns killed by their own demand. They asked for what was threatened; what was threatened came dressed as mercy and turned out to be a storm.

That structure is why the sūrah ends the verse with a sentence that is not merely descriptive: *wa-mā kānū muʾminīn* — they were not believers. The clause secures the fairness of the account. What was destroyed was not a town of innocent people; it was a town that had lived through its own century-scale warning and rejected it, and the Book's reader is expected to keep that fact in view when he condemns the destruction as excessive.

**The Remnant and the Mercy**

The other half of the verse — *him and those with him* — returns to the pattern established in Noah's account, and the sūrah will keep it. In this sūrah's narratives, the rescue is always small, always named in the same breath as the town's destruction, and always attributed to mercy. The Book's later chapters add the detail of how the remnant was preserved; Sūrat al-Ḥūd records that they were saved *by a mercy from Us* from a punishment that came as a cry and an earthquake (11:58, 11:67 in the two accounts), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has the town ask, at the last moment, whether there is any remnant to be spared (26:139 in its wording).

The narrative's shape is worth stating in a sentence: in this sūrah, the mercy of God and the judgment of God arrive together, and the difference between the two populations is not their circumstances but their response to a message. That is the sūrah's thesis about history, and it will now be demonstrated three more times with the same structure and different scenery.

**The Verse's Place in the Sequence**

ʿĀd's story is the second of the five towns, and its closing sentence — *they were not believers* — completes a triplet that the reader has now heard twice and will hear four times: the messengers warn, the elite mock, the people disappear. The sūrah's towns have been given varying degrees of detail, and ʿĀd is the one granted a small masterpiece of irony by the Book's later chapters: an end that arrived in the shape of a promise fulfilled and a rain cloud that was something else entirely.

The reader who has just been told, in verse 57, that God drives clouds to a dead land to bring it to life, is now shown a cloud driven to a living town to bring it to death. The sūrah's imagery is deliberately reversable, and what determines the direction is never the weather.


**Uprooted: Cutting Off the Last of Them**

The verb of destruction here is *qaṭaʿnā*, from *q-ṭ-ʿ*, to cut. The full phrase in the Arabic is *qaṭaʿnā dābir alladhīna kadhdhabū* — we cut off the *dābir* of those who denied. *Dābir* is the active participle of the same root as *ʿaqib*, the heel: it names the one who comes last, the rear of a group. To cut off the *dābir* is to cut off the last of them, so that none remains behind.

Al-Anʿām uses the same verb for the same outcome: *“So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.”* (6:45)

The idiom is stronger than a report of death. A people whose *dābir* is cut has no remainder: no survivor to carry a name, no descendant to inherit a claim


**Saved by a Mercy From Us**

The verse’s first clause is *fa-anjaynāhu wa-alladhīna maʿahu bi-raḥmatin minnā* — “So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy.” (7:72). The rescue is attributed to mercy rather than to the people’s conduct, and the same attribution appears in Hūd’s account: *“When Our command came, We rescued Hûd and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, saving them from a harsh torment.”* (11:58). The two verses use the same construction — a mercy *from Us* — for the same event in the cycle.

The parallel fixes the shape of every deliverance the sūrah reports. Lūṭ and his household are saved except the wife (7:83); Hūd and the believers are saved by a mercy (11:58); Ṣāliḥ and the believers are saved “by a mercy from Us” (11:66); Shuʿayb and the believers are saved (7:93). In each case the salvation is stated as given, and in each case the destruction is stated as earned: the sūrah’s summaries attach the outcome to the people’s denial (7:72, 7:78, 7:92).

That asymmetry is the verse’s doctrinal content and the reason it is placed where it is. The cycle of towns opens at 7:59 with a messenger’s fear for his people and closes at 7:93 with the last of them buried; 7:72 stands early enough to establish the rule that governs all of them. The remnant is not the majority, the mercy is not earned, and the uprooting is not arbitrary — three propositions the sūrah will not argue again, because it has stated them here.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:73

> **And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord: this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you. So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her, or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Thamūd and the She-Camel**

*Wa-ilā Thamūda akhāhum Ṣāliḥan* — and to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ. The third town enters the sequence with the same formula, and its messenger brings a new element: a sign that lives among the community and makes demands on it. *Hādhihi nāqatu Allāhi lakum āyatan* — this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you — *fa-dharūhā taʾkul fī arḍi Allāh wa-lā tamassūhā bi-sūʾin* — so leave her to eat in Allah's land and do not harm her, or a painful punishment will seize you.

The Book gives this sign more space than any other pre-Mosaic miracle, and the reason is its peculiar design. The she-camel is not a spectacle performed once and debated afterwards; it is an animal pastured on the town's land, drinking from the town's water, and its presence is the test. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ states the arrangement in the town's own hearing: *“Ṣâliḥ said, ‘Here is a camel. She will have her turn to drink as you have yours, each on an appointed day. And do not ever touch her with harm, or you will be overtaken by the torment of a tremendous day.’”* (26:155–156). Sūrat al-Qamar compresses the whole affair into four verses: the warning, the consultation, the hamstringing, and the cry (54:23–31).

**The Sign as a Neighbour**

What is theologically remarkable about the she-camel is that it turns a natural resource into a test of obedience. Thamūd's people did not need to accept an argument or assent to a doctrine in order to pass the test; they needed to share the water. The Book elsewhere names the sign as one of the reasons the town's destruction was inevitable, and it is worth noting the tradition's interest in this verse: classical exegetes discuss how the animal's daily access to the spring displaced the town's own use, and how the distribution was arranged. The details are less important than the principle, which the sūrah states in a single clause: *do not harm her*.

The Book's use of the sign also protects the messengers from the charge of magic. A wonder that appears at will and vanishes is a claim about the man; an animal that stays and requires restraint is a claim about the hearers. The Qur'an notes that the sign was *for them*, and the Book's language around it is transactional: a proof given, and a limit set.

**Ṣāliḥ's Address and Its Additions**

Ṣāliḥ's opening speech is the same as Noah's and Hūd's — the call to the worship of the One God — with the addition of the sign and the warning of the punishment to follow its violation. The sūrah gives him no new doctrine. What the account adds is the mechanism of the town's doom: not a philosophical error, not a failure of argument, but a collective decision to kill a particular animal in order to demonstrate that the messenger's God could not protect it.

Sūrat al-Shams tells the same story in its own way and supplies the reason the refusal became fatal: *“when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺. … But the messenger of Allah warned them, ‘˹Do not disturb˺ Allah’s camel and her ˹turn to˺ drink!” … Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their …’* (91:12–14). The Book's analysis locates the sin in the act of hamstringing and in the rejection that made it deliberate. The town had been given a sign that was also a daily ordinance, and it chose to destroy the ordinance in public.

**The Geography of Thamūd**

The sūrah's next verse will describe the town's achievements, but the Book supplies its own portrait in several places, and the archaeological details are consistent: the carving of dwellings in the rock, and the trading of security for wealth. Sūrat al-Ḥijr records that the people *“They carved their homes in the mountains, feeling secure.”* (15:82), and Sūrat al-Fajr names Thamūd with the people who *hollowed out the rock in the valley* (89:9). This sūrah's own memory of the tribe is Ṣāliḥ's reminder of their carved homes in the next verse (7:74), and the Qur'an returns to the empty houses of Thamūd as a lesson: *“So their homes are there”* (27:52).

The picture is of a people who had solved the problem of nature — water, shelter, defence — and had begun to think of security as a property they possessed. The sign they were given was a living interruption in that sense of possession: an animal that drank their measured water and could not be touched. The Book's towns are consistently destroyed by the one thing they cannot incorporate into their systems, and Thamūd's system had been built precisely to minimize interruptions.

**The Sign the Town Chose to Kill**

The sūrah does not yet say what will happen, but its audience had heard the story in the markets and the Book has told it elsewhere: the she-camel was hamstrung, the town was given three days, and the cry took them (11:65, 54:31). Verse 73 closes with the warning attached to the sign — *or a painful punishment will seize you* — and the reader who knows what comes next reads the sentence as the last free warning the town ever received.

The arrangement of the sūrah's three towns so far is the same in each case: a message, an elite who object, a sign or an argument, and a deadline. Noah's town had a century; ʿĀd had generations; Thamūd was given an animal that any shepherd could see. The Book's escalation of proximity is deliberate, and the next verse shows the town at ease in the middle of it, boasting about its real estate.


**The Sign’s Terms: A Share of Water and of Grazing**

Ṣāliḥ’s sign arrives with conditions. The sūrah states the first of them here — *“So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her, or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment!”* (7:73) — and ash-Shuʿarāʾ’s parallel account states the second: *“Here is a camel. She will have her turn to drink as you have yours, each on an appointed day.”* (26:155). The she-camel is given grazing and a scheduled share of water; the town is given the same schedule and told not to touch her.

Ṣāliḥ’s own words in Hūd make the terms explicit: *“And O my people! This she-camel of Allah is a sign for you. So leave her to graze freely on Allah’s earth and do her no harm, or a swift punishment will overtake you!”* (11:64). The verse contains the three elements of the arrangement: attribution (she is God’s, not the town’s), permission (the earth is open to her), and sanction (harm brings a punishment that does not wait).


**The Command Not to Harm Her, and Its Breach**

The prohibition in 7:73 is *lā tamassūhā bi-sūʾ* — literally do not touch her with harm — which the translation renders *“do not harm her”* (7:73). The preposition makes the harm an instrument: not merely do not harm her, but do not come at her with harm. 11:64 states the sanction for breach, and ash-Shams states the command in its shortest form: *“But the messenger of Allah warned them, ‘Do not disturb Allah’s camel and her turn to drink!’”* (91:13) — where the thing protected is not only the animal but her share.

The sūrah reports the breach and its consequence in the verse that follows this one: the hamstrung camel, the defiance of the command, the punishment (7:77–78). Ash-Shams adds the detail that the act was undertaken by the town’s most wretched (91:12). The exegetes read the sequence as a demonstration of what a sign with terms looks like when the terms are broken: not a natural catastrophe but a sanction stated in advance, invoked, and executed.

7:73 therefore does more than introduce a miracle. It installs a legal arrangement inside a town — an animal with rights to land and water, guaranteed by a prophet, with a stated penalty — and the town’s response is the response the sūrah has been describing since its opening: the proof is given, the terms are announced, and the people destroy what they were told not to touch.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:74

> **Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land—˹and˺ you built palaces on its plains and carved homes into mountains. So remember Allah’s favours, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Established in the Land**

*Wa-dhkurū idh jaʿalakum khulafāʾa min baʿdi ʿĀdin wa-bawwaʾakum fī al-arḍ* — and remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land. The verse repeats the argument Hūd used against ʿĀd, addressed now to their heirs, and the repetition is itself the message. Thamūd occupies the territory ʿĀd lost, and their claim to it is the same claim their predecessors made: possession as evidence of favour.

The word *bawwaʾakum* — settled you, established you — is the vocabulary of placement by a host. The Book uses it for Israel in the promised land (10:93) and for the settlement of the believers after their trials (22:41). The verb's grammar keeps Thamūd's tenancy in the gift: the town did not occupy an empty peninsula by its own strength; it was placed, in the same way that its predecessor had been displaced.

**Palaces on the Plains and Homes in the Mountains**

*Tabnūna bi-suhūlihā qaṣūran wa-tanḥitūna al-jibāla buyūtan* — you build palaces on its plains and carve the mountains into homes. The description is precise and it matches the Book's other accounts: Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has Ṣāliḥ asking, *“˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity, and construct castles, as if you are going to live forever,”* (26:128–129), and Sūrat al-Ḥijr records the practice of carving dwellings from the rock *“feeling secure”* (15:82). The two halves of the verse's image — the tower on the plain and the chamber in the cliff — form a catalogue of defensive achievement, and the Book's readers have always recognized the picture: an architecture designed to make attack impossible and time irrelevant.

The Qur'an's treatment of this architecture is consistently theological. The stones are not criticized as luxury; the Book's objection is to what such building expresses about its builders' estimate of their own permanence. Sūrat al-Fajr's description of Iram's pillars is framed by the same thought — *the like of which was never created in the lands* — and immediately followed by the account of a people who thought their strength made them immune to judgment (89:6–13). What Thamūd had converted into self-confidence was, in the Book's account, a loan by which it was being tested.

**"So Remember the Favours of Allah"**

*Fa-dhkurū ālāʾa Allāh* — so remember the favours of Allah. The instruction is repeated verbatim from Hūd's address (7:69), and the sūrah's towns are shown to receive identical counsel from identical messengers. The word *ālāʾ* covers the whole inventory the verse has just listed: the succession, the settlement, the plains, the cliffs, and the skill to use them. Nothing in the list is described as a product of Thamūd's own creative power; the city is presented as a set of gifts that happens to be inhabited by people with names.

The Book's later verses about Thamūd make the same point from the ruins: *“So their homes are there”* (27:52). Whatever the town thought its architecture was for, the Book's epitaph is empty buildings — an inventory of materials with the tenants gone. The verse's instruction to remember is thus the only defence the sūrah offers against that outcome, and it is offered at the last moment before the town's refusal is sealed.

**"Do Not Spread Corruption in the Land"**

The verse ends with the prohibition that the sūrah placed at the head of its practical instructions at 7:56: *wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍ mufsidīn* — and do not go about the land spreading corruption. The verb *ʿathā* adds to *fasād* the sense of violent, ruinous action — the destruction that leaves wreckage behind — and the Book uses it for those whose conduct goes beyond mere disobedience into devastation (2:27, 2:60, 26:151–152, 29:36).

The placement of this clause in Ṣāliḥ's speech connects the town's coming crime to the sūrah's broader moral framework. Thamūd's destruction will not be triggered by an abstract dispute about the names of gods; it will be triggered by the deliberate killing of an animal placed under the town's protection as a sign. The sūrah's vocabulary makes that act a form of *fasād* in the literal sense: the ruin of a living thing in an ordered land, performed as a public gesture. And the Book's portraits of these towns are consistent in presenting their crimes as acts of vandalism against a world that had been set right (7:56) — a correspondence the sūrah's audience, watching their own sacred precinct put to tribal uses, was equipped to notice.

**The Third Warning and Its Heirs**

The verse's function inside the narrative is to lay the foundation for verse 75, where the town's elite will turn on the lowest of their own people. It has just reminded Thamūd of every advantage they possess, and it has named them the heirs of a drowned generation — and the two facts together are the sūrah's case for their accountability. They inherited the lesson and the land at the same time.

The reader of this sūrah has now watched three towns receive the same message and answer it in three dialects: Noah's town with a label, ʿĀd with a demand and a taunt, Thamūd with a living sign they were told not to touch. What remains to be seen, in the verses that follow, is the internal cost of the refusal — the split inside the town between those who believed and those who owned the plains and the cliff-houses. That split, and not the she-camel, will occupy the next several verses, and it is the sūrah's most exact diagnosis of how a community talks itself into destruction.


**The Carving in Two Other Accounts**

The sūrah reports Thamūd’s building as a fact about their skill, and the two other accounts add the quality of the work and the state of mind behind it. Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ puts the question to them directly: *“to carve homes in the mountains with great skill?”* (26:149). Sūrah al-Ḥijr supplies the motive in a single participle: *“They carved their homes in the mountains, feeling secure.”* (15:82).

The three accounts together give a complete picture of the town, and each element answers one of the charges this verse brings. Skill is the capacity; security is what the capacity was believed to buy; and the sūrah’s command — remember the favours — is the correction to both. Cutting habitations into stone is a work of engineering that presupposes a settled people, tools, surplus food and time, and every one of those is among the favours the verse asks them to remember. The security named in al-Ḥijr is what happens when a people begin to read the surplus as their own achievement.


**Succession, and the Town That Came Before**

The verse opens by naming the town whose place Thamūd took: successors after ʿĀd. The Book returns to that succession in its own register of the destroyed: *“Did you not see how your Lord dealt with ’Ȃd—”* (89:6), a passage that goes on to name the pillars of Iram and the stonemasons of Thamūd in the same breath, so that the two towns stand in one sequence.

The succession is the verse’s argument rather than its chronology. A people who inherit the place of a destroyed people have in front of them the one piece of evidence no messenger needs to supply: the remains. That is why the sūrah’s histories always travel in order and always mention the predecessor, and why its charge against each town is not ignorance but inattention. Thamūd is established in the land ʿĀd lost, building in the same landscape, and the verse asks it to remember both facts at once — the establishment and the succession — before it forbids the corruption that follows from forgetting the second.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:75

> **The arrogant chiefs of his people asked the lowly who believed among them, “Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?” They replied, “We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question the Elite Ask the Poor**

*Qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna istakbarū min qawmihi li-lladhīna istuḍʿifū li-man āmana minhum* — the arrogant chiefs of his people said to the weak ones among them who had believed. The sūrah has been building to this sentence since its first pages, and the sentence's structure contains its whole social analysis. The town is divided into two vocabularies: the *malaʾ* who are *mustakbirūn*, arrogant, and the *mustaḍʿafūn*, those treated as weak. The Book's terminology is not neutral descriptive sociology; it assigns responsibility. One group inflates itself; the other is made small, and the passive voice in *istuḍʿifū* says who did it.

The Qur'an uses this pair of terms across its narratives of the prophetic age, and it repeatedly describes the same alliance of the powerful and the same constituency of the message. Sūrat Sabaʾ records the exchange between the arrogant and the weak in the Hereafter and has the weak say to the arrogant, *“The disbelievers vow, ‘We will never believe in this Quran, nor in those ˹Scriptures˺ before it.” If only you could see when the wrongdoers will be detained before their Lord, throwing blame at each other! The lowly ˹followers˺ will say to the …’* (34:31–33). Sūrat al-Furqān describes the objection of the disbelievers with the same social logic: *“And they say ˹mockingly˺, ‘What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺? If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner,”* (25:7) — the objection of those who expected the message to arrive with attendants.

**"Are You Certain That Ṣāliḥ Has Been Sent?"**

*A-taʿlamūna anna Ṣāliḥan mursalun min rabbihi* — are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord? The question is one of the finest pieces of villainy in the Book. It contains no argument, no counterclaim, and no denial of Ṣāliḥ's credentials; it is a probe. The elite of Thamūd do not ask the believers to defend their faith before God; they ask whether the believers are *sure*, and they address the question to people whose poverty had taught them to hedge every statement and whose standing in the town depended on those above them.

The wording the sūrah gives the question — *do you know* — is the language of certainty, and the answer it receives is expressed in the language of confidence: *we certainly believe in what he has been sent with*. The Book's care here is worth noting. The believers are not asked about their degree of assurance, and they do not claim to know everything about the messenger's mission. They testify to what they trust, and the two verbs — *we know* / *we believe* — are the sūrah's comment on the difference between the elite's epistemological posturing and the poor's actual faith.

**The Answer of the Lowly**

*Qālū innā bimā ursila bihi muʾminūn* — they said: we certainly believe in what he has been sent with. The sentence is a monument of the sūrah, and its composition deserves attention. The believers do not answer with a proposition about Ṣāliḥ; they answer with a proposition about the *message*. What they affirm is *bimā ursila bihi* — "what he has been sent with" — which is precisely the ground on which the elite hoped to unsettle them.

The reply has been quoted by Muslims in every generation facing official pressure, and the Book itself prepares the reader for it earlier in the sūrah: the reader has already heard the divine voice describe the saved of the end times as those who *“As for those who believe and do good—We never require of any soul more than what it can afford—it is they who will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.”* (7:42), and has already watched the lowly appear on the sūrah's wall of separation while the tyrants stand in the Fire (7:48–49). The sūrah's structure is designed to let the reader see the answer of verse 75 from both directions at once: inside the town, where it looks like weakness; and inside the Hereafter, where the same people are the ones told to enter Paradise.

**The Poor as the Book's Constant Constituency**

The Qur'an's sociology of belief is one of its least fashionable and most consistent features. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's version of the towns' objection is explicit: *“How can we believe in you, when you are followed ˹only˺ by the lowest of the low?”* (26:111; see also 11:27, where the chiefs say that no one follows Noah except the lowliest, and note that Noah refuses to drive them away). The Book does not romanticize poverty; it says that power and wealth systematically make their holders less able to accept a message that costs them precedence.

Sūrat al-Anʿām's instruction to the Prophet is the doctrine in action: *“˹O Prophet!˺ Do not dismiss those ˹poor believers˺ who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure.”* (6:52), and Sūrat al-Kahf repeats it: *“Patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not let your eyes look beyond them, desiring the luxuries of this worldly life.”* (18:28). Both verses were revealed in a Makkah where the Prophet was under pressure to send away the poor in order to attract the notables — the same pressure the sūrah's Thamūd applies from below.

**A Question About Others' Faith**

The elite's question has one more feature that deserves notice: it is about somebody else's belief. The chiefs do not ask whether *they* owe the messenger anything; they interrogate the poor about what the poor think. The Book's consistent portrait of the towns' leaders is of people who find it easier to manage the religious life of others than to examine their own, and the pattern repeats in the sūrah's account of the Hereafter — where the leaders of the world discover that the faith of the lowly, whose certainty they had mocked, was the one thing they themselves had never bothered to possess (7:49).

The verses that follow will give the elite their slogan and their deed, and the sūrah will report both without commentary beyond the facts. The reader who has followed the sūrah from its opening — the scales, the gates, the wall, the crowds — already knows how the two sentences in this exchange will be judged, and which of them will be quoted in the Garden.


Belief in What He Was Sent With: The Object Named

The answer of the lowly at 7:75 is brief and precise: we believe in what he has been sent with. The object of the belief is not the man but the message, and the Book states the same object in its fullest form: *“The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”* (2:285)

The precision of the answer is what defeats the question. The chiefs asked whether the lowly knew that Ṣāliḥ had been sent by his Lord, and the answer names what he had been sent with rather than what they knew about his sending

What the exchange shows about knowledge is the sūrah's point. The chiefs ask for certainty about a sending, which is a matter they cannot verify; the lowly answer with belief in a message, which is a matter they have received


The Reply That Ends the Exchange

The chiefs' response is recorded in a single sentence: *“We surely reject what you believe in.”* (7:76). The symmetry is exact. The lowly believed in what the messenger was sent with; the chiefs reject what the lowly believe in. Neither party addresses the content, and the exchange closes with two statements about each other's belief rather than about the message

What the closure establishes is the ground of the destruction that follows. A dispute that has become a comparison of positions cannot be settled by a sign, and the sūrah reports that the sign was given and harmed anyway. The she-camel at 7:73 was the sign, and the hamstringing at 7:77 was the answer to it; the exchange at 7:75–76 is the verbal form of the same refusal

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:76

> **The arrogant said, “We surely reject what you believe in.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"We Reject What You Believe In"**

*Qāla al-ladhīna istakbarū innā bi-mā āmantum bihi kāfirūn* — the arrogant said: we reject what you have believed in. The reply is a sentence about the believers rather than about God, and its grammar reveals how religious rejection actually works in the sūrah's towns. The chiefs do not say *we disbelieve in the messenger* or *we deny the Lord of all worlds*; they say they are *kāfirūn* with respect to the faith of the lowly. The object of their denial is another group's confidence.

The Book records this structure repeatedly, and it is one of its sharpest psychological observations. Sūrat al-Baqarah's accounts of the prophets' audiences show the leaders' objections moving from the message to the messenger to the messenger's followers. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's Noah narrative has the chiefs objecting that *only the lowest of the people follow him*, as though the composition of a community were evidence about its God (26:111; see also 11:27). And the Qur'an's description of the disbelievers' own logic at the Judgment places exactly this sentence in a larger diagnosis: *“And they will lament, ‘If only we had listened and reasoned, we would not be among the residents of the Blaze!’”* (67:10).

**The Maintenance of Rank**

The social mechanism behind the sentence is worth stating plainly. In a town structured by lineage and standing, the acceptance of a message involves more than a change of belief; it involves a change of position. If the poor of Thamūd are right, then the elite's ancestors were wrong, the town's sanctuaries were frauds, and the pillars and cliff-dwellings were paid for by the labour of people whose judgment the elite had treated as negligible. The Book's narratives repeatedly show that this is the objection that cannot be answered by argument, because it is not an argument. Verse 76 is the sūrah's cleanest specimen: the elite's theology is a function of their social position, and the sūrah states it in five Arabic words.

Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own Hereafter scenes put the machinery on display for the reader's benefit. The arrogant and the lowly argue in the Fire (7:38–39); each side blames the other; the Book's verdict is that the leaders carry the teaching-load and the followers carry the imitation-load, and neither gets to transfer the bill. The exchange of verses 75 and 76 is the earthly version of that scene, and the sūrah's reader is meant to recognize that the two arguments are the same argument, staged twice with a lifetime in between.

**Rejection as Group Identity**

The Book's vocabulary adds a nuance that translations often lose. *Kāfirūn* in this sentence functions socially as much as doctrinally: to *kafara bi-shayʾ* is to cover, deny, and repudiate — and in the towns of the sūrah, the repudiation is an act of tribal self-definition. The chiefs are asserting what they are, not what is true.

Sūrat al-Baqarah's refutation of the same habit is aimed at a different community but makes the identical point: *“And when they are told, ‘Believe as others believe,’ they reply, ‘Will we believe as the fools believe?’ Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know” (2:13)* (2:13). The Book's reply is to take the towns' word for the believers and apply it to the mockers, and this sūrah has already done exactly that in its scale verses: the light scale belongs to those the towns laughed at, and the heavy one to those they trusted.

**What the Sentence Concedes**

It is worth noticing what the chiefs' sentence quietly grants. They do not dispute that the believers exist, nor that their belief is sincere, nor that Ṣāliḥ has been with them. Their objection is neither evidential nor moral; it is social. Sūrat al-Zukhruf catches the same concession at the highest level, where the Makkans, unable to attack the message, attack the recipient: *“And they exclaimed, ‘If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities!’”* (43:31) — a sentence that presumes the Qur'an might be genuine and objects only to its address.

The Book's later sūrahs preserve the end of this argument at the Judgment, when the elite and their followers exchange recriminations. Sūrat Sabaʾ reports the followers' answer to their leaders — *“No! It was your plotting by day and night — when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and to set up equals with Him”* (34:33) — and their final plea is preserved in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb: *“Our Lord! We obeyed our leaders and elite, but they led us astray from the ˹Right˺ Way. Our Lord! Give them double ˹our˺ punishment, and condemn them tremendously”* (33:67–68). Verse 76's sentence — *we surely disbelieve in what you believe in* — will therefore be spoken twice in the Book's history: once by Thamūd's elite in the town's assembly, and once on the Day when the order of speakers is reversed.

The sūrah's towns are not usually asked to deny that a revelation exists; they are asked whether they are willing to accept that it has arrived among people they had written off. The verse that follows shows what a community does when the answer is no, and the Book does not need to editorialize. The she-camel was a sign, and the town's elite had just announced — two verses before touching it — that the people who called it God's sign were people whose faith they would not share.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:77

> **Then they killed the she-camel —defying their Lord’s command—and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, “Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Argument to Slaughter**

*Fa-ʿaqarū al-nāqata wa-ʿataw ʿan amri rabbihim* — then they killed the she-camel, defying their Lord’s command. The sūrah's third town now crosses the line its predecessors approached, and the verb the Book chooses is significant: *ʿaqara* — to hamstring, to cut the tendon that makes a creature useless. It is not a description of a general massacre; it is the precise act of crippling an animal. The crime of Thamūd, in the Book's account, is an act of deliberate vandalism against a sign left among them.

Sūrat al-Qamar names the town's own agent: *“But they roused a companion of theirs, so he dared to kill ˹her˺”* (54:29), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records the outcome: *“But they killed her, becoming regretful”* (26:157). Sūrat al-Shams names the demagogue: *“when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺.”* (91:12). The Book's account of the events shows a division of responsibility that the sūrah's narrative has already prepared: a designated agent performs the deed, and the town consents — the Qur'an reports that they were all pleased with it — and so the punishment falls on all of them (91:14).

**"Defying Their Lord’s Command"**

The second clause, *wa-ʿataw ʿan amri rabbihim* — defying their Lord’s command — states the theological content of the act. *ʿAtā* is to overstep the limit placed in front of a person; the phrase is used throughout the Book for the violation of an explicit divine prohibition (2:61, 5:78, 7:166). What makes Thamūd's act different from the pagan rites of their neighbours is that the command they defied was not a general moral law they had never heard; it was the specific instruction attached to the sign visible in their pasture: *do not touch her with harm*.

The Book's narratives consistently give each town exactly one decisive prohibition — a small, checkable, public command that tests the community's willingness to be governed by anything other than its own judgment. For Thamūd it was an animal; for Adam it was one tree; for the people of the sabbath it was the fishing net (7:163); for Abraham's people there was no such command but a fire. The sūrah's reader is being taught that the form of the test is not the point; the point is whether the hearers accept any limit at all, and Thamūd's answer was recorded in the architecture they left behind: unrestricted.

**"Bring Us What You Threaten Us With"**

*Wa-qālū yā Ṣāliḥu ʾtinā bimā taʿidunā in kunta mina al-mursalīn* — and they challenged him: “O Ṣâliḥ, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.” The pattern of ʿĀd returns, now with the taunt sharpened by the deed: the town has just killed the sign, and it demands the consequence in the same speech. The sentence is a public demonstration of impunity — a community establishing, before its own members, that the messenger's warnings have no force.

The Book records the taunt at several points with a consistency that shows how central the challenge was to the prophetic experience: *“Our Lord! Hasten for us our share ˹of the punishment˺ before the Day of Reckoning.”* (38:16); *“They said, ‘Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!’”* (7:70); *“Bring us then whatever you threaten us with”* (46:22). And the Book's replies repeat the fact that the demanded item has already been scheduled: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘A Day has ˹already˺ been appointed for you, which you can neither delay nor advance by a ˹single˺ moment.’”* (34:30; see also 71:4). The sūrah's audience, hearing verse 77 read aloud, already knows what follows in the next verse. So did Thamūd, in principle.

**The Silence of the She-Camel**

One element of the story is worth noticing because it belongs to the sūrah's rhetoric of signs: the she-camel does nothing. She is not a wonder that performs; she is an animal that nurses, grazes, and drinks. The Book's most durable sign is the one the community has become used to — the ordinary creature whose ordinary existence has been declared the possession of God. The town was not asked to accept a miracle; it was asked to accept a boundary around a living thing.

And the boundary is what it destroyed. The Qur'an's account of what follows places the hamstringing at the centre of the judgment: *“Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their crime, levelling all to the ground.”* (91:14); *“Indeed, We sent against them ˹only˺ one ˹mighty˺ blast, leaving them like the twigs of fencebuilders.”* (54:31). The sūrah's sequence closes with the town wiping out the last evidence of its own warning, and the Book's manner of reporting the collapse — one verse, in the next lines — is a comment on the difference between the years of patient speech and the instant of the answer.

**The Inversion the Sūrah Keeps**

The reader has now watched three towns move at increasing speed from argument to action. Noah's town needed a century of preaching; ʿĀd needed a taunt; Thamūd needed only the sight of a sign and the confidence of a ruling class. The Book's point is that the pattern accelerates: the more evidence a community has, the less patience it musters for the messenger who brings it.

Verse 77 closes with the town's challenge still hanging in the air, and the next verse supplies the fulfilment in a form they did not choose. The Book's narratives of the towns are, among other things, a lesson in the way the warned describe their own coming destruction — as an accusation to be tested rather than a fact to be prepared for. Thamūd's last words in this account are a dare, and the answer arrives before the sentence has had time to settle.


**Three Days in Your Homes**

The verse reports the killing and the challenge. Hūd gives the warning that followed the killing: *“But they killed her, so he warned ˹them˺, ‘You have ˹only˺ three ˹more˺ days to enjoy life in your homes— this is an unfailing promise!’”* (11:65).

The three days are the answer to the challenge. The people asked for the threatened thing to be brought; the messenger named a term and called the naming a promise that will not fail. The sūrah’s account of the killing is therefore completed by a timetable rather than by an argument.

The exegetes read the three days as the last instance of the respite the sūrah describes everywhere. A term is named, an interval is given, and the interval is not used to return — which is the pattern 7:182–183 states as a rule. 11:65’s phrase about enjoying life in their homes is the same interval described from inside it: the time is spent as though it were ordinary.


**Saved From the Disgrace of That Day**

The verse of Hūd reports the outcome in two clauses: *“When Our command came, We saved Ṣâliḥ and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us and spared them the disgrace of that Day.”* (11:66). Al-Aʿrāf reports it in one: *“Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes.”* (7:78).

The two accounts describe the same event from the two parties. The saved are described by a mercy and by an exemption from disgrace; the destroyed are described by the manner of their falling and by the place — in their homes, the same homes in which they were told to enjoy three days.

This is the inversion the sūrah keeps. The challenge at 7:77 asked for the threatened thing to be brought, and it was brought to the ones who asked. The verse’s own phrase — defying their Lord’s command — describes the act as defiance rather than as doubt, and 11:66 supplies the counterparty: a prophet and those with him, saved by a mercy and spared a disgrace whose name is the same word the sūrah used of the disgraced at 7:13.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:78

> **Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Tremor**

*Fa-akhadhat-humu al-rajfatu fa-aṣbaḥū fī dārihim jāthimīn* — so the tremor seized them, and they became, in their homes, fallen on their knees. The sūrah's account of Thamūd's end is one sentence long, and every word of it is chosen to close an argument. The instrument of destruction is *al-rajfah*: the quake, the shudder — the punishment that arrives through the ground the town had built its palaces on.

The Book uses different instruments for different towns, and the variation is a teaching device. Noah's people drowned (7:64); ʿĀd's were carried off by a wind (69:6–7); Thamūd's were shaken; the people of Lot were overwhelmed by a rain of stones and a deafening cry (7:84, 15:73–74); Madyan's were seized by the quake and the day of the shadow (7:91, 26:189). The sūrah's list of penalties matches the towns' accounts of their own invulnerability: a maritime people would not have feared a quake, a mountain people would not have feared a flood. The Book gives each town a destruction that its own pride had ruled out.

**"In Their Homes"**

*Fa-aṣbaḥū fī dārihim jāthimīn* — and in the morning they were in their home, fallen. The details deserve the attention the sūrah gives them. The town of carved mountains is destroyed *in their home* — inside the buildings that were supposed to be shelter from exactly this kind of judgment. The Book's earlier verse has just listed their architecture as evidence of their blessings; the next sentence cancels it. The Qur'an repeats the formula for ʿĀd and Madyan (46:25; 7:91; 11:94) and uses it again in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt: *“So their homes are there”* (27:52), and in Sūrat Hūd: *“And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes,”* (11:67).

*Jāthimīn* is a precise posture-word: kneeling, fallen on the chest, crouched. The image the sūrah is drawing is not of a battlefield but of a settlement stopped in the middle of an ordinary morning — the corpse as a domestic object. The Book's Hereafter scenes use the same language in a different register when the towns stand before the Judge: *“And you will see every faith-community on its knees. Every community will be summoned to its record ˹of deeds˺.”* (45:28). The sūrah's reader is meant to link the two: the posture that filled the morning in Thamūd's streets is the posture of the Day, and one of them happened without warning.

**The Speed of the Verdict**

The single sentence of verse 78 has another function: at the level of the narrative, it delays nothing. The reader of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf has watched the sūrah build its case for the justice of the Hereafter across seventy verses — the question, the record, the scale, the gates, the wall, the conversations. Here is the verdict in the world, and it arrives in the time it takes to recite a line of poetry.

The Book's speed in these narratives is deliberate, and its own explanation of the mechanism appears in the sūrah of Hūd: *“When Our command came, We saved Ṣâliḥ and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us and spared them the disgrace of that Day.”* (11:66). The pattern of rescue is stated there with the same words used for the towns: a command arrives, the believers are taken out by mercy, and the place is emptied. Nothing in the sūrah's accounts of the towns is drawn out, because the interest is never in the destruction itself.

**What the Book Says About the Warnings**

The Book's repeated judgments on the towns are not merely narrative; they are evidence in the sūrah's argument about the Hereafter. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf itself will make this explicit in a few verses, in a passage about the towns of the peninsula whose ruins are visible: *“Did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep? Or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play?”* (7:97–98). The question is asked in the present tense, in the sūrah's own voice, and it is addressed to its audience.

Verse 78 supplies the display case for that question. Nothing the town possessed — the plains, the fortresses, the treasuries, the standing army, the legitimacy conferred by generations of possession — altered the outcome by a single day. The Book's narration of the destruction is not gloating; its tone is the tone of a man who has watched the ruins on the road, and its purpose is stated in its own vocabulary: *a reminder*.

**The Verse as a Turning Point**

Inside the sequence, Thamūd's destruction is the middle of the five towns, and the sūrah uses it differently from the earlier two. Noah's account ended with the ark and a blind people; ʿĀd's ended with a rescue and an uprooting. Verse 78's glimpse of the corpses in the houses sets up the most affecting verse of the whole sequence — the next one, in which Ṣāliḥ addresses the ruins.

The reader should notice the placement: the sūrah does not end the town's story with a moral until the messenger has had the last word over the bodies. That word, in verse 79, is not a condemnation but an account of a mission that has now ended badly, pronounced by the one man the town could have listened to. The Book's arrangement of the sequence gives the town its destruction and then immediately gives its messenger the elegy, and the sūrah is by that arrangement making a claim about who the narrative is for.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:79

> **So he turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Eleventh Hour and the Eleventh Verse**

*Fa-tawallā ʿanhum wa-qāla yā qawmi laqad ablaghtukum risālata rabbī wa-naṣaḥtu lakum wa-lākin lā tuḥibbūna al-nāṣiḥīn* — so he turned away from them, saying: “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”

The verse is the sūrah's elegy, and its structure is exact. The messenger turns his back — *tawallā* — and then speaks, which is to say that the speech is delivered to a town already emptied of hearers, or to the reader, or to the record. The Book's narratives use this farewell posture at the close of a mission in several places; Sūrat al-Muʾminūn gives Noah the same words, and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own Shuʿayb will turn away with an almost identical sentence a few verses later (7:93). What the sūrah is showing its reader is the shape of a completed argument: the messenger has no further speech, and the town has no reply.

**"I Have Conveyed the Message"**

*Laqad ablaghtukum risālata rabbī* — surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message. The verb *ablagha* is the strongest form of conveyance: to deliver something to its destination in full, to bring a thing all the way. It is the term the sūrah used for the messengers' duty in their opening speeches (7:62, 7:68) and the term the Book uses for the completion of the prophetic commission. The messenger's claim, made in the presence of a destroyed town, is not that the town refused to listen but that the terms of the delivery are complete: whatever comes next is not a failure of transmission.

That claim is important in the Book's moral economy. The sūrah's reader is repeatedly shown that the messengers are not blamed for the outcome of their preaching, and the Book's instruction to the last Prophet repeats the principle: *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:21–22; see also 42:48). Verse 79 teaches the same lesson with the town's corpse as the visual aid.

**"Sincere Advice" for the Third Time**

The word *naṣaḥtu* — I gave sincere advice — appears in the sūrah's sequence now for the third time, after Noah (7:62) and Ḥūd (7:68), and it is used again by Shuʿayb (7:93). The repetition is the sūrah's way of defining the prophetic office through the term that the towns most thoroughly misread. The messenger's counsel had been free, patient, uninterested in reward, and addressed to the town's own interest; the town experienced it as interference.

The sūrah's final clause states the reason the advice failed, and it is devastating in its modesty: *wa-lākin lā tuḥibbūna al-nāṣiḥīn* — but you do not love sincere advisers. The Book does not say that the town did not understand, or lacked evidence, or was deceived by a stronger power. It says the town did not love the counsel, and the word *love* shifts the whole explanation to the level of preference. Thamūd's problem was not epistemic but affective; they disliked being counselled, and the sūrah's last word on the town is about a taste.

**The Role of Reproach in the Book**

The sūrah's messenger does not curse the town in this verse and does not invoke punishment upon it; he reports his own conduct and the town's dislike. It is worth comparing the Book's other farewells: Shuʿayb's in the same sūrah ends with *“We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it. It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge.”* (7:89), and Noah's prayer over his people in Sūrat Nūḥ is recorded at length — *“My Lord, do not leave a single disbeliever on earth”* (71:26). The Qur'an's messengers are not uniformly gentle, and they are not uniformly severe; what the Book's portraits share is that none of them takes the town's answer personally. Their reproach is always directed at the refusal of the message, and their grief is always for the people, not for themselves.

Ṣāliḥ's sentence is the cleanest statement of the pattern in the entire sequence: the mission is complete, the counsel was given, and the failure is located in the hearers' appetite. If the sūrah had wanted the reader to pity the town, this verse would be the place; instead it hands the reader a mirror, because the Book's narratives of the towns are not mainly about the past. Its audience was told that these stories were *reminders*, and the reminder in verse 79 is that a community can spend its entire window of opportunity disliking the people who told it the truth.

**The Silence After**

The verse's last feature is what the sūrah does next: it begins the story of Lot. There is no pause for lament and no comment from the narrator, and the reader is left holding a scene of one man speaking to an empty street. The sūrah's sequence moves the way the Book's histories move — the town falls, the messenger speaks, the narrative advances — and the accumulation is the argument. Five towns will be laid end to end in this chapter, and the reader who arrives at the end of them will have heard three words repeated in the mouths of the messengers and never once answered: *worship Allah; you have no god besides Him*.


**Turning Away, and the Command to Do It**

The verse’s first act is a turning: he turned away from them. The verb denotes both a refusal and a departure, and the Book gives it to the Prophet ﷺ as a command in the same form: *“So turn away from them ˹O Prophet˺.”* (54:6), followed by an instruction to wait for a Day whose summons will be a horrifying one.

The parallel fixes the sense of Ṣāliḥ’s turning. It is not a withdrawal in anger or a failure of patience; it is the end of an address that has been completed. The prophet has conveyed and advised — the two acts named in his own sentence — and the turning follows from the fact that nothing further can be said to people who dislike advisers. The sūrah marks the moment by giving him the last word in the passage and no reply from the town. The silence after the reproach is how the sūrah reports that the earthquake came.


**Liking the Adviser**

The final clause is not about the advice but about the taste of those who received it: you do not like sincere advisers. The verb is from the root for love, so the charge concerns affection rather than judgment. The town did not fail to understand the counsel. It disliked the man who brought it, and the dislike is reported as the reason the counsel failed.

The Book states the right order of loves and treats a reversal of it as the thing to be feared: *“If your parents and children and siblings and spouses and extended family and the wealth you have acquired and the trade you fear will decline and the homes you cherish”* (9:24) — if these are dearer than God, His Messenger and struggle in His way, then wait for God’s command. Verse 79 shows the same reversal in a town that had been given its own prophet and could not bear him. What the sūrah asks its readers to examine is therefore not their opinions about counsel but their appetite for it, since the diagnosis here is a preference, and preferences are what a person is answerable for.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:80

> **And ˹remember˺ when Lot scolded ˹the men of˺ his people, ˹saying,˺ “Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot and the Crime Without Precedent**

*Wa-Lūṭan idh qāla li-qawmihi a-taʾtūna al-fāḥishata mā sabaqakum bihā min aḥadin mina al-ʿālamīn* — and ˹remember˺ when Lot rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people: *“You certainly commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before you.”* (29:28) The sūrah's fourth town is introduced without the word *brother*, and the omission is itself a comment: Lot's relationship to Sodom is one of residence rather than kinship, and the Book's account elsewhere notes that he was a stranger among them (21:74; 29:26).

The phrase the verse uses for the crime is *al-fāḥishah* — the sūrah's standard term for sexual immorality, used at 7:28 for the circumambulation, at 6:151, and at 4:22. What distinguishes Sodom's offense in the Book's telling is the qualifier: *mā sabaqakum bihā min aḥadin mina al-ʿālamīn* — no one before you among the worlds had done it. Whether the clause means that no people before them had committed this particular act, or that no one had committed an indecency of this brazenness in public, the effect is the same: Sodom's crime is presented as historically unprecedented, which is to say that the town had reached a refinement of transgression its neighbours had not imagined.

**The Crime in the Book's Other Accounts**

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has Lot name the deed and its inversion of creation: *“Why do you ˹men˺ lust after fellow men, leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you? In fact, you are a transgressing people.’”* (26:165–166). Sūrat al-Naml's version has the town's own view of the matter: *“And ˹remember˺ Lot, when he rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people, ‘Do you commit that shameful deed while you can see ˹one another˺?’”* (27:54), and Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt adds the detail of their public councils: *“Do you really lust after ˹other˺ men, abuse the travellers, and practice immorality ˹openly˺ in your gatherings?” His people’s only response was to say ˹mockingly˺: “Bring Allah’s punishment upon us, if what you say is true.’”* (29:29). The picture the Book builds is not of a private vice but of a town that had made the deed part of its public culture.

The Qur'an's rhetoric on the point is worth noting for what it does not do. The Book never argues that the act is unnatural in the modern sense of a category violation; its arguments are those it makes against every sin in the sūrah: the deed is described as a transgression of bounds, a corruption in a land that had been set right, and — decisively — an act performed against the messenger sent to correct it. The town's judgment in the sūrah hangs on that last point, and verse 82 will show the town conflating the two.

**The Difference Between Sodom and Its Neighbours**

The sūrah's towns have so far at least argued with their messengers. ʿĀd demanded proof, Thamūd killed a sign, Noah's chiefs pronounced a verdict. Sodom's response, recorded in the next verse, will contain no theological content at all — no gods are defended, no ancestors are cited, no claim is made about the messenger's truthfulness. What the town says is that the messenger and his household must leave. The Book's narratives treat that difference as the town's most damning feature: a community so settled in its practice that the only question raised by a prophetic summons was the inconvenience of the summons.

Sūrat al-Qamar preserves the town's atmosphere with the same emphasis: *“He had already warned them of Our ˹crushing˺ blow but they disputed the warnings.”* (54:36), and the Book repeatedly describes the towns as being destroyed *while they were still in their transgression, asleep at dawn* (15:66; 15:73; 7:97–98). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf gives the town one verse of speech in the next lines, and the whole town has nothing to say about God.

**The Messenger as a Resident**

Lot's standing in the sūrah's sequence is unusual because he is not a founder of the town he addresses. The Qur'an nowhere claims that Sodom received a legislative covenant from him; the Book's portrait is of a righteous man living among a people committed to a practice he denounced, so that the town's history became a contest between a resident's conscience and its demand for conformity. Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ and Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt both record that Lot was a recipient of judgment and knowledge (21:74) and that he emigrated for the sake of his Lord (29:26), and the Book's account in Sūrat al-Ṭahrīm names his wife as an example of a believer's household member who failed the test (66:10).

That last detail is doing important work in the Book's teaching about family and faith, and the sūrah will state it factually in verse 83: the rescue passed through the household and took all but one. The narrative therefore has two poles — a man out of place in his city, and a wife out of place in the ark of her family — and the sūrah reports both with the same flatness, as facts about which community a person's life actually belonged to.

**A Verse About Precedent**

One further observation belongs to the verse's opening clause. The phrase *no one among the worlds has done it before you* contains an argument that the sūrah's readers cannot miss: the towns of the prophetic era are being compared with one another, and Sodom's failure is a novel rather than inherited form of corruption. The Book's view of moral history is not cyclical; it allows for moral invention, and it treats novelty in evil as a distinctive kind of responsibility.

That is why the sūrah's account of the town is so compressed and yet so severe. Sodom did not fall because its people were weaker than the populations destroyed before them, or because they had been given less light. It fell because a community that had been warned chose to make its practice the measure of its life, and the sūrah's next verse shows what such a community says when a prophet interrupts its evening.


**Lusting and Leaving: The Two Verbs**

The verse puts the charge as a question about precedent; ash-Shuʿarāʾ puts it as a question about desire and its object: *“Why do you ˹men˺ lust after fellow men, leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you? In fact, you are a transgressing people.”* (26:165–166).

The two verbs in the verse are the argument. *Taʾtūna*, you approach or come to, describes an act; *tadharūna*, you leave, describes an omission. The charge is not framed as an excess of desire but as a substitution — one thing approached and another left — and the thing left is described as created for them.

The exegetes note that the verse of ash-Shuʿarāʾ makes the substitution explicit in a way 7:80 leaves to the reader. Al-Ṭabarī reads both as describing a departure from what was given rather than an addition to it, and the verdict is the same in both: a transgressing people, using the sūrah’s own word for leaving a limit behind.


**Fāḥishah: The Word and Its Range**

The deed is named *fāḥishah*, from *f-ḥ-sh*, which describes what is excessive to the point of being unseemly. Al-Isrāʾ uses the same noun of unlawful intercourse: *“Do not go near adultery. It is truly a shameful deed and an evil way.”* (17:32).

The word is therefore not specific to one act but describes a class: a deed that exceeds a limit in a way that is visible as excess. 17:32 adds the prohibition of approach — *lā taqrabū*, do not go near — which is the same form of address the sūrah gives about the tree (2:35, 7:19). The prohibition is placed before the act rather than at it.

This is why 7:80 can put the charge as a question about precedent and still be a statement about a limit. The people are asked whether they do something no one did before, and the word used for it names excess rather than novelty. 17:32 supplies the range of the word, and the two verses together describe the deed as an approach forbidden and an excess committed.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:81

> **You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Specification of the Charge**

*Innakum la-taʾtūna al-rijāla shahwatan min dūni al-nisāʾ* — you approach men with desire, instead of women. Lot's opening address continues with the detail that makes the town's crime specific: the substitution. The Book's phrasing is careful. It is not a general accusation of sexual disorder; it names the act, the object, and the perversion of the design — *min dūni al-nisāʾ*, to the exclusion of women. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's version adds the created order to the charge: *“leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you? In fact, you are a transgressing people.’”* (26:166). The argument in the Book is thus about authorship: the pairing of male and female was a creation, and the town's practice was a repudiation of the arrangement in favour of an invention.

The Qur'an records the same indictment against Sodom across six sūrahs, and its constancy is itself part of the teaching: this is not a prohibition the Book is embarrassed about, and it never softens the account under pressure. Sūrat al-Naml puts the accusation in the mouth of the town rather than of the prophet — *“And ˹remember˺ Lot, when he rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people, ‘Do you commit that shameful deed while you can see ˹one another˺?’”* (27:54) — and Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt expands the catalogue with the town's other practices: the cutting of the road, the shameful assembly (29:29).

**"You Are a People Transgressing"**

*Bal antum qawmun musrifūn* — rather, you are a people exceeding the limits. The word *musrif* is the sūrah's vocabulary for the one who goes past the boundary in any domain: the spendthrift in property, the tyrant in power, the glutton in appetite, and here the community that has made excess its norm. The Book uses *isrāf* across the whole field of conduct, and its consistent point is that the sin is not located in a single appetite but in the decision that there is no limit to be respected.

The Quranic treatment of Sodom's offense is thus framed by the same doctrine the sūrah applied to the towns' religion. Noah's people thought worship was inherited property; ʿĀd thought strength was authorization; Thamūd thought they could define the sign. Sodom thought that desire was the only law there was, and the town's culture had been arranged around the assumption. The verse names the underlying error with a single adjective.

**The Town's Public Dimension**

It is worth noting how many of the Book's accounts of Sodom place the crime in the street or in an assembly. Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's version has the town's own question — *“Do you really lust after ˹other˺ men, abuse the travellers, and practice immorality ˹openly˺ in your gatherings?” His people’s only response was to say ˹mockingly˺: “Bring Allah’s punishment upon us, if what you say is true.’”* (29:29) — and Sūrat al-Naml has the deed performed with the knowledge of the community, which is what its rhetorical question about *seeing* implies (27:54). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records the response of the townsmen to Lot's guests as a mob action (26:165). The Book's picture is of a vice that had become an institution, defended as a culture, and enforced by the town's collective will.

That is the context in which the next verse is to be read. When a community arranges itself around an inversion, the presence of a man who will not conform becomes a scandal rather than an eccentricity. The Book's judgment against Sodom, in its own framing, is not pronounced on private acts discovered in the dark; it is pronounced on a public order that had decided to define itself by them.

**The Comparative Context**

The Qur'an's severity on this subject has been noted by every generation of its readers, and the Book's own comparative treatment is instructive. Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, in legislating against an unrelated sexual offense, uses a term that connects the two: *“And the two among you who commit this sin—discipline them. If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them.”* (4:16, read by the majority of the commentators as a general indecency). Sūrat al-Nūr establishes the evidentiary and penal structure for illicit sexual conduct and closes the door on slander (24:4). The Book's approach to sexual ethics is thus consistent and structural: a fixed boundary, a heavy penalty, and a strong guard against accusation.

Sodom's singularity lies then in its scale. The town had made of the transgression a civilization. It is the same judgment the sūrah has applied to every one of its five towns: the crime is almost never the individual act; it is the collective decision to arrange a community — its laws, its gatherings, its walls — on the wrong side of a limit.

**"Instead of Women" and the Book's Argument From Design**

The clause *min dūni al-nisāʾ* has traditionally been read as the Book's argument from design, and the sūrah of al-Shuʿarāʾ makes that reading explicit by naming the mates as *what your Lord created* (26:166). The Book's sexual ethic in this verse is therefore anchored in the creation order rather than in tribal convention, which is precisely why the sūrah's presentation is so direct: the town did not merely break a law; it rewrote the human arrangement in the ledger of created things.

The point has a corollary that the sūrah's narrative will press. If the arrangement of the sexes is a creation, then a community's authority over the practice runs only as far as a creature's authority over the design of its own species — which is to say, it has none. The town's response, in the next verse, is to expel the one resident who said so, and the Book records the sentence without ironic comment. What follows — the rain, the stones, the overturned towns — is the sūrah's answer to a community that thought its culture could overrule its Creator.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:82

> **But his people’s only response was to say, “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Drive Them Out — They Want To Be Pure"**

*Wa-mā kāna jawāba qawmihi illā an qālū akhrijūhum min qaryatikum innahum unās yataṭahharūn* — but his people’s only response was to say: “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!” The sentence is the sūrah's finest specimen of the rhetoric of resentment, and its cruelty lies in the last word.

The town could have defended its practice, cited its ancestors, disputed the messenger's claims, or demanded a sign — as the previous four towns had done. It did none of it. What it said instead was that the presence of people who insist on purity is intolerable. The mockery is not directed at Lot's message about God; it is directed at the household's chastity. The Book's other account of the same remark makes the verb even blunter: *“But his people’s only response was to say, ‘Expel Lot’s followers from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!’”* (27:56).

**Purity as an Accusation**

The word *yataṭahharūn* is the fifth form of the root *ṭ-h-r*, with the reflexive and intensive sense: they seek to purify themselves, they make a show of purity. The town's sentence treats moral cleanliness as an affectation — something a person pretends to, something that embarrasses an honest community, something to be expelled for. The sūrah's reader already knows how the Book regards that reversal, because its opening had made purity of heart one of the definitions of the saved (7:42–43), and because the Book's own community would spend its history being told that *“Allah loves those who purify themselves”* (9:108).

There is a further indictment in the grammar. The townspeople do not say *Lot is a hypocrite*; they say the household *wants* to be pure, as though the desire itself is the offense. What Sodom objected to was not the performance of virtue — a town can accommodate a few performers — but its presence as a standing contradiction of their own order. Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn's picture of the mockers at the gate — *“Indeed, the wicked used to laugh at the believers,”* (83:29) — is the same social mechanism at a smaller scale; the sūrah's verse is the mechanism with a decree attached.

**The Town That Could Not Tolerate a Neighbour**

The Book's interest in the towns of the prophets consistently turns on this question: what does a community do with a member who will not conform? The five towns answer in escalating terms — a label, a taunt, a killed animal, an expulsion — and the sūrah arranges their answers so that the reader can see them as a scale of intolerance. Sodom's answer is the most radical because it begins from the premise that the community has the right to define the conditions of belonging, and the one condition it cannot meet is the presence of a conscience.

That is why the Book's account of Sodom has always been read by its communities as a description of something more than a sexual history. Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's version adds the crime of highway robbery (29:29); the sūrah of Hūd records the town's assembly proposing to the guests (11:78–79); the Book's overall portrait is of a walled community whose walls were its main achievement. Verse 82 tells the reader what such a community does when something on the inside refuses to match the outside.

**The Book's Irony**

The Book does not need to comment; the reader supplies the irony. The inhabitants of a town whose practice has been called unprecedented, whose assemblies have been named in the Book of God, stand in the street and expel the only family that could have stayed in it on the terms God set. The sentence they pronounce — *they want to be pure* — will be quoted in Muslim liturgies for the rest of history as the model of mockery, and the Book of the sūrah's own chapter of the events states the answer in the following verse: a rain from the sky, and a morning that found the towns turned over.

That sequence is the sūrah's method in miniature. It reports speech, and then it reports consequence, and it refuses to editorialize between them, on the assumption that the reader's conscience will supply the verdict. The verdict in this case is available from the earlier verses of the same passage: Sodom's mockery happened in the world where the scale of 7:8 applies, and the deed it mocked was called, by its own messenger, the same purity the Book commends.

**A Town That Expelled What It Needed**

The final observation on the verse belongs to the Book's use of Sodom as a warning to the towns of its own audience. The sūrah has described the town's answer to the messenger as an expulsion — *akhrijūhum min qaryatikum* — and it is not incidental that the Qur'an's account of the migration that follows, in other sūrahs, makes Lot's departure from Sodom the one journey that saved his family (29:26; 51:35). What Sodom did to Lot, God arranged for his rescue.

The Book's narratives of the towns are full of such reversals, and the sūrah's audience in Makkah had its own version of them under way. The Prophet would be expelled from a city which the Book describes as a town of traders who could not tolerate sincere counsel, and the expulsion would be the beginning of a migration rather than an end. The verse of the Aʿrāf records the formula in the mouths of Sodom: *they are people who want to be pure*. The Book's silent response is that this is exactly why they were let go.


**The Same Answer in al-Naml**

The reply of Lūṭ’s people is reported twice, and the two versions agree word for word in the charge: *“Expel Lot’s followers from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”* (27:56). Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ gives the same demand with the threat attached: *“If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.”* (26:167).

The agreement is significant because the charge is the least likely thing for a town to state about itself. The accounts do not report a defence of the town’s practice, an argument that it is permitted, or a denial that it happens. They report an expulsion justified by the purity of the people being expelled, which means the town understood exactly what Lūṭ’s household stood for and objected to it as such. The sūrah’s irony is not manufactured by the narrator; it is in the town’s own sentence, preserved identically in two places so that the reader cannot take it as a paraphrase.


**The Word for Keeping Oneself Pure**

The phrase the town uses is built on *ṭ-h-r*, the root of ritual and moral purity, and the form is one of seeking or holding a state — people who keep themselves pure. The same root and the same form appear elsewhere in a sentence of praise, and the contrast between the two uses is the sharpest in the Book: of the mosque founded on righteousness, *“In it are men who love to be purified. And Allah loves those who purify themselves.”* (9:108).

The verses describe the same disposition from opposite sides. In al-Tawbah the love of purity is a quality God loves in men who built a place of worship on it; here the same quality is the reason given for an expulsion. The sūrah is not making purity ambiguous. It is reporting that a town can name purity correctly and hate it, and that the naming is the most reliable evidence of what the town has understood. The verse that follows this one records the outcome — the rescue of the household except the one who stayed behind — and the rescue is of the people the town had just described accurately.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:83

> **So We saved him and his family except his wife, who was one of the doomed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Family and the One Who Stayed**

*Fa-anjaynāhu wa-ahlahu illā imraʾatahu kānat mina al-ghābirīn* — so We saved him and his family, except his wife, who was one of the doomed. The rescue is stated in the sūrah's familiar form, and one clause alters the pattern that Noah's and ʿĀd's towns had established. In the earlier narratives, the remnant was defined by belief; here the household itself is named as the saved unit, and the exception is spelled out.

The Book's other accounts supply the drama the sūrah leaves out. Sūrat al-Ḥijr and Sūrat Hūd record the angels arriving at Lot's door and the instruction that he should travel by night with his family and that no one should look back (15:65; 11:81). Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt has them leave before dawn (51:35), and 11:76 records the negotiation over the guests. The wife's sympathy for the town's order is named only in the phrase *who was one of the doomed* — *al-ghābirīn*, literally those who stayed behind.
