The word's root carries both the sense of remaining and of delay, and the Book uses it for those left inside a punishment when the righteous are extracted.

**The Doctrine of the Household**

The exception is one of the Book's clearest statements about the limits of kinship. The Qur'an's teaching that ties of blood do not transmit faith is not a side note; it is stated in several places, and this verse is one of its canonical instances: *“Indeed, some of your spouses and children are enemies to you, so beware of them.”* (64:14); *“You will never find a people who ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day loyal to those who defy Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their parents, children, siblings, or extended family. For those ˹believers˺, Allah has instilled faith in their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Him. He will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. They are the party of Allah. Indeed, Allah’s party is bound to succeed.”* (58:22). Sūrat al-Taḥrīm makes the point with two examples and both of them are women married to prophets: *“Allah sets forth an example for the disbelievers: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. Each was married to one of Our righteous servants, yet betrayed them. So their husbands were of no benefit to them against Allah whatsoever. Both were told, ‘Enter the Fire, along with the others!’”* (66:10).

The Book's prophets are thus shown to be without a special power over their own households. Noah's son drowned (11:42–43); Abraham's father died in his error (9:114); the Prophet's uncle was condemned in a sūrah named for him (111:1–5). The sūrah's narrative keeps the record honest, and verse 83's exception — one woman in a rescued house — is the scripture's protection against treating a believing household as a charm.

**"She Was One of Those Who Stayed Behind"**

The sūrah's manner of stating the wife's fate is worth pausing over. She is not described as having committed any act; she is named by her position. The Book states no crime for her, and the phrase *one of the doomed* — *al-ghābirīn*, literally those who remained behind — locates her with the town rather than with the family that was extracted. The Qur'an's moral accounts often use this form of description; its most economical examples are the statements about those who *have not believed* and *have turned away*, where the label sums up a life rather than a moment.

The sūrah's own later verse on the entry to Paradise makes the complementary point: the community of the Hereafter is built on the criterion of response, not of family (7:49; 7:38–39). The sūrah's narrative of the towns has been putting that principle on display for three verses running: families divided by belief inside the same house, a household saved entire except for one, a town wiped out around a single righteous man.

**The Rescue and Its Terms**

*Anjaynā* — the verb that has closed each narrative in the sūrah — appears again, and the Book's consistent account of the deliverances is that they are accomplished by mercy and by the faithful transmission of instructions. In the fuller versions, the rescued are given a deadline, a direction, and a prohibition against looking back; the Book's narrative interest is in the fact that the rescue was arranged in advance and announced as an event. Sūrat al-Ḥijr's version is the most vivid: the angels tell Lot that the town's term is the morning, *“We revealed to him this decree: ‘Those ˹sinners˺ will be uprooted in the morning.’”* (15:66; see also 11:81).

The saved household's smallness is part of the sūrah's persistent theme. The narrative does not rescue a city; it removes a handful of people under cover of night. The Book's account of the migration that follows places Lot's journey in the tradition of Abraham's departure and Joseph's and Moses's — the pattern of the righteous person operating without a community and trusting a promise. Verse 83 leaves the wife behind as the narrative's one fixed point: not everyone who shares a house shares a direction.

**What the Verse Leaves in the Reader's Hands**

The verse's last clause is stated without explanation, and the sūrah has already given the reader enough to understand it. The town's crime was a culture of the limitlessness; the wife's position was inside that culture; the rescue required a departure that she did not make. The Book's narratives refuse the consolation that family is the same as fate, which is why the sūrah's account of the towns has been so insistent that each community receives its own sentence. Lot's house and Lot's town were separated by a decision, and the Book records that decision under the plainest term: she remained.


**She Will Suffer the Same Fate**

The verse states the exception: *“So We saved him and his family except his wife, who was one of the doomed.”* (7:83). Hūd gives the instruction in which the exception was made: *“O Lot! We are the messengers of your Lord. They will never reach you. So travel with your family in the dark of night, and do not let any of you look back, except your wife. She will certainly suffer the fate of the others.”* (11:81).

The verse supplies the terms the sūrah leaves implicit. The departure is at night, the family is included, looking back is forbidden, and the wife is named twice — once in the exception and once in the sentence that follows it. The reason given is not her presence in the household but what will befall her.

The exegetes read the double naming as the point of the exception. A household departs together and one member does not arrive; the narration refuses to explain this by kinship, and the sūrah’s own formulation is the shortest possible: she was of those who remained. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse is cited as evidence that salvation is not transmitted through a household.


**A Rain Poured on Them**

The verse that follows reports what befell those who remained: *“We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺. See what was the end of the wicked!”* (7:84). The verb is *amṭarnā*, to rain, and the sūrah uses the same verb of the rain sent on the towns as a sign of mercy (7:57).

The two uses of the verb are the sūrah’s sharpest instance of a single word carrying opposite outcomes. Rain is the provision described at 7:57 as a mercy sent to dead land; rain is the punishment described here. The difference is not in the water but in what is sent with it, and the verse names the addition.

This is why the sentence that closes 7:84 is addressed to a reader rather than to a character. *Fa-ẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibat al-mujrimīn* — see what the end of the criminals was — is the sūrah’s refrain, and it appears here at the close of the shortest of its five narratives. The exception of the wife and the rain on the town are given in two verses, and the refrain is what turns them into a lesson.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:84

> **We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺. See what was the end of the wicked!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rain and the End**

*Wa-amṭarnā ʿalayhim maṭaran fa-nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mujrimīn* — and We rained down upon them a rain; then see what was the end of the criminals. The sūrah's fourth town closes with the shortest and harshest of its endings, and the sequence of verbs is exact: the rain is sent, and the reader is addressed directly.

The Book's other accounts of the event supply the materials of that rain. Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt names the stones: *“To send upon them stones of ˹baked˺ clay, marked by your Lord for the transgressors.”* (51:33–34). Sūrat al-Ḥijr records the hour and the direction: *“So the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise. And We turned the cities ˹of Sodom and Gomorrah˺ upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.”* (15:73–74). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ and Sūrat al-Qamar describe the morning and the overturned place (26:172–173; 54:37–38); and the Book's characteristic evaluation of the rain is stated at 25:40: *“They have certainly passed by the city ˹of Sodom˺, which had been showered with a dreadful rain ˹of stones˺.”*.

**"See What Was the End of the Criminals"**

*Fa-nẓur* — then look, consider, see. The imperative is directed at the sūrah's reader and it turns the narrative into evidence. This is the same move the sūrah made after Noah's rescue, where the blindness of the town was named as its own verdict, and it is the move the Book makes repeatedly in the Makkan sūrahs: the ruins of the prophetic age are presented as available, inspectable data. Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's account of the same history ends with the same address to the reader: *“You ˹Meccans˺ certainly pass by their ruins day and night. Will you not then understand?”* (37:137–138).

The term for the town is *al-mujrimīn*: the criminals, from the root *j-r-m*, which carries the sense of cutting off and of a harvest of guilt. The sūrah has used it in its own verdicts before (7:40, 7:41) — the residents of the Fire and the wrongdoers. The reader is therefore being told exactly where Sodom's category sits in the sūrah's moral taxonomy: the town is not an exotic curiosity of the ancient world but an instance of the category the sūrah has been describing since the gates were closed on the arrogant.

**The Pattern Complete in Four Towns**

With verse 84 the sūrah's town sequence reaches the end of its first run, and the shape of the series can now be assessed. Each narrative contains a messenger, a message that is always the same, an elite who lead the rejection, a refusal that takes the form of mockery, a sign that is either a natural event or an animal or a resident's conscience, a rescue of a small group, and a destruction that fits the town's own account of its strengths. Four towns, four variations, and no exceptions to the rule.

This is why the sūrah gives the narratives so little documentary texture and so much doctrinal uniformity. The Book is not writing the history of the peninsula; it is running a comparative experiment and reporting the constant. And the constant is stated in the verse that closes each story: the end of the criminals is what the reader is invited to observe.

**Rain, Water, and the Sūrah's Own Imagery**

There is a final resonance in the word *maṭar* that ties the narrative to the sūrah's earlier verses. In 7:57 the sūrah described God driving clouds to a dead land and sending down water as mercy, and it drew the argument for the resurrection from the rain that brings a barren place to life. Here the same vocabulary is used for the punishment: a rain that kills rather than revives. The Book's imagery is deliberately capable of either direction, and what determines whether water is mercy or judgment is the same thing that determines whether Hūd's cloud is a season's hope or a wind of destruction.

The sūrah's parallels fill out what this verse compresses. Sūrat Hūd describes the instrument and its maker: *“When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay, marked by your Lord ˹O Prophet˺. And these stones are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers!”* (11:82–83). Sūrat al-Ḥijr gives the hour and the deed: *“So the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise. And We turned the cities ˹of Sodom and Gomorrah˺ upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.”* (15:73–74). Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt states the same with the economy of this verse (51:33–34). And Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt records that the site was left as evidence: *“And We did leave ˹some of˺ its ruins as a clear lesson for people of understanding”* (29:35) — ruins on the route the sūrah's first audience travelled north on its trade journeys. The command *then see* is therefore not rhetorical: it points to a road the reader had walked and to remains that outlived the town's laughter.

The sūrah's reader is left with the comparison and the imperative. The rain fell on Sodom while the message was still in the town's streets; Lot's counsel was still audible in the ears of the men who mocked it. Verse 84's request — *then see* — is thus addressed to people who have the whole account in front of them and to their own conduct, and the sūrah has given them the interpretive tools in advance: the scale of verse 8, the parables of the land, the soil that answers the rain and the soil that does not.


**The Rain in Its Other Accounts**

The verse reports the rain without describing it, and the other accounts supply the description. Sūrah Hūd: *“When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay,”* (11:82). Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt names the material in the commission given to the angels: *“to send upon them stones of ˹baked˺ clay,”* (51:33).

The three accounts together give the sequence the sūrah’s single verb compresses: a command, an inversion, and a rain of stones. The inversion is what makes the rain intelligible — the cities’ highest part became their lowest, and the stones fell on what had been underneath. The sūrah’s economy here is a feature of its method throughout the histories: it names the punishment in the fewest possible words and leaves the detail to the accounts it assumes the reader knows, because the point it is making is not the mechanism but the sentence that follows it.


**The Word for the End**

The verse closes with the imperative the sūrah repeats after every history: see what the end of the criminals was. The word for the end is *ʿāqibah*, from a root meaning to follow at the heel, and it denotes what comes after a thing rather than merely its termination. The Qurʾān uses it of the outcome of a conduct, and the sūrah’s command to look at it is therefore a command to look at what followed, not at how it stopped.

That is why the imperative is addressed to a reader rather than to a witness. The towns’ end is not something the sūrah’s audience saw; it is something they can inspect in the remains and in the sequence the sūrah has just narrated. The same command appears in this sūrah at the end of the Midian history (7:86) and before the Egyptian narrative (7:103), and in al-Naml after the account of the court that denied the signs while convinced of them (27:14), so that each history closes not with the punishment but with the instruction to examine it. The verse’s final words make the reader a party to the case rather than an audience at the execution.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:85

> **And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord. So give just measure and weight, do not defraud people of their property, nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. This is for your own good, if you are ˹truly˺ believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet of the Market**

*Wa-ilā Madyana akhāhum Shuʿayban* — and to Madyan, their brother Shuʿayb. The sūrah's last town before Moses is a trading city, and the crime it is charged with is the one its economy makes possible: *fa-awfū al-kayla wa-l-mīzān* — so give full measure and weight — *wa-lā tabkhasū al-nāsa ashyāʾahum* — and do not defraud people of their goods.

The Book's association of prophecy with commercial honesty is one of its most distinctive features, and this verse states the connection at its strongest: the messenger's first duty after the call to worship is the correction of the scales. Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn opens the Qur'an's only sūrah named for a mercantile crime: *“Woe to the defrauders! Those who take full measure ˹when they buy˺ from people, but give less when they measure or weigh for buyers.”* (83:1–3). Sūrat al-Isrāʾ lists the honest scale among the commandments of the Decalogue tradition: *“Give in full when you measure, and weigh with an even balance. That is fairest and best in the end.”* (17:35). And Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records Shuʿayb's version of this verse with an addition about the danger of the practice: *“and do not defraud people of their property. Nor go about spreading corruption in the land.”* (26:183).

**The Order of the Commandments**

The verse's arrangement repays attention. It begins with the sūrah's standard formula — worship the One God — and then moves immediately to a list of economic obligations: full measure, honest weight, no defrauding of what belongs to others. The sūrah does not treat the second as a mere corollary of the first; it presents them as one message, and the Book's prophets are consistently the defenders of both. Sūrat al-Nisāʾ turns the connection into a warning: *“O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent. And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you.”* (4:29), and Sūrat al-Baqarah's catalogue of the people of the Book includes the crime of consuming wealth unjustly and of devouring the property of the weak (2:188).

The Madyan narrative in Sūrat Hūd records the town's own understanding of Shuʿayb's demand, and their objection is revealing: *“They asked ˹sarcastically˺, ‘O Shu’aib! Does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our forefathers worshipped or give up managing our wealth as we please? Indeed, you are such a tolerant, sensible man!’”* (11:87). The answer implicit in the verse is that the question marks the boundary the message crosses: the worship of God is inseparable from the use of the scales, and the town's assumption that trade is a zone of moral freedom is precisely what Shuʿayb was sent to deny.

**"Do Not Spread Corruption in the Land"**

*Wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍ mufsidīn* — and do not spread corruption in the land — this is the third time the sūrah has used the prohibition, after its general instruction at 7:56 and Ṣāliḥ's warning at 7:74, and in this town it acquires a sharp economic meaning. The verb *ʿathā* names destructive action, and its objects in the Book's usage are crops, property, and people. A market in which the buyer cannot trust the measure is not a private vice; it is the mechanism by which a whole town's wealth is transferred to its unscrupulous, and it corrupts the land in the precise sense that it makes the exchange of goods — the lifeblood of a trading city — unsafe.

The Qur'an's later treatment of Madyan states the outcome in the Book's own idiom: *“So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud. That was really a torment of a tremendous day.”* (26:189), and Sūrat Hūd records the cry and the quake that took them (11:94–95). The narrative's severity is proportionate to the crime's social reach: a town that cheats its customers is punishing the strangers who have no clan to defend them, and the Book's sentence on it is the same as its sentence on the towns that mocked the prophets.

**"That Is Better for You, If You Are ˹Truly˺ Believers"**

*Dhālikum khayrun lakum in kuntum muʾminīn* — that is better for you, if you are ˹truly˺ believers. The clause is the sūrah's central practical claim, and it is worth noting that it is an argument from advantage rather than from fear. Shuʿayb does not say that the short measure will be paid for in the Fire; he says that honesty is better. The Book makes the same move in the story of Madyan's fuller version, where Shuʿayb urges his people with a reminder of God's own largesse: *“He has blessed me with a good provision from Him”* (11:88).

The Book's economic doctrine will be stated in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's later verse: *“O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent.”* (4:29), and its view of the market is that a working economy is a form of the trust the sūrah has been describing since its first pages. The hadith the tradition received on the same point is among the shortest and sharpest in the corpus: the Prophet ﷺ passed a heap of grain, put his hand into it, found its lower part damp, and said, *“Whoever cheats is not one of us”* (Muslim 102, from Abū Hurayrah). Verse 85 is that hadith's doctrinal foundation, and the sūrah's last town is judged by whether it could be trusted with a scale.

**The Prophet Who Speaks First to the Merchants**

Madyan's position in the sūrah's sequence is deliberate. Noah's city, ʿĀd, and Thamūd were countries of tenants, shepherds, and builders; Sodom was a city of transgression; Madyan is the town of commerce, . The sūrah's arrangement thus covers the whole range of the peninsula's societies and gives each one a prophet whose specific charge matches its specific temptation. The reader is meant to see that no department of life stands outside the message — least of all the one that measures, weighs, and takes.


**An Even Balance: The Same Command in al-Isrāʾ**

Shuʿayb’s address begins with a proof: *“A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord.”* (7:85), and then turns to measure and weight. Al-Isrāʾ gives the same two commands in the same order: *“Give in full when you measure, and weigh with an even balance. That is fairest and best in the end.”* (17:35).

The verse of al-Isrāʾ adds the reason in two adjectives — fairest, and best in the outcome. The first describes the act, the second its end, and the pair is the form in which the Book states a commercial command: a practice and its consequence named together. 7:85 makes the same addition in its own terms, calling the conduct better for those who believe.

The exegetes read the two verses as one instruction given twice. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the command to full measure is stated positively and the prohibition of short measure negatively, so that neither the act nor its omission is left unnamed. 55:9 states the negative form — weigh with justice and do not give short measure — and 17:35 states the positive.


**Not Defrauding People of Their Property**

The sūrah’s third command is not to defraud people of their goods. Hūd gives the same three commands in the same messenger’s mouth: *“O my people! Give full measure and weigh with justice. Do not defraud people of their property, nor go about spreading corruption in the land.”* (11:85).

The verse is almost a duplicate of 7:85, and the small differences are instructive. Hūd’s version names the property as *ashyāʾ*, things, and puts the corruption as a second prohibition; al-Aʿrāf’s version names the goods and attaches the prohibition to the settled state of the land after its reform. Both end with the same pair of offences: defrauding and corrupting.

This is why the sūrah calls Shuʿayb the messenger of the market in the exegetical tradition — not because his message is only commercial but because the two offences it names are the two by which a settled people damages itself from inside. The corruption forbidden is not invasion but practice, and the property defrauded belongs to neighbours rather than to enemies.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:86

> **And do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. Remember when you were few, then He increased you in number. And consider the fate of the corruptors!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ambush on the Road**

*Wa-lā taqʿudū bi-kulli ṣirāṭin tūʿidūna wa-taṣuddūna ʿan sabīli Allāh man āmana bihi wa-tabghūnahā ʿiwajan* — and do not lie in ambush on every road, threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. The verse is the sūrah's most concrete description of the crime it announced at 7:45: the definition of the *ẓālimūn* as those who turn others from the road of God and seek to make it crooked is here given a location, a method, and a target.

The location is *every road* — the trade routes of Madyan, the caravan tracks that made the town's economy and connected the peninsula. The method is intimidation: *tūʿidūna* — you threaten, issuing warnings to travelers, taxing, harassing, and turning back the ones who might have come to hear the message. The target is stated with an exactness that the sūrah's earlier verse left implicit: *man āmana bihi* — whoever believes in Him. The town's roadblocks were not set against strangers in general but against believers in particular, and the sūrah's phrasing suggests an organized policy rather than casual banditry.

**The Book's Interest in Roads**

The Qur'an's concern with the safety of the roads is not incidental; the roads are how revelation travels and how the community of believers grows. The Book's prohibition of highway robbery appears in its legal and moral codes (5:33; 7:86; see also 29:29), and its description of a believing merchant's world is one where the movement of goods and persons is protected. The Prophet's own city would be built on a trade route, and the security of the roads would become one of the practical concerns of the Sharīʿah.

Madyan's crime is therefore the inverse of the sūrah's own opening command: where verse 3 told the Prophet's audience to follow what has been sent down and not to take other guardians, the town of Madyan physically stood in the way of anyone who tried. The narrative makes the town's judgment the most socially detailed of the five, and it is the only one whose crime is described as an ongoing public operation — people stationed on roads with threats.

**"Remember When You Were Few"**

*Wa-dhkurū idh kuntum qalīlan fa-kaththarakum* — and remember when you were few and He multiplied you. The verse turns from the crime to the town's history, and it uses the same argumentation as Ḥūd's address to ʿĀd and Ṣāliḥ's to Thamūd: the community's present standing is a gift with a history. Madyan had been small, marginal, and dependent; it had grown into a settled trading center; and the measure of its growth is also the measure of its obligation.

The Book's use of demographic history as a religious argument is consistent from its earliest sūrahs. Sūrat al-Takāthur mocks the city's pride in numbers (102:1–2); Sūrat al-Anfāl reminds the first Muslim community in Madinah of its weakness and God's protection: *“Remember when you had been vastly outnumbered and oppressed in the land, constantly in fear of attacks by your enemy, then He sheltered you.”* (8:26). Verse 86's instruction to Madyan is thus part of a general pattern: the Book reads a community's success as a ledger entry, not as a trophy.

**"See What Was the End of the Corrupters"**

*Wa-nẓurū kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mufsidīn* — and see what the end of the corrupters was. The closing clause returns to the second person plural and points the town at the fate of its predecessors, which the sūrah has just narrated. Noah's town, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Sodom are the visible record the verse is invoking; Madyan's merchants, whose caravans passed the ruins the sūrah's earlier verse 69 called to the memory of ʿĀd, are being asked to read the same landscape they traded through.

The term *mufsidūn* — corrupters — is the sūrah's own word for what the towns were (7:74, 7:85, 7:86), and the verse binds the whole sequence together: the crime of Madyan, in the Book's framework, is the same crime as the crime of the towns before it, committed in a different department of life. The cheated customer, the threatened believer, and the bribed official are the same phenomenon in the sūrah's moral grammar — a community treating what does not belong to it as its own.

**The Second Half of the Sūrah's Definition**

It is worth setting this verse beside 7:45, because the sūrah has now supplied the full portrait it announced there. That verse defined the wrongdoers as those who hinder others from the path, seek to make it crooked, and deny the Hereafter. Verse 86 supplies a working example of the first two, and the surrounding narrative supplies the third: Madyan's elite will reject Shuʿayb's message and threaten expulsion (7:88), and their confidence is built on the assumption that no account is being kept.

The sūrah's arrangement makes this the last of the towns because it is the most immediately recognizable to its own audience. Makkah was a trading city; its notables were merchants; its caravans passed Madyan's ruins on the road north; and the sūrah's readers were about to be asked, in their own streets, what a scale is worth and what a believer's road is for. The verse's imperative — *see* — is addressed as directly to them as it was to the town.


**Crookedness, and the Law the Verse Gave the Jurists**

The verse’s third charge uses a word the Book reserves for a defect in a road and in a book. The crookedness the ambushers strive to give the path is *ʿiwaj*, and the same word is denied of the revelation in the opening of Sūrah al-Kahf: Allah *“has revealed the Book to His servant, allowing no crookedness in it”* (18:1). The pairing sets the two operations against one another. The Book is straight and admits no bending; the work of the ambushers is to bend the road people take to it — not by arguing against it, but by making the way to it unsafe.

The jurists read the first clause as a legal text and not only as a moral one. Lying in wait on the roads to threaten and to take is what the tradition calls *ḥirābah*, brigandage, and its ruling is given in Sūrah al-Māʾidah: *“Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread mischief in the land is death, crucifixion, cutting off their hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile from the land.”* (5:33). The connection drawn between the two verses is that the ambush here is against the path of God rather than against a traveller’s purse, and that the corruption named in this verse’s last clause is the same *fasād* the ruling in al-Māʾidah punishes.


**The Refrain of Increase**

The verse’s second sentence is one of three in this sūrah built on the same pattern, addressed to three different towns. To ʿĀd: *“Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you greatly in stature.”* (7:69). To Thamūd: *“Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land.”* (7:74). To Midian, here: remember when you were few, and He increased you in number. In each case the increase is given as a fact to be remembered before the charge is made, and in each case it is the fact that converts the town’s confidence into evidence against it.

The three increases differ in kind, and the difference is exact. ʿĀd is increased in stature, Thamūd in establishment — palaces on the plains and homes cut into the mountains — and Midian in number. Each town is given the thing it was known for, and each is asked to remember that the thing was received. The refrain’s function in the argument is to remove the ground of a town’s independence: what it took for its own strength is listed among the favours. That is why the verse closes on the fate of the corrupters, and why the sūrah turns next to the rule of the towns — that none was taken without first being tried with hardship and then with ease (7:94–95).

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:87

> **If some of you do believe in what I have been sent with while others do not, then be patient until Allah judges between us. He is the Best of Judges.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Be Patient Until Allah Judges"**

*Wa-in ṭāʾifatun minkum āmanū bi-lladhī ursiltu bihi wa-ṭāʾifatun lam yuʾminū fa-ṣbirū ḥattā yaḥkuma Allāhu baynanā* — and if a group among you has believed in what I have been sent with, and another group has not, then be patient until Allah judges between us; for He is the best of judges.

The verse is the sūrah's clearest statement of the prophetic method, and it arrives at the point in the Madyan narrative where the town's division has become visible. Shuʿayb does not call for the believers to separate, does not threaten the unbelievers with the community's authority, and does not offer the town a deadline. He proposes patience, and the reason he gives is that judgment belongs to God.

**The Argument Against Compulsion**

The Qur'an's most famous statement on coercion is Sūrat al-Baqarah's *“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.”* (2:256), and verse 87 is one of the places where the principle is displayed in the conduct of a prophet. The Book's messengers do not enforce; they convey, warn, and leave the verdict to its owner. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ gives the same logic to Noah: *“So judge between me and them decisively, and save me and the believers with me”* (26:118), and this sūrah gives Shuʿayb the prayer it prepares: *“Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge”* (7:89).

The doctrine is important in the sūrah's own historical setting, where the towns' elites enjoy the power of coercion and use it. The narrative's inversion is total: the group with the police is the group that rejects the message, and the messenger's only weapon is a wait. The Book's later legislative sūrahs will build the community on the same premise — belief cannot be produced by force — and the Prophet's own career would be a long education in patience with a hostile majority before any question of governance arose.

**The Community in Transit**

The verse also gives a picture of a community in the middle of a decision, and the picture is unsparing in its realism: some believe, some do not, and both groups are standing in the same marketplace, trading with one another, sharing the same wells. The Book does not describe the believers of Madyan as a separate enclave; the sūrah's earlier narrative of Ṣāliḥ showed the believers as the town's underclass (7:75), and Shuʿayb's town has its own version of the split.

That realism is the basis of the sūrah's instruction to patience. A community that must live beside its opponents for years needs a discipline that does not depend on the outcome of the argument. The Book names it in the sūrah of the Cave: *“And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening”* (18:28), and in Sūrat al-ʿAṣr's summary of salvation: *“except those who have faith, do good, and urge each other to the truth, and urge each other to perseverance.”* (103:3). The verse of the Aʿrāf supplies the same discipline to a merchant town that has just been told its scales are crooked.

**"He Is the Best of Judges"**

*Wa-huwa khayru al-ḥākimīn.* The phrase is one of the Qur'an's recurring doxological formulas, and it appears at points where human judgment is being contrasted with divine: Sūrat Yūnus has the Prophet told to follow what is revealed and to be patient *until Allah judges, for He is the best of judges* (10:109); Sūrat Yūsuf puts the phrase in the mouth of Jacob's sons (12:80); Sūrat al-Tīn closes with the same question: *“Is Allah not the most just of all judges?”* (95:8).

In the sūrah's narrative, the phrase has a practical edge: the town has judges of its own — the elite who will shortly threaten Shuʿayb with expulsion (7:88) — and the verse is relocating the case to a higher court. The messenger's patience is not passivity; it is the transfer of a case that the local bench cannot try fairly. The Book's audiences have always read this verse as the charter of a community that does not take the law into its own hands, and the Madyan narrative remains its canonical exhibit.

**The Waiting as a Position**

The Book's readers have noticed that Shuʿayb's patience is not the patience of a man without an argument. He has just delivered the most detailed of the sūrah's messages: the call to worship, the scale, the prohibition of defrauding, the warning about the ambush on the roads. Verse 87 comes after that case is complete, and the sequence matters: the patience is prescribed to a community that has said what it had to say, and its function is to prevent the messenger's followers from thinking that the lack of an immediate verdict means the case has failed.

That is the sūrah's own lesson to its audience in Makkah, which was watching the same wait unfold in its own streets. The Book's instruction to its Prophet in the middle of the persecution uses the same verb and the same limit: *“So endure patiently, as did the Messengers of Firm Resolve. And do not ˹seek to˺ hasten ˹the torment˺ for the deniers.”* (46:35). Madyan's verse is the model for that instruction, and it says what the Qur'an says everywhere: the delay is not the absence of the judgment but the mercy that precedes it.


**The Same Sentence to Two Other Messengers**

The instruction to wait for a judgment is given to the Prophet ﷺ in the same words: *“And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah passes His judgment. For He is the Best of Judges.”* (10:109). Shuʿayb states the same position from inside a confrontation that has already failed: *“O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine.”* (11:93).

The three statements share a structure that is worth naming, because it is what makes patience a position rather than a mood. Each contains a refusal to escalate, a continuation of the speaker’s own work, and an appeal to a judgment that is not his to deliver. In Yūnus the continuation is stated positively — follow what is revealed to you; in Hūd it is stated as a parallel course, each side persisting in what it holds. This verse states it as a waiting inside one community, where the split has already happened and the parties are still living beside one another.


**Patience Under a Decree**

The Book distinguishes this waiting from mere endurance by attaching it to a decree: *“So be patient with your Lord’s decree, for you are truly under Our ˹watchful˺ Eyes.”* (52:48). The patience asked for is not the patience of someone who has no options but of someone who has been told how long the matter will take and by whom it will be settled.

That is the function of the verse’s closing sentence. *He is the best of judges* is not a compliment to the judgment’s fairness alone, though the commentators read it as including that; it is a statement about jurisdiction. A dispute between a messenger and his town cannot be settled by either party, because one is the claimant and the other has refused to hear the claim. Naming a judge removes the dispute from the hands of the people having it, and the waiting that follows is not inactivity but the discipline of leaving a case with the court that has it. The sūrah will spend the rest of its length documenting what that court has already decided in the cases of the towns.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:88

> **The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened, “O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land, unless you return to our faith.” He replied, “Even if we hate it?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Threat of Expulsion**

*Qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna istakbarū min qawmihi la-nukhrijannaka yā Shuʿaybu wa-lladhīna āmanū maʿaka min qaryatinā aw la-taʿūdunna fī millatinā* — the arrogant chiefs of his people threatened: “O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land, unless you return to our faith.”

The sentence is the sūrah's most explicit statement of the towns' ultimate argument. Sodom had said *expel them*; Madyan formalizes it as a policy, with a condition attached: return to our religion and you may stay. The Book's record of the exchange shows the towns moving from argument to coercion over the course of the sequence, and it makes the coercive threat the last position of a losing case. The elite of Madyan cannot answer Shuʿayb's case about the scales, so they answer it with the town's boundary.

**The Word Millah**

*Millah* is the Book's term for a community's religion regarded as a shared way of life — the word used of Abraham's way (2:130, 3:95, 16:123), of the idolaters’ religion in Joseph’s prison (12:37), and of the Prophet’s own faith in Sūrat al-Kāfirūn (109:6, *“You have your way, and I have my Way.”*). That Shuʿayb's opponents call their system a *millah* shows what they are defending: not a doctrine but a community's inheritance, the package of customs that made Madyan Madyan. The verse's threat is therefore an identity claim: conform, or leave.

The Qur'an's own address to the Prophet would later use the same word in the opposite direction, commanding him to follow the *millah* of Abraham (16:123), which is the Book's way of acknowledging that communities do possess corporate identities — and of insisting that the identity be traceable to a prophet rather than to an ancestor's invention.

**"Even If We Detest It?"**

*Qāla a-wa-law kunnā kārihīn* — he said: even if we detest it? The reply is three words in Arabic and it dismantles the threat. The elite's proposal had treated religion as a matter of choice in principle; Shuʿayb's question reveals what the choice actually involves. They are asking him to profess a faith he regards as false, and the interrogative — *even if we hate it?* — forces them to say aloud what coercion means.

The Book has a consistent position on this demand, and it states it in several registers. Sūrat al-Baqarah forbids compulsion in religion (2:256); Sūrat al-Naḥl's command to the Prophet to invite to the way of the Lord *with wisdom and good counsel* (16:125) rules out the alternative; Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah tells the Prophet, in the same sūrah, that he is not a controller over them (88:22). And the Book's own account of the hypocrites in Madinah makes the same point from the other side: a profession produced by pressure has no spiritual content, and the Book treats it as worse than the honest rejection because it corrupts the community's integrity.

Shuʿayb's question remains one of the sharpest three-word arguments in the Book, and its application reaches any community tempted to measure loyalty by recitation rather than by conviction.

**The Expulsion and the Sūrah's History**

The threat of expulsion is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the sūrah's portrait of the towns' last instrument. The narrative will note that the punishment took the town before the threat could be executed — Sūrat Hūd records the cry and the earthquake that seized them (11:94–95) — and the Book's pattern in such cases is to let the persecuted community outlive its persecutors. The sūrah's Makkan audience, hearing the verse recited, had its own expulsion in view: the Prophet's plan to leave a city whose establishment had made the same calculation.

The verse's details are also worth noting for what they say about the believers of Madyan: the threat is addressed to *those who believe with you*, which means the community had grown visible enough to be a targeted group. The sūrah's earlier narratives had let the believers of the towns appear in a single sentence; here they are a party whose removal is the town's condition for peace.

**The Last Resort of a Bankrupt Case**

The sūrah's sequence has now given the towns an inventory of arguments: Noah's chiefs used a label, ʿĀd used a taunt, Thamūd killed a sign, Sodom expelled a neighbour. Madyan's elite produce the same instrument as Sodom's — the boundary and the exit — but the sūrah places it in the mouth of the town's leadership as a formal decision, which is the clearest statement the sequence offers about what is really at stake. The town's rulers did not fear Shuʿayb's God; they feared that his followers would remain in Madyan and prove that another way of life was possible there.

That fear is the sūrah's diagnosis of the towns' motives, and it is stated by the verse's own vocabulary: *alladhīna istakbarū*, those who had made themselves great. The expulsion order comes from men whose standing is threatened by a scale that measures honestly. The narrative's judgment on them is delivered a verse later, in the answer of the prophet they proposed to expel, and the answer is a refusal to trade the truth for a residence permit.


**Millah, Dīn, and Sharīʿah**

The chiefs’ demand is phrased with the word *millah* — return to our *millah* — and the choice is not incidental. The Book distinguishes three words that English collapses into religion. *Dīn* is religion as a way of judgment and obedience. *Sharīʿah* and *minhāj* are the ordained way given to a particular community: *“To each of you We have ordained a code of law and a way of life.”* (5:48). *Millah* is the creed as inherited and followed, and it nearly always takes a personal genitive — the *millah* of Ibrāhīm.

That genitive is what gives the chiefs’ phrasing its significance. They do not say return to the truth, or return to our *dīn*; they say *our millah*, the way of our fathers, which is a claim of descent rather than of evidence. The Book uses the same construction of the true path, and so exposes the argument actually being made. The answer given to those who say follow our faith is that the faith followed is defined by its founder: *“We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”* (2:135); and the community of the Prophet ﷺ is told to hold to a *millah* likewise defined by a father — *“the way of your forefather Abraham”* (22:78). The grammar is the same in both cases. What differs is whether the father was upright.


**Expulsion in the Sūrah’s Other Histories**

The threat to drive Shuʿayb and those who believed with him out of the town is not particular to Midian. It is the second move in the sūrah’s histories, and the Book records it in nearly the same words to other messengers. Nūḥ’s people threaten him with stones: *“If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be stoned ˹to death˺.”* (26:116). Lūṭ’s people threaten him with precisely what Midian threatens here: *“If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.”* (26:167). The threat reaches the Prophet ﷺ himself: *“They were about to intimidate you to drive you out of the land ˹of Mecca˺, but then they would not have survived after you ˹had left˺ except for a little while.”* (17:76).


**Coercion Cannot Produce Faith**

The second half of the threat — or you return to our *millah* — makes the chiefs’ aim explicit: not silence but assent. The Book’s answer is that the aim is unreachable. *“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood.”* (2:256). The commentators explain the principle rather than the politics of the verse: force can produce a sentence spoken aloud, and a sentence spoken under force is not belief, so coercion can manufacture the appearance of a return and nothing behind it.

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:89

> **We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it. It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Then We Would Have Fabricated a Lie Against Allah"**

*Qad iftaraynā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban in ʿudnā fī millatikum baʿda idh najjānā Allāhu minhā* — we would have fabricated a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah saved us from it. The answer to the expulsion threat is the sūrah's clearest statement of the cost of a return, and it names the cost with the vocabulary the sūrah reserves for the gravest crime in its book: *iftirāʾ*, the fabrication of a lie against Allah.

The term has been in the sūrah since verse 37, where the interrogative formed its most solemn sentence: *who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah?* For Shuʿayb to say that a return to Madyan's religion would make him one of those people is to accept the town's frame and reverse its polarity. The elite had argued in terms of public order; the messenger answers in terms of truth\. To profess a religion he knows to be false in order to keep a place in a town is not prudence but a claim about God that God has not made.

**"After Allah Has Saved Us From It"**

The clause *baʿda idh najjānā Allāhu minhā* adds a second layer: what the town offers as a homecoming, Shuʿayb describes as a rescue already accomplished. The believer's relationship to his former religion is not that of a person who has left a village but of someone who has been taken out of a ruin. The Book's vocabulary for conversion in several places uses this language of deliverance: Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own account of the followers of the messengers, Sūrat al-Māʾidah's promise that God will bring a people whom He loves, and Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's description of the one who says, *“I was among the heedless”*. The town's proposal is an offer to return to what the messenger regards as the disease from which he has been cured.

The Book's later sūrahs make the refusal the duty of the community and the point of its identity: *“Whoever disbelieves in Allah after their belief—not those who are forced while their hearts are firm in faith, but those who embrace disbelief wholeheartedly—they will be condemned by Allah and suffer a tremendous punishment”* (16:106). The narrative places that absolute in the mouth of a prophet who is being offered a practical way out.

**"Unless Allah Wills"**

*Wa-mā yakūnu lanā an naʿūda fīhā illā an yashāʾa Allāhu rabbunā* — and it does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. The exception is one of the Book's characteristic qualifications, and it is a statement about the limits of the human will rather than a loophole in the refusal. The Qur'an places the clause on the believer's tongue in matters of resolve: *“you cannot will ˹to do so˺ unless Allah wills”* (76:30; see also 81:29), and it teaches the community to say *God willing* about its own plans.

The clause protects the refusal from the sin of claiming absolute autonomy. Shuʿayb does not say *we will never return even if God wills it*; he says that a return is not open to them as agents, because the human will is itself a created thing. The Book's doctrine of the will is stated most precisely in Sūrat al-Insān's closing verse: *“you cannot will ˹to do so˺ unless Allah wills”* (76:30, from His decree). The phrase is thus the deepest level of the verse's answer to the town: even the refusal to return is not a personal achievement.

**"Our Lord Has Encompassed Everything in Knowledge"**

*Wasiʿa rabbunā kulla shayʾin ʿilman* — our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. The Book's omniscience verses typically appear at decisive moments, and this one is placed where the town's leaders are weighing a private calculation and the messenger is declaring that no calculation is private. Sūrat al-Talāq's famous verse uses the same concept: *“Allah is the One Who created seven heavens ˹in layers˺, and likewise for the earth. The ˹divine˺ command descends between them so you may know that Allah is Most Capable of everything and that Allah certainly encompasses all things in ˹His˺ knowledge.” (65:12). Sūrat al-Anʿām states it in a form that would make any conspiracy absurd: *“With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea. Not even a leaf falls”* (6:59).

**"In Allah We Put Our Trust"**

*ʿAlā Allāhi tawakkalnā* — in Allah we have placed our trust. The Book's *tawakkul* is the disposition of a person who has done what can be done and then released the outcome, and the sūrah of the family of ʿImrān explains the sequence: *“And consult with them in ˹conducting˺ matters. Once you make a decision, put your trust in Allah. Surely Allah loves those who trust in Him.”* (3:159). Shuʿayb's community had delivered its case, refused the coercion, and been told to wait; the trust is the state in which the waiting is possible.

The declared trust is also the community's answer to the threat of expulsion. What Madyan controlled was a place in Madyan, and the verse's sentence says that the believers' security is held elsewhere. The Book's later account of the believers' answer to Pharaoh uses the same formula: *“Your rage towards us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, and let us die while submitting ˹to You˺.’”* (7:126; see also 10:85).

**The Prayer for Judgment**

*Rabbanā iftaḥ baynanā wa-bayna qawminā bi-l-ḥaqqi wa-anta khayru al-fātiḥīn* — our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth; You are the best of judges. The closing petition is the sūrah's own version of the prophets' final resource. ʿĀd's messenger was told to wait; Noah was given a century; Shuʿayb asks for the verdict. The verb *fataḥa* — to open, to decide, to give the opening judgment — is used for legal and military verdicts throughout the Book, and the psalm-like echo of the request in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's later narratives (26:118) shows how consistently the Qur'an's prophets place the dispute in the court of the One who cannot err.


Guidance Not Owned: Why a Return Would Be a Lie

The refusal at 7:89 is stated as a claim about fabrication: returning to the rejected faith after being saved from it would be a lie against Allah. The ground of the claim is that the guidance was not the speakers' own achievement, and the Book states that ground plainly: *“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills”* (28:56)

If the guidance had been acquired by the speakers, abandoning it would be a loss of their own. Since it was given, abandoning it is a denial of the gift, and a denial of the gift is a statement about the giver. This is the logic of 7:89, and it explains why the verse uses the language of fabrication rather than of weakness

The verse's next clause places the matter inside Allah's knowledge and will: the Lord has encompassed everything in knowledge, and a return could happen only if He willed it. The two clauses do the same work from two sides


Judge in Truth: The Same Prayer in al-Anbiyāʾ

The prayer of 7:89 asks for a judgment between the two parties with truth, and the Book records the same prayer on the Prophet's tongue: *“My Lord! Judge ˹between us˺ in truth.”* (21:112). The verse of al-Anbiyāʾ adds the description of the One addressed, that He is the Most Compassionate whose help is sought against what is claimed, and the addition is what makes the prayer possible

What the two prayers share is their setting. Both are made by a messenger whose people have refused him and threatened him, and both ask for a decision rather than for a punishment. The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf places this prayer at the end of its account of the people who expelled their messenger from the town, and the request for judgment is the last word the account gives him

## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:90

> **The disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened, “If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"If You Follow Shu’aib, You Will Surely Be Losers"**

*Wa-qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi la-in ittabaʿtum Shuʿayban innakum idhan la-khāsirūn* — and the disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened: “If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!” The town's last argument is not about God, revelation, or the resurrection. It is about the price of conversion, and the sūrah reports it in the plainest commercial grammar Madyan knew.

The word *khāsirūn* — losers — belongs to the ledger that this town's narrative has been about since its first verse: short measure, honest weight, defrauded goods, ambushed caravans. The elite of Madyan spoke the vocabulary of the market, and the sentence they choose is a market assessment: a man who follows a reformer in a trading city forfeits his standing with the men who control the routes. Sūrat al-Zumar reports the same calculus in the mouth of the Makkan leadership: *“The disbelievers say to the believers, ‘˹Just˺ follow our way, and we will bear ˹the burden of˺ your sins.’ But they would never ˹want to˺ bear any of the believers’ sins. They are simply lying.”* (29:12). The leadership’s own dismissal is recorded in the same sūrat al-Zumar: *“Worship then whatever ˹gods˺ you want instead of Him.”* (39:15).

**The Cost of Conversion in a Trading Town**

The sūrah's setting makes verse 90 a study in social pressure. Madyan's believers were not being asked to accept a doctrine in private; they were being told that the town's notables would treat adherence to Shuʿayb as a form of commercial suicide. The Book's portrait of such pressure appears throughout its Makkan material: the believers of the Prophet's town were confronted with the loss of family protection (the *ḥilf* system), the boycotts, and the economic leverage of the Quraysh.

Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt describes the mechanism as a test: *“Do people think once they say, ‘We believe,” that they will be left without being put to the test? … We certainly tested those before them. And ˹in this way˺ Allah will clearly distinguish between those who are truthful and those who are liars.’* (29:2–3). And Sūrat al-Baqarah's lines about the cost of fidelity are aimed precisely at merchants who feared the loss of their livelihood: *“Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, ‘When will Allah’s help come?’ Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near.”* (2:214; see also 2:155). Madyan's elite were delivering the warning in advance, and the sūrah's reader is meant to hear in their sentence the voice of every establishment that has priced loyalty.

**The Book's Answer: a Different Ledger**

The Qur'an's rebuttal of the town's arithmetic is not that losing money does not matter; it is that the town's ledger omits its largest column. Sūrat al-Ṣaff puts the whole sequence in commercial terms: *“O believers! Shall I guide you to an exchange that will save you from a painful punishment?”* (61:10) — followed by faith, struggle, and the promise of forgiveness, gardens, and noble dwellings (61:11–13); Sūrat al-Tawbah uses the language of purchase outright: *“Allah has indeed purchased from the believers their lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise.”* (9:111).

The sūrah of al-Baqarah states the failure of the alternative with the same metaphor: *“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (2:16). Against that, the Book's promise to those who pay the price of following is stated in the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf's own later chapters and in Sūrat al-Naḥl: *“Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth. Those who leave their homes and die while emigrating to Allah and His Messenger—their reward has already been secured with Allah.”* (4:100); *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life”* (16:97).

**The Word That Comes Back**

The sūrah's sharpest composition is the word's return. Verse 90's townsmen call the believers *losers*; verse 92 — two verses later, after the earthquake and the city's erasure — declares, in the Book's own voice, that the ones who rejected Shuʿayb *were the true losers*. The Qur'an performs this reversal repeatedly: the mocking sentence of the disbelievers is quoted back as a verdict, sometimes with the same vocabulary, sometimes with the same syntax. Sūrat al-Anʿām's version puts the challenge and the answer in a single exchange: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine. You will soon know who will fare best in the end. Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.’”* (6:135).

Madyan's elite had the accounting exactly backwards, and the sūrah lets its reader watch the correction arrive within two lines. The narrative's point is not that the believers would eventually be compensated; it is that the towns were already, at the moment of their taunt, inside a ledger whose balance they could not see. The Book's word for that condition is the one it uses in the verse about the sealed hearts a few lines later: a people who cannot hear what is being said about them (7:100).

**The Threat That Failed**

The verse's function in the narrative is to record the elite's last instrument before the punishment. The sūrah's towns have run through their repertoire — arguments from ancestry, demands for signs, mockery, expulsion orders — and Madyan's ending is the bluntest of them all: a warning about the cost of dissent. What the record shows is that the threat accomplished nothing. The believers did not recant; the messenger did not moderate; and the town was destroyed without its notables having gained a day.

The Book's later history would prove the same point at scale. The trade routes of Madyan's region passed to other cities; the Muslims who had been warned of loss inherited the commercial networks of the Near East within a century; and the verse's sentence survives as the sūrah's standard example of a ruling class mistaking the future for an extension of the present. The town bet on the permanence of its own arrangements, and the sūrah's next verse reports what happened to the bettors.


As If They Had Never Lived There: The Outcome of the Threat

The chiefs' threat at 7:90 declares the followers of Shuʿayb to be losers, and the sūrah answers it two verses later in the same terms: *“Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there. Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers.”* (7:92). The answer repeats the word the chiefs used and applies it to the party that used it, and it adds a description of the erasure that makes the loss complete.

The erasure is what distinguishes this outcome from the destructions reported elsewhere in the sūrah. A people destroyed leave ruins, and the sūrah treats the ruins as instruction at 7:100; a people wiped out as if they had never lived there leave nothing to be instructed by

The threat's ground was economic. Following Shuʿayb meant accepting his regulation of the measure and the weight, and in a trading town that regulation was a loss of profit. The sūrah's account of the threat therefore concerns a ledger, and the answer at 7:92 concerns the same ledger settled in full


A Decree Against the Threat

The threat of 7:90 is a prediction made by one party about another, and the Book records a prediction made in the other direction: *“I and My messengers will certainly prevail.”* (58:21). The verse of al-Mujādilah states the outcome as a decree already written, which is the same form as the chiefs' threat but with a different author

What the comparison establishes is that a threat's force depends on its source rather than on its confidence. The chiefs threatened with certainty and were wiped out; the decree was stated once and was fulfilled in the destruction reported at 7:92

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:91

> **Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them and they fell lifeless in their homes.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Earthquake at Madyan**

*Fa-akhadhat-humu al-rajfatu fa-aṣbaḥū fī dārihim jāthimīn* — so the tremor seized them, and they became, in their homes, fallen on their knees. The sūrah closes Madyan with the exact formula it used for Thamūd at 7:78: same instrument, same posture, same morning. The towns have been presented to the reader as a series of variations on a theme, and the two identical endings bind Madyan and Thamūd into a single lesson.

The Qur'an's other accounts of Madyan's end preserve details the sūrah leaves out. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ describes the instrument as a shadow and a day: *“So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud. That was really a torment of a tremendous day.”* (26:189). Sūrat Hūd has the cry and the quake together and adds that the town's dwellings were left uninhabited: *“When Our command came, We saved Shu’aib and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us. And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes, as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd!”* (11:94–95). The Book's use of several terms for one event — cry, blast, quake, shadow — is characteristic: the destruction is described from the viewpoint of the people who experienced its different phases.

**The Word Rajfah**

*Rajfah* is the shudder, the violent trembling of the ground; the Book uses it for Thamūd (7:78), for the punishment that seized the people of Shuʿayb here (7:91), and for the quake at the destruction of the town in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt (29:37). Its choice for a trading city is deliberate in a Book that matches penalties to settings: Madyan's wealth was stored in stone and mud-brick, its caravans were somewhere on the road, and its people were confident in the solidity of the ground they had built on.

The Qur'an's habit of selecting the punishment a town could not imagine is consistent through the sūrah. Noah's people, who travelled by land, were drowned; ʿĀd, who considered themselves unassailable, were destroyed by a wind; Thamūd, who carved their security from the rock, were shaken out of it; Sodom, whose walls were famous, were destroyed from above and below. The Book's narrations of these endings are short because the interest is never in the mechanics, but the choice of each instrument is a sentence on the town's own account of its strengths.

**"In Their Homes" and the Morning**

*Fa-aṣbaḥū* — and they became in the morning — is a favourite construction of the sūrah's narratives and the Book's warnings more generally. The ending of a people is typically reported at dawn: Sūrat al-Ḥijr gives Sodom the sunrise and the cry (15:73); Sūrat Hūd has Madyan's destruction by the cry, its people left lifeless in their homes (11:94); the sūrah's own 7:97 will ask the Makkans whether they feel secure from a punishment that arrives *by night while they sleep*, or *by day while they play*. The morning is the hour when a community is most confident of the day ahead; the Book's verdicts arrive there.

The clause *fī dārihim* — in their homes, in their own dwelling — has the same function as it did for Thamūd: it converts the town's private architecture into a display of the punishment. The sūrah's reader is invited to picture the merchants of Madyan at home, in the rooms built from the profits of the trade they defended against the messenger's warning.

**The Town Without a Legacy**

Madyan's disappearance in the Book is complete, and the sūrah states it in the next verse: the town became *as though it had never been lived in* (7:92). The Book's interest in the destruction is not archaeological; it is the erased record that matters. The town's practices, its measures, its caravans, its liturgies, and its arguments all vanished, while the message that its elite had priced as a threat to their standing continued to be recited in every Muslim city within a generation.

That contrast is the sūrah's own running theme, and the sequence of the towns has now completed its purpose. Five communities, five messengers, five refusals, and five endings compressed into the few verses the sūrah allots each — with one difference: Madyan's death is followed by the sūrah's fullest reflection on the meaning of the entire series, a passage that will generalize the pattern for every society left standing. The next verses are the sūrah's commentary on the ruins it has just described.

**What the Earthquake Confirms**

The town's threat in verse 90 was that believers would become losers. The quake in verse 91 answers the threat without a word of commentary, because the sentence that follows it will do the talking. The sūrah moves from the domestic image to the monetary verdict with the same unadorned grammar it used for the scale and the gates, and it leaves the reader with a picture rather than an argument: the men who owned the roads of Madyan, fallen in their own houses in the posture the Book keeps for the condemned at the Judgment.

The narrative's speed is part of its severity. The sūrah does not grant Madyan a farewell scene in which its elite reconsider, and it does not report a single conversion from the town's leadership after the threat. The Book's histories are written this way because they are warnings rather than biographies, and the warning to the sūrah's own city was direct: the same threat, the same commerce, and the same option were on the table in Makkah, which read Madyan's story on the same page as its own fate.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:92

> **Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there. Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"The True Losers"**

*Alladhīna kadhdhabū Shuʿayban ka-an lam yaghnaw fīhā* — those who rejected Shuʿayb were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there — *alladhīna kadhdhabū Shuʿayban kānū humu al-khāsirīn* — those who rejected Shuʿayb were the true losers.

The verse answers the town's sentence of two verses earlier, and it answers it in the town's own currency. The elite had warned the townsmen that following Shuʿayb would make them losers; the sūrah assigns the word to the elite and to everyone who accepted their warning. The Book performs this reversal throughout its narratives — the accusers' vocabulary is quoted back as the verdict — and verse 92 is one of the cleanest examples of the technique, because the same Arabic word *khāsirūn* carries both sentences and only the subject has changed.

**"As If They Had Never Lived There"**

The image is the sūrah's most complete statement of what the destruction of a society means. *Ka-an lam yaghnaw fīhā* — as if they had never been settled there, never prospered there, never been at home. The verb *ghaniya* carries dwelling and sufficiency at once: it is the word for being settled in a place and the word for being well off in it. Madyan's disappearance erases both at the same time.

The Book uses the phrase for other destroyed towns and gives it additional weight each time. Sūrat Hūd's account of Thamūd ends with the same formula — *as if they had never lived there* (11:68) — and its account of Madyan repeats it (11:95). In both cases the phrase follows the observation that the towns' messengers had delivered their warnings and that the towns had possessed every material reason to listen. The Book's choice of words makes the erasure total: not conquered, not merely defeated, but unwritten — their buildings, names, and generations absorbed into a landscape that no longer remembered them.

**Why the Book Erases**

Modern readings of the sūrah sometimes take the verse for a piece of poetry about history's indifference. The Book's own framing of the same image is theological and, in its idiom, exact. Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ states the principle that the erasure is a judgment: *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly. And We ˹alone˺ were the Successor.”* (28:58). Sūrat al-Naml's version states the ruin plainly: *“So their homes are there, ˹but completely˺ ruined because of their wrongdoing.”* (27:52; see also 29:38).

The theological claim is that a community's existence is a tenure, and its continuity is the gift of the One who granted it. When the Book says a town became as if it had never prospered in it, the sentence is not about memory; it is about ownership. The land's real proprietor had reclaimed what He had lent, and the record of the tenants was closed without ceremony.

**The Sūrah's Answer to the Threat**

The verse also completes the town's transformation from the inside. In verse 90 the elite spoke for the town's future and offered its members a choice: the message or their livelihood. In verse 92 the same town is described in two clauses, both of which name it by its rejection — not Madyan, not the merchants, not the tribe, but *those who rejected Shuʿayb*. The Book's habit of naming its communities by their response rather than their lineage is one of the ways it keeps the sequence of towns from reading as an ethnic history. The subject of both clauses is defined by what it did with the message.

And the repetition of the verb *kadhdhabū* — they rejected, they called him a liar — is the sūrah's way of fixing responsibility. The disaster did not befall a town; it befell a rejection. Everything the town had — its position on the caravan routes, its water, its skilled labour, its generations — was available to it as long as it was, and the Book's verdict treats the rejection as the cause of its removal from the land.

**The Loss That the Word Names**

The final clause's construction — *humu al-khāsirūn*, they are the true losers — is emphatic and restrictive in Arabic: the pronoun separates the subject and the definite noun claims the category. The sūrah's scale has already provided the definition: whoever comes to the Day with a light scale has lost himself (7:9). The elite of Madyan spent their political capital trying to prove that devotion to a prophet would bankrupt their city; the sūrah's answer is that the city's actual bankruptcy was recorded in a different account, under a different entry, and on a day when its notables had nothing left to protect.

The verse's position — between the quake and the messenger's farewell — is also significant. The reader meets the town's erasure and its verdict before he hears Shuʿayb speak again, and when the messenger does speak, in the next verse, he will not gloat over the ruins. His sentence returns to the same vocabulary the sūrah's prophets have used throughout, and the reader is reminded that the one person who had the right to be satisfied with the outcome was the one who had spent his life trying to avoid it.


**A Merchant’s Word for Ruin**

The verdict of the verse is *khasirū* — they lost — and the root *kh-s-r* is commercial before it is moral. To lose, in the Qurʾān’s usage, is to come out of a transaction holding less than one put in: the capital is gone and the goods never arrived. The sūrah’s first audience were traders who would have heard the word as a ledger entry, and the Book argues with them in that register throughout: *“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (2:16).


**Dwelt in Sufficiency**

The clause rendered as if they had never lived there is built on a verb that means more than residence. *Yaghnaw* comes from *gh-n-y*, whose sense is to be sufficient, to be free of want, to have enough that one can stay; the same root gives *ghanāʾ*, sufficiency and wealth together. What the verse denies the destroyed town is not the bare fact of occupation. It denies that their dwelling ever reached sufficiency — as if they had never prospered there, never been at home, never had enough for it to count.

The precision matters, because these towns were prosperous. They had wealth, gardens, measures and scales, and the confidence that went with them. The claim of the verse is that none of it reached the threshold the root names: a sufficiency that lasts. In the sūrah’s own terms the town that denied its messenger was already poor while it was standing, and the earthquake only published the fact.


**The Erasure Formula and the Ruins Left Behind**

Sūrah Hūd closes the same story with the same formula and adds the town’s name to the erasure: *“as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd!”* (11:95). Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ generalises it into a rule about cities: *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly.”* (28:58).

The Book does not leave the ruins merely empty; it makes them evidence and asks the reader to go and look. *“And the people of ’Ȃd and Thamûd ˹met a similar fate˺, which must be clear to you ˹Meccans˺ from their ruins.”* (29:38). The invitation is put as a command to travel: *“Have they not travelled throughout the land so their hearts may reason, and their ears may listen? Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind.”* (22:46). The erasure of verse 92 is thus double. The town is removed from the present, and what remains of it is placed where a traveller can verify the removal — the ruins are the verse’s footnote, left standing on the trade routes the sūrah’s audience actually used.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:93

> **He turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Shuʿayb's Farewell**

*Fa-tawallā ʿanhum wa-qāla yā qawmi laqad ablaghtukum risālāti rabbī wa-naṣaḥtu lakum fa-kayfa āsā ʿalā qawmin kāfirīn* — he turned away from them, saying: “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”

The sūrah's fifth town closes with the third of its farewells, and the differences between them measure the sūrah's composition. Noah left a drowned world for an ark; Ṣāliḥ left a city prostrate and spoke to it of counsel that was disliked; Shuʿayb leaves a town erased from the ground, and his final sentence is not about the town's response but about his own grief, ending in a question he answers himself. The Book's account of Madyan in Sūrat Hūd closes with the same erasure: *“as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd!”* (11:95). The Hūd narrative also gives Shuʿayb a last line that is not grief but a warning: *“And watch! I too am watching with you!”* (11:93).

**"I Have Delivered the Messages of My Lord"**

*Laqad ablaghtukum risālāti rabbī* — I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord. The verb is the one the sūrah's messengers have used in their opening speeches (7:62, 7:68) and it returns here as the last word of the sequence's commercial prophet. The claim is not that the town heard, or that it understood, or that anyone was persuaded; it is that the transmission is complete, and the Book treats the completion as the messenger's whole responsibility.

The point is one the Book returns to in its instruction to the Prophet: *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:21–22); *“Respond to evil with what is best. We know well what they claim. And say, ‘My Lord! I seek refuge in You from the temptations of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, that they ˹even˺ come near me.’”* (23:96–98). The sūrah's own narrative has now shown five messengers fulfilling a duty whose results were not their property, and the farewells are the sūrah's way of setting the record straight about what a prophetic career is measured by.

**"Sincere Advice" — the Fourth Occurrence**

*Wa-naṣaḥtu lakum* — and I gave you sincere advice. The word *nāṣiḥ* has now appeared in the sūrah's sequence for the fourth time, after Noah (7:62), Ḥūd (7:68), and Ṣāliḥ (7:79), and its repetition across five towns is the sūrah's deliberately monotonous answer to the towns' accusations of folly. The messengers were not rulers, miracle-workers, or tribal champions; the Book's one-word summary of their function is the term for the man who mends what is torn without leaving a seam.
