The sūrah's arrangement has the word do double duty. In Ṣāliḥ's farewell it names what the town refused to love (7:79). In Shuʿayb's it names what the messenger did anyway. The Book's account of that persistence is one of its quietest themes: the counseling continued through the insults, the threats, the expulsion order, and the ambush on the roads, and it continued to the day when the town's options closed.

**"How Could I Grieve?"**

*Fa-kayfa āsā ʿalā qawmin kāfirīn.* The question is rhetorical and its subject is the messenger's own capacity for sorrow — the Arabic *āsā* carries grief with the sense of consoling oneself. Shuʿayb's sentence does not say that he is glad the town is gone. It says that grief has nowhere to stand, because grief over a people requires that they still might have turned, and the sūrah records the towns' destruction as the closure of a decision rather than an accident.

The Book teaches the same discipline to the Prophet repeatedly, and its most reassuring form is in Sūrat al-Kahf: *“Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message.”* (18:6), followed by the sūrah's answer that the message is not the messenger's to enforce. Sūrat Fāṭir's instruction is the direct counterpart to Shuʿayb's question: *“Are those whose evil-doing is made so appealing to them that they deem it good ˹like those who are rightly guided˺? ˹It is˺ certainly Allah ˹Who˺ leaves to stray whoever He wills, and guides whoever He wills. So do not grieve yourself to death over them ˹O Prophet˺. Surely Allah is All-Knowing of what they do.”* (35:8). The sūrah's farewell is thus not coldness; it is the boundary between a prophet's service and a final outcome that belongs to God.

**The End of the Five Towns**

Verse 93 ends the sūrah's first narrative cycle, and the sequence's design can now be seen whole. Five towns, five messengers, five summary messages — worship the One God, live by His limits — five refusals expressed through the local vocabulary of power, and five endings reported in a verse apiece. Noah's people drowned because they could not be drawn out of a routine; ʿĀd's vanished into a wind from the direction of their own optimism; Thamūd's were shaken out of the stone they trusted; Sodom's were erased from above and below; Madyan's, the last and the most like the sūrah's own audience, became as though they had never lived there.

The sūrah now begins its general reflection on what those towns mean. The verses that follow are no longer narrative but law — a statement of the pattern that governed all five histories and that now applies to every society on earth, including the one being addressed. Shuʿayb's farewell is the hinge: after it, the sūrah stops describing particular towns and starts describing the rule.


**Do Not Grieve: The Command Given to the Prophet**

Shuʿayb’s question — *“How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”* (7:93) — is put as a rhetorical question in the first person

The three verses describe one problem from three positions. Fāṭir states the prohibition and grounds it in God’s knowledge of what they do; an-Naḥl states the prohibition and supplies the patience required to keep it, noting that the patience itself is God’s help; 7:93 shows a prophet arriving at the same position by his own account of what he has already done

The conclusion is drawn from the delivery: the messages were delivered and the advice was given, so grief has no remaining object. Al-Qurṭubī reads the verse as a statement about the limits of a messenger’s responsibility rather than about the hardness of his heart, and cites it alongside the commands to the Prophet as evidence that grief over a people who refuse is grief over something already discharged


**Messages Plural: Delivery and What Is Delivered**

Shuʿayb says *risālāt rabbī* — the messages of my Lord — in the plural. The plural is used in the sūrah of a delivery made over time and more than once, and the same plural appears in his other address (7:85). Al-Māʾidah states the duty in the singular and in the imperative: *“O Messenger! Convey everything revealed to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message.”* (5:67).

The two formulations describe the same office from different sides. 5:67 addresses the one who delivers and makes delivery the whole of the duty — a failure to convey is a failure of the mission itself. 7:93 reports the duty discharged and asks what remains after it. Read together they define the office precisely: the messenger is responsible for the conveying and for nothing downstream of it, and the plural of the messages indicates the repetition that the conveying required.

The sūrah’s own record of that repetition is in its structure. Shuʿayb speaks at 7:85, is answered at 7:88, speaks again at 7:93 in the past tense — *balaghtu*, I have delivered — and the narration ends. The plural *risālāt* is therefore not a general phrase but a count: the messages were delivered more than once, and the verse reports the last of those deliveries as complete.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:94

> **Whenever We sent a prophet to a society, We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity, so perhaps they would be humbled.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Law of Adversity**

*Wa-mā arsalnā fī qaryatin min nabiyyin illā akhadhnā ahlahā bi-l-baʾsāʾi wa-l-ḍarrāʾi laʿallahum yaḍḍarraʿūn* — and We never sent a prophet to any town without seizing its people with suffering and hardship, so that they might humble themselves. With this verse the sūrah stops telling the stories of towns and begins to state the law that governed them all.

The two nouns are a fixed pair in the Qur'an's language of trial: *baʾsāʾ* is the hardship that touches property and circumstances — poverty, hunger, loss — and *ḍarrāʾ* is the hardship that touches the body and the self — illness, pain, injury. The Book uses them together whenever it describes the afflictions by which a message is brought home: *“Indeed, We have sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ to other people who We put through suffering and adversity ˹for their denial˺, so perhaps they would be humbled”* (6:42), and the sūrah's own verse states the same purpose in the same pair of nouns (7:94). Sūrat al-Baqarah applies the pair to the Prophet's community: *“They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken”* (2:214).

**The Purpose Stated in the Verse**

*Laʿallahum yaḍḍarraʿūn* — so that they might humble themselves — the clause is the verse's whole doctrine, and its verb is one of the Qur'an's most precise religious terms. *Taḍarruʿ* is the self-abasement of a creature who has run out of resources; it is the root the sūrah used for the manner of supplication in its instruction at 7:55: *call upon your Lord humbly and secretly*. The Book's teaching here is that the hardships that visit a society are not random and not only retributive; they are summonses, and their intended outcome is the posture of a person who has stopped relying on his own strength.

Sūrat al-Anʿām's parallel passage uses the same word with the same purpose and adds a lament: *“so perhaps they would be humbled. Why did they not humble themselves when We made them suffer? Instead, their hearts were hardened, and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them”* (6:42–43). The sūrah's verse hides the rest of the story in its optative form — *so that they might humble themselves* — and the next verse will show what actually happened in the towns the sūrah has been describing.

**Hardship as a Language**

The Qur'an's doctrine of the trial of nations is unlike a simple theory of punishment, and the difference is the purpose clause. A penal system looks backward at an offense; the Book's afflictions look forward at a possible change. The distinction appears in the Book's own use of the term *ibtilaʾ*, testing: the trials of a person or a community are described as exposure rather than merely as payment, and the object of the exposure is a response that only the tested can give.

Neither is the doctrine a denial of suffering's severity; the Book describes the destitution of the tested communities with an unromantic precision and regards their relief as a mercy when it comes. Sūrat Yūnus states the response that saves: *“When We give people a taste of mercy after being afflicted with a hardship, they swiftly devise plots against Our revelations! Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Allah is swifter in devising ˹punishment˺. Surely Our messengerangels record whatever you devise.’”* (10:21). And the Qur'an's own account of the Prophet's community at Badr has the same structure at the level of the individual: hardship, then an answer, and the answer decides what the hardship was for.

**Why the Verse Precedes the Diagnosis**

The placement of 7:94 is worth noting: it arrives after all five towns and before the sūrah's closing analysis of them. The reader has just watched the towns destroyed, and the sūrah now tells him that the destruction was not the first word but the last — the first word was a period of hardship quietly addressed to each community while its messenger was still among it. The Book repairs the historical record before the reader can protest, and it does so with a single sentence covering every town it has described.

The remaining verses of the sūrah will state the rest of the sequence: what happened when prosperity replaced the hardship (7:95), what the towns said, and how the seizure came. The sūrah's reader is being prepared for a diagnosis of the whole phenomenon, and verse 94's function is to establish the premise that the destruction was always preceded by an invitation.

**The Hudaybiyyah Hadith and the Personal Scale**

The Book's law for nations has its counterpart in the Prophet's teaching about individuals, and the tradition preserved the analogy in a well-known report: *“No fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim — not even the prick of a thorn — but that Allah expiates some of his sins for it”* (al-Bukhārī 5641; Muslim 2573, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Hurayrah). The two doctrines operate at different scales, and both teach the same thing about the meaning of pain in the Book's universe: hardship is not evidence of abandonment, and the community that reads its troubles as a summons is the community that escapes the sūrah's next verse.

The sūrah's attention now turns to the outcome that makes the whole passage necessary — the astonishing fact that the towns, given hardship and then given relief, drew not humility but a false conclusion. That is the subject of the next line, and it is the sūrah's most exact account of how people misread their own history.


**The Second Movement of the Test**

The verse states the first movement of the sūrah’s law — a town seized with hardship so that it might be humbled — and the verse after it states the second: *“Then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished”* (7:95). The towns then offer the argument the verse records: *“Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.”* (7:95).

The reply is a generalisation, and generalisation is what defeats it. A town that has been humbled by hardship and then enriched can read the sequence two ways: as a summons and its answer, or as weather. The argument from the fathers converts the sequence into weather — these things have always happened — and the sūrah treats that conversion as the point at which the town becomes unreachable. What follows is not a further summons but the seizure described in the verse’s last clause, taken by surprise, while unaware. The two verses together give the law in full: hardship, then ease, then either humility or an explanation that makes both meaningless.


**The Same Purpose Clause Elsewhere**

The clause *so perhaps they would be humbled* is the sūrah’s, and the Book uses the same construction elsewhere with the same end in view. Of the corruption people have made on land and sea: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (30:41). Of the punishment before the punishment: *“We will certainly make them taste some of the minor torment ˹in this life˺ before the major torment ˹of the Hereafter˺, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (32:21).

The three passages agree that the lesser affliction exists for the sake of the return, and that its being tasted is part of its function — a consequence has to be felt before it can instruct. They differ in scale: al-Rūm speaks of corruption visible across the land and sea, al-Sajdah of a torment minor beside the major one to come, and this verse of the discipline applied to a single town by a single prophet. The sūrah’s version is the smallest of the three and the most concrete, which is why it precedes the histories rather than following them: the reader is given the law in one town before being shown it operating in four.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:95

> **Then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished and argued ˹falsely˺, “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.” So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Wrong Conclusion From Relief**

*Thumma baddalnā makāna al-sayyiʾati al-ḥasanata ḥattā ʿafaw wa-qālū qad massa ābāʾanā al-ḍarrāʾu wa-l-sarrāʾu* — then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished and argued ˹falsely˺: “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.” The verse is the sūrah's account of what the towns did with the mercy that followed their trials, and its analysis is one of the most penetrating in the Book.

The sequence is exact. A community receives the message; hardship arrives, and its function was stated in the previous verse — to make the people humble. Then the hardship is lifted, the community prospers, and at the moment of prosperity it draws the conclusion that had been prepared for it: the alternation of hardship and ease is a natural cycle that all previous generations experienced without consequence. The Book reports the sentence as a piece of false reasoning that explains itself: if our fathers went through both and nothing happened to them, then nothing follows from either.

**"Our Fathers Had Both"**

The argument the towns construct is the argument from normalcy, and the Book names it as the last stage of the deception. Its Qur'anic parallel appears in Sūrat al-Anʿām, where the sequence is stated almost as a law: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!”* (6:44). The same pattern is repeated in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn, where the sūrah describes a community receiving mercy after hardship and using it as an argument for security (23:75–77 in the sequence).

The Book's diagnosis of the error is worth stating precisely. The men of the towns were not denying that history contains cycles of fortune; their error was to read the cycles as evidence that no one was managing them. The Qur'an's answer appears at 7:95's heels in the following verses: the alternation is itself the test, and the community that treats its prosperity as a licence has misread the ledger of the One who granted it.

**The Suddenness**

*Fa-akhadhnāhum baghtatan wa-hum lā yashʿurūn* — so We seized them by surprise while they were unaware. The adverb *baghtatan* — suddenly — is the Book's standard attribute of the seizure that ends a heedless generation, and the pairing with *lā yashʿurūn*, while they were not aware, is stated at several points in the Makkan sūrahs: Sūrat al-Aʿrāf will repeat the formulation in its account of the Hour (7:187); Sūrat Yūsuf asks whether people feel secure that the Hour will not take them by surprise when they least expect it (12:107); Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's version of the punishment of the towns uses the same logic (29:53); and Sūrat al-Naḥl's series of questions states the doctrine plainly: *“Do those who devise evil plots feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them? Or that the torment will not come upon them in ways they cannot comprehend? Or that He will not seize them while they go about ˹their day˺, for then they will have no escape?”* (16:45–46).

The wording is not merely picturesque. The Book's teaching is that the timing of judgment is a deliberate concealment: the generation that has made its peace with a warning cannot see the hour of the settlement, and the warning itself becomes part of the ordinary furniture of its life. Sūrat Yūnus gives the reason the delay exists: *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed. But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their defiance.”* (10:11; see also 16:61, 35:45).

**Prosperity as the Heavier Test**

The verse's most important claim is that the good condition after the bad was the actual trial, and the sūrah's own earlier material supports it. The rain that revives a dead land was described at 7:57 as a sign; the good soil's yield at 7:58 was an argument; and the sūrah's address to ʿĀd at 7:69 named *the favours of Allah* as the thing to remember. The Book's position is that abundance carries a heavier obligation than scarcity, because abundance removes the pressure that produces humility.

Sūrat Luqmān puts the same thought in the mouth of its warning: *“So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah.”* (31:33) — and Sūrat al-Anʿām's verse about the opening of the gates of everything is followed by the sūrah's own explanation: *“So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.”* (6:45). The sentence is typical of the Book's manner: the destruction of a community is reported with the doxology, because the standard being vindicated is the one the community had been writing off as a cycle.

**The Sentence the Towns Never Said**

The verse's careful composition can be appreciated by noting what the towns did not say. They did not attribute the relief to God and thank Him; the sūrah's earlier verse on the good soil identified the faculty that learns from such things — *for a people who are thankful* (7:58) — and the towns' sentence shows the faculty atrophied. They did not ask whether their hardship had signalled anything. They did not notice that their messenger's presence tracked the pattern.

Instead they produced the one sentence that made the later seizure possible: our fathers had both, and nothing happened. The sūrah has now shown its reader how a community talks itself into destruction, and the mechanism is not vice or violence but a theory of history — the theory that the alternations of fortune are weather, and that a generation may therefore live in the calm with no obligation to ask who sends it. The Book's answer is stated in the next verse as a counterfactual that flips the towns' reasoning: the prosperity they treated as proof of impunity was the very thing that could have saved them.


Until They Increased: The Growth That Sealed the Term

7:95 describes a substitution and then a growth. Adversity is changed to prosperity, and the change continues *until they increased*, at which point the argument of the forefathers is produced and the seizure follows. The verb of increase is the hinge of the verse, and the Book states the same hinge in terms of a test whose two forms are mistaken for verdicts: *“whenever a human being is tested by their Lord through ˹His˺ generosity and blessings”* (89:15) the person boasts of honour, and *“when He tests them by limiting their provision”* (89:16) the person protests at humiliation. The two verses of al-Fajr name the error that 7:95 narrates, namely the reading of a change in circumstances as a statement about the person rather than as a test.

The growth is what makes the argument possible. A people in adversity do not produce the claim that the forefathers had both; a people who have flourished do, because the flourishing supplies the precedent they cite. The sūrah states the same mechanism at 7:94–95 in sequence: the messenger is sent, the people are afflicted, then they are relieved, and the relief is what generates the false reading

The substitution itself is a mercy in form and a test in operation. The sūrah says elsewhere that no community was destroyed without a prior warning, and the warning here is the prosperity: it is given so that the people may be grateful, and the gratitude is what the verse finds absent


Honoured or Humbled: The Two Readings of a Change

The argument of the forefathers is the boast of 89:15 put into a communal mouth. Our forefathers too had been visited by adversity and prosperity, the people say, and the saying treats the alternation as a feature of the world rather than as an address

The sūrah's own sentence about the towns that never spoke is the counterpart of this argument. Had they said what the verse of al-Fajr implies, the relief would have been received as a test and the prosperity as a call to gratitude; instead the precedent of the forefathers was cited and the term ran out

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:96

> **Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth. But they disbelieved, so We seized them for what they used to commit.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counterfactual**

*Wa-law anna ahla al-qurā āmanū wa-ttaqaw la-fataḥnā ʿalayhim barakātin mina al-samāʾi wa-l-arḍ* — had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth. The verse is the sūrah's answer to the theory of history that the towns had constructed in the previous verse, and it states the alternative in the most concrete terms the Book possesses: rain, harvest, security.

The phrase *barakāt mina al-samāʾi wa-l-arḍ* — blessings from the sky and the earth — is one the sūrah of al-Māʾidah also uses of the People of the Book: *“And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below. Some among them are upright, yet many do nothing but evil.”* (5:66). The Book's imagery of blessing is always agricultural and economic before it is spiritual, because the audience of the Qur'an measured well-being in crops, flocks, and caravans; the verse is telling the towns that their prosperity was not the neutral climate they assumed but a response, and that its size depended on their conduct.

**Faith and Mindfulness**

The condition the verse attaches to the promise is a pair of terms the sūrah has used throughout: *āmanū*, they believed — trust in the message and the messenger — and *ittaqaw*, they were mindful — the practical restraint that the sūrah's prophets kept demanding, the honest scale at Madyan, the untouched she-camel at Thamūd, the undefiled sign at Sodom. The Book's grammar of blessing is consistently conditional in this way, and its statements are equally consistently corporate: the covenant is with a community, and so is the consequence.

Sūrat al-Naḥl's parable of the town states the two conditions under a single image: *“And Allah sets forth the example of a society which was safe and at ease, receiving its provision in abundance from all directions. But its people met Allah’s favours with ingratitude, so Allah made them taste the clutches of hunger and fear for their misdeeds.”* (16:112). The verse is the sūrah's own theology in narrative form, and its details — security, ample provision, the denial of favour, the garment of hunger and fear — are the exact reversal of verse 96's promise. Sūrat Sabaʾ's account of the people of Sheba makes the same point with garden imagery: *“Indeed, there was a sign for ˹the tribe of˺ Sheba in their homeland: two orchards—one to the right and the other to the left. ˹They were told:˺ ‘Eat from the provision of your Lord, and be grateful to Him. ˹Yours is˺ a good land and a forgiving Lord.’”* (34:15) — until the town turned away and was given, in place of its gardens, a flood and bitter fruit (34:15–17).

**"But They Rejected"**

*Wa-lākin kadhdhabū fa-akhadhnāhum bimā kānū yaksibūn* — but they disbelieved, so We seized them for what they used to commit. The second half of the verse returns from the counterfactual to the record, and it repeats the vocabulary of the previous verses: the seizure, what they used to commit, the rejection. The sūrah has now stated the towns' whole history in the form of a conditional sentence with one clause filled in and one left open — and the open clause is the historical fact, that the towns did not believe and were not mindful.

The verb *kasaba*, to earn, is the Book's commercial term for moral action, and its appearance here is pointed in a sūrah whose last town was judged by its scales. The seizure is not described as an act of caprice; it is a harvest of what the towns had been accumulating in the only ledger that outlasts a civilization. The sūrah's reader has watched five communities make exactly the same mistake, and the verse's final clause names the mechanism without embellishment.

**The Doctrine of Blessing in the Book**

The Qur'an's promise that faithfulness produces abundance is not a formula for material success, and the Book's own accounts of its prophets prevent that reading: Noah's century produced a handful of believers, and the sūrah's own messenger in Makkah was boycotted, stoned, and expelled. What the verse promises is a community's collective well-being in the world when it accepts the terms on which the world was made — the honest scale, the protected road, the undefiled sign, the remembered favour.

And the Book's warnings about the alternative are equally corporate. Sūrat al-Anʿām's verse about the opening of every gate and the sudden seizure (6:44) is followed by the sūrah's statement of the purpose: *“So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.”* (6:45). The sūrah's own 7:96 states the terms of the exchange, and the next three verses will ask the reader the only question that remains: whether he has considered the alternative.

**What the Towns Lost in the Trade**

The verse's pairing of belief with mindfulness is also a claim about what the towns thought they were buying. Madyan's merchants had calculated that following Shuʿayb would cost them their standing and their profit, and verse 90 recorded the calculation. Verse 96 states the price of the other choice: not merely the loss of prosperity but the loss of the supplier. The blessings from the sky and the earth had been available; the towns had been living on credit; and the verse's conditional perfect tense — *We would have opened* — records what the world would have been for a community that accepted the terms, said in the voice of a narrator who knows what happened instead.

The sūrah will now make the question explicit. The next three verses consist of nothing but questions addressed to the sūrah's own readers and to the towns: did they feel secure in the night, in the day, in the plan itself?


**From Heaven and Earth: The Two Sources Described**

The blessings the verse promises come from two directions: *“We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth.”* (7:96). Al-Muʾminūn describes the two movements: *“We send down rain from the sky in perfect measure, causing it to soak into the earth. And We are surely able to take it away.”* (23:18) and *“With it We produce for you gardens of palm trees and grapevines, in which there are abundant fruits, and from which you may eat.”* (23:19).

The two verses supply what 7:96 compresses. Blessings from heaven are rain sent in measure; blessings from earth are what the lodged water produces. The clause in between — *wa-innā ʿalā dhahābin bihī la-qādirūn* — states the contingency that makes both blessings rather than mechanisms.

This is why the counterfactual at 7:96 is stated as it is. The blessings are described as an overwhelming, *la-fataḥnā ʿalayhim barakāt*, from a verb whose primary sense is to open. What is opened is a supply that was available, and the condition on which it was available is the two terms the verse names first — faith and mindfulness.


**Seized for What They Used to Earn**

The verse’s second half reports the seizure: they disbelieved, so they were taken for what they used to earn. Ar-Rūm states the same relation between conduct and consequence: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (30:41).

The verse supplies the purpose 7:96 leaves implicit — the tasting is partial and is meant to produce a return. The sūrah’s own histories follow exactly this shape: years of shortage given so that they might come back (7:130), signs sent in succession so that they might humble themselves (7:133). In every case the seizure is a taste and not the whole.

7:96 therefore states the doctrine the histories narrate. The blessings are conditional, the seizure is proportionate, and both are described in the language of earning: what a people acquires determines what is opened to it and what is closed. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse is the sūrah’s summary of its own method — it explains in one sentence why five towns ended the same way.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:97

> **Did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Did They Feel Secure by Night?"**

*A-fa-aminu ahlu al-qurā an yaʾtiyahum baʾsunā bayātan wa-hum nāʾimūn* — did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep? The verse opens the sūrah's most direct address to its own audience, and it does so with a question whose answer is meant to be embarrassing.

The scene is precise: night, and a town asleep. The Book's choices of hour are never accidental, and its narratives of destruction have already prepared the reader for this one. Sodom was destroyed at dawn (15:66); Thamūd's punishment came in the morning (15:83); the sūrah's own accounts of the townships mostly arrive at the beginning of a day. The night question adds the condition of sleep — the hours when a community has no defences, no sentries, and no consciousness of anything beyond its own walls and its own rest.

The Qur'an's parallel questions make the same point with the same architecture. Sūrat al-Mulk's address to the secure is the purest instance: *“Do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up as it quakes violently? Or do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not unleash upon you a storm of stones. Only then would you know how ˹serious˺ My warning was!”* (67:16–17). Sūrat al-Naḥl's list of possibilities — swallowing, seizure from beneath, confusion, a wasting punishment, an enemy — is followed by its own warning: *“But your Lord is truly Ever Gracious, Most Merciful.”* (16:47), which is the verse's way of saying the delay in all those scenarios is mercy, not immunity.

**The Sleep of the Secure**

*Wa-hum nāʾimūn* — while they were asleep. The phrase, like its counterpart in the next verse, describes a state of mind as much as a physical condition. The towns that the sūrah has destroyed were not destroyed in war or in preparation for a crisis; they were ended in the middle of ordinary life, and the Book's word for that condition is the vocabulary of sleep. The Qur'an's own assessment of such security appears in the verse's closing question at 7:99, in the phrase the Book will use for the feeling of safety itself.

The Book's accounts of its prophets' enemies often show them at their ease immediately before the judgment arrives. Sūrat al-Isrāʾ states the rule by which a society is destroyed — its elite commanded to obey and rebelling instead (17:16); Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's account of the destruction of certain towns comes while their owners are unaware (29:53). The Book's rhetoric is designed so that the reader experiences a small version of the shock: the punishment arrives at the hour when no one is watching, because the whole point of the pattern is that vigilance is not a human possession but a discipline of the faithful.

**Living by Nightfall**

The verse's question is directed at the sūrah's audience, and its subject is not an ancient town. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's Makkan readers walked past the empty sites of the towns their caravans traded with; the question that follows each description of the ruins is always the same, and the Book asks it with the same forms: *do you feel secure*. The imperative is addressed to people who had read the warning, heard the recitation, watched the Prophet's community persist through hardship, and continued to assume that the ordinary arrangements of their city would hold.

The Book's own answer to the feeling of security is stated in the next verse and completed in the third question of the series, whose phrase the sūrah has already used in another context: *none would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers* (7:99). The whole sequence is a piece of spiritual instruction, and its object is the reader's own estimate of his position in the world.

**The Sense of the Hour**

There is one more layer in the verse's composition. The night and its sleep are the Book's standing symbols of heedlessness in this world — Sūrat al-Furqān describes the believing servants as those who *“spend ˹a good portion of˺ the night, prostrating themselves and standing before their Lord.”* (25:64), Sūrat al-Sajdah commends those *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them.”* (32:16), and the sūrah of al-Muzzammil opens with the command to *“Stand all night ˹in prayer˺ except a little”* (73:2). The sūrah's question asks what the sleeping town thought was protecting it during the hours when the faithful are described as awake.

The contrast is between two ways of passing a night: the town that sleeps in the confidence of its walls, and the believer who rises in the confidence of his Lord. The Qur'an's instruction to the Prophet about the Day's nearness uses the same imagery of the night and its end: *“So be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say. And glorify the praises of your Lord before sunrise and before sunset”* (20:130), and the sūrah of al-ʿAṣr's warning about humanity in loss is preached against the background of time's march. Verse 97 is thus the sūrah's invitation to a discipline, in the form of a question that no city can answer for itself.

**The Question the Reader Must Answer**

The sūrah's sequence has now ended its narratives and turned, with three questions, to its audience. The reader is placed among the people of the towns, not as a spectator to their history but as a participant in the same condition: the message recited, the signs visible, the delay extended, the ordinary life proceeding. What the verse asks is not whether he expects the punishment today; it is whether he has arranged his life as though it cannot come at all.

The Book's characteristic way of closing such a passage is to give the reader not a threat but a practice, and the practice appears in the sūrah's own earlier instructions: call on your Lord humbly and secretly (7:55); do not corrupt the earth after it has been set right (7:56); remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, in the mornings and the evenings (7:205). The questions of verses 97 to 99 are the other side of those commands, and the Book's reader is expected to hear in the first the reason the second exist.


Feeling Secure: The Same Question in al-Mulk

The question of 7:97 asks whether the people of the towns felt secure against a punishment arriving at night, and the Book puts the same question in al-Mulk with two images attached: *“Do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up as it quakes violently?”* (67:16), *“Or do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not unleash upon you a storm of stones.”* (67:17)

The security named in both is a state rather than a judgment. A people who feel secure have not concluded that a punishment is impossible; they have stopped attending to it. This is why the sūrah's question is rhetorical and why the verses of al-Mulk end with a statement about the warning being known only when it arrives

The two instruments of al-Mulk correspond to the two destructions the sūrah reports. The earth swallowing and the stones from the sky are the shaking and the rain of the towns' accounts, and the sūrah describes both as arriving during sleep or rest


Hardened When They Should Have Humbled Themselves

The sūrah's cycle of affliction and relief has a counterpart in al-Anʿām that names what went wrong inside it: *“We have sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ to other people who We put through suffering and adversity ˹for their denial˺, so perhaps they would be humbled.”* (6:42)

The two verses supply the interior of the sūrah's cycle. 7:94–95 reports the affliction, the relief, and the argument from the forefathers; 6:42–43 reports the hardening and the appealing that made the argument possible. A heart that hardens under suffering does not read the suffering as an address, and misdeeds made appealing do not appear as misdeeds

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:98

> **Or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Or by Day, While They Play?"**

*Aw-aminū an yaʾtiyahum baʾsunā ḍuḥan wa-hum yalʿabūn* — or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play? The second question mirrors the first and changes two words. Night becomes day; sleeping becomes playing.

The substitution is the verse's whole argument, and it deserves the weight the Book gives it. The towns of the sūrah were destroyed in the middle of their ordinary occupations, and the Qur'an's choice of the word *play* places those occupations in the light of the sūrah's earlier verdict on the same vocabulary. At 7:51 the Book described the condemned as those who *took their religion as amusement and play*; the verse's question turns the word back on the security of the prosperous. What the towns called business, pleasure, and the normal conduct of life, the Book calls by the name they reserved for other people's amusements.

**The Daytime and Its Confidence**

The pairing of night with day means that the sūrah's question covers the whole human clock. There is no hour of the day or night at which a society is, by its own arrangements, safe; the two conditions the verses name — sleep, the absence of consciousness, and play, the absence of seriousness — are the two modes of heedlessness, and both are described as the normal activity of the well-off.

The Book uses this double question elsewhere, and its versions are worth setting side by side. Sūrat al-Naḥl's series of possibilities covers seizure from above, from below, in confusion, or by a slow wasting (16:45–47). Sūrat al-Mulk's questions come in a pair with the earth's swallowing and the storm of stones (67:16–17). And Sūrat al-Isrāʾ's account of the towns destroyed uses the night explicitly: *“Whenever We intend to destroy a society, We command its elite ˹to obey Allah˺ but they act rebelliously in it. So the decree ˹of punishment˺ is justified, and We destroy it utterly.”* (17:16). In every version, the point is the same: the destruction arrives in the middle of a routine.

**The Play of the Prosperous**

*Yalʿabūn* is the Book's word for what a community does when it confuses the interval of mercy with a permanent concession. The Qur'an's use of the term is not confined to recreation; it covers the serious business of societies that have decided that the questions the prophets raise can be deferred indefinitely. Sūrat al-Anʿām's confrontation with the townspeople who made a game of their religion (6:70's *lahw wa-laʿib*) and Sūrat al-Ḥadīd's description of the world's own texture — amusement, play, adornment, boasting, competition in wealth and children (57:20) — express the same judgment.

Verse 98's question thus belongs with the sūrah's earlier diagnosis of the towns. The elites of Madyan and ʿĀd and Thamūd were not frivolous people; they were serious about their trade, their monuments, and their standing. What the Book calls play is the seriousness of a person who has excluded the one serious question from the ledger. Sūrat al-Muʾminūn's summary of the contrast puts the two lives side by side: the believers who turn away from idle talk (23:3) and the heedless who are described by the sūrah's recurring image of play (21:1–3; 44:9; 52:12).

**Why the Questions Have No Answer**

The two questions of verses 97 and 98 are constructed so that no reader can supply the answer they expect. To say *no, we do not feel secure* is to indict one's own community; to say *yes* is to claim knowledge that no creature possesses. The Book's method here is to let the reader stand in the silence of his own possible answers, while the third question of the series supplies the doctrinal term for the position: *the plan of Allah*.

The sūrah is also, in these verses, completing the work it began at 7:94. That verse established that hardship was the summons; 7:95 showed the towns misreading relief; 7:96 stated the counterfactual; and 7:97–98 ask whether the survivors of history have understood the lesson of those who have not survived. The Book's addressee has now been given the law, the case, the evidence, and the question. The verses that follow close the argument with one sentence about the only disposition that can be called sane.

**The Blessedness of Not Feeling Secure**

Read in the context of the sūrah's earlier teachings, the questions are not an accusation aimed at the reader; they are an invitation to a state of mind the Book calls *taqwā*. The faithful are described elsewhere as those who *fear their Lord unseen* and as those whose hearts tremble when His name is mentioned (22:35; 8:2). The night and day questions put the reader in the same position as the sūrah's towns in order to produce the opposite result: not paralysis and not dread, but the alertness that makes a person's ordinary day an act of worship.

Sūrat al-Zumar leaves the door of that interval open in the widest terms: *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins”* (39:53). The question of verse 98 is severe precisely because the same span of ordinary days is offered to the reader as time to turn.

The sūrah's remedy for the towns' condition has been present in it since verse 55: supplication, humility, honest dealing, the remembrance of blessings, and the conscious expectation of the meeting. The next verse names the alternative to all of them — a security that the Book regards as the deepest form of loss.


**Security, and Where the Book Says It Comes From**

The verse’s subject is a feeling — security — and the Book treats it as something that either has a ground or has none. Of those whose faith is not mixed with wrongdoing: *“It is ˹only˺ those who are faithful and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood who are guaranteed security and are ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (6:82). The security is guaranteed, and it is guaranteed to a described conduct rather than to a place or a lineage.

The Book also reports a security given as a provision, and asks what it obliges: *“Have they not seen how We have made ˹Mecca˺ a safe haven, whereas people ˹all˺ around them are snatched away?”* (29:67). The towns of this sūrah were secure in the same way, and the verse asks whether that security made them feel safe from a punishment that could arrive in daylight, while they were at play. The two verses together give the sūrah’s diagnosis: a safety that was granted and then read as a permanent condition is the state in which a town stops listening to anything.


**The Word for Play**

The activity named here is *lahw*, and the Book pairs it constantly with *laʿib* — amusement and play — in its description of what the life of this world is when it is taken for the whole of things: *“Know that this worldly life is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children.”* (57:20).

The pairing matters because the verse is not describing wickedness but occupation. The towns are not reported as committing crimes in the daytime; they are reported as playing, and the punishment arrives inside the play. The sūrah’s charge against prosperity is precisely this — that it fills a day so completely that nothing can enter it. The verse before this one asks whether the towns felt secure against a punishment arriving by night while they slept, and the two questions divide the day between them: asleep or at play, and in neither condition able to notice.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:99

> **Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Did They Feel Secure From Allah's Plan?"**

*A-fa-aminū makra Allāh* — did they feel secure from the plan of Allah? The third question of the series introduces the sūrah's sharpest theological term, and its sharpness has troubled readers for centuries. *Makr* in Arabic is the word for a stratagem, a scheme, a plan worked out with cunning; the Qur'an applies it to human scheming when it reports the plots of the disbelievers, and it applies it to God when it describes the counter-plot by which their schemes are undone.

The Book's instances of the pairing are numerous and deliberate. *“And the disbelievers made a plan ˹against Jesus˺, but Allah also planned —and Allah is the best of planners.”* (3:54). *“And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when the disbelievers conspired to capture, kill, or exile you. They planned, but Allah also planned. And Allah is the best of planners.”* (8:30). Sūrat al-Naml's account of the plot against Ṣāliḥ states the principle in the sūrah's own terms: *“And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware.”* (27:50). The term's use is not a description of God's character in the abstract; it is the Book's way of saying that the schemes of the powerful are never the last move in a situation, because the One whose plan they are ignoring has already answered them.

**The Security That Is the Real Danger**

The verse's target is a state of mind that the Qur'an regards as the terminal spiritual illness: the conviction that one's arrangements are beyond the reach of consequence. The sūrah's towns have been shown displaying that conviction in a dozen forms — the pillars of Iram, the carved cliffs, the profitable scales, the expulsion orders — and the Book's sentence on it is stated in the second half of the verse: *none would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers*.

The clause's construction is exact. It does not say that the secure are punished for their confidence; it says that their confidence is itself the loss. The word *khāsirūn* returns to the sūrah for the third time in the passage (7:90, 7:92, 7:99), and in each use it names a different party: the believers, as the towns calculated the cost of following Shuʿayb; the towns themselves, as the Book struck the balance; and now anyone who mistakes the interval for immunity. The sūrah is teaching its reader the Book's definition of a loser, and it does so by repetition.

**The Believer's Fear and the Prophet's Prayer**

The Book's positive doctrine of fear appears throughout the Makkan sūrahs and is stated most fully in the sūrah of the Cave and the sūrah of al-Raʿd: *“and those who maintain whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, stand in awe of their Lord, and fear strict judgment.”* (13:21); *“and those who fear the punishment of their Lord—”* (70:27). The Prophet's own practice is recorded in the hadith, where fear and hope are held together in his instruction: the Companions heard him say, *“None of you should wish for death because of a calamity befalling him; but if he has to wish for death, he should say: ‘O Allah! Keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and let me die if death is better for me’”* (al-Bukhārī 5671; Muslim 2680, from Anas ibn Mālik). The sūrah's own earlier instruction — call upon God *with hope and fear* (7:56) — is the positive form of the same discipline.

The verse's function in the sūrah's argument is to prevent the reader from resolving the two previous questions too comfortably. It is easy to say that one does not feel secure while continuing to live as though one were; the sūrah's term for the alternative is the one it used for supplication in verse 55, where the manner of prayer is *humble and quiet*, the posture of a person who has no claim to press.

**The Doctrine Stated and Restated**

Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's third question is not the Book's only statement of the principle, and its other formulations fill out what the verse intends. Sūrat al-Mulk's questions about the security of the heaven-dwellers are answered with the observation that gratitude and walking humbly are the alternatives (67:16–22). Sūrat al-Rūm's account of the cycles of fortune warns that the alternation is by design (30:34–36) and Sūrat Fāṭir's passages on the same theme conclude with the phrase that sums up the sūrah's theology: *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, ‘Have you considered your associate-gods which you invoke besides Allah?’”* (35:40). The message of all of it is the one the sūrah has been stating since the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf opened with the clear Book: the created order runs on terms that no community can alter, and the security of a heedless generation is not a refuge but a debt.

**The Passage Complete**

With verse 99 the sūrah's meditation on the towns is complete, and its shape can be seen whole: the law of adversity (7:94), the misread relief (7:95), the counterfactual (7:96), the two questions about night and day (7:97–98), and the question about the plan itself (7:99). The five towns of the earlier narrative are the evidence, and the passage's four general verses are the sūrah's doctrine of history.

What follows will apply the doctrine to the sūrah's own readers with two more questions about inheritance and the seal on the heart (7:100–101), then draw the moral of the nations (7:102) and turn the page toward Moses and Pharaoh (7:103). The sūrah's reader, having been asked whether he feels secure, is about to be asked whether he has understood what he is standing on.


**The Root That Gives Both Faith and Security**

The verb in this verse is *yaʾmanu*, from *ʾ-m-n*, to be secure, to be safe from a thing. The same root in the fourth form, *āmana*, means to believe — to put oneself in safety by trusting. The Book’s vocabulary therefore makes faith and security cognate: the one who believes is the one who is safe, and the word for safety is the word for belief in another form.

Al-Anʿām states the connection positively: *“It is ˹only˺ those who are faithful and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood who are guaranteed security and are ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (6:82)

The distinction the root makes available is the verse’s whole argument. There is a security that belongs to faith and a security that is felt in place of it


**The Losers Named**

The verse’s exception is *illā al-qawmu al-khāsirūn* — except the losing people. *Khāsir* is the active participle of *khasira*, to lose, to suffer diminution in a transaction. The word is commercial: the loser is the one whose trade ended below what he put in. Az-Zumar names the loss at its maximum: *“The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day. That is indeed the clearest loss.”* (39:15).

The sūrah uses the same participle at its own turning points. It is the word of the first confession — *“we will certainly be losers”* (7:23) — and of the people of the light scales (7:9), and it appears in the histories of the towns (7:92). In each case the loss is stated by the ones who suffer it or by God about them, never as an accusation thrown at an opponent. 7:99 is the sūrah’s summary use: the security that is not faith is a loss, and the people who feel it are the losers.

39:15 supplies the measure of the loss 7:99 names. To lose oneself is to lose the only thing whose loss cannot be repaired by another gain, and to lose one’s family is to lose the second thing a person counts on. The verse calls this *al-khusr al-mubīn*, the clear loss — the same adjective the sūrah uses of the warning at 7:184. What is clear in one place is the office of the warner; what is clear in the other is the size of the loss he warns against.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:100

> **Is it not clear to those who take over the land after ˹the destruction of˺ its former residents that—if We will—We can punish them ˹too˺ for their sins and seal their hearts so they will not hear ˹the truth˺?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Do They Not See Who Inherits the Land?"**

*A-wa-lam yabīn li-lladhīna yarithūna al-arḍa min baʿdi ahlihā an law nashāʾu aṣabnāhum bi-dhunūbihim wa-naṭbaʿu ʿalā qulūbihim fa-hum lā yasmaʿūn* — is it not clear to those who take over the land after ˹the destruction of˺ its former residents that—if We will—We can punish them ˹too˺ for their sins and seal their hearts so they will not hear ˹the truth˺?

The verse closes the sūrah's meditation on the towns by turning from the dead to the survivors. Its addressees are the people who moved into the abandoned houses, irrigated the abandoned fields, and took over the caravan stops whose former owners the Book has just described being shaken out of them. The Book's question to them is a question about evidence: the ruins are visible, the story is public, the mechanism is documented — is all of that not plain?

**The Book's Doctrine of Succession**

The Qur'an consistently treats the succession of peoples as an office and not an accident. *“Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act.”* (Yūnus 10:14). *“Have they not seen how many ˹disbelieving˺ peoples We destroyed before them? We had made them more established in the land than you. We sent down abundant rain for them and made rivers flow at their feet. Then We destroyed them for their sins and replaced them with other peoples.”* (Anʿām 6:6). The Book's formula — establishment, abundance, destruction, replacement — is the same sequence the sūrah has just narrated in five instalments, and 6:6 states it as a general law addressed to the Prophet's contemporaries.

The doctrine cuts the other way as well. Sūrat al-Nūr makes the succession a promise to the faithful — *“Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good that He will certainly make them successors in the land, as He did with those before them”* (24:55) — and Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ states the condition plainly: *“Surely, following the ˹heavenly˺ Record, We decreed in the Scriptures: ‘My righteous servants shall inherit the land.’”* (21:105). The verse's warning and the Book's promise are the two faces of one law: the land changes hands, and the tenants' conduct decides the tenancy.

**The Seal on the Heart**

*Wa-naṭbaʿu ʿalā qulūbihim fa-hum lā yasmaʿūn.* The verse's second threat is graver than the first, and it names the penalty that makes the whole meditation on the towns intelligible. The Book's vocabulary of the sealed heart appears in several forms — *khatama* (2:7), *ṭabaʿa* (7:101, 10:74, 40:35), *rān* (83:14), *ghulf* (4:155) — and in each place it is the settled result of a person's own persistence rather than a sentence imposed from outside. Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn states the mechanism with the most precision: *“But no! In fact, their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit!”* (83:14).

The Prophet's teaching preserved the same image in one of the best-known explanations of that verse. Abū Hurayrah reported him saying: *“When the servant commits a sin, a black spot appears in his heart; if he repents and desists, his heart is polished clean; but if he returns, it increases until it covers his heart — and that is the covering (rān) which Allah mentions: 'No indeed, what they used to earn has covered their hearts.'”* (al-Tirmidhī 3334, from Abū Hurayrah; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by al-Tirmidhī and ḥasan by Dār al-Salām).

**"So They Will Not Hear"**

The verse's consequence is stated in terms of hearing rather than punishment, and the choice is deliberate in a sūrah that has been about speech and its reception from its first page. The Book's own description of the loss appears at 7:179, where the condemned have eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, and at 7:198, where the idols' claimants are called and do not hear the call. Sūrat Yā Sīn states the same condition in the form of a barrier: *“and have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them and covered them ˹all˺ up, so they fail to see ˹the truth˺”* (36:9), followed immediately by the Book's own summary — *“It is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe”* (36:10).

Sūrat al-Anʿām gives the same loss a first-person form: *“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first”* (6:110). The sūrah's 7:100 therefore states, in one conditional sentence, the whole arithmetic of the Book's warnings: the punishment a nation fears may take away its cities, but the punishment that ends its possibility is the closing of the organ by which the message is received.

**What the Ruins Are For**

 The Book's recitation of the towns' ends is not an attempt to prove God's power in the abstract; it is a demonstration arranged for tenants who believe themselves permanent. Sūrat Ṭāhā's formulation is the closest parallel: *“Is it not yet clear to them how many peoples We destroyed before them, whose ruins they still pass by? Surely in this are signs for people of sound judgment.”* (20:128). Sūrat al-Sajdah's version adds the Book's own lament: *“Is it not yet clear to them how many peoples We destroyed before them, whose ruins they still pass by? Surely in this are signs. Will they not then listen?”* (32:26) — and the verse ends with the very faculty that 7:100's seal removes.

**The Warning the Sūrah Leaves Open**

The verse's grammar leaves the reader inside the condition: *if We willed* — the strike is available, the seal is available, and the only thing standing between the inheritors and the towns' fate is not an absence of precedent but the interval described at 7:97–99. The sūrah has already given the reader the remedy in the same passage: the towns would have been opened upon with blessings had they believed and been mindful. The verse extends the option to the new tenants: the sealed heart of 7:100 is stated as a possibility precisely because it can still be avoided.

The sūrah's next verse will explain that the seal has a history in every people the Book has addressed, and that the recounting of the towns is itself the instrument by which the door is kept open. Between the law of the ruins and the doctrine of the seal, the sūrah's reader is being taught to hear — the one verb the verses keep pressing on him.


Left to Stray Knowingly: The Sealing as an Act

7:100 warns those who inherit the land that their hearts could be sealed so that they do not hear, and the Book describes the same sealing as something done with knowledge: *“Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts, and placed a cover on their sight.”* (45:23). The verse of al-Jāthiyah names the ground of the sealing — desires taken as a god — and it names the three faculties closed: hearing, heart, and sight.

The sealing is therefore not arbitrary. It is performed knowingly, on people who had taken a desire as their god, and it closes the faculties by which a warning is received. This is what makes the warning of 7:100 severe: the inheritors of the land are told that the possibility of not hearing is real, and the verse of al-Jāthiyah shows how it becomes real

The question at the end of 45:23 completes the warning: who can guide them after Allah. The sūrah's own question at 7:100 is put in the same form, asking whether it is not clear to the inheritors that the same could be done to them


Affliction and What Hands Committed

The punishment threatened at 7:100 is for sins, and the Book states the relation between affliction and conduct as a general rule: *“Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have committed. And He pardons much.”* (42:30)

What the pardon adds is the measure of the warning. A people afflicted for their sins are afflicted for less than their sins, and the remainder is pardoned; the inheritance of the land at 7:100 is therefore an inheritance under a suspension rather than under a settled account

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:101

> **We have narrated to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of those societies. Surely, their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but still they would not believe in what they had already denied. This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"These Are the Societies Whose Stories We Relate to You"**

*Tilka al-qurā naquṣṣu ʿalayka min anbāʾihā* — those are the towns; We relate to you some of their tidings. The verse is the sūrah's own caption on the narrative block that has just concluded, and it states the purpose of the material: the account of the five communities has been transmitted to the Prophet as information, for him first of all.

The Book gives the same caption to its stories in several places, and the repeated formula deserves attention because it defines what kind of book the Qur'an claims to be. *“And We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the stories of the messengers to reassure your heart. And there has come to you in this ˹sûrah˺ the truth, a warning ˹to the disbelievers˺, and a reminder to the believers.”* (11:120). *“This is how We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of the past. And We have certainly granted you a Reminder from Us.”* (20:99). *“We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the best of stories”* (12:3). *“We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ their story in truth.”* (18:13). *“We narrate to you ˹O Prophet˺ part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for people who believe.”* (28:3). The word *anbāʾ*, tidings, is the Book's term for the reports of the communities that its audience could not have known — and it classifies its own narratives as news rather than literature, historical verdicts rather than legends.

**"Their Messengers Came With Clear Proofs"**

*Wa-laqad jāʾat-hum rusuluhum bi-l-bayyināt.* The clause gathers the towns' experience into a single formula. Each of the sūrah's five narratives contained a demand for proof and a response: Noah's people called him in error, ʿĀd's demanded wonders, Thamūd's pointed to their own supremacy, Sodom's wanted the threat carried out, Madyan's argued about the scale and the roads. What all of them received, in the sūrah's own account, were clear proofs — the messenger's signs, the mechanism of the natural world, the testimonies of their own history. The Book's verdict on the towns' objections is therefore terse: *their messengers came with proofs*.

**"They Were Not To Believe What They Had Already Denied"**

*Fa-mā kānū li-yuʾminū bimā kadhdhabū bihi min qabl.* This is the verse's hardest clause, and the Book repeats it in nearly identical form elsewhere: *“Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors!”* (7:103); *“So We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood—all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people.”* (7:133); and the clause that closes the same pattern in Sūrat Yūnus: *“Then after him We sent ˹other˺ messengers to their ˹own˺ people and they came to them with clear proofs. But they would not believe in what they had rejected before. This is how We seal the hearts of the transgressors.”* (10:74).

The clause states the Book's doctrine of settled disbelief. The refusal the towns were practicing at the moment of the messenger's arrival was not a fresh decision; it was the continuation of a posture already adopted, and Sūrat al-Anʿām identifies the process in God's own voice: *“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance”* (6:110). Sūrat al-Baqarah's opening states the same verdict in its starkest form: the disbelievers are those whom warning and its absence leave equally unmoved, hearts, hearing, and sight alike covered (2:6–7).

**"Thus Allah Seals the Hearts of the Disbelievers"**

*Kadhālika yaṭbaʿu Allāh ʿalā qulūbi al-kāfirīn.* The doctrine of the seal is not a blot on the Book's justice; it is the explanation of why the towns' stories repeat with such monotony. The Qur'an's own remedy for a heart that is hardening is stated repeatedly in the imperative: remember, turn back, seek forgiveness, recite. Sūrat al-Zumar leaves the door open in the widest terms: *“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ ‘O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”* (39:53), and Sūrat al-Furqān's verse on repentance promises the substitution of good deeds for bad: *“As for those who repent, believe, and do good deeds, they are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds. For Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”* (25:70).

The Prophet's own practice shows what the seal's alternative looks like in a life. Umm Salamah reported that he used to say in his supplication: *“O Turner of hearts, keep my heart firm upon Your religion”* (al-Tirmidhī 3522, from Umm Salamah; graded ḥasan by al-Tirmidhī). The request is telling, because it treats firmness of heart as a gift continually asked for rather than a possession, and it is the exact opposite of the condition the sūrah's verse describes.

**Why the Sūrah Tells the Stories at All**

The verse's placement answers a question the reader of the sūrah may have been asking through five narratives: why is the Book's argument so heavily historical? The answer is the one Sūrat al-Ṭāhā gives, and it is the sūrah's own: *“So narrate ˹to them˺ stories ˹of the past˺, so perhaps they will reflect”* (7:176). The towns are gone, but the mechanism they illustrate is present, and the Book's claim is that the mechanism is knowable — by evidence, by warning, and by the public record of what happened to peoples who treated their prosperity as a permanent concession. The next verse will state what the survey of those peoples found.


**Some of Their News: The Partitive and the Unreported Rest**

The verse says *min anbāʾ al-qurā*, rendered *“We have narrated to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of those societies.”* (7:101). Two words carry the weight. *Nabaʾ* is not any report; it is news of consequence, the word the Book uses of its own accounts, *anbāʾ al-ghayb*, news of the unseen, and of the tidings brought by messengers. And *min* is partitive: what has been narrated is a portion, not the whole.

The Book states the same thing expressly of the messengers: *“We already sent messengers before you. We have told you the stories of some of them, while others We have not.”* (40:78). The sūrah’s histories are therefore an excerpt — selected, not exhaustive. That has a consequence for how they are read. The towns named are not the towns that existed, and the lesson of each is not limited to what happened there; the selection is itself part of the argument. Aṭ-Ṭabarī notes that the sūrah reports what serves the admonition, and the exegetes take the unnamed remainder as a standing reminder that the Book is not a chronicle.


**The Seal Stated in al-Baqarah**

The verse closes: *“This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers.”* (7:101). Al-Baqarah opens with the same statement in the same terms: *“Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.”* (2:7). The two verses belong to different books and different contexts — one summarising a history of destroyed towns, one describing a class of people in the Prophet’s own city — and they use the same vocabulary and the same finality.

The comparison is instructive on two points. First, the sealing in both places follows something: in 7:101 it follows the messengers’ coming with clear proofs and the towns’ refusal to believe what they had already denied; in 2:7 it follows the description of a people who knowingly reject. The seal is not a decree issued before the act; it is the act’s completion. Second, both verses mention the organs — heart, hearing, sight — because both describe a failure of reception: the proof arrived, and the faculties that should have taken it in were closed.

This is the answer 7:101 gives to the question the sūrah has been asking since its opening. The towns were not destroyed for ignorance; they were destroyed because the faculties that would have ended their ignorance were sealed by their own prior refusal. And the reader is meant to feel it: the same faculties are at work in him.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:102

> **We did not find most of them true to their covenant. Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"We Found Most of Them Faithless to the Covenant"**

*Wa-mā wajadnā li-aktharihim min ʿahdin wa-in wajadnā aktharahum la-fāsiqīn* — We did not find most of them true to their covenant; rather, We found most of them truly rebellious. The verse is the sūrah's summary verdict on the communities it has surveyed, and its two nouns — covenant and transgression — name the two halves of the Book's anthropology.

**Which Covenant?**

The Qur'an's language of *ʿahd* and *mīthāq* refers to more than the agreements made with particular prophets. The Book describes a covenant taken from every human being before their earthly life: *“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify regarding themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ ‘Am I not your Lord?’ They replied, ‘Yes, You are! We testify.’”* (7:172) — the verse belongs to this very sūrah, and it is the reason the sūrah's summaries can speak of a covenant that every people has broken. Sūrat Yā Sīn restates the same primordial undertaking: *“Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, not to follow Satan, for he is truly your sworn enemy, but to worship Me ˹alone˺? This is the Straight Path.”* (36:60–61).

The Book also speaks of covenants with the prophets (33:7), with the People of the Book (3:187, 5:12–14), and with the Prophet's community *“Surely those who pledge allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ are actually pledging allegiance to Allah.”* (48:10), and it gives the ordinance its general form in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: *“Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. And honour ˹your˺ pledges, for you will surely be accountable for them.”* (17:34). The verse's verdict that *most* of the towns kept no covenant is therefore a statement about the species and not only about Madyan: the human person knows an obligation that his conduct routinely ignores.

**The Anatomy of Transgression**

*Fāsiqīn* is the Book's precise term for that condition, and its root meaning is instructive: *fisq* in Arabic describes a date emerging from its skin, the fruit leaving the husk that should have contained it. The Qur'an's own definitions show the term operating in the realm of conduct rather than doctrine. Sūrat al-Ḥashr defines the transgressors as those who forgot God and were consequently made to forget themselves: *“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. It is they who are ˹truly˺ rebellious.”* (59:19). Sūrat al-Nūr treats the slanderer's offense as transgression (24:4), and Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt warns that a careless report may be a transgression with consequences (49:6–7).

Most telling for this verse is Sūrat al-Baqarah's linkage of transgression to covenant-breaking in a single passage: the sūrah's parable of the gnat misleads by it *many*, and the ones it misleads are defined immediately as those who break the covenant of Allah after ratifying it, sever what Allah commanded to be joined, and spread corruption in the earth (2:26–27). The Book's own sequence — covenant, breach, corruption, loss — is the sūrah's sequence in miniature, and the towns of al-Aʿrāf have just enacted it five times.

**The Weight of "Most"**

The verse's word *aktharihim*, most of them, prevents two errors. It refutes the notion that the towns were uniformly wicked, since the Book elsewhere insists that in every community there remains a remnant of those who hold to the covenant: *“And had they observed the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have been overwhelmed with provisions from above and below. Some among them are upright, yet many do nothing but evil.”* (5:66), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own later passage promises that *“And among those We created is a group that guides with the truth and establishes justice accordingly.”* (7:181). And it refutes complacency in the sūrah's readers, because the statistic is a warning: the majority is not the measure of the truth, and the pattern the Book documents is that the majority of every people addressed by a messenger has broken faith.

The sūrah's earlier verse on the towns' accounting made the same point with different words: the blessings were available to the faithful and mindful, and the record says that most preferred otherwise. The Qur'an returns to the theme insistently — *“most people will not believe”* (12:103); *“most people do not believe”* (13:1); *“most of them do not know”* (6:37 and elsewhere), *“We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood. ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks.”* (7:10) — because the reader's instinct is to infer truth from numbers, and the Book's histories are written to sever that inference.

**The Verdict and the Road Ahead**

Verse 102 closes the sūrah's account of the nations, and its phraseology recurs at the sūrah's opening address to the Prophet's own audience: the towns' failure was not a deficit of information but a failure of covenant-fidelity, and the Book's narrator reports it as a finding of fact. The Book states the same verdict about communities that have gone before and the generations that inherit them: *“That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done”* (2:134; the same sentence closes 2:141).

The five towns have now been surveyed, explained, and generalized; the law of adversity, the misread mercy, the seal on the heart, and the broken covenant are all stated. The sūrah now performs the transition it has been preparing since its opening: with verse 103 it leaves the ruins of Arabia and returns to the story of Moses, the longest narrative in the Book, and the model against which the towns' history has been arranged.


**The Rebellious: The Word and Its Sense**

The verse’s verdict uses *fāsiq*: *“Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious.”* (7:102). The root *f-s-q* means to depart or to come out, and the participle names one who has gone out from something — in the Book’s usage, out of obedience. Al-Baqarah uses it of those who depart by means of a parable: *“And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—”* (2:26).

The two verses connect a state to an act of leaving. In 2:26 the departure is what makes the parable mislead rather than guide; in 7:102 it is what the finding reports. The exegetes note that *fisq* in the Book is not unbelief in general but a departure from a position already occupied, which is why the verse can speak of a covenant that was made and then not kept.

This is the word’s weight in the sūrah’s argument. The towns are not described as people who never had anything; they are described as people who left what they had. The verse’s first clause states the leaving as a finding — *wajadnā*, we found — and the second names what was found.


**Covenant Violated After It Was Affirmed**

Ar-Raʿd describes the same conduct in three acts: *“And those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land—it is they who will be condemned and will have the worst abode.”* (13:25).

The three acts belong together and correspond to what 7:102 summarises. The covenant is the testimony taken from the descendants of Ādam (7:172); the ties ordered to be maintained are the relations that testimony established; and the corruption in the land is what the sūrah’s histories report town by town. The verse of ar-Raʿd gives the sequence, and 7:102 gives the verdict on it.

The comparison also fixes the meaning of *most*. 13:25 describes a class by its acts; 7:102 quantifies a finding. The sūrah’s histories supply the instances — a remnant saved in each town, a majority destroyed — and the two verses together state the rule the histories follow: the covenant was affirmed before it was violated, so the violation is a departure and not an ignorance.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:103

> **Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Then After Them We Sent Moses"**

*Thumma baʿathnā min baʿdihim Mūsā bi-āyātinā ilā Firʿawna wa-malaʾihi fa-ẓalamū bihā fa-nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mufsidīn* — then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them; see what was the end of the corruptors!

The verse is the sūrah's hinge. Twenty-three verses have surveyed the towns of Arabia and the region; from here the sūrah enters the story of Moses, the longest single narrative in the Qur'an, which the Book develops across al-Baqarah, al-Aʿrāf, Yūnus, Ṭāhā, al-Shuʿarāʾ, al-Qaṣaṣ, and al-Muʾmin in extended form and mentions in dozens of other places. The word *Moses* occurs in this translation more often than the name of any other prophet — 178 times, against 82 for Abraham and 57 for Joseph.

**The Chain of Prophecy**

*Min baʿdihim* — after them — places Moses in the succession the sūrah has been tracing. The Book's own sense of prophetic history is genealogical and continuous: *“Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers.”* (2:87); *“We already sent messengers before you.
