The Book's narratives and its polemics serve the same teaching, and the sūrah's readers are given both forms.

**The Next Verse's Declaration**

The command to the Prophet to issue the challenge is followed immediately by his own declaration of protection (7:196), and the sequence gives the passage its shape: the idols are dismissed, the challenge is issued, and the ground of the messenger's security is named. The sūrah's readers are shown the answer to the challenge before it is made.

**The Reader's Own Test**

The verse's questions are directed at every reader who has ever placed his confidence in something other than God, and the inventory can be applied to whatever that thing is. The Book's argument is not confined to statues, and the sūrah's closing instructions about remembrance and recitation describe the alternative practice.

**The Passage's Movement**

The sūrah's final treatment of the idols now proceeds from their creation (7:191) through their help (7:192), their response (7:193), their servitude (7:194), and their bodies (7:195), and the next verses repeat and complete the examination. The Book's method in the passage is exhaustive on purpose, and the reader is meant to reach the end of the list without finding a case.

**The Confidence That Replaces Fear**

The sūrah's readers are shown a messenger who can invite conspiracy against himself and then state that his Protector is the One who revealed the Book. The Book's teaching about reliance is thus delivered in the form of a life rather than a proposition, and the passage's closure is a declaration of trust.

The verse's inventory also serves the sūrah's closing contrast, since the next verses name the Protector who hears and acts, and the final verse of the sūrah describes the angels who worship and prostrate. The Book's readers are given three orders of being in a few lines: the idle image, the protected messenger, and the angers who serve — and the passage's argument is complete when the three are compared.


**Four Questions, Each With Its Instrument**

The verse’s inventory is built on a grammatical detail that survives poorly in translation. Each faculty is followed by the preposition *bi*, with or by means of: feet to walk *with*, hands to hold *with*, eyes to see *with*, ears to hear *with*. The questions are therefore not about possession. Idols of stone have feet, hands, eyes and ears in abundance, and the sūrah’s audience knew it.

What the preposition asks about is function — whether the faculty is exercised by the one who has it. The question form puts the answer beyond argument, since the audience could see the images and could see that nothing walked, held, saw or heard. That is why the challenge in the second half of the verse is issued in the imperative rather than as a further question: call on them and conspire against me. Once the inventory has been taken, the only remaining test is practical, and the verse sets it in terms that make the outcome visible to everyone standing there.


**The Book’s Other Tests for a God**

Two other passages apply the same method, and both put the test in a form the audience can run. Sūrah al-Ḥajj: *“O humanity! A lesson is set forth, so listen to it ˹carefully˺: those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah can never create ˹so much as˺ a fly, even if they ˹all˺ were to come together for that.”* (22:73). Sūrah Yūnus: *“Can any of your associate-gods originate creation and then resurrect it?”* (10:34).

The three tests differ in the faculty they examine and converge on the same conclusion. Al-Ḥajj tests production at its smallest, and adds the second half of the image — if a fly took something from them they could not recover it. Yūnus tests the two ends of creation, its beginning and its return, which are the acts no rival can claim. This verse tests the organs of a person: walking, holding, seeing, hearing. Together they cover what a god would have to be able to make, to undo and to notice — and the verse in al-Aʿrāf supplies the one test that can be performed in a temple, in an afternoon, by anyone with eyes.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:196

> **“Indeed, my Protector is Allah Who has revealed this Book. For He ˹alone˺ protects the righteous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Indeed, My Protector Is Allah"**

*Inna waliyyi Allāhu alladhī nazzala al-kitāba wa-huwa yatawallā al-ṣāliḥīn* — indeed, my Protector is Allah Who has revealed this Book. For He ˹alone˺ protects the righteous.

**The Declaration of Protection**

The verse answers the challenge of the previous sentence with a statement about the Prophet's Protector, and the Book's readers are given the ground of the messenger's confidence. The Qur'an's declarations of reliance are a fixed feature of its addresses to the Prophet, and this one names the protector as the One who revealed the Book.

**The Word for Protection**

*Walī* — the Book's word for the guardian, the ally, the one who takes charge of a person's affairs — describes a relationship of both authority and care, and the Qur'an uses it for God throughout. The same word appears in the Book's account of Jacob's trust: *“But ˹only˺ Allah is the best Protector, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful”* (12:64).

**"Who Has Revealed This Book"**

The verse identifies the Protector by His act rather than by an attribute: the One Who has revealed this Book is the One who protects. The sūrah's readers are shown the connection between the messenger's mission and his security — the same authority that commissioned him sustains him — and the Book's language of revelation and protection is joined in a single sentence.

**"For He Protects the Righteous"**

*Wa-huwa yatawallā al-ṣāliḥīn* — the protection is extended to the righteous as a class, and the sūrah's readers are told that the messenger's security is an instance of a general law. The Book's promises to the righteous run through the Qur'an, and the sūrah's readers have met the description of the righteous repeatedly in its narratives.

**The Prophet's Reliance in the Sūrah**

The sūrah had already stated the Prophet's disavowal of power and knowledge in the previous passage (7:188), and the present declaration completes it: he possesses nothing, and he is protected by the One who possesses everything. The Book's portrait of the messenger is consistent in both directions, and the sūrah's readers are given the two statements side by side.

**The Ground of the Messenger's Challenge**

The invitation to the idolaters to conspire against him (7:195) makes sense only in the light of this declaration, and the sūrah's readers are shown the reasoning of a man who does not rely on his own strength. The Book's readers are given a model of confidence that is not self-confidence, and the passage states the difference explicitly.

**The Book's Other Statements of Protection**

The Qur'an's statements about God's protection of the believers and the messengers are numerous, and their vocabulary is the same as the verse's. The Book's readers are told that the protection is not a privilege of the messenger's office alone but the standing provision for those who act rightly, and the sūrah's readers are invited to place themselves among them.

**The Verse's Structure**

The sentence has two parts: a personal declaration and a general statement, and the transition from *my Protector* to *the righteous* widens the address to include the reader. The Book's rhetoric in such verses consistently moves from the particular to the general, and the sūrah's readers are shown the doctrine's application to themselves.

**The Tradition's Reading**

The commentators took the verse as a statement of the Prophet's reliance and as a promise to the believers, and the tradition's literature of trust in God drew on it and on its companions. The sūrah's readers were meant to understand that the protection described is available to those who fulfill the conditions the sūrah has been describing.

**The Contrast With the Idols**

The verse's positive statement stands directly against the previous verses: the idols can help neither their worshippers nor themselves (7:192, repeated in the next verse), while the Protector of the Prophet is the One who revealed the Book and who takes charge of the righteous. The sūrah's arrangement makes the contrast unavoidable.

**The Reader's Reliance**

The sūrah's readers are asked to identify what they rely on, and the verse supplies the criterion: what is relied on must be able to act, and the only being who acts without limit is the One named here. The Book's teaching about reliance is thus stated in positive form at the end of the passage's critique of the idols.

**The Next Verse's Repetition**

The next verse repeats the idols' incapacity once more (7:197) before the sūrah turns to the question of hearing (7:198), and the repetition is the Book's way of concluding the argument. The passage's readers are given a final negative statement and then the sūrah's closing instructions, and the transition is from refuge in God to the practice of the community.

The verse's identification of the Protector with the giver of the Book also tells the sūrah's readers something about how the messenger's authority and his safety are connected: the same act that made him a messenger made him a dependent, and the Book's readers are shown that the office carries the protection of the One who conferred it. The passage's readers are given the ground of the Prophet's confidence in a single sentence.

The verse's readers are also shown the difference between the messenger's dependence and the idolaters' reliance: both groups look outside themselves, and the Book's argument is about what is there when they look. The sūrah's closing instruction to seek refuge with God (7:200) applies the same reasoning to the ordinary moments of a believer's day, and the passage's doctrinal statement thus becomes a practice.


**The Righteous and the Protection Promised Them**

The second clause states the protection as a fact about a class: He protects the righteous. The commentators ask whether that makes the protection conditional, and the sūrah answers by defining the class elsewhere in terms of conduct rather than status. The towns are told what would have happened had they been faithful and mindful: *“Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth.”* (7:96) — a blessing attached to two acts, faith and mindfulness, and withheld when they are withheld.

The same three marks reappear in the ordaining of mercy at 7:156, and the righteousness named here is the righteousness those verses describe. The clause is therefore not a promise to a group identified in advance but a statement of where the protection is found: with the conduct, in whoever performs it. The verse’s speaker is a messenger under threat from a town that has just threatened to stone him or expel him, and the protection he claims is the one his own conduct has been described as qualifying for.


**The Same Declaration in Hūd’s Mouth**

The declaration has a close parallel in the sūrah of Hūd, spoken in the same situation — a prophet facing a town that has refused him and threatened him: *“I have put my trust in Allah—my Lord and your Lord. There is no living creature that is not completely under His control. Surely my Lord’s Way is perfect justice.”* (11:56).

The two declarations differ in their images and agree in their ground. Hūd’s uses the forelock, the hair by which a beast is led, and states that no living thing is outside that hold; the verse in al-Aʿrāf names the Book as the ground of protection, since the one who revealed it is the one who defends the messenger carrying it. Both put the speaker’s safety outside his own management, and both do it in the hearing of the people threatening him — which is what makes the declaration a challenge as well as a prayer. The verse that follows here repeats it in the plural, extending the reliance from the messenger to whoever hears him.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:197

> **But those ˹false gods˺ you call besides Him can neither help you nor even themselves.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Can Neither Help You Nor Even Themselves"**

*Wa-alladhīna tadʿūna min dūnihi lā yastaṭīʿūna naṣrakum wa-lā anfusahum yanṣurūn* — but those ˹false gods˺ you call besides Him can neither help you nor even themselves.

**The Repetition and Its Function**

The verse restates almost verbatim what verse 192 had said, and the repetition frames the Prophet's declaration of protection (7:196) on both sides. The Book's habit of repeating a proposition around a central statement is a feature of its rhetoric, and the sūrah's readers are given the idols' incapacity and the Prophet's security in a single enclosed unit.

**Why the Qur'an Repeats**

The Qur'an's repetitions are not redundancies but instruments of emphasis and structure, and the sūrah's readers have met the technique in its repeated statements about guidance (7:178, 7:186) and in its repeated formulas about the signs. The Book's teaching is delivered by re-statement, and the passage at the sūrah's close is an example.

**The Worshippers' Position Stated Again**

The verse addresses the idolaters directly as those who call upon others besides God, and the Book's readers are shown the charge in the second person rather than as a description. The sūrah's polemic thus closes as it began, with an address to the people who invoke the associate-gods.

**The Idols' Double Failure**

The two clauses of the verse — no help for the worshippers and none for themselves — recapitulate the passage's argument, and the second clause is the more decisive. The Book's readers are shown that the beings invoked cannot even serve their own interests, and the conclusion about their worship follows.

**The Judgment Scene Recalled**

The sūrah's readers have been told how the associate-gods will behave on the Day of Judgment: they will disown their worshippers and testify that they were unaware of the worship offered them (10:29), and Sūrat al-Naḥl reports their rebuttal of the polytheists' appeal (16:86). The verse's statement about help in this world is completed by the Book's account of the next.

**The Argument's Conclusion**

The passage that began with the question about creation (7:191) now ends with the statement that the idols cannot help, and the reader is left with no attribute of divinity that the idols retain. The Book's method is to close a case with a restatement rather than with a new premise, and the sūrah's readers are given the conclusion in the form of a verdict.

**The Next Verse's Change of Subject**

The following verse turns from the idols' incapacity to their deafness and their sightless appearance (7:198), and the passage's argument is extended by one more clause. The sūrah's examination of the associate-gods is thus complete, and the reader is carried to the sūrah's final instructions for the community.

**The Doctrine of Reliance Stated Positively**

The sūrah's contrast between the idols and the Protector of the righteous (7:196) is the passage's positive teaching, and the Book's readers are given a doctrine of reliance in which the object of trust is able to act. The sūrah's closing verses about seeking refuge with God (7:200) and remembering Him (7:205) apply that doctrine to the community's daily practice.

**The Pastoral Force of the Repetition**

For a community surrounded by the claims of the Makkan cults, the repetition of the idols' incapacity was a steady reminder rather than a novelty, and the sūrah's readers were given a formula they could carry. The Book's repetitions in its Makkan sūrahs served the community's formation as much as its instruction.

**The Verse's Address to Every Reader**

The verse's second person addresses the sūrah's audience directly, and the Book's readers are asked to consider what they call upon besides God. The question's relevance is not confined to a particular cult, and the sūrah's teaching about reliance is meant to be applied in the reader's own circumstances.

**The Sequence Completed**

The sūrah's treatment of the associate-gods now includes their creation (7:191), their help (7:192), their response (7:193), their servitude (7:194), their bodies (7:195), and their final restatement (7:197), with the Prophet's declaration (7:196) at the center. The Book's readers are given a complete dossier, and the sūrah moves on to its closing instructions.

**The Turn to the Community**

The remaining verses of the sūrah address the Prophet and the believers: the command to be gracious and to turn from the ignorant (7:199), the instruction to seek refuge (7:200), the description of the mindful (7:201), the account of the devils' persistence (7:202), the answer about signs (7:203), the command to listen to the recitation (7:204), the remembrance morning and evening (7:205), and the prostration of the angels (7:206). The passage about the idols ends, and the sūrah's practice begins.

The verse's repetition of the idols' failure also prepares the reader for the sūrah's final command to seek refuge: the Book's readers are told that nothing besides God can help, and then instructed where help is to be sought. The sūrah's closing verses are thus a practical conclusion drawn from the argument of the preceding passage, and the transition is one of the sūrah's most deliberate.

The verse's wording also closes the door on the possibility that the associate-gods might act on the worshippers' behalf at some future point, since the verb addresses the present and permanent condition of the objects invoked. The sūrah's readers are told that nothing about the idols will change, and the Book's statements about the Day of Judgment depict the same incapacity in its final form.


**No Protector and No Helper**

The verse’s two denials use the Book’s standard pair for what a person relies on: a *walī*, one who holds your affair, and a *naṣīr*, one who comes to your aid. The same pair is used where the impossibility is stated without reference to idols at all: *“And you cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven. Nor have you any protector or helper besides Allah.”* (29:22).

The pairing distinguishes two kinds of need, and the verse denies both to the objects of worship. A *walī* is required before trouble arrives — the one who manages, guards and stands in for a person; a *naṣīr* is required once it has arrived. An object that cannot do either is not a partial help but no help, and the verse’s clause *nor even themselves* removes the smallest concession available: something that cannot assist its own case has nothing to give. That is why the sūrah’s declaration in the preceding verse is phrased as it is, naming a protector who revealed a Book and who defends the righteous — the two functions the pair describes, held by one who performs both.


**The Closing Movement’s Five Steps**

The passage this verse belongs to proceeds by steps, and the steps are tests rather than assertions. The idols are asked to respond to a call for guidance and cannot (7:193); they are inventoried for organs and found without function (7:195); the messenger states whose protection he holds (7:196); they are asked to help and cannot help themselves (7:197); and they are shown facing their worshippers without seeing them (7:198).

The order is deliberate. It moves from the act of calling, to the body called upon, to the caller’s alternative, to the practical consequence, and finally to the perception that would have made any of it a relationship. A reader who follows the five steps has not been given a polemic but an inspection, and the inspection is one he can perform. The sūrah closes its argument about the gods of its audience this way — not by denouncing them but by asking what they can do — and then turns, in the verses that remain, to the conduct of the one who has finished asking.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:198

> **If you ˹idolaters˺ call them to guidance, they cannot hear. And you ˹O Prophet˺ may see them facing towards you, but they cannot see.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Cannot Hear"**

*Wa-in tadʿūhum ilā al-hudā lā yasmaʿū wa-tarāhum yanẓurūna ilayka wa-hum lā yubṣirūn* — if you ˹idolaters˺ call them to guidance, they cannot hear. And you ˹O Prophet˺ may see them facing towards you, but they cannot see.

**The Verse and Its Companion**

The verse repeats the argument of 7:193 in a shorter form and adds a detail: the idols appear to face the worshipper. The Book's readers are shown the difference between appearance and capacity, and the sūrah's treatment of the associate-gods closes with an image rather than a syllogism.

**"They Cannot Hear"**

The Qur'an's statement about the idols' deafness appears in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf, where the gods are unaware even of the calls of those who invoke them (46:5), and in the sūrah's own earlier verse about response (7:193). The Book's readers are told that the beings addressed in the sanctuaries receive nothing, and the point is made in the plainest terms.

**"You May See Them Facing Towards You"**

The image of idols with faces turned toward the worshipper is one of the Book's most economical pieces of satire, and its target is the appearance of a relationship. The sūrah's readers are shown the semblance of attention and told that nothing accompanies it, and the contrast between the sculpted gaze and the absent perception is the verse's whole content.

**The Book's Irony**

The Qur'an's polemics against the idols frequently work by such irony: the image that seems to look, the god that must be carried, the deity that cannot defend its own temple. The sūrah's readers are invited to see the objects of the cult as their makers designed them, and the verse's last clause states what the design cannot supply.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Treatment of Sight**

The sūrah had used the vocabulary of vision and hearing in its description of the heedless who have eyes and do not see (7:179), and in the catalogue of the faculties given to the human being. The Book's readers are thus given two kinds of blindness in the same sūrah: the blindness of creatures who refuse to use their senses and the blindness of objects that have none.

**The Doctrine of Dead Objects**

The Book's readers are told that the idols are not merely powerless but inanimate, and the Qur'an's account of the calf had made the point in Israel's history: the golden image could not speak or guide (7:148). The sūrah's final verse about the idols states the same fact for the cult of Arabia, and the two scenes belong to one teaching.

**The Worshippers' Vision**

The verse leaves the worshippers to their own sight: they can see the idols, and the idols cannot see them. The Book's readers are shown the worshipper's position in its starkest form — a person standing before an object that appears to look at him and cannot — and the sūrah's argument closes with that picture.

**The Next Verse's Command**

The sūrah's next verse turns to the Prophet with an instruction about conduct: to be gracious, to enjoin what is right, and to turn away from the ignorant (7:199). The Book's order is significant: the argument against the idols is followed by the community's ethic, and the reader is carried from polemic to practice.

**The Qur'an's Understanding of Guidance Stated Again**

The verse's phrase about calling the idols to guidance repeats the sūrah's concern with the theme, and the Book's readers are reminded that guidance is God's to give. The sūrah's final verses about the recitation, the remembrance, and the prostration of the angels describe the community's participation in that guidance, and the passage moves from the denial of false sources to the practice of the true one.

**The Reader Addressed**

The verse's second person addresses both the idolaters and the sūrah's own community, and the Book's readers are invited to consider where they look for guidance. The question's relevance extends past the sanctuaries of Makkah, and the sūrah's closing instructions supply the answer in the form of a discipline.

**The Passage's End and the Sūrah's Turn**

The examination of the associate-gods is complete with this verse, and the sūrah's last eight verses address the community's conduct, refuge, recitation, and worship. The Book's arrangement places the sūrah's practice after its argument, and the reader is given the doctrine and the discipline in the order the Book chose.

**The Closing Movement Anticipated**

The sūrah's readers are about to be told to be gracious to those who wrong them, to seek refuge in God, and to listen to the Qur'an in silence — instructions that presuppose everything the sūrah has taught. The final verse's angels, who are not too proud to worship and who prostrate, complete the passage's contrast: the idols have no faces to turn and cannot see, and the nearest to God bow before Him.

The verse's clause about the idols facing the worshipper also carries a warning about the appearance of religion: the Book's readers are shown that a cult can have all the marks of devotion — a fixed direction, a gaze, a posture — and none of the reality. The sūrah's readers are asked to consider what distinguishes the worship of the living God from the service of an image, and the sūrah's final instructions supply the answer: hearing, remembrance, and prostration before the Lord.


**The Three Faculties the Sūrah Names**

Two verses earlier the sūrah drew up its own inventory of the faculties and reported them as unused: *“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with. They are like cattle. In fact, they are even less guided!”* (7:179). Verse 198 applies the inventory to the idols, and that transfer is the passage’s argument. The organs denied function in the worshippers are denied existence in the worshipped: the idols cannot hear a call to guidance, and they cannot see the faces turned toward them.

The comparison to cattle belongs to the same argument. A beast hears a sound and does not take it as speech; the charge against the heedless is that they reduced their own hearing to that level and then assigned the same incapacity to the objects of their devotion. The order matters. It is not that dead matter was first mistaken for a god and afterwards discovered to be unresponsive. It is that a hearing which had already stopped working chose for itself an object that never had any, and the verse reports the two facts in that sequence — they cannot hear, and you may see them facing you while they cannot see.


**The Book’s Two Comparisons: the Flock and the Grave**

Elsewhere the Book makes the same charge with two images, and both are addressed to the one who calls rather than to the one who does not answer. Of the callers: *“The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding.”* (2:171). Of the call itself: *“Nor are the dead and the living equal. Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ makes whoever He wills hear, but you ˹O Prophet˺ can never make those in the graves hear ˹your call˺.”* (35:22).

Both images locate the failure in the receiver, and both leave the caller’s work intact, which is the instruction carried inside the polemic. The shepherd goes on calling to a flock that cannot take the call as speech; the messenger goes on speaking to graves. Neither is told to stop, and neither is promised that calling will produce hearing. Verse 198 belongs to that family: it states the incapacity of the object so that the one who invites will not measure his work by its effect. The direction the sūrah gives the Prophet immediately afterwards — take what is offered, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant (7:199) — is the conduct that follows from knowing it.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:199

> **Be gracious, enjoin what is right, and turn away from those who act ignorantly.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Be Gracious, Enjoin What Is Right, and Turn Away"**

*Khudhi al-ʿafwa wa-mur bi-l-ʿurfi wa-aʿriḍ ʿani al-jāhilīn* — be gracious, enjoin what is right, and turn away from those who act ignorantly.

**The Three Commands**

The verse gives the Prophet three instructions in a single line, and the tradition treated them as a summary of the sūrah's ethic. The command to be gracious comes first, then the charge to enjoin what is right, then the direction to turn away from the ignorant, and the order moves from the Prophet's own disposition to his public duty to his handling of opposition.

**"Be Gracious"**

*Khudhi al-ʿafwa* — the Book's phrase for taking what is easy, for accepting the surplus, for pardoning. The Qur'an's teaching about pardon appears throughout: *“The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent. But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation, then their reward is with Allah”* (42:40); the description of the believers as those who control their anger (3:134); and the instruction to the Prophet's community to pardon and bear with the People of the Book's hostility (2:109). The verse gathers that teaching into an imperative.

**"Enjoin What Is Right"**

*Wa-mur bi-l-ʿurf* — the Book's term for what is recognized as good, the customary right that reason and revelation both acknowledge. The sūrah's own description of the Prophet includes the same charge — he commands what is good and forbids what is evil (7:157) — and the Qur'an's address to the believers names the duty as a mark of the community (3:104). The verse is thus the Prophet's commission in miniature.

**"Turn Away From Those Who Act Ignorantly"**

*Wa-aʿriḍ ʿani al-jāhilīn* — the instruction is about conduct rather than about debate, and the Book's ethic of restraint is stated in similar terms elsewhere: the servants of the Most Compassionate respond to the foolish with peace (25:63), and the Book's counsel to answer evil with what is best (23:96, 41:34) belongs to the same teaching. The sūrah's readers are given a policy rather than a tactic.

**The Verse and the Prophet's Conduct**

The Book's accounts of the Prophet's dealings with his opponents show the instruction being carried out, and the Qur'an's own address in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān attributes the Prophet's leniency to God's mercy (3:159). The sūrah's readers are shown that the ethic of verse 199 is not an abstraction but the description of a life the community had observed.

**The Book's Ethic of Restraint**

The Qur'an's teaching about forbearance is not passivity: the same Book commands the establishment of justice, the defense of the wronged, and the correction of abuses. What the verse rules out is retaliation for insults and the pursuit of arguments with those who are not seeking the truth, and the sūrah's readers are given the boundary in a line.

**The Tradition's Reading**

The commentators and jurists treated the verse as a foundational statement of the Prophet's missionary conduct, and they noted that the command to pardon concerns wrongs done to the Prophet personally rather than the rights of others or the limits God has set. The sūrah's readers are shown how the tradition distinguished the personal and the public in applying the verse.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah**

The verse follows the long examination of the idols (7:191–198) and precedes the instruction to seek refuge (7:200), and its position gives it the character of a conclusion drawn from the argument. The sūrah's readers are shown what the doctrine looks like in conduct: the rejection of the idols is accompanied by a refusal to imitate the manner of their worshippers.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Statements of the Same Ethic**

The sūrah had described the Prophet's community as those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is evil (7:157) and had reported the warners of the town by the sea as the saved party (7:165). The sūrah's readers are given the ethic in narrative and in command, and the two forms reinforce each other.

**The Community's Practice**

The verse's instructions were received by the Muslim community as a standard for its own conduct toward those who oppose it, and the tradition's literature on daʿwah drew on it repeatedly. The sūrah's readers are told that the manner of the invitation belongs to the invitation, and the Book's readers are given the Prophet's own disposition as the model.

**The Order of the Commands**

The verse's sequence is significant: the Prophet is first to take hold of the generous course, then to call others to the recognized good, and only then to deal with the ignorant. The sūrah's readers are shown a method in which self-discipline precedes proclamation, and the passage's readers are invited to apply the order to themselves.

**The Next Verse's Refuge**

The command to turn away from the ignorant is followed by the instruction to seek refuge with God from Satan (7:200), and the pairing tells the reader where the strength for the first command comes from. The sūrah's closing verses address the community's inner life directly, and the ethic of verse 199 rests on the practice the next verse prescribes.

The verse's first command also has a juristic history: the scholars discussed whether *al-ʿafw* in this context means the surplus of generosity, the pardon of offenses, or the acceptance of what people can bear, and the readings converged on the third sense as the Prophet's manner in inviting his people. The sūrah's readers are shown a directive that the tradition applied to the conduct of the caller rather than to the content of the call.

The verse also names the community's relationship to the ignorant without permitting contempt: the instruction is to turn away, not to despise, and the Book's address to the Prophet elsewhere prescribes patience with what the opponents say. The sūrah's readers are given a policy whose motive is stated later in the passage, where the instruction to seek refuge with God locates the source of the strength required.


**Responding With Peace**

The verse’s third command is to turn away from those who act ignorantly. Al-Furqān describes the same posture as a mark of God’s servants: *“The ˹true˺ servants of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on the earth humbly, and when the foolish address them ˹improperly˺, they only respond with peace.”* (25:63).

The two verses describe one behaviour in three parts. A manner of walking — humility; a reception of speech — the foolish addressing them; and a reply — peace. 7:199 gives the same three in the form of commands: be gracious, enjoin what is right, turn away from the ignorant.

The exegetes note that the reply in al-Furqān is not a rebuttal. The word *salām* here is a dismissal without harm, and the sūrah’s command to turn away is the same act stated as an instruction. Al-Qurṭubī reads the verse as the practical form of the sūrah’s larger ethic: the messenger is commanded to enjoin and to leave, and the two are not in tension because the enjoining has already been done.


**Sticking With Those Who Call Morning and Evening**

The verse’s command to turn away has a counterpart in al-Kahf, which states what the turning is toward: *“And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not let your eyes look beyond them, desiring the luxuries of this worldly life.”* (18:28).

The verse pairs a company with a patience. The ones to be kept company with are described by their prayer and its times — the same times 7:205 commands for remembrance — and the prohibition that follows is about the eyes: not to look beyond them toward the life of this world.

Read with 7:199 the two verses describe the whole of the posture. Turning away from the ignorant is not a withdrawal into solitude but a movement toward a company defined by worship. The sūrah states the same arrangement in its closing sequence: refuge from the provocation (7:200), remembrance at the two times (7:205), and the angels who are not too proud to worship (7:206).

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:200

> **If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Seek Refuge With Allah"**

*Wa-immā yanzaghannaka mina al-shayṭāni nazghun fa-staʿidh bi-llāhi innahu samīʿun ʿalīm* — if you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**The Instruction and Its Occasion**

The verse follows the command to turn away from the ignorant (7:199), and its placement shows what the previous instruction requires: the provocation such encounters produce is answered by recourse to God rather than by retaliation. The Book's readers are given the practical mechanism of the ethic stated in the line before.

**The Word for the Provocation**

*Nazgh* — a prick, a goad, the sudden incitement — describes the impulse that arrives before reflection, and the Book's use of the term is precise: what is at issue is not a settled intention but a movement that can be met at once. The sūrah's readers are shown that the cure is available at the moment of the irritation.

**"Seek Refuge With Allah"**

*Fa-staʿidh bi-llāhi* — the Book's term for seeking protection, and the Qur'an returns to it in a verse almost identical in wording: *“And if you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Indeed, He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”* (41:36). The sūrah's readers are given the practice rather than a theory of temptation, and the repetition of the formula in two sūrahs makes it a fixed feature of the community's discipline.

**"All-Hearing, All-Knowing"**

The two names closing the verse state why the recourse works: the One addressed hears the unspoken petition and knows the provocation that prompted it. The sūrah's earlier verse about the heedless had described ears that do not hear and hearts that do not understand (7:179), and the names at the end of this verse supply the contrast.

**The Book's Other Refuge Instructions**

The Qur'an commands the same recourse in several places, and the tradition of recitation before reading the Qur'an rests on Sūrat al-Naḥl's instruction: *“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed”* (16:98). The sūrah's readers are given a practice that the Book attaches to recitation, to provocation, and to the moments of anger.

**The Supplication in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn**

The Qur'an also provides the words: *“My Lord! I seek refuge in You from the temptations of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, that they ˹even˺ come near me”* (23:97–98). The sūrah's readers are shown that the refuge is sought both from the incitement and from the approach that precedes it, and the two verses together define the practice.

**The Two Protecting Sūrahs**

The Qur'an's final sūrahs consist entirely of refuge-seeking, and their language — the Lord of the daybreak, the Lord of humankind (113:1, 114:1) — is the Book's most concentrated statement of the practice the sūrah's verse prescribes. The readers of the sūrah are shown the same doctrine at the beginning of the Book's closing sequence.

**The Psychology of the Verse**

The verse treats temptation as something external in its origin and momentary in its effect, and it prescribes an act rather than an analysis. The sūrah's readers are told that the provoked moment is not the place for argument with oneself, and the instruction's brevity is part of its point.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**

The verse does not say that the tempted person has sinned, nor that the thought is his own creation, and the Book's distinction between the provocation and the consent appears elsewhere in its treatment of responsibility. The sūrah's readers are shown that the attack is met at the threshold rather than punished after it.

**The Next Verse's Description**

The following verse describes the mind of the God-conscious under the same attack: when the devils whisper to them, they remember God and begin to see clearly (7:201). The sūrah's readers are given the practice in verse 200 and its result in verse 201, and the two verses answer each other.

**The Community's Recourse**

The Muslim community's practice of seeking refuge before recitation, before anger, and at the onset of unworthy thoughts derives from passages such as this one, and the sūrah's readers were given the habit with the doctrine. The Book's method here is to attach a small verbal act to the moment of danger, and the passage's teaching is carried in the practice.

**The Sūrah's Doctrine of Reliance**

The verse belongs with the sūrah's earlier declarations of reliance — the Prophet's Protector who revealed the Book (7:196) and the statement that the idols can neither help nor harm. The sūrah's readers are shown a religion in which protection is sought from the One who hears and knows, and the sūrah's final verses about remembrance and prostration continue in the same register.

The Muslim tradition placed the verse at the head of its teaching about the etiquette of anger, and its manuals of conduct instructed the believer to say the refuge formula at the moment of provocation. The sūrah's readers are shown a discipline that operates before deliberation, and the Book's readers are given the practice as a habit of the community rather than as advice for exceptional cases.

The verse's form is also notable: the Book does not describe the temptation in detail or invite the reader to examine it, but prescribes the turn to God at once. The sūrah's readers are shown the Book's confidence that the remedy is sufficient, and the passage's terseness is a statement about what the community is expected to need.

The two names closing the verse were read by the tradition as the ground of the supplication's efficacy: the appeal is to the One who hears the whispered word of the heart and knows the intention behind it. The sūrah's readers are told that the recourse is met with attention rather than with silence, and the verse's theology is contained in its final three words.


**No Authority Over My Servants**

The verse gives a command for a moment: if a provocation from Satan touches you, seek refuge. Al-Ḥijr states the limit that makes the command workable: *“you will certainly have no authority over My servants, except the deviant who follow you”* (15:42). The authority is denied, and the exception is defined by following rather than by weakness.

The two verses describe one situation from two sides. 15:42 states the position as a fact about the enemy’s power; 7:200 states it as an instruction to the one provoked. The instruction is not to resist a force but to take refuge from a suggestion, and the reason it is sufficient is that the suggestion has no authority behind it.

The exegetes read the sequence in the verse accordingly. The provocation is named first as a touching — *nazgh*, a pricking, a goading — and the refuge is commanded immediately, before any deliberation


**An Appointed Number of Your Servants**

The sūrah has already recorded the enemy’s own claim, in the verses that describe his expulsion. An-Nisāʾ reports it as part of a cursed declaration: *“I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants.”* (4:118). The next verse states the methods: *“I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah’s creation.”* (4:119).

The claim is to a portion, and the methods are described in the order in which they operate: misleading, then the arousal of false hopes, then commands that are obeyed in matters as small as the marking of cattle. The verse ends by naming the loss of the one who takes him as a guardian instead of Allah (4:119).

7:200 is the answer available at each of those stages. A portion is claimed; the sūrah’s reply is not a counter-claim but an instruction — take refuge when the goading touches you. The claim in 4:118 is about a number, and the exception in 15:42 is about a kind of person: the deviant who follow. What separates the two is not strength but the act of following, which is why the instruction in 7:200 is given to the individual and in the singular.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:201

> **Indeed, when Satan whispers to those mindful ˹of Allah˺, they remember ˹their Lord˺ then they start to see ˹things˺ clearly.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"They Remember Their Lord and Start to See Clearly"**

*Inna alladhīna ittaqaw idhā massahum ṭāʾifun mina al-shayṭāni tadhakkarū fa-idhā hum mubṣirūn* — indeed, when Satan whispers to those mindful ˹of Allah˺, they remember ˹their Lord˺ then they start to see ˹things˺ clearly.

**The Description of the Mindful**

The verse describes the effect of the refuge prescribed in the previous line, and its subject is the God-conscious rather than the Prophet alone. The Book's readers are shown the practice being performed by the community, and the sūrah's closing movement turns from the messenger's instruction to the believers' condition.

**The Word for the Whisper**

*Ṭāʾif* — a visitation, a passing touch — describes the suggestion as something that comes and goes, and the Book's vocabulary for the devil's work consistently presents it as an approach rather than a possession. The sūrah's readers are told that the intrusion is not the same as the intention, and the verse's grammar keeps the two apart.

**"They Remember Their Lord"**

*Tadhakkarū* — the Book's verb for recalling what one already knows — and the sūrah has used the same root for the community that forgot the reminder (7:165's narrative) and for the command to remember what is in the Scripture (7:171). The sūrah's readers are shown that the remedy for the whisper is a remembering, and the Book's teaching about remembrance runs through its addresses to the community.

**"Then They Start to See Clearly"**

*Fa-idhā hum mubṣirūn* — the recovered sight is stated as the immediate outcome of the remembrance, and the sūrah's readers are given the contrast with the blindness of the heedless stated earlier in the sūrah (7:179). The Book's use of sight for understanding is consistent, and the verse describes the restoration of a faculty rather than the acquisition of new information.

**The Doctrine of the Two Responses**

The sūrah's readers are shown two reactions to the same attack: the mindful remember and see, and the devils' associates are plunged deeper (7:202). The Book's presentation of the two groups in consecutive verses makes the passage a study in contrast, and the reader is invited to locate himself in the pair.

**The Book's Teaching About the God-Conscious**

The Qur'an's descriptions of the God-conscious recur throughout its sūrahs, and their common element is precisely this responsiveness: the believer is described as one who remembers when reminded. The sūrah's early verses had described the revelation as a reminder for the believers, and the verse shows what a reminder is for.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Commands to Remember**

The sūrah's community has been instructed to remember what it has been given, and the command appears at the covenant of the mountain (7:171) and in the sūrah's account of the generations who forgot. The sūrah's readers are shown that the practice recommended in verse 200 is the same faculty the earlier narratives had tested.

**The Verse's Consolation**

The verse assures the community that the attack of the devil does not define the believer, and the Book's readers are given a description of the ordinary experience of temptation followed by recollection. The sūrah's readers are told that the momentary disturbance is not the loss of the state, and the verse's sequence — the touch, the remembering, the sight — is its anatomy.

**The Tradition's Use of the Verse**

The commentators connected the verse with the practice of seeking refuge and with the doctrine of repentance after the whisper, and the tradition's literature on the heart's fluctuations drew on it. The sūrah's readers were given both the instruction and the assurance, and the passage's two verses supplied the practice and its fruit.

**The Next Verse's Contrast**

The verse that follows describes the devil's associates who are plunged deeper without resistance (7:202), and the sūrah's readers are given the pair explicitly. The Book's method in this closing passage is to place the two conditions side by side, and the reader is left with the choice that the sūrah has been presenting since its first pages.

**The Community's Condition**

The verse's description of the mindful is offered to the community as its own portrait, and the sūrah's recipients were told what they could expect of themselves. The Book's readers are shown that the standard is not the absence of the attack but the speed of the remembrance, and the verse's wording measures the response rather than the temptation.

**The Passage's Movement Forward**

The sūrah's next verses turn to the demand for signs (7:203) and to the recitation, remembrance, and prostration that end the sūrah (7:204–206). The verse's account of the community's inner life is thus the hinge of the closing passage, and the reader is carried from the devil's whisper to the angels' worship.

The verse's description of the recovery also distinguishes it from mere regret: what follows the remembrance is sight, which the Book uses for understanding the situation as it is. The sūrah's readers are shown the difference between a person who has been disturbed and one who has been deceived, and the verse's sequence is meant to convey the restoration of judgment.

The passage's assurance was also read as a statement about the ordinary life of the believer rather than about extraordinary sanctity, and the tradition's discussions of the heart's states used the verse to define the normal pattern. The sūrah's readers are given a doctrine in which the fall is momentary and the return is immediate, and the verse's verbs are in the habitual form to say so.


**A Whisper That Passes**

The word for what reaches the mindful here is *ṭāʾif*, from a root meaning to go round a thing, and it denotes something that comes around and passes — a visitor, a circuit, a touch. The Book’s other word for the same operation is *waswās*, a repeated whispering: *“from the evil of the lurking whisperer—who whispers into the hearts of humankind”* (114:4–5). The two words describe different phases of one process, and the verse that uses the first is describing the earliest of them.

That is why the remedy in this verse is as quick as the thing it answers. A *ṭāʾif* has not settled; it has come round and is passing, and a remembrance that arrives in the same moment meets it while it is still outside. Sūrah al-Nās describes the whisperer as lurking and retreating, which is the same picture from the other side: the approach is intermittent, and the response that works against an intermittent approach is an intermittent readiness. The verse does not promise that the mindful will not be addressed. It says that when they are, they remember, and the sequence takes one step.


**Then They Are Seeing**

The second half of the verse is a nominal sentence introduced by the particle of suddenness: *fa-idhā hum mubṣirūn* — then, behold, they are seeing. The grammar states an achieved condition rather than an action in progress; there is no verb of becoming, only a subject and a participle. What the verse describes is therefore not a process of recovery but its completion, and the particle marks it as arriving without interval.

The choice of the participle from *b-ṣ-r* belongs to the sūrah’s running vocabulary of sight, which it has used of the sign given for the gazers, of the idols that cannot see the faces turned toward them, and of the faculties listed as instruments and left unused. This verse supplies the positive case: sight that returns in a moment, in people who had been addressed by something passing. The contrast with verse 198 is exact and deliberate. The idols cannot see; their worshippers cannot see; the mindful are addressed by the same enemy and, remembering, see at once — and the difference between the two groups is not the organ but what happens when it is used.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:202

> **But the devils persistently plunge their ˹human˺ associates deeper into wickedness, sparing no effort.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"The Devils Plunge Their Associates Deeper"**

*Wa-ikhwānuhum yamuddūnahum fī al-ghayyi thumma lā yuqṣirūn* — but the devils persistently plunge their ˹human˺ associates deeper into wickedness, sparing no effort.

**The Contrast Stated**

The verse completes the pair begun in 7:201, and its subject is the other category of people: those whose association with the devils is reciprocal. The Book's readers are shown two conditions rather than two natures, and the verse's verb — the devils' persistence — describes a process that continues as long as it is not interrupted.

**The Word for the Associates**

*Ikhwānuhum* — their brothers — and the Book's use of kinship for the relation between the devils and the wicked is deliberate: the sūrah's readers are shown a companionship rather than a servitude, and the Qur'an's language about evil presents it as a society as well as a condition.

**"Plunge Them Deeper"**

*Yamuddūnahum fī al-ghayy* — the verb is one of extension, of stretching a rope, of drawing a thing out; the image is of a deepening that is willed from both sides. The sūrah's readers are shown that the plunging is not an assault on the unwilling, and the Book's narrative of the fall of Adam's adversary had already portrayed the devil's method as invitation (7:20).

**"Sparing No Effort"**

*Thumma lā yuqṣirūn* — the clause states the persistence of the process, and the Qur'an's warnings about the devil's patience are stated elsewhere in the Book. The sūrah's readers are told that the associate's situation does not stabilize, and the passage's image of deepening water is meant to convey the direction of travel.

**The Book's Doctrine of Companionship**

The Qur'an states repeatedly that the company a person keeps becomes his company in the next life: whoever turns away from the Reminder is assigned a devil as a companion (43:36), and the Book's readers are given the same teaching in the sūrah's own accounts of communities that followed their leaders into ruin. The verse's word for brotherhood belongs to that doctrine.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah's Close**

The verse stands between the description of the mindful (7:201) and the answer about signs (7:203), and its function is to state what happens when the practice of verse 200 is not performed. The sūrah's readers are thus given both the remedy and the alternative in consecutive lines.

**The Book's Account of the Devil's Work**

The Qur'an's statements about the devil describe his activity as temptation, embellishment, and companionship, and it consistently presents his power as limited by the creature's response. The sūrah's earlier narrative of his refusal to prostrate had already stated the terms of his relation to the human being (7:11–18), and the verse's description of his persistence belongs with that account.

**The Reader's Position**

The verse describes a class rather than an individual case, and the sūrah's readers are given the two options in the passage as a whole. The Book's teaching here is that the difference between the groups lies not in the intensity of the attack but in the answer given to it, and the verse's contrast makes the point without comment.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Warnings**

The sūrah had warned its readers about the communities that were overtaken while unaware (7:95) and had described the heedless who have the faculties and do not use them (7:179). The verse's image of a deepening course belongs to the same sequence of warnings, and the sūrah's readers are given the diagnosis in several registers.

**The Next Verse's Question**

The following verse answers the demand for a sign with the Prophet's statement that he follows only what is revealed to him (7:203). The transition from the discussion of the devils to the discussion of the revelation is significant: the sūrah's readers are shown what the alternative to the devils' company is, and the answer is stated as the Book itself.

**The Community's Vigilance**

The verse was read by the community as a caution about complacency in the practice of remembrance, and the tradition's teaching about the heart's hardening drew on passages such as this. The sūrah's readers are told that the plunge is gradual and unnoticed, and the Book's remedy has been given in the preceding verse.

**The Passage Complete**

The sūrah's account of the two responses is now complete: refuge and remembrance on one side (7:200–201), and the deepening course on the other (7:202). The Book's arrangement leaves the reader between the two, and the sūrah's final four verses supply the practice that ends the passage.

The verse's description of the devils' persistence also implies the community's part in the process, since the associates are being drawn by beings they have chosen as brothers. The Book's readers are shown that the companionship is the result of a prior agreement, and the sūrah's earlier narrative of the devil's refusal had stated the terms: he asked for respite and was granted it until the appointed day (7:15).

The Qur'an's warnings about the devil's patience are matched by its assurances about God's protection, and the sūrah's passage places the two in sequence: the refuge and remembrance of verses 200–201 stand before the account of the plunge in verse 202. The sūrah's readers are given the remedy before the diagnosis, and the order is the Book's usual provision for its community.

The passage's vocabulary of drawing and stretching is also used by the Book for its own dealings with the obstinate, and the sūrah's readers are shown that the same image can describe the extension of a term or the deepening of a course. The verse's context leaves no doubt which of the two the associates receive.


**The Extension of a Course**

The verb describing what the devils do to their associates is from *m-d-d*, to stretch, extend, lengthen — the word used of extending a rope, of prolonging a shade, and of supplying more of a thing already present. What is described is not a push but a lengthening: the associates are kept going in the direction they had already taken.

The Book states the same operation from the other side, as a respite whose purpose the recipients misread: *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment.”* (3:178). The extension looks identical from inside and is opposite in source. This verse assigns one kind of lengthening to the devils, and the sūrah’s preceding verse assigns the counter-movement — remembrance, and then sight — to the mindful. Both are described as continuous rather than as single acts, which is why the sūrah’s instruction to its readers concerns keeping a practice rather than making a decision.


**The Company the Associates End In**

The verse’s word for the associates is *ikhwān*, brothers, and the Book describes how that brotherhood ends. On the Day, the companion is wished away by the one who had him: *“I wish you were as distant from me as the east is from the west! What an evil associate ˹you were˺!”* (43:38).

The distance named is the widest the language has, and it is asked for by the one who followed. This verse supplies the mechanism that produced the wish: an associate who extends a course without sparing effort, and a companion who does not notice the extension because it is gradual. The two verses are one case seen at its two ends — the working of the partnership and its dissolution — and the sūrah places its account of the partnership immediately before its closing instructions, so that the instructions reach a reader who has just been shown what he is being kept from.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:203

> **If you ˹O Prophet˺ do not bring them a sign ˹which they demanded˺, they ask, “Why do you not make it yourself?” Say, “I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This ˹Quran˺ is an insight from your Lord—a guide and a mercy for those who believe.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Why Do You Not Make It Yourself?"**

*Wa-idhā lam taʾtihim bi-āyatin qālū lawlā ijtabaytahā qul innamā attabiʿu mā yūḥā ilayya min rabbī hādhā baṣāʾiru min rabbikum wa-hudan wa-raḥmatun li-qawmin yuʾminūn* — if you ˹O Prophet˺ do not bring them a sign ˹which they demanded˺, they ask, "Why do you not make it yourself?" Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This ˹Quran˺ is an insight from your Lord—a guide and a mercy for those who believe."

**The Demand Restated**

The sūrah's closing verses return to the demand for signs, which had occupied the sūrah's earlier polemics, and the verse gives the demand its most revealing form: the opponents ask the Prophet to produce a sign himself. The Book's readers are shown a request that has ceased to be about evidence and become a request about authority.

**The Book's Many Accounts of the Demand**

The Qur'an records the same demand in sūrah after sūrah, and each version adds a detail: the challenge to bring a sign from his Lord (6:37), the complaint that no sign had been sent (13:7), the demand that he bring one (20:133), the oath that they would believe if a sign came (6:109), and the request to produce a different Qur'an altogether (10:15). The sūrah's readers are given the demand's whole history.

**"Why Do You Not Make It Yourself?"**

The question's premise is that the Prophet's authority includes the disposal of signs, and the Book's answer denies the premise at once. The sūrah's readers are shown that the messenger is not a magician with a repertoire at his command, and the reply that follows — that he follows only what is revealed — settles the matter by stating his office.

**The Answer's Content**

*Qul innamā attabiʿu mā yūḥā ilayya min rabbī* — I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. The sūrah's readers are given the Prophet's position in a sentence: he is a follower of revelation before he is anything else, and the Book's accounts of the other messengers' replies to the same demand say the same thing: signs are only with Allah (6:109, 29:50).

**Why the Signs Are Withheld**

The Book states the reason in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: the signs were not sent because the earlier peoples denied them and the demand would have been followed by the same denial (17:59), and Sūrat al-Anʿām states that even the descent of the angels and the speaking of the dead would not produce belief without God's will (6:111). The sūrah's readers are shown that the demand is not an argument but a posture.

**"An Insight From Your Lord"**

*Baṣāʾiru* — the plural of insight, of clear perception — is the Book's term for what the revelation supplies, and the Qur'an's self-descriptions in this register are numerous: a healing and mercy for the believers (17:82), a warning, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide and a mercy (10:57). The sūrah's readers are told that the sign they already have is of a different kind from the one they demanded.

**"A Guide and a Mercy for Those Who Believe"**

The verse's closing description repeats the Qur'an's standard formula for itself, and the conditional at the end is the sūrah's recurring note: the Book's guidance and mercy are realized in those who believe. The sūrah's readers have met the same qualifying phrase in the sūrah's earlier verses, and its repetition here closes the argument about signs with an account of what a sign is for.

**The Answer to the Demand for Something New**

Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt answers the same demand by pointing to what had already been given: *“Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, ˹which is˺ recited to them. Surely in this ˹Quran˺ is a mercy and reminder for people who believe”* (29:51). The sūrah's verse belongs to that family of answers, and its readers are shown the Book's consistent reply to those who ask for something other than the recitation.

**The Demand's Real Nature**

The Book's diagnosis of the demand appears in Sūrat al-Baqarah's account of the earlier communities who said that God should speak to them or a sign should come (2:118), and in the statement that their hearts are alike. The sūrah's readers are given the demand's genealogy, and the sūrah's answer to it is the verse's declaration of the Prophet's office.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Treatment of the Messenger's Limits**

The sūrah had already stated that the Prophet knows neither the unseen nor the Hour and possesses no power over benefit or harm (7:188), and the present verse completes the portrait by adding the signs to the list. The sūrah's readers are given a consistent account of the messenger's position, and the verses are meant to be read together.

**The Community's Use of the Verse**

The Muslim community's understanding of the Prophet's relation to revelation rests on passages such as this one, and the sūrah's readers were told that the messenger's authority is the authority of what he was given. The verse's answer was also used in the tradition's discussions of the Qur'an's sufficiency as the sign, and the Book's own statement in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt supplied the argument's positive form.

**The Sūrah's Closing Movement**

The verse stands at the head of the sūrah's final four verses, and it gives them their subject: the revelation, the listening, the remembrance, and the worship. The Book's readers are shown what the alternative to the demand for signs is, and the alternative is the recitation they have been hearing.

**The Verse's Instruction**

The verse's command to the Prophet is to state his position rather than to defend himself, and the Book's readers are given a model of how the messenger handled the demand for credentials. The sūrah's readers are shown that the answer to a demand for something other than the revelation is the revelation.

**The Recitation That Follows**

The next verse commands the listeners to be silent when the Qur'an is recited (7:204), and the placement is deliberate: the sign that was demanded is being recited to them at that very moment. The sūrah's readers are given the demand, the answer, and the command to attend in three consecutive sentences, and the passage's argument is thus complete.


Only Following What Is Revealed: The Limit Stated on the Messenger

The answer at 7:203 is a statement of limits, and the Book states the same limits in the first person: *“I am not the first messenger ever sent, nor do I know what will happen to me or you. I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.”* (46:9). The verse of al-Aḥqāf gives three refusals and one affirmation. The messenger is not original, does not know the unseen, and is not sent with anything but warning; what he does is follow what is revealed to him.

The three refusals answer the demand of 7:203 at its root. A sign made by the messenger would require him to be an originator, and the verse of al-Aḥqāf removes that possibility; a sign produced on request would require knowledge of what is unseen, and that is removed as well

The limit is stated without diminishing the message. The verse at 7:203 calls the Book insight, guide, and mercy, and the verse at 46:9 calls its bearer a clear warner. Both descriptions are of a thing received, and the sūrah's insistence on this is what separates its messengers from the miracle-workers its peoples demand


The Unseen With Allah: The Demand Answered in Yūnus

The demand for a sign is recorded elsewhere with the same answer: *“Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?”* (10:20), and the reply is that *“˹The knowledge of˺ the unseen is with Allah alone. So wait! I too am waiting with you.”* (10:20)

What the waiting adds is the messenger's position relative to his people. He waits with them rather than above them, and the sūrah's own answer makes the same point by describing the Book as insight from their Lord — a thing addressed to them and available to them now

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:204

> **When the Quran is recited, listen to it attentively and be silent, so you may be shown mercy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Listen to It Attentively and Be Silent"**

*Wa-idhā quriʾa al-Qurʾānu fa-stamiʿū lahu wa-anṣitū laʿallakum turḥamūn* — when the Quran is recited, listen to it attentively and be silent, so you may be shown mercy.

**The Command and Its Occasion**

The verse follows the Prophet's declaration that the Book is an insight, a guide, and a mercy (7:203), and its instruction supplies the response the declaration requires. The sūrah's readers are told what to do with the sign they have just been offered, and the command's position in the sūrah's final movement gives it the weight of a summary of the community's discipline.

**The Two Verbs**

*Fa-stamiʿū lahu wa-anṣitū* — the first verb is listening with the ear and the attention, and the second is the silence that accompanies it. The pair is the Book's most precise statement about the reception of recitation, and the sūrah's readers are shown that attendance on the Qur'an is an act with two parts, one of them abstention.

**The Tradition's Rulings**

The scholars drew from the verse their teaching about listening to the Qur'an in prayer and outside it, and their discussions distinguished the recitation that is obligatory to attend from the recitation that is heard incidentally. The sūrah's readers are shown that the verse was received as a legal principle as well as an exhortation, and the community's practice of silence during public recitation rests on it.

**"So You May Be Shown Mercy"**

The command's purpose is stated in the Book's vocabulary of mercy, and the sūrah's readers are told that the act of listening is not a courtesy but a means. The Qur'an attaches mercy to specific practices throughout — the sūrah's earlier commands about returning, remembering, and seeking refuge all close with a similar clause — and the verse's grammar keeps the outcome in God's hand.

**The Book's Treatment of Hearing**

The Qur'an's addresses consistently treat hearing as the first step of faith: the Book's description of the heedless is that they have ears and do not hear (7:179), and its account of the earlier communities' failure is repeatedly phrased as a refusal to listen. The sūrah's readers are shown that the command of verse 204 is the positive form of the sūrah's long indictment.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Accusations**

The sūrah had reported that the idols cannot hear those who call upon them (7:193, 7:198), and the Book's readers are given the contrast: the objects of worship are deaf, and the worshippers of God are commanded to listen. The verse's placement at the end of the sūrah's examination of the idols makes the comparison explicit.

**The Recitation in the Prophet's Practice**

The Book's accounts of the Prophet's night recitation and of the community's prayer describe the practice the verse commands, and the Qur'an's instruction to recite in a measured manner belongs to the same discipline. The sūrah's readers are shown a religion centered on a recited text, and the command to be silent is the necessary condition of its reception.

**The Verse's Audience**

The command addresses everyone present at the recitation, and the Book's readers are told that the obligation is not restricted to believers: the sūrah's readers in the Prophet's city included those who had not yet accepted the message, and the verse's requirement of silence applied to them as well.

**The Discipline of Silence**

The Book's readers are also shown the inward form of the command, since the silence of the tongue is a figure for the attention of the heart, and the sūrah's earlier verses had made the heart the seat of understanding (7:179). The community's tradition drew from the verse its teaching about attentiveness rather than mere quietness, and the two verbs of the verse were read together.

**The Qur'an's Self-Presentation**

The verse's command presupposes the Book's account of itself as a recitation that works on its hearers: the sūrah's readers have been told that the Book is an insight and a mercy, and elsewhere that the Qur'an's recitation increases the believers' humility (17:109). The sūrah's readers are shown a text that accomplishes something in the one who attends to it.

**The Mercy Extended**

The verse's closing clause gives the reason for the command in the Book's usual manner, and the sūrah's readers are told that the act of listening places them in the way of mercy. The same word appears in the sūrah's earlier descriptions of the righteous and in its closing verse's command to remember, and the passage's vocabulary is deliberately repeated.

**The Next Verse's Remembrance**

The following verse commands the remembrance of God inwardly, with humility, morning and evening (7:205), and the two commands together describe the community's daily practice: listening to the recitation and remembering the Lord. The sūrah's readers are given the outward and inward halves of the discipline, and the final verse supplies the model of those who perform it.

**The Passage's Order**

The sūrah's last three verses move from hearing to remembering to prostrating, and the sequence is the Book's account of how revelation becomes worship. The sūrah's readers are shown a progression that leads from the recited word to the daily remembrance to the posture of the angels, and the sūrah ends at the point to which its whole argument has been directed.

The verse also served the community as a rule about the conduct of the mosque: the recitation is to be heard rather than competed with, and the tradition's teaching about not raising one's voice above the imam's drew on it. The sūrah's readers are shown that the Book's final instructions concern the manner of the community's assembly as much as its private devotion.


**The Same Word in the Listening of the Jinn**

The command to be silent uses a verb that appears in one other scene in the Book, and that scene is a listening. The group of jinn sent to hear the Qurʾān say to one another: *“Listen quietly!”* (46:29), using the same imperative this verse gives, and then return to their people as warners.

The parallel is exact and it fixes the quality of the silence required. The jinn are not told to refrain from speech as a rule of assembly; they are told to be still so that what is being recited can be taken in, and the sūrah in al-Aḥqāf reports the result — a listening that produced warning and transmission. Verse 204 attaches the same result to the same act in the form of a purpose clause: so that you may be shown mercy. The silence commanded is therefore instrumental rather than disciplinary. It is what a person does when something worth hearing is being said, and the verse treats its audience as people who are in that position.


**The Public Listening and the Private Remembrance**

The verse that follows moves the same subject indoors: *“Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless.”* (7:205). The two verses give the sūrah’s account of hearing in two registers — one public and shared, the other inward and continual.

The pairing answers a question the first verse raises on its own. If listening is commanded when the Qurʾān is recited, what happens when it is not being recited? The second verse supplies the practice for the interval: remembrance, inwardly, in a moderate voice, at the two ends of the day. The sūrah’s closing verses are therefore not an appendix to its argument but its instruction for living inside it — a discipline for when the recitation is heard, and a discipline for the hours between. Both are stated with a purpose clause or a prohibition attached, and both end on heedlessness as the state they exist to prevent.

---
## Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:205

> **Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"Remember Your Lord Inwardly"**

*Wa-dhkur rabbaka fī nafsika taḍarruʿan wa-khīfatan wa-dūna al-jahri mina al-qawli bi-l-ghuduwwi wa-l-āṣāli wa-lā takun mina al-ghāfilīn* — remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless.

**The Command and Its Manner**

The verse commands remembrance and specifies its manner in four particulars: inwardly, with humility, with awe, and in a voice between silence and loudness. The Book's readers are shown that the practice has a form, and the sūrah's readers are given the discipline that the recitation of the previous verse had prepared.

**"Inwardly"**

*Fī nafsika* — the sūrah's readers are directed to the interior, and the Book's teaching about the heart as the seat of understanding (7:179) gives the instruction its setting. The Qur'an's other descriptions of remembrance make the same point: the believers remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on their sides (3:191), and the Book's readers are shown a practice that does not depend on posture or place.

**"With Humility and Reverence"**

*Taḍarruʿan wa-khīfatan* — the two words describe the disposition of the suppliant: a turning toward God in need, and a fear of His displeasure. The Qur'an's prayers are full of both notes, and the sūrah's readers have met the combination in the sūrah's narrative of Moses' entreaties and in the Book's instructions to its community.

**"In a Moderate Tone of Voice"**

*Wa-dūna al-jahri mina al-qawli* — the Book's instruction about the voice appears in almost identical form in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: *“Do not recite your prayers too loudly or silently, but seek a way between”* (17:110). The sūrah's readers are shown that the community's worship is neither display nor concealment, and the verse's phrase supplies the standard the tradition applied to the recitation and the supplication alike.

**"Morning and Evening"**

*Bi-l-ghuduwwi wa-l-āṣāl* — the two ends of the day are named, and the Qur'an's instructions about the times of glorification recur: the command to glorify before sunrise and before sunset (20:130, 50:39), during the night (50:40, 76:26), and the statement that the shadows of all things bow in the morning and the evening (13:15). The sūrah's readers are given a rhythm rather than a single occasion.

**The Book's Times of Worship**

The Qur'an's treatment of time is structured around the daily cycle, and the sūrah's readers are shown that remembrance belongs to the ordinary course of a day rather than to exceptional moments. The tradition's collections of morning and evening supplications took their warrant from passages such as this one, and the verse's pair of times became the community's daily anchor.

**"Do Not Be One of the Heedless"**

*Wa-lā takun mina al-ghāfilīn* — the verse closes with a prohibition, and its word is the sūrah's own term for those who do not attend: the heedless are described earlier as those who have hearts and do not understand (7:179), and the sūrah's readers were told that the destruction of the towns came upon people who were unaware (7:95). The command is thus the sūrah's final warning against the condition it has been diagnosing throughout.

**The Verse's Moderation**
